concepts/commonwealth-and-protectorate.title: The Commonwealth and Protectorate
concepts/commonwealth-and-protectorate.content:
The Commonwealth and Protectorate
Summary
The Commonwealth and Protectorate (1649–1660) was the eleven-year republican interregnum between the execution of Charles I and the Restoration of Charles II. It is conventionally divided into two phases: the Commonwealth proper (1649–1653), during which England was governed by the Rump Parliament and a Council of State as a self-proclaimed republic, and the Protectorate (1653–1659), when Oliver Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector under the Instrument of Government. Though brief, this period saw the most radical constitutional experiments in English history — the abolition of monarchy and the House of Lords, the first written constitution, the conquest of Ireland and Scotland, a victorious naval war against the Dutch, and the emergence of England as a major Protestant military power in Europe.

The Rump Parliament and the Commonwealth Declared
After the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649, the remnant of the House of Commons — reduced by Pride’s Purge (December 1648) to about sixty members, derisively called the “Rump” — moved swiftly to consolidate power. The monarchy was abolished on 17 March 1649; the House of Lords was dissolved on 19 March. On 19 May, England was declared “a Commonwealth and Free State,” governed by the representatives of the people. A Council of State of thirty-eight members, including Cromwell, was appointed to execute the laws and direct military and naval affairs.
The Commonwealth rested on narrow foundations. The Rump controlled perhaps a hundred and fifty members after readmitting some of the excluded and issuing writs for new elections in sympathetic constituencies, but the nation at large was deeply hostile. Royalists, Presbyterians, and the mass of ordinary Englishmen regarded the new regime as a usurpation. Hume records that the Commonwealth found “every thing in England composed into a seeming tranquillity by the terror of their arms” — but it was terror, not consent, that maintained order. An engagement to support the Commonwealth “without king or house of peers” was imposed under severe penalties, yet the people’s reluctance forced the Rump to abandon enforcement.

Cromwell’s Campaigns: Ireland and Scotland
The greatest immediate threats to the Commonwealth were in Ireland and Scotland. In Ireland, the Marquis of Ormond had assembled a royalist army of sixteen thousand men and threatened Dublin. Cromwell was appointed Lord Lieutenant of Ireland in March 1649 and arrived in Dublin on 15 August, after Colonel Michael Jones had already routed Ormond at Rathmines.
Cromwell’s Irish campaign was swift and brutal. At Tredah (Drogheda) in September 1649, he stormed the town after two repulses, and ordered that no quarter be given. The garrison of three thousand men was slaughtered; even those who survived the assault were butchered the next day. At Wexford, the same severity was exercised when English troops rushed in before a capitulation could be completed. Hume writes that Cromwell “pretended to retaliate by this severe execution the cruelty of the Irish massacre: but he well knew that almost the whole garrison was English; and his justice was only a barbarous policy, in order to terrify all other garrisons from resistance.” The policy worked: town after town opened its gates, and within nine months Cromwell had subdued most of Ireland.
In Scotland, the Presbyterians — enraged by the execution of the king and the refusal of the Independents to establish Presbyterian discipline — proclaimed Charles II as king, on condition that he swear to the Covenant. Cromwell, now Captain-General after Fairfax resigned rather than invade Scotland, marched north with sixteen thousand men in July 1650. The Scots, under David Lesley, outnumbered him two to one but were dominated by fanatical clergy who forced Lesley into a rash engagement at Dunbar on 3 September 1650. Cromwell won a decisive victory: three thousand Scots slain, nine thousand taken prisoner. Edinburgh and Leith fell, and the remnant of the Scottish army fled to Stirling.
Charles II, having landed in Scotland and been crowned at Scone (January 1651), led a Scottish army into England in August 1651, hoping that royalist sympathisers would rise. They did not. Cromwell intercepted him at Worcester on 3 September 1651 — exactly one year after Dunbar — and destroyed the royal army. Charles escaped after six weeks of wandering in disguise, famously hiding in an oak tree at Boscobel House, before reaching France. The “crowning mercy,” as Cromwell called Worcester, ended the civil wars.

Naval War and the Dutch Republic
The Commonwealth inherited a formidable navy, and the Rump used it aggressively. The Navigation Act of 1651, which required that goods imported into England be carried in English ships or ships of the country of origin, struck directly at the Dutch carrying trade. Tensions escalated into the First Anglo-Dutch War (1652–1654).
Admiral Robert Blake, who had distinguished himself as a land commander at Taunton and Lyme, proved an admiral of genius. He chased Prince Rupert’s royalist squadron into the Tagus, made prize of twenty Portuguese ships, and threatened Lisbon. In the Channel, Blake, Monk, and Dean fought a series of savage battles against the Dutch admirals Tromp and De Ruyter. The most famous engagement was the battle of 29 July 1653, in which Tromp was shot through the heart. “Though near thirty ships of the Dutch were sunk and taken,” Hume writes, “they little regarded this loss compared with that of their brave admiral.” The war ended with the Treaty of Westminster (April 1654), yielding the honour of the flag to England, an indemnity from the Dutch East India Company, and a secret article excluding the House of Orange from the Stadtholderate.

Expulsion of the Rump and Barebone’s Parliament
By April 1653, the Rump had become increasingly unpopular even within the army. The members, who had sat since 1640, showed no inclination to dissolve themselves and call new elections. On 20 April 1653, Cromwell — acting with a party of musketeers — entered the House and expelled the members by force. “You are no parliament,” he is said to have declared. “I will put an end to your prating.”
Cromwell then summoned a nominated assembly of 128 “godly persons” — five from Scotland, six from Ireland, the rest from England — which met on 4 July 1653. Derisively called “Barebone’s Parliament” after Praise-God Barebone, a London leather-seller and prominent Fifth Monarchist, this body was composed largely of religious radicals: Fifth Monarchists, Anabaptists, Antinomians, and Independents. They set about abolishing tithes, the clerical function, the court of Chancery, and the entire system of English law, intending to replace it with the Mosaic code. Hume describes them as “the very dregs of the fanatics.” Alarmed and embarrassed, Cromwell allowed the moderate members to stage a dissolution on 12 December 1653, restoring authority into his hands.

The Protectorate: Instrument of Government
On 16 December 1653, Cromwell was installed as Lord Protector under the Instrument of Government — England’s first and only written constitution. Drafted by Lambert and the Council of Officers in just four days, the Instrument established a single chief magistrate with extensive but bounded powers. The Protector was supreme magistrate; justice was administered in his name; he had the power of war, peace, and alliance (with council consent); he could pardon all crimes except murder and treason; and he commanded the armed forces jointly with parliament. A standing army of thirty thousand men (twenty thousand foot, ten thousand horse) was established with independent funding. The Protector was obliged to summon a parliament every three years and allow it to sit for five months without dissolution. Bills not receiving the Protector’s assent within twenty days would become law by parliamentary authority alone — the one exception being the army, which could not be reduced without his consent.
The first Protectorate Parliament met on 3 September 1654 — the anniversary Cromwell regarded as fortunate. Though the electoral arrangements were more equitable than the old system (borough-mongering was suppressed, county representation increased, and a 200-pound estate qualification was required for voters), the Commons proved restive. Republicans, Presbyterians, and concealed royalists all opposed the Protectorate. Cromwell was forced to require members to sign a “Recognition” accepting the Instrument before they could sit, and he dissolved the parliament in January 1655 when it showed signs of refusing supply.

Foreign Policy: the Western Design
Cromwell’s foreign policy was a mixture of Protestant crusading zeal and commercial calculation. His “Western Design” — an ambitious plan to seize Spanish colonies in the Caribbean — led to the expedition of 1655 under Admiral Penn and General Venables. The attack on Hispaniola failed disgracefully, but the fleet seized the poorly-defended island of Jamaica in May 1655, which became a permanent English possession.
The war with Spain (1655–1658) was more successful in Europe. Blake blockaded Cadiz and destroyed the Spanish West Indies fleet at Santa Cruz de Tenerife in April 1657. In alliance with France, Cromwell captured Dunkirk from the Spanish in June 1658 — the only continental foothold England held during the century. Blake died in August 1657 off Plymouth, just as his ship entered harbour.
Domestically, Cromwell’s rule grew increasingly authoritarian. After a royalist rising in 1655, he divided England into eleven military districts governed by Major-Generals with sweeping powers. The constitution was replaced in 1657 by the Humble Petition and Advice, which offered Cromwell the crown. After two months of agonised deliberation, he refused — fearing the army’s reaction — but accepted the right to name his successor and the establishment of a second chamber (the Other House).

Richard Cromwell’s Fall and the Restoration
Oliver Cromwell died on 3 September 1658 — his lucky day — and was succeeded by his eldest son, Richard. Richard Cromwell lacked his father’s authority, military backing, or political skill. The army, divided between republicans and officers loyal to the Protectorate, forced Richard to dissolve his parliament and, in May 1659, to abdicate. The Rump Parliament was restored.
The year that followed was one of chaos: the Rump was expelled again by the army, a Committee of Safety was established, General Monk — the commander in Scotland — marched south. Monk, a professional soldier whose motives remain debated, entered London in February 1660, declared for a free parliament, and restored the members secluded by Pride’s Purge. The Long Parliament finally dissolved itself on 16 March 1660, and a Convention Parliament was elected. On 8 May 1660, Charles II was proclaimed king. He landed at Dover on 25 May, and entered London on 29 May — his thirtieth birthday.

Legacy
The Commonwealth and Protectorate left a deep imprint on English political thought. The abolition of monarchy, however brief, demonstrated that kingship could be dispensed with — a precedent that haunted the restored Stuarts and shaped the Revolution of 1688. The constitutional experiments of the Instrument of Government and the Humble Petition and Advice introduced ideas of written constitutions, triennial parliaments, and the separation of powers. Cromwell’s military and naval reforms made England a European power for the first time since the Armada. The Navigation Act and the conquest of Jamaica laid foundations for the British Empire. But the period also established a deep English suspicion of military rule, Puritan austerity, and religious radicalism — a reaction that would characterise the Restoration years.
The term “Interregnum” (Latin for “between reigns”) is the traditional label, but it implicitly denies the regime’s claim to legitimacy. The Commonwealth and Protectorate were, for eleven years, the actual government of England, Scotland, and Ireland — and, for a time, the most formidable military and naval power in Protestant Europe.

concepts/glorious-revolution.title: The Glorious Revolution
concepts/glorious-revolution.content:
The Glorious Revolution
Summary
The Glorious Revolution (1688–1689) was the bloodless overthrow of James II by his nephew and son-in-law, William of Orange, Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic, and the subsequent establishment of a constitutional monarchy on foundations of parliamentary sovereignty and Protestant succession. It was at once an invasion, a national rising, and a constitutional settlement: the last successful invasion of England, the most decisive assertion of parliamentary authority over the crown, and the event that fixed the religious and political character of the British state for the next three centuries. The revolution was remarkable for the speed and unanimity with which the nation turned against its lawful sovereign; for its almost complete absence of bloodshed on English soil; and for the durable legal framework — the Bill of Rights, the Toleration Act, the Mutiny Act, the Triennial Act — that it bequeathed to posterity.

Causes: James II’s Catholicising Policy
James II succeeded his brother Charles II in February 1685 with the most loyal Parliament and the most devoted Church party any Stuart had ever commanded. Within three years he had squandered both. The cause was his open and unwavering project to restore Catholicism as the religion of England — a design he pursued with an inflexibility that Hume judged the product not of vice but of a “bigotry so absolute” that it overrode every consideration of policy or constitutional obligation.
Having persuaded or intimidated a docile Parliament in 1685 to vote him a revenue for life, James proceeded to dispense with the Test Act by appointing Catholics to military and civil offices. The collusive case of Sir Edward Hales (1686) secured a judicial sanction for the dispensing power. He created a Court of Ecclesiastical Commission, after the model of the High Commission abolished under Charles I, and used it to suspend the Bishop of London for refusing to discipline an anti-Catholic preacher. He expelled the fellows of Magdalen College, Oxford, and installed Catholics in their place. Catholic peers were admitted to the Privy Council; a papal nuncio was received at court for the first time since the Reformation; and in Ireland, the Earl of Tyrconnel systematically replaced Protestant officers and magistrates with Catholics.
In April 1687 James issued a Declaration of Indulgence, suspending all penal laws against Catholics and Dissenters. When the Anglican clergy refused their cooperation, he issued a second declaration in April 1688 and ordered it to be read in every church. Seven bishops, headed by Archbishop Sancroft, petitioned the king against it on the ground that the dispensing power was illegal. James committed them to the Tower. Their trial in June 1688 ended in acquittal, to universal rejoicing throughout the kingdom. The soldiers on Hounslow Heath, whom the king had reviewed that very day, broke into such tumultuary joy that James, hearing the commotion, was told it was only the soldiers rejoicing at the acquittal of the bishops. “Do you call that nothing?” he replied. “But so much the worse for them.”
The decisive event came on 10 June 1688, when Queen Mary of Modena gave birth to a son — James Francis Edward Stuart, the Prince of Wales. For the Protestant nation, the birth of a Catholic heir transformed the prospect of temporary inconvenience into the certainty of a Catholic dynasty. A calumny spread that the child was supposititious, smuggled into the queen’s bed in a warming-pan. It was almost certainly false, but it was widely believed, and it gave William of Orange the pretext he needed for intervention.

The Invitation and the Dutch Invasion
William of Orange, the husband of James’s elder daughter Mary, had been the centre of European resistance to Louis XIV since 1672. He had maintained a secret correspondence with English grandees for two years, and the trial of the bishops had convinced him that the nation was ready to rise. Burnet records that William insisted on “formal and direct invitations” before he would commit himself. On 30 June 1688 — the very day the bishops were acquitted — seven men, the Immortal Seven, dispatched a letter to the Hague urging William to intervene. The signatories were the Earls of Devonshire, Danby, and Shrewsbury; Lord Lumley; the Bishop of London (Compton); Edward Russell; and Henry Sidney.
William obtained the consent of the States General for an expedition of unprecedented scale. He assembled a fleet of nearly five hundred vessels — transports, men-of-war, and support craft — carrying an army of some fourteen thousand men, with a full train of artillery and cavalry. The first attempt to sail in October was driven back by storms. A second attempt fared no better. On 1 November a third departure succeeded, with the fleet clearing Helvoet-Sluys and standing down the Channel under the command of Admiral Herbert. A strong easterly wind — the “Protestant wind” — carried the armada through the Straits of Dover while bottling up the English fleet under Lord Dartmouth in the Thames estuary.
Burnet, who sailed in the van of the fleet, gives a vivid first-hand account of the voyage. He describes how the pilot misjudged the course and overshot Torbay, so that it seemed the fleet must sail on to Plymouth — a disaster, since Plymouth’s governor, the Earl of Bath, had not yet committed himself. “While Russel was in no small disorder,” Burnet writes, “on a sudden to all our wonder it calmed a little. And then the wind turned into the South: And a soft and happy gale of wind carried in the whole Fleet in four hours time.” On 5 November 1688 — the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot — William landed his army in Torbay. “As soon as the Prince and Marshal Schomberg got to shore,” Burnet recounts, “they were furnished with such horses as the village of Broxholme could afford; and rode up to view the grounds.”

The Advance and the Defections
The landing was at first greeted with caution. The whole county of Devon was so terrified by the executions that followed Monmouth’s rebellion that “no one for several days joined the prince,” Hume notes. The Bishop of Exeter fled to London. But within a week the gentry of Devon and Somerset began to appear. Sir Edward Seymour proposed an association, which everyone signed. Lord Delamere took arms in Cheshire; the Earl of Danby seized York; the Earl of Bath, governor of Plymouth, declared for the prince. The nobility and gentry of Nottinghamshire embraced the same cause.
The most decisive blows came from the army. Lord Cornbury, son of the Earl of Clarendon, carried over three regiments of cavalry. John Churchill — the future Duke of Marlborough, who owed his entire fortune to James’s favour — deserted with the Duke of Grafton and Colonel Berkeley. When James arrived at Salisbury, his headquarters, he received the news of Churchill’s defection with bitter astonishment. Then Prince George of Denmark, James’s own son-in-law, deserted him at Andover together with the young Duke of Ormond. When the news reached London, Princess Anne fled to Nottingham in the company of Lady Churchill. James, on hearing of his daughter’s abandonment, burst into tears. “God help me,” he cried, “my own children have forsaken me!”

James’s Flight
James, having lost his army, his family, and his nerve, made panicked concessions: he dismissed the Ecclesiastical Commission, restored the charters of London and the corporations, and reinstated the fellows of Magdalen College. But these were read as symptoms of terror, not repentance. On the night of 11 December 1688 James sent the queen and the infant prince to France under the escort of Count Lauzun. He himself disappeared the same night, attended only by Sir Edward Hales, and threw the Great Seal into the Thames as he crossed it. His intention was to reach a ship waiting at the mouth of the river, but he was seized by fishermen at Faversham and roughly handled before being recognised. He was brought back to London, where the populace received him with unexpected acclamation. William, having no intention of allowing James to remain, ordered him to leave Whitehall. James retired to Rochester and, on 23 December, privately embarked for France. Louis XIV received him with the highest generosity at the palace of St. Germains-en-Laye.

The Convention Parliament
With James in France, William summoned an assembly of peers and former MPs, which then issued writs for a Convention Parliament — so called because it was not summoned by royal authority. The Convention met on 22 January 1689. The Commons, elected under the influence of the prevailing Whig sentiment, were more decisive than the Lords. They passed a resolution declaring “that King James II, having endeavoured to subvert the constitution of the kingdom, by breaking the original contract between king and people, and having, by the advice of Jesuits and other wicked persons, violated the fundamental laws, and withdrawn himself out of the kingdom, has abdicated the government, and that the throne is thereby vacant.”
The Lords debated this resolution clause by clause. The Tories, feeling the sting of their recent abandonment of non-resistance principles, proposed instead a regency. The question was carried for a king by only two votes — fifty-one against forty-nine. All the prelates except the Bishops of London and Bristol voted for a regent. After a free conference between the houses, the lords acquiesced in the commons’ formulation.
William, meanwhile, made clear his own terms. He told Halifax, Shrewsbury, and Danby that he would not be regent, nor would he hold a crown dependent on the will or life of another. “If they judged it proper to settle a regent,” Hume records him saying, “he had no objection: he only thought it incumbent on him to inform them, that he was determined not to be the regent.” Mary, with characteristic deference, made known that she would accept no authority but from and through her husband.

The Declaration of Rights and the Offer of the Crown
Before offering the crown, the Convention drew up a Declaration of Rights, enumerating the illegal acts of James’s reign and asserting the ancient rights and liberties of the subject. It declared the dispensing and suspending power illegal, condemned the Court of Ecclesiastical Commission, affirmed that elections ought to be free and parliaments held frequently, and prohibited standing armies in peacetime without parliamentary consent. On 13 February 1689, William and Mary were jointly offered the crown at a ceremony in the Banqueting House at Whitehall. William accepted in his own name and that of his wife. They were crowned together in Westminster Abbey on 11 April 1689.

The Revolution Settlement
The Declaration of Rights was enacted into law later in 1689 as the Bill of Rights — one of the fundamental statutes of the English constitution. It settled the succession: the crown was vested in William and Mary jointly, with the administration remaining in William; the remainder went to the Princess Anne and her descendants, then to William’s descendants by any future marriage. Catholics and those who married Catholics were excluded from the throne.
Three other statutes completed the settlement. The Toleration Act (1689) granted freedom of worship to Protestant Dissenters, though it left the Test Act and corporation acts intact, so that Catholics and nonconformists remained excluded from public office. The Mutiny Act (1689) placed the army under parliamentary control by requiring regular renewal of the authority to maintain military discipline. The Triennial Act (1694) required that parliaments be summoned at least once every three years, preventing the crown from governing without them as Charles II and James II had done.

Constitutional Significance
The Glorious Revolution resolved the great constitutional questions that had vexed English politics since the accession of the Stuarts. The crown could not suspend or dispense with the laws; it could not maintain a standing army without parliamentary consent; it could not govern without parliaments. The revolution established what Hume called a “mixed monarchy” — a constitution in which the powers of the crown were narrowly circumscribed and those of parliament, particularly the Commons, decisively enlarged. It gave England “the most entire system of liberty that ever was known amongst mankind,” in Hume’s judgment.
The revolution settlement was not democratic: the landed gentry and the merchants who dominated parliament governed in their own interest, and the Toleration Act did not extend to Catholics or to those who rejected the Trinity. But it created the framework within which parliamentary government and cabinet responsibility would develop over the following century. The principle that the crown’s authority derived from a contract with the people — implicit in the Convention’s language of “original contract” and “abdication” — became the foundational myth of Whig constitutionalism.

Jacobite Opposition
The revolution created its own opposition. Those who remained loyal to James II — the Jacobites (from the Latin Jacobus, James) — refused to accept the legitimacy of William’s title. The Jacobite cause drew on the doctrine of divine right and non-resistance, the sentimental attachment to the ancient royal line, and the resentment of those who had lost office, influence, or estates in the revolution. The non-juring schism split the Church of England: Archbishop Sancroft and some four hundred clergy refused to take the oaths to William and Mary and were deprived of their livings. Jacobite risings in Scotland and Ireland followed in 1689–1690. The Jacobite threat persisted through the Williamite and Annean reigns, flaring into open rebellion in 1715 and 1745, and was not extinguished until the destruction of the Highland clans at Culloden. But the revolution had, as Hume observed, “put the nature of the English constitution beyond all controversy.”

Historiographical Interpretations
The Whig interpretation, given classic expression by Thomas Babington Macaulay in his History of England (1848), presented the Glorious Revolution as the culminating triumph of English liberty: a conservative revolution that preserved ancient rights against Stuart tyranny, established the supremacy of law, and secured the Protestant religion. Macaulay called it the “preserving revolution” — the bloodless vindication of the constitution.
The revisionist interpretation, associated with J. C. D. Clark and others, has challenged this narrative. Revisionists argue that the revolution was not a victory for popular liberty but a coup by a narrow oligarchy of landowners and merchants, motivated more by fear of Catholicism and French power than by constitutional principle. They note that the settlement preserved the monarchy, the House of Lords, the established church, and the tight property qualification for the franchise — a settlement designed not to empower the people but to secure the dominance of a Protestant landed class. The revolution, in this reading, was profoundly conservative: it changed the dynasty to preserve the social order.
Between these positions stands Hume, writing a century before Macaulay. Hume saw the revolution as a necessary correction of constitutional imbalance, but he refused the Whig tendency to treat the Stuart monarchs as tyrants and their opponents as saints. He judged Charles I and James II with a measured scepticism that acknowledged their defects without demonising their characters. The revolution, for Hume, was a fortunate event — but fortune, not virtue, had chiefly determined its outcome.

concepts/petition-of-right-and-ship-mone.title: The Petition of Right and Ship Money
concepts/petition-of-right-and-ship-mone.content:
The Petition of Right and Ship Money
Summary
The Petition of Right (1628) and the Ship Money controversy (1634–1640) were the two defining constitutional conflicts of the Personal Rule of Charles I. Between them, they crystallised every major grievance that would drive England into civil war: the crown’s claim to tax without parliamentary consent, the imprisonment of subjects without cause shown, the billeting of soldiers on civilians, the imposition of martial law in peacetime, and — above all — the assertion that the king’s prerogative could override the common law and the ancient liberties of the subject. The Petition of Right was the first comprehensive statutory statement of English liberties since Magna Carta; Ship Money was the most ambitious assertion of royal prerogative finance since the Tudor period. Together, they made the constitutional question — who rules, the king by his prerogative or the king-in-parliament by law? — the central issue of the age.

The Petition of Right (1628)
Context: The Forced Loan and the Five Knights’ Case
The crisis that produced the Petition of Right began with the failure of Charles I’s first parliament (June 1625 — August 1625). The Commons, distrustful of the Duke of Buckingham’s management of the war with Spain, granted only two subsidies — a fraction of what the crown needed. Charles prorogued and then dissolved the parliament, and resolved to govern without one. He resorted to a Forced Loan — a demand for money not authorised by parliament, assessed on the counties and collected by commissioners under the threat of imprisonment for refusal. Privy councillors and judges who objected were dismissed; over seventy gentlemen were committed to prison for refusing to contribute.
Five of these prisoners — the most famous being Sir Thomas Darnel, Sir John Corbet, and Sir John Hampden (the same Hampden who would later resist Ship Money) — applied for a writ of habeas corpus in the King’s Bench in November 1627. The return to the writ stated that they were imprisoned “by the special command of His Majesty.” The question was stark: could the crown imprison a subject without showing cause? The judges, led by Chief Justice Hyde, gave an evasive answer — they refused bail but did not explicitly affirm the crown’s right. The prisoners remained in custody. The “Five Knights’ Case” left the law in a state of dangerous uncertainty, and it created the political atmosphere in which the Petition of Right was conceived.
The Five Rights
The Petition of Right was the work of the third parliament of Charles I, which met on 17 March 1628. The Commons was dominated by lawyers and country gentlemen who understood the constitutional stakes perfectly. Sir Edward Coke, then in his mid-seventies, returned to the Commons after years in retirement and became the leading voice for the petition. He was joined by John Selden, John Pym, Sir John Eliot, and Sir Dudley Digges.
After weeks of debate and a celebrated conference between the two Houses, the Lords and Commons presented the Petition to the king on 2 June 1628. It was not a statute but a petition — a declaration of existing law, not a grant of new liberties. It recited the relevant clauses of Magna Carta and a series of statutes confirming it, and then prayed that no subject should be compelled to contribute to any tax, loan, or benevolence without the consent of parliament; that no freeman should be imprisoned or detained without cause shown (the habeas corpus principle); that soldiers and sailors should not be billeted on private houses against the will of the owner; and that commissions for proceeding by martial law should be revoked and not issued in future.
These were the five rights: no taxation without parliamentary consent, no imprisonment without cause shown, no billeting of troops, no martial law in peacetime, and — implied throughout — the supremacy of the common law over the prerogative. Hume writes that the Petition “was a declaration of the rights of the subject, and a confession of the limitations of prerogative” — but he also noted that it was “conceived in terms so general and ambiguous, that it might be eluded by any king who was not restrained by a regard to his engagements.”
Charles’s Reluctant Assent
Charles resisted the Petition for weeks. He offered a counter-declaration affirming Magna Carta but refusing to concede the specific points. The Commons would not accept it. Desperate for supply — the war with France and Spain was going badly, and Buckingham’s expedition to La Rochelle was about to fail — Charles finally gave way. On 7 June 1628, he came before both Houses and pronounced the formula of royal assent: “Soit droit fait comme est désiré” — Let right be done as is desired.
But even as he gave his assent, Charles made clear that he did not regard the Petition as altering the constitution. He told the Commons that he intended “to keep the laws in full force and vigour, but that the king’s prerogative was also to be maintained.” The qualification was ominous. Within months, Charles had violated the spirit of the Petition by continuing to enforce martial law in the districts where troops were quartered, and by raising another forced loan — this time disguised as a “free gift” — to finance the disastrous Rochelle expedition.
Violation and Aftermath
The assassination of Buckingham on 23 August 1628 removed Charles’s most unpopular minister, but it did not reconcile the king to parliamentary government. When the parliament reassembled in January 1629, remonstrances against the violation of the Petition of Right were met with demands for further supply. The Commons passed resolutions declaring anyone who introduced innovations in religion, who advised the collection of tonnage and poundage without parliamentary grant, or who paid those duties, to be “a capital enemy to the kingdom.” The Speaker was held down in his chair while the resolutions were read. Charles dissolved the parliament on 10 March 1629 and resolved never to call another. The eleven-year Personal Rule — the period derisively called the “Eleven Years’ Tyranny” by later Whig historians — had begun.

Ship Money
The Revival of an Ancient Tax
Ship Money was not a new invention. It was an ancient right of the crown, exercised since the time of the Saxon kings, to require the maritime counties to provide ships (or their monetary equivalent) for the defence of the realm in time of danger. Elizabeth I had used it sparingly; James I had let it lapse. In 1634, Charles I revived it, citing the threat of Dutch and Dunkirk privateers to English commerce. Writs were issued to the ports and maritime counties demanding a fleet of ships — or, more conveniently, the money to build and equip them.
The writs were issued on the advice of Attorney General William Noy, who had unearthed precedents from the reign of Edward I. The sum demanded was reasonable, the purpose (naval defence) was legitimate, and the maritime counties complied without serious objection. In 1635, however, Charles extended the tax to the inland counties — to the whole kingdom — on the ground that the defence of the realm concerned all subjects equally. The principle had shifted: what began as a feudal obligation of the ports had become a general tax levied by the crown without parliamentary consent.
John Hampden’s Trial (1637)
The extension of Ship Money to the inland counties raised the constitutional question directly. John Hampden, a Buckinghamshire gentleman of considerable fortune and Puritan sympathies, refused to pay his assessment of twenty shillings on his lands. The case was tried before all twelve judges of the Court of Exchequer Chamber in the autumn of 1637.
The crown’s argument, presented by Attorney General Sir John Bankes and Solicitor General Sir Edward Littleton, rested on the doctrine of necessity: in time of danger, the king as sovereign was the sole judge of what was necessary for the defence of the realm, and his judgment could not be questioned in the courts. Hampden’s counsel — led by Oliver St John and Robert Holborne — conceded the king’s right to defend the realm but insisted that the mode of defence was regulated by law: the king could not levy a general tax without parliamentary consent, and the danger must be proved to be actual and imminent, not merely hypothetical.
The case divided the nation. Hume records that “the eyes of all England were fixed on this great cause, which was regarded as the dernier resort of national liberty.” The judges deliberated for months. In February 1638, the verdict was delivered: seven judges found for the crown, five for Hampden. The majority, led by Chief Baron Finch, held that the king was the sole judge of the necessity, and that Ship Money was a lawful charge upon the whole kingdom. But the narrowness of the decision — a bare majority, with three of the seven majority opinions resting on reasoning so strained that even contemporaries dismissed them — was a moral victory for Hampden and the parliamentary opposition. The law might be with the crown, but public opinion was not.
Financing the Navy and the Constitutional Principle
Between 1634 and 1640, Ship Money yielded over eight hundred thousand pounds — a sum greater than any subsidy ever granted by parliament. It enabled Charles to build the most formidable navy England had possessed since Elizabeth’s reign: the Sovereign of the Seas, the largest ship in Europe, was launched in 1637 as a direct result of Ship Money revenue. For six years, the crown was financially independent of parliament. The navy patrolled the Channel, suppressed piracy, and projected English power without the need for parliamentary supply.
But the constitutional price was immense. Hume observes that Ship Money “was a tax levied without consent of parliament, and was a violation of that fundamental principle of the constitution, that no money could be imposed upon the subject without the consent of the Commons.” By making the king financially independent, Ship Money menaced the entire structure of parliamentary government. If the king could finance the navy, the army, and the civil government from prerogative revenues, what need had he of parliaments at all? The question answered itself in the eleven-year interval between the dissolution of 1629 and the summoning of the Short Parliament in 1640.

The Roots of Civil War
The Petition of Right and Ship Money were not isolated grievances. They were parts of a coherent constitutional pattern: the assertion by Charles I of a prerogative power above the law, and the resistance of the parliamentary gentry to that assertion. The Petition of Right had declared, in law, that the king could not tax without parliament, could not imprison without cause, could not govern by martial law. Ship Money demonstrated that the king could and would do so anyway, so long as the judges upheld his prerogative and no parliament sat to call him to account.
When the Scots rebellion of 1639–1640 forced Charles to summon parliament — first the Short Parliament (April–May 1640), then the Long Parliament (November 1640) — these grievances were the first order of business. The Long Parliament impeached the judges who had upheld Ship Money, declared Ship Money illegal, and passed the Triennial Act to prevent the crown from governing without parliaments. The Petition of Right was cited in the Nineteen Propositions (1642) and in the Grand Remonstrance. It became, alongside Magna Carta, the foundational text of the parliamentary cause.
The Petition of Right and Ship Money established what contemporaries called “the liberties of the subject” and what later generations would call the constitutional principle of no taxation without representation. The blood of the Civil War, the scaffold of the king, and the settlement of 1688 were, in a direct line, the consequences of these two conflicts. They are the constitutional hinge on which the 17th century turns.

concepts/popish-plot-and-exclusion-crisi.title: The Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis
concepts/popish-plot-and-exclusion-crisi.content:
The Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis
Summary
The Popish Plot (1678) and the Exclusion Crisis (1679-1681) were the most convulsive political events in England between the Restoration and the Glorious Revolution. A fabricated Jesuit conspiracy to assassinate Charles II, burn London, and massacre Protestants threw the nation into a frenzy of anti-Catholic terror that lasted nearly three years. Scores of innocent Catholics were executed on perjured testimony. The plot in turn ignited a constitutional struggle over whether the king’s brother and heir, the openly Catholic James, Duke of York, should be excluded from the succession by act of parliament. This struggle produced the first organised political parties — the Whigs and the Tories — and ended only when Charles II dissolved the Oxford Parliament in 1681 and ruled without parliaments for the remainder of his reign, pursuing a Tory reaction that included the execution of Lord Russell and Algernon Sidney on charges arising from the Rye House Plot.

The Popish Plot
Titus Oates
The plot was the invention of Titus Oates, the most infamous informer in English history. Oates was the son of an Anabaptist preacher who had conformed to the Church of England. He himself took orders but was indicted for perjury and dismissed from a naval chaplaincy on complaint of “unnatural practices, not fit to be named,” in Burnet’s phrase. He converted to Catholicism, lived among the Jesuits at St. Omers and in Spain, and returned to England in 1678 with a manufactured knowledge of their secrets.
Oates’s narrative, first communicated to the council in September 1678, was a tissue of absurdities. He claimed the pope had assumed sovereignty over England and Ireland and had delegated it to the Jesuits. Lord Arundel was to be chancellor, Lord Powis treasurer, Coleman secretary of state, Lord Bellasis general of the papal army. The king was to be shot with silver bullets, stabbed with a consecrated knife, or poisoned; the great fire of London had been the Jesuits’ work; a general massacre of Protestants was planned; the army in Flanders was to invade. Hume calls these “such absurdities as no human testimony was sufficient to prove.” Yet the nation, already inflamed by anti-Catholic prejudice and fear of a popish successor, believed them.
Coleman’s Letters
What gave Oates’s fictions plausibility was the seizure of papers belonging to Edward Coleman, secretary to the Duchess of York. Coleman had carried on a voluminous correspondence with Père la Chaise, the French king’s confessor, and with other continental Catholics, discussing schemes for the conversion of England and the extirpation of heresy. His letters did not mention assassination or massacre, but they revealed that the Catholic party in England had long been plotting with France to restore the old religion. Hume observes that Coleman’s letters were “sufficient alone to destroy all the credit” of Oates’s narrative — for if such a vast conspiracy existed, how could Coleman’s voluminous correspondence contain no trace of it? — but the public mind was past reasoning. Oates’s plot and Coleman’s letters were confounded together; the evidence of the latter, being unquestionable, gave credit to the former.
Godfrey’s Murder
The murder of Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey on 17 October 1678 completed the delusion. Godfrey was a London magistrate before whom Oates had laid his deposition. After being missing for several days, his body was found in a ditch at Primrose Hill, run through with his own sword. The marks of strangulation were about his neck. The cry rose instantly that he had been assassinated by the Papists for taking Oates’s evidence.
Hume is characteristically sceptical. Godfrey had lived on good terms with Catholics; he was a friend of Coleman himself. That the Catholics would murder him — thereby confirming every suspicion against them — seemed to Hume “utterly improbable.” He canvasses the alternative: that Shaftesbury and the popular party contrived the murder to throw odium on the Catholics. But Oates’s fictions were so absurd that no man of sense could have invented them; a fool was more likely to succeed than a wise man. Hume concludes that Godfrey’s murder, in all likelihood, had no connection with the popish plot whatever, and may have been suicide.
Nevertheless, the public drew no such nuanced conclusion. Godfrey’s body was carried through the streets of London, exposed for two days, and buried with immense pomp. Seventy-two clergymen marched before the coffin; above a thousand persons of quality followed. At the funeral sermon, two divines stood on either side of the pulpit lest the preacher himself be murdered by the Papists. The city prepared its defences; chains and posts were put up. Sir Thomas Player, the chamberlain, declared that without these precautions all the citizens might rise next morning with their throats cut.
The Terror
Parliament met in October 1678 in a mood of blind fury. Oates and a succession of accomplices — Bedloe, Prance, Dugdale, Dangerfield, Turberville — multiplied accusations. The Commons voted that there was a damnable and hellish plot contrived by the Papists for assassinating the king, subverting the government, and massacring the Protestants. A Test Act was rushed through, excluding all Catholics from both houses of parliament. The Duke of York himself was compelled to withdraw from the council and retire to Brussels.
The trials that followed were a travesty of justice. Coleman was tried and executed in December 1678. Ireland, a Jesuit, went to the gallows in January 1679. Five Catholic peers — Arundel, Powis, Petre, Stafford, and Bellasis — were committed to the Tower. William, Lord Stafford, was impeached by the Commons, tried by the Lords, and executed on Tower Hill in December 1680, protesting his innocence to the last. In all, some thirty-five Catholics were executed on the perjured testimony of Oates and his confederates. Oates himself was given a state apartment in Whitehall, a pension, and the title of “Doctor of Divinity” from the Protestant colleges at Oxford and Cambridge.

The Exclusion Crisis
Shaftesbury and the Green Ribbon Club
The popish plot gave Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury, the political instrument he needed. Shaftesbury had been a member of the Cabal ministry under Charles II, but after the Declaration of Indulgence was withdrawn he crossed to opposition and became the most formidable parliamentary leader of the age. Dalrymple, drawing on French dispatches, asserts that Shaftesbury “framed the fiction of the popish plot in the year 1678, in order to bury the Duke, and perhaps the King, under the weight of the national fear and hatred of popery.” When pressed on the absurdity of Oates’s narrative, Shaftesbury is reputed to have answered: “The more nonsensical the better; if we cannot bring them to swallow worse nonsense than that, we shall never do any good with them.”
Shaftesbury organised his followers in the Green Ribbon Club, which met at the King’s Head Tavern in Chancery Lane. The club was the organisational centre of the “country party” — soon to be called Whigs — coordinating elections, managing the press, distributing propaganda, and orchestrating the monster petitioning campaigns that demanded the sitting of parliament and the exclusion of the Duke of York.
The Three Exclusion Parliaments
The first Exclusion Parliament met in March 1679. Charles, seeing the temper of the Commons, attempted to forestall exclusion by offering limitations on a popish successor: the Duke of York should have only the title of king, with real power vested in a regent chosen by parliament; Catholics should be excluded from the privy council and both houses. The Commons rejected these offers and proceeded with a Bill of Exclusion, which passed the Commons but was rejected by the Lords after a great debate in which Halifax — “the Trimmer” — distinguished himself by his eloquence against the bill. Charles prorogued and then dissolved the parliament.
The second Exclusion Parliament met in October 1680. The Commons again passed the Exclusion Bill. The Lords debated it through November; Halifax again led the opposition, arguing that exclusion would alter the fundamental succession of the crown and produce civil war. The bill was defeated by sixty-three votes to thirty. The Commons, enraged, impeached several of the king’s ministers, including the Lord Chief Justice Scroggs, who had begun to check the excesses of the plot trials. Charles prorogued parliament in January 1681 and dissolved it soon after.
The Oxford Parliament 1681
Charles summoned the third Exclusion Parliament to meet at Oxford in March 1681, where the royalists had a stronger electoral advantage. The king came in state, attended by his guards; the Whig leaders arrived in a body, armed, as if expecting a coup. The Commons immediately revived the Exclusion Bill. After only a week, Charles dissolved the parliament in person, having kept the secret so well that the black rod came to the door while the Commons were in full debate. The members were left stunned and dispersed.
This was the decisive victory for the crown. Charles had resolved to endure any extremity rather than submit to exclusion. He governed for the remaining four years of his reign without summoning another parliament, relying on French subsidies and strict economy — Tangiers was abandoned, the navy neglected, the household retrenched — to make the crown independent of parliamentary supply.

The Tory Reaction
With the dissolution of the Oxford Parliament, the tide turned violently against the Whigs. The clergy, encouraged by the court, preached the doctrine of non-resistance from every pulpit. Addresses poured in from the counties, congratulating the king on his escape from parliaments and condemning the exclusionists. The reality of the plot itself was openly called in question. Oates was stripped of his pension and lodgings and eventually convicted of perjury.
The court now turned the weapons of perjury and informers against the Whigs themselves. Edward Fitzharris, a Catholic informer, was executed in 1681 after attempting to implicate the exclusionists. Stephen College, “the Protestant joiner,” a zealous Whig partisan, was tried at Oxford before a packed jury and executed. The charter of the City of London was forfeited by a writ of quo warranto, and the corporations that had returned Whig MPs were systematically remodelled.
The Rye House Plot
In 1683 a conspiracy was discovered — or perhaps manufactured — by the government. A small group of desperate republicans, including old Cromwellian soldiers, had allegedly plotted to assassinate Charles and the Duke of York at the Rye House in Hertfordshire, as the king returned from Newmarket. The plot was betrayed by one of the conspirators. Whether Shaftesbury, by then in exile and dying in Holland, was directly involved is uncertain; but the government seized the opportunity to destroy the Whig leadership.
Shaftesbury himself had fled to Holland in 1682 and died at Amsterdam in January 1683. Hume records his epitaph: “He died in a foreign land, deserted by his friends, and loaded with the imprecations of his countrymen.” This was written before the Rye House confessions made the name of Shaftesbury still more odious.
Execution of Lord Russell and Algernon Sidney
William, Lord Russell, the son of the Duke of Bedford, was the most respected of the Whig leaders. A man of unimpeachable personal integrity — he alone among the opposition leaders had refused French money — he was nevertheless implicated in the Rye House conspiracy by the testimony of Lord Howard of Escrick and Colonel Rumsey. The evidence was weak; Russell protested that he had never countenanced assassination or rebellion. He was tried before Chief Justice Pemberton, convicted of high treason, and beheaded in Lincoln’s Inn Fields on 21 July 1683. He met his death with composure and dignity, and the public never forgave the king for refusing to pardon him.
Algernon Sidney, the republican theorist and author of the Discourses Concerning Government, followed Russell to the scaffold in December 1683. Sidney’s trial was even more scandalous. The evidence against him was scantier than against Russell, but the court — now presided over by Jeffreys — admitted as evidence Sidney’s unpublished manuscript, which argued that the people had a right to resist tyrants. This was enough. Sidney was convicted and executed on Tower Hill on 7 December 1683. His death made him a martyr for the Whig cause and gave his writings a posthumous influence far beyond what they had enjoyed in his lifetime.

Constitutional Significance
The Popish Plot and Exclusion Crisis were the crucible in which the first modern political parties were formed. The terms “Whig” and “Tory” entered the English political vocabulary during these years: Whig, from the Scottish Whiggamores (anti-Catholic Presbyterian rebels), was the insult hurled at the exclusionists; Tory, from the Irish tories (Catholic outlaws), was hurled back at the court party. The names stuck and have endured for more than three centuries.
The crisis posed the fundamental question of the English constitution: could parliament alter the succession to the crown? The Whigs argued yes — that the original contract between king and people gave parliament the right to exclude a popish successor who would subvert the constitution. The Tories argued no — that the succession was fixed by divine right and statute, and that to alter it was to invite civil war. Charles II’s victory in 1681 seemed to vindicate the Tory position. But the question would not die. When James II succeeded in 1685 and pursued his Catholicising policies, the Whig arguments were vindicated by the Revolution of 1688, which altered the succession by act of parliament and excluded James and his heirs forever.
Both Hume and Burnet are deeply sceptical of Oates and the plot. Hume’s account is laced with irony: the plot, he says, “contained such low absurdity, that it is impossible to have been the invention of any man of sense or education.” Burnet, who was personally approached by Dr. Tonge before the discovery and who knew Coleman well, gives a detailed narrative that shows how “the whole town was all over enflamed” and how Coleman’s letters — which Burnet himself examined — were confused with Oates’s fictions. Dalrymple, writing a century later with access to the French archives, is the most emphatic in attributing the plot to Shaftesbury’s contrivance. All three historians agree on one point: that the Popish Plot was a fabrication, and that the men who died on the scaffold — Catholic and Whig alike — were victims of a national madness.

concepts/royal-society.title: The Royal Society
concepts/royal-society.content:
The Royal Society
Summary
The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge, incorporated by Royal Charter in 1662, was the first permanent institution devoted to experimental natural philosophy in the English-speaking world. Conceived during the Civil Wars and Commonwealth at Oxford, formally established in London at the Restoration, and patronised by Charles II, the Society became the institutional engine of the English Scientific Revolution. Its founders — John Wilkins, Robert Boyle, Christopher Wren, William Petty, John Wallis, Seth Ward, and others — were Baconians who rejected scholastic authority in favour of systematic experiment, collaborative observation, and plain descriptive prose. Over the next half-century, under the presidencies of Lord Brouncker, Sir Joseph Williamson, and finally Isaac Newton, the Society transformed English intellectual life and projected its influence across Europe through the Philosophical Transactions, the world’s first exclusively scientific periodical.

Origins: The Oxford Group (c. 1645–1660)
The Royal Society did not spring fully formed from the Restoration court. Its roots were in the private, extra-curial gatherings of natural philosophers that began during the Civil Wars. The most important of these met at Oxford, in the lodgings of John Wilkins at Wadham College — a man whose extraordinary gift for conciliation, Burnet wrote, “made him to be beloved by all parties.” Sprat, himself a Wadham man, marks this as the true birthplace: “Some space after the end of the Civil Wars at Oxford, in Dr. Wilkins his Lodgings, in Wadham College, which was then the place of Resort for Virtuous, and Learned Men, that the first meetings were made, which laid the foundation of all this that followed.”
The Oxford group included the mathematician John Wallis, the astronomer Seth Ward, the physician Thomas Willis, the anatomist Thomas Goddard, the natural philosopher Robert Boyle, the architect and astronomer Christopher Wren, and the political economist William Petty. They met regularly to perform experiments, discuss natural phenomena, and read the works of Francis Bacon, whose New Atlantis and Novum Organum supplied both the ideological programme and the institutional model for what they were attempting. The Civil War and the Interregnum made the university a refuge for learned men who wished to avoid politics and theology; natural philosophy was, as Sprat put it, “Nature alone, which could pleasantly entertain them, in that estate.”
A second group met in London at Gresham College, under the auspices of Samuel Foster, the professor of astronomy. These two circles overlapped and corresponded, and when the Restoration came, the London meetings rapidly eclipsed the Oxford ones.

Foundation at Gresham College (1660)
On 28 November 1660 — twelve weeks after Charles II entered London — twelve men met at Gresham College, in Bishopsgate, after a lecture by Christopher Wren (the professor of astronomy). They resolved to form “a Colledge for the Promoting of Physico-Mathematicall Experimentall Learning.” The minute book records the first list of forty-one names, including the Earl of Brouncker, Robert Boyle, John Wilkins, Christopher Wren, William Petty, and the king’s physician, Sir Thomas Millington. Lord William Brouncker was elected the first President. John Wilkins and Henry Oldenburg were appointed Secretaries. Regular weekly meetings were established, and the Society began immediately to collect instruments, perform experiments, and correspond with foreign philosophers.
The speed of the foundation is itself a Restoration phenomenon. During the Interregnum, the Oxford group had operated informally and discreetly. With the return of monarchy came the possibility of public, legal incorporation. The Society’s founder-members were overwhelmingly royalists or moderate parliamentarians; they had survived the Commonwealth by keeping their heads down, and they presented themselves to the restored King as natural allies of the crown — sober, learned, useful men whose work would strengthen the state.

The Royal Charter (1662)
Charles II granted the Society its first Royal Charter on 15 July 1662, incorporating it as “The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge.” The King, who had a genuine if dilettantish interest in chemistry and navigation, expressed his favour in terms that Sprat records: “Your Majesty was the first, who confirm’d this Noble Design of Experiments, by Your own Example, and by a Public Establishment.”
The Charter named Brouncker as President, appointed a Council of twenty-one, and empowered the Society to hold land, elect Fellows, appoint officers, and publish its proceedings. A second Charter in 1663 enlarged the privileges and added the King as Founder and Patron — a role symbolised by the Society’s motto, Nullius in Verba (“On no man’s word”), a declaration of independence from ancient authority and a commitment to experimental evidence as the sole arbiter of truth.
The Charter was more than a legal formality. It gave the Society a permanent corporate identity, independent of the life of any individual patron or sovereign, and it placed the new experimental philosophy under the protection of the English crown — a public endorsement that the French Académie des Sciences (founded 1666) and other continental bodies would later emulate.

Early Leadership and Fellows
Lord William Brouncker (c. 1620–1684), the first President, was a mathematician of genuine ability — he had published the first systematic treatment of continued fractions and served as Chancellor to Queen Catherine. He presided over the Society’s most formative decade, from 1662 to 1677, and was succeeded by Sir Joseph Williamson (1677–1680), the Secretary of State, and then by Sir Christopher Wren (1680–1682).
The early Fellowship was a remarkable concentration of talent. Robert Boyle (1627–1691) was the Society’s most prolific experimentalist — his work with the air pump, published as New Experiments Physico-Mechanical (1660), established the relationship between pressure and volume now known as Boyle’s Law, and his Sceptical Chymist (1661) laid the foundations of modern chemistry. Robert Hooke (1635–1703) was appointed first Curator of Experiments in 1662, charged with preparing three or four experiments for each weekly meeting; his Micrographia (1665) revealed the microscopic world with unprecedented clarity. Christopher Wren contributed anatomical drawings, astronomical observations, and the design of the Society’s meeting rooms. John Wilkins (1614–1672), the Society’s first Secretary, was the intellectual organiser and conciliator whose Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language (1668) attempted to create a universal language for science. William Petty (1623–1687) brought the quantitative methods of the “political arithmetic” to the Society. Henry Oldenburg (c. 1619–1677), the first Secretary, built the European correspondence network that made the Society the clearing-house of European science — corresponding with Spinoza, Huygens, Leibniz, Malpighi, and dozens of others.
Isaac Newton (1642–1727) was elected a Fellow in 1672, on the strength of his reflecting telescope and his early optical papers. He was an active correspondent of the Society through Oldenburg, though his relationship with the Fellowship was often prickly — his disputes with Hooke over the theory of light and with Leibniz over the calculus soured his temper. He became President in 1703 and was re-elected annually until his death in 1727, presiding over the Society’s most celebrated period.
Burnet records that the Society was also joined by “many Physicians, and other ingenious men,” including Samuel Pepys (President 1684–1686), whose diary records numerous visits to Gresham College to see experiments, and John Evelyn, whose Sylva (1664) on forestry was published under the Society’s auspices.

The Baconian Method and the Programme of Experiments
The Society’s intellectual programme was explicitly Baconian. Francis Bacon had argued in The Advancement of Learning and the Novum Organum that natural philosophy must abandon the syllogism for experiment, that knowledge must be built inductively from particulars, and that science should be a collaborative, institutional enterprise — a vision he had set out fictionally in New Atlantis (1627), with its House of Salomon, the model for the Royal Society itself.
The Society translated this vision into practice. At each weekly meeting, experiments were performed before the assembled Fellows — not as demonstrations of established truths but as genuine investigations. The Curator of Experiments (Hooke) was responsible for designing and executing these trials. Sprat describes the method: “They have a constant succession of experiments, in which every man may take part, either by his hands or his eyes.” The results were recorded, debated, and often repeated publicly to ensure reproducibility — an innovation as important as any single discovery.
The range of early experiments was vast. The air pump, constructed for Boyle by Hooke, generated a vacuum that allowed experiments on respiration, combustion, and the weight of air. Blood transfusion was attempted between dogs in 1665, and a human transfusion — in which Arthur Coga, a “harmless lunatick,” received sheep’s blood — followed in 1667. Microscopic observations by Hooke revealed the cellular structure of cork (coining the word “cell”) and the compound eyes of insects. The Society weighed the earth, tested the strength of gunpowder, observed the transit of Mercury, dissected dozens of animals, and collected natural specimens from every corner of the known world.

The Repository and the Philosophical Transactions
Two institutional innovations of the 1660s proved decisive for the Society’s long-term influence.
The Repository was the Society’s museum of natural and artificial curiosities — specimens, instruments, preserved animals, fossils, minerals, and ethnographic objects. It was housed at Gresham College and later moved with the Society to Crane Court. The Repository served as a physical archive of Baconian natural history, a library of nature against which hypotheses could be tested and from which generalisations could be drawn. Its keeper was Hooke, who curated it alongside his duties as Curator of Experiments.
Far more consequential was the Philosophical Transactions, first published on 6 March 1665 under the editorship of Henry Oldenburg. It was the world’s first periodical devoted exclusively to scientific research. Oldenburg printed letters and papers from correspondents across Europe — often in English or Latin, occasionally in French — and distributed them to subscribers. The Transactions created a public sphere for science. For the first time, a discovery made in London could be read in Paris, Leiden, or Florence within weeks. The publication of Newton’s early optical papers in the Transactions in 1672 — and the ensuing controversy with Hooke — demonstrated both the power and the difficulty of open scientific debate. The Transactions were interrupted by Oldenburg’s death in 1677 but revived by the Society under successive editors; they have been published continuously ever since, making them the oldest scientific journal in the world.

The Great Fire, the Move to Crane Court, and the Eighteenth Century
The Great Fire of London in September 1666 destroyed the Royal Exchange and much of the City, but Gresham College survived — though its neighbourhood was devastated. The Society continued to meet at Gresham until 1710, when the College premises were needed for other uses. In that year, the Society purchased a house at Crane Court, off Fleet Street, which served as its premises until the move to Somerset House in 1780.
The later decades of the seventeenth century saw the Society’s work deepen and specialise. Newton’s Principia Mathematica (1687) — published with the encouragement of the Society and dedicated to it — transformed natural philosophy, establishing universal gravitation and the laws of motion. Newton’s presidency from 1703 marked a shift: the Society became more hierarchical, more mathematical, and more cautious in its experimental programme. Newton himself was a formidable but overbearing President, dominating the Council and directing the Society’s activities with an iron hand. The great days of the 1660s — the air pump, the microscope, the transfusion experiments — receded into institutional memory.

The Society’s Role in the Scientific Revolution
The Royal Society was not the only scientific institution of the seventeenth century — the Académie des Sciences in Paris (1666), the Leopoldina in Germany (1652), and the Accademia del Cimento in Florence (1657) all preceded or paralleled it. But the Society was unique in its combination of features: it was a private corporation, not a state academy; it was open in its membership to gentlemen, physicians, clergymen, and merchants (not merely professional philosophers); it published a regular journal open to external contributors; and it maintained an active experimental programme at its weekly meetings.
The Society’s most important contribution was not any single discovery but the creation of a public, institutional, collaborative model for natural knowledge. Before the Royal Society, science was largely the pursuit of isolated individuals — Kepler, Galileo, Harvey — who published their results privately and corresponded with a small circle. After the Society, science became a profession with a permanent institutional home, a periodical press, a standard of experimental reproducibility, and a rhetoric of public utility. The Society’s motto — Nullius in Verba — captured the epistemological revolution: authority no longer resided in ancient texts, the church, or the prince, but in the disciplined observation of nature by a community of peers.

concepts/social-orders-and-ranks.title: Social Orders and Ranks in 1688
concepts/social-orders-and-ranks.content:
Social Orders and Ranks in 1688
Summary
Gregory King, Lancaster Herald of Arms, included in his Natural and Political Observations upon the State and Condition of England (1696) a celebrated classification of the English population by social degree. This scheme, titled “A Scheme of the Income & Expence of the Several Families of England, Anno 1688,” divided the nation into 26 distinct ranks, from the highest Temporal Lords down to Vagrants. For each rank, King recorded the number of families, the average income per family, and the total income and total expense for the group. It was the most detailed quantitative description of English social structure ever attempted in the 17th century.

King’s Categories
King’s 26 ranks, listed in descending order of social degree, were as follows.
Nobility
Temporal Lords. The highest temporal rank. King divided this category into the five degrees of the peerage: Dukes, Marquesses, Earls, Viscounts, and Barons. The Temporal Lords were the smallest of all the ranks in number of families.
Spiritual Lords. The Archbishops, Bishops, Deans, and other dignitaries of the Church of England who sat in the House of Lords.
Baronets. A hereditary order of knighthood created by James I in 1611.
Knights. Those who had received the honour of knighthood, whether Knights of the Garter or Knights Bachelor.
Gentry
Esquires. The principal gentry, entitled by law or custom to bear arms.
Gentlemen. The broad lower tier of the gentry, including those who lived on their rents and claimed the status of gentleman by birth, education, or reputation.
Office-Holders and Professionals
Persons in greater offices. Higher civil servants, judges, and senior government officials.
Persons in lesser offices. Clerks, excise officers, and the lower rungs of the civil establishment.
Commerce
Eminent merchants. The wealthiest wholesale traders and overseas merchants, chiefly in London and the outports.
Merchants by sea. The lesser merchants trading overseas, including ship captains trading on their own account.
Shopkeepers and tradesmen. The retail traders of town and country.
Artisans and handicrafts. Skilled craftsmen in all trades.
Military and Naval
Naval officers. Commissioned officers of the Royal Navy.
Military officers. Commissioned officers of the army.
Clergy
King divided the clergy into two tiers. The superior clergy included bishops, deans, and benefited clergy with substantial livings. The inferior clergy included curates and vicars of poor benefices.
Law
Lawyers. Barristers, solicitors, attorneys, and all others practising the law.
Land
Freeholders of the better sort. Those who held land in freehold to the value of £50 per annum and upwards.
Freeholders of the lesser sort. Those who held freehold land of less than £50 per annum.
Farmers. Tenant farmers who rented the land they cultivated.
Labour
Labouring people and outservants. Agricultural labourers, industrial workers, and domestic servants who lived out.
Cottagers and paupers. The rural poor, living in cottages with little or no land, together with those receiving parish relief.
Maritime and Military Enlisted
Common seamen. Ordinary sailors in the merchant and naval service.
Soldiers. Enlisted men in the army.
Marginal
Vagrants. Hawkers, pedlars, crate carriers, gipsies, thieves, and beggars — those with no fixed habitation or settled means of support.

Key Figures from the Tables
King’s aggregations across all 26 ranks produced the following totals for the nation in 1688.
The total number of families in England was 1,360,000. The total number of inhabited houses was 1,300,000, giving an average of slightly over four persons per house. The total population was 5,500,000 souls, comprising 530,000 in London and the Bills of Mortality, 870,000 in the other cities and market towns, and 4,100,000 in the villages and hamlets.
The yearly income of the nation stood at £43,500,000 sterling. The yearly expense of the nation was £41,700,000. The excess of income over expense yielded a yearly increase of national wealth amounting to £1,800,000.
Of the £43,500,000 total income, £13,000,000 came from rents of lands, houses, and other hereditaments, while £30,500,000 came from the produce of trade, arts, and labour.
The total number of transitory people — seamen and soldiers not accounted in the house-by-house assessments — was 140,000. Of these, some 60,000 had no place in the marriage, birth, and burial assessments. Vagrants of all kinds numbered 30,000, of whom about 20,000 were not recorded in the assessments.

The Distribution
King’s scheme revealed a steep concentration of income at the top of the social order. The Temporal Lords, numbering between 160 and 200 families, had an average income per family several times greater than that of any other rank. The Spiritual Lords, though far fewer in number, also stood at a level of income far above the common sort. The Baronets and Knights followed, their incomes placing them among the wealthiest families in the kingdom.
At the opposite end of the scale, the Labouring people and outservants formed the single largest group, with hundreds of thousands of families subsisting on incomes that barely covered their yearly expense. The Cottagers and paupers were the poorest settled group, their expenses often exceeding their incomes, making them a net drain on the national account. Below them stood the Vagrants, whose income was the least of all.
The middle ranks — the Freeholders, Farmers, Shopkeepers, Artisans, and the lesser Clergy — together constituted the broad centre of English society. Their incomes, though modest individually, collectively formed the bulk of the nation’s productive capacity.

The Social Pyramid
King’s numbers described a society shaped like a broad-based pyramid. At the apex stood the few hundred families of the peerage and higher clergy, commanding incomes that placed them among the richest subjects in Europe. Below them came several thousand gentry families — Baronets, Knights, Esquires, and Gentlemen — whose rents and offices supported a life of leisure and local authority. The middle of the pyramid was occupied by the tens of thousands of freeholders, farmers, shopkeepers, and artisans, whose labour and trade generated the greater part of the nation’s wealth. The base of the pyramid was formed by the hundreds of thousands of labouring people, cottagers, and paupers, whose numbers far exceeded all the other ranks combined. At the very bottom, outside the settled order, were the vagrants.
The shape of this pyramid reflected the distribution of income: the wealth of the few was drawn largely from the land, while the labour of the many sustained the commerce and agriculture upon which the whole depended. King’s scheme showed an England in which the majority of families lived at or near subsistence, while a small minority controlled a disproportionate share of the nation’s income.
