concepts/the-restoration.title: The Restoration
concepts/the-restoration.content:
The Restoration
Summary
The Restoration of 1660 was the re-establishment of monarchy in England, Scotland, and Ireland after the eleven-year republican interregnum of the Commonwealth and Protectorate. Charles II, the exiled son of the executed Charles I, returned from continental exile to claim the throne on 29 May 1660 — his thirtieth birthday. The event was not a conquest or a coup but a national settlement, negotiated by a Convention Parliament and ratified by acclamation. It restored the monarchy, the House of Lords, the Church of England, and the ancient constitution, but it also settled the crown on a new financial footing, abolished feudal tenures, and confirmed — in practice if not in law — many of the constitutional changes forced by the Long Parliament. The Restoration proved remarkably durable: though it was followed by religious persecution, plague, fire, and two foreign wars, the monarchy itself was never seriously threatened until the Revolution of 1688.

The Collapse of the Protectorate
Oliver Cromwell died on 3 September 1658 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Richard. Richard Cromwell lacked his father’s military reputation, political authority, and personal force. Hume describes him as a young man “of no experience, educated in the country, accustomed to a retired life, unacquainted with the officers and unknown to them.” The army, dominated by republican officers meeting in cabal at Wallingford-house, forced Richard to dissolve his parliament in April 1659 and soon after to abdicate. The Rump Parliament — the same remnant that Cromwell had expelled by force in 1653 — was restored. But the Rump proved unable to govern: it was expelled again by the army in October 1659, and a Committee of Safety was established. England descended into near-anarchy. Royalist risings were suppressed, but the military factions could settle on no stable form of government. The nation, exhausted by civil war and military usurpation, longed for a settled order.

Monk’s March to London
General George Monk, the commander of the English forces in Scotland, was the pivotal figure. A professional soldier who had served the king in Ireland, fought for the parliament, and later served Cromwell faithfully, Monk held his cards close. In January 1660 he marched his army south from Coldstream. As he advanced, the gentry of every county flocked to him with addresses urging the restoration of a free parliament. At St. Albans, he demanded that the Rump remove the regiments that had recently expelled it. He entered London on 6 February 1660. After initial hesitation — he appeared to temporise, even negotiating with the Rump — Monk revealed his hand. On 21 February, he restored the members of the Long Parliament who had been secluded by Pride’s Purge in 1648. The restored Long Parliament dissolved itself on 16 March 1660, having ordered new elections for a “free parliament.”

The Declaration of Breda and the Convention Parliament
The elections returned a Convention Parliament dominated by moderate Presbyterians and concealed royalists. It met on 25 April 1660. On 1 May, Sir John Granville arrived with a letter from Charles II, accompanied by the Declaration of Breda. The declaration was a masterpiece of political calibration. In it, Charles promised:

A general amnesty to all who would acknowledge his authority, “excepting only such persons as shall be excepted by parliament”
Liberty of conscience, to be settled by parliamentary advice
The settlement of all disputes over land purchases and alienations by act of parliament
The payment of all arrears to the army

Hume records that the letter and declaration were “greedily read: without one moment’s delay, and without a contradictory vote,” the Commons voted to receive them. On 8 May 1660, Charles II was proclaimed king at Palace-yard, Whitehall, and Temple-bar. The rapidity of events “discovered the passionate zeal and entire unanimity of the nation.”

The Landing at Dover
Charles II landed at Dover on 25 May 1660. General Monk received him on the beach. The king entered London on 29 May, his thirtieth birthday. The coincidence was interpreted as a happy omen. London greeted him with an outpouring of joy that, by all contemporary accounts, was overwhelming and universal. The Puritan austerity of the Interregnum was swept aside. Bells rang, bonfires blazed, conduits ran with wine. The nation, in Burnet’s phrase, had experienced “the great turn.”

The Restoration Settlement
The Act of Indemnity
The Convention Parliament’s first great work was the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion. Charles, who had promised at Breda to leave exceptions to parliament, pressed for the widest possible mercy. He came to the House of Lords “in the most earnest terms” and urged “the obligation of his former promise; a promise, he said, which he would ever regard as sacred; since to it he probably owed the satisfaction, which at present he enjoyed, of meeting his people in parliament.” The lords were vengeful — they wished to except everyone who had sat in any high court of justice — but the king’s intervention carried the day. In the end, only the regicides — those who had directly signed Charles I’s death warrant — were excepted. Even of these, only nine were executed: Harrison, Scot, Carew, Clement, Jones, Scrope, Axtel, Hacker, and Coke, together with Hugh Peters, the fanatical preacher who had inflamed the army to regicide. Hume observes that the “severities which followed such furious civil wars and convulsions” were remarkably few. The dead Cromwell, Ireton, and Bradshaw were attainted and their estates forfeited. Vane and Lambert were excepted but not executed at once. All others who had borne arms against the king received a full and free pardon.
The Land Settlement
The land question was the most delicate issue. During the Interregnum, vast estates had been confiscated from the crown, the church, and the royalists, and resold — often to speculators who had no connection to the original owners. The Declaration of Breda had promised that all such questions would be settled by parliament. The Convention Parliament confirmed the purchasers in their possession, to avoid a wholesale unsettling of titles, but those who had bought crown or church lands were required to surrender them, receiving a modest compensation. The old royalists, who had sacrificed everything for the crown, were largely left unrecompensed — a bitter disappointment that Clarendon privately acknowledged.
The Revenue Settlement
The Convention Parliament settled the king’s revenue with great care, and with an eye to limiting royal independence as well as providing for the crown. Feudal tenures — wardship, livery, purveyance — which had been long resented as a burden on the gentry, were abolished. In compensation, the crown was granted a perpetual revenue of 100,000 pounds a year from the excise. Tonnage and poundage and the other half of the excise were granted to the king for life. The parliament voted that the settled revenue of the crown should be 1,200,000 pounds a year — more than any English monarch had ever enjoyed — but assigned funds that yielded scarcely two-thirds of that sum. Hume notes that the parliament “shewed no intention of parting with” the engine of supply, and left the crown dependent on future parliaments. The army was disbanded, retaining only a small force of guards and garrisons — about one thousand horse and four thousand foot: the first appearance of a standing army under the monarchy.

The Religious Settlement
Prelacy Restored
The religious settlement was dictated largely by the royalist reaction. The bishops were restored to their sees, the ejected clergy recovered their livings, and the Book of Common Prayer was readmitted into the churches. Initially, Charles issued a declaration promising moderation: suffragan bishops for large dioceses, the advice of presbyters in ordination and jurisdiction, alterations to the liturgy, and a relaxation of ceremonies — the surplice, the cross in baptism, and bowing at the name of Jesus were not to be rigidly insisted on. This declaration, issued by the king as supreme head of the church, assumed a legislative authority in ecclesiastical matters that was constitutionally questionable but practically necessary in the aftermath of civil war.
The Savoy Conference
In March 1661, a conference was held at the Savoy between twelve bishops and twelve leading Presbyterian ministers, ostensibly to bring about an accommodation between the two parties. Hume dismisses the conference as an exercise in futility: “To enter into particulars would be superfluous. Disputes concerning religious forms are, in themselves, the most frivolous of any; and merit attention only so far as they have influence on the peace and order of civil society.” The bishops and Presbyterians separated, in Hume’s words, “more inflamed than ever, and more confirmed in their several prejudices.”
The Corporation Act and the Act of Uniformity
The Cavalier Parliament, elected in May 1661, was dominated by royalists and zealous churchmen; not more than fifty-six Presbyterian members obtained seats. It proceeded to dismantle the religious settlement of the Interregnum. The Corporation Act (1661) required all municipal magistrates to renounce the Solemn League and Covenant, swear that it was not lawful to resist the king, and receive the Anglican sacrament. The Act of Uniformity (1662) went further: every clergyman was required to receive episcopal ordination (or be re-ordained), declare his assent to everything in the Book of Common Prayer, take the oath of canonical obedience, abjure the Covenant, and renounce the principle of taking arms against the king on any pretence. The act was supported by a coalition of interests: the church party seeking revenge for years of suffering, the Independents and sectaries eager to see their Presbyterian rivals crushed, and the Catholics at court who feared a united Protestant front.
The Great Ejection
The Act of Uniformity took effect on St. Bartholomew’s Day, 24 August 1662. Nearly two thousand Presbyterian ministers — about a fifth of the English clergy — refused to comply and were ejected from their livings. This was the Great Ejection. Many of the ejected ministers, men of learning and piety, ended their days in poverty. Hume writes that the king’s promises of toleration were “eluded and broken,” though he adds that Charles “did not voluntarily concur with this violent measure” but was forced by Clarendon, the church party, and the Catholic faction at court.

Restored Court Culture
The Restoration court was a deliberate repudiation of the Puritanism that had dominated the Interregnum. Charles II, by nature “totally devoid of resentment,” presided over a court of gaiety, wit, and pleasure. Hume characterises the shift: “The melancholy austerity of the fanatics fell into discredit, together with their principles. The royalists, who had ever affected a contrary disposition, found in their recent success new motives for mirth and gaiety.” The king himself set the tone: “The king himself, who bore a propensity to pleasure, served, by his powerful and engaging example, to banish those sour and malignant humours.”
The court became the centre of English cultural life. The theatre, suppressed by the Puritans, was revived with unprecedented splendour. Women’s roles — previously played by boys — were now performed by actresses for the first time on the English stage. The Royal Society, chartered by the king in 1662, became the institutional home of the new experimental philosophy (though Hume himself was sceptical of its achievements). Literature flourished in the witty, cynical verse of Dryden and the comedies of the Restoration stage. Architecture, music, painting — all felt the influence of French and Italian taste imported by the king and his courtiers in exile. The court was also a place of scandal: the king’s mistresses — Barbara Villiers (Lady Castlemaine), Nell Gwyn, Louise de Keroualle (Duchess of Portsmouth) — were as prominent in public life as the ministers. Clarendon lamented the corruption of morals, but the nation as a whole, weary of enforced godliness, embraced the new licence.

entities/archbishop-laud.title: William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury
entities/archbishop-laud.content:
William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury
Summary
William Laud (1573–1645), Archbishop of Canterbury from 1633 until his impeachment by the Long Parliament, was the architect of the Arminian and ceremonial revival that provoked the Puritan rebellion and hastened the English Civil War. Hume describes him as a man of learning, severity, and unrelenting zeal — “virtuous, if severity of manners alone, and abstinence from pleasure, could deserve that name” — whose passion for ritual order and priestly authority made him the most hated man in England outside the court. Burnet calls him “a learned, a sincere and zealous man, regular in his own life, and humble in his private deportment; but was a hot, indiscreet man.” His prosecution and execution in January 1645, after four years in the Tower, were the second great act of parliamentary vengeance (after Strafford’s) and a decisive step toward the destruction of the established church.

Early Career at Oxford
Laud was born at Reading, Berkshire, in 1573, the son of a clothier. He was educated at Reading School and St John’s College, Oxford, where he took his BA in 1594 and was elected a fellow. He was ordained and rose rapidly in academic administration, becoming President of St John’s College in 1611. At Oxford he became known for his opposition to the dominant Calvinist orthodoxy and for his attachment to the ceremonies and liturgy of the primitive church. In 1616, James I appointed him Dean of Gloucester. There he immediately ordered the communion table, which Puritan reformers had moved into the chancel, to be replaced at the east end of the cathedral — an early sign of the policy he would later impose on the whole kingdom.

Bishop of St David’s and London
Laud was consecrated Bishop of St David’s in 1621, but his influence remained modest until the accession of Charles I. The new king shared Laud’s reverence for ecclesiastical order and his suspicion of Puritan theology. In 1627, Laud was appointed Bishop of Bath and Wells, and in 1628 he was translated to the wealthy see of London. From this position he became the king’s principal adviser on church affairs, eclipsing the more moderate Archbishop Abbot.

Arminian Theology and Opposition to Calvinism
The theological controversy that defined Laud’s career was the conflict between Calvinism and Arminianism. The English Reformation had been built on the Calvinist doctrines of predestination and absolute decrees — tenets embedded in the Thirty-Nine Articles and preached by the first reformers. The Dutch theologian Arminius and his followers had challenged this system, arguing for human free will and a conditional election. Hume records that the Arminians, “finding more encouragement from the superstitious spirit of the church than from the fanaticism of the Puritans, gradually incorporated themselves with the former.” Laud, along with Bishops Neile and Montague, became the leader of this party. The Commons, dominated by the Puritan faction, saw the spread of Arminianism as a mortal threat and repeatedly censured its adherents. Laud’s identification with Arminianism tied him, in the Puritan mind, to Rome itself.

Archbishop of Canterbury (1633)
Upon Abbot’s death in 1633, Laud was appointed Archbishop of Canterbury. He now controlled the ecclesiastical patronage of the entire realm and used it ruthlessly to promote high-church clergymen and to suppress Puritan lecturers. Hume observes that Laud “seems not to have been altogether so great an enemy to the Catholics” as his predecessors — an indulgence that, together with his severity toward Puritans, aroused the deepest suspicion. The court of Rome twice offered him a cardinal’s hat, which he declined, saying “something dwelt within him which would not suffer his compliance, till Rome were other than it is.” A court lady, asked by Laud why she had turned Catholic, replied: “I perceive your grace and many others are making haste to Rome; and therefore, in order to prevent my being crowded, I have gone before you.”

The Laudian Church: Beauty of Holiness and Altar Rails
Laud’s programme for the church was one of uniformity, decency, and what might be called the “beauty of holiness.” He ordered the communion table — which had stood in the middle of the chancel since the Reformation — to be removed to the east end of every church, railed in, and denominated an altar. The officiating clergyman was to be called a priest. Copes and other embroidered vestments were to be worn in administering the sacrament. Bowing toward the altar was required. Crucifixes and painted windows were encouraged. Burnet records that Laud’s innovations included “setting the communion table by the east walls of churches, bowing to it, and calling it the Altar,” the suppression of lectureships, and the encouragement of Sunday sports.
The consecration of St Catherine’s Church in 1630 became a cause celebre. As described by Hume, Laud approached the west door and a voice cried: “Open, open, ye everlasting doors, that the king of glory may enter in.” He fell on his knees, pronounced the ground holy, several times took up dust and threw it in the air, bowed repeatedly toward the communion table, marched around the church reciting psalms, and pronounced imprecations upon those who would profane the place. To the Puritans, these ceremonies were indistinguishable from popish superstition.

Persecution of Puritans: Prynne, Bastwick, and Burton
Laud’s enforcement of uniformity was most notoriously displayed in the Star Chamber prosecutions of the Puritan writers Prynne, Bastwick, and Burton. Prynne, a barrister of Lincoln’s Inn, had published a thousand-page quarto called “Histrio-Mastyx,” attacking stage-plays, music, dancing, and Christmas-keeping, but also the hierarchy, ceremonies, and innovations of Laud. He was sentenced to the pillory in two places, the loss of both ears, a 5000 pound fine, and imprisonment for life.
In 1637, Burton (a divine) and Bastwick (a physician) were tried in the Star Chamber for seditious and schismatical libels against the church, and condemned to the same punishment. Prynne was tried again for a new offence and lost what remained of his ears. Hume notes that the Star Chamber’s severity was “generally ascribed to Laud’s passionate disposition.” The public was deeply offended, and the alacrity with which the three men suffered increased still further the indignation against the archbishop.

The Scottish Prayer Book Crisis
The crisis that ultimately destroyed Laud and his king began in Scotland. Determined to impose liturgical uniformity across both kingdoms, Laud and Charles introduced a new Prayer Book and canons for the Church of Scotland in 1637 — a liturgy modelled on the English Book of Common Prayer but even more ceremonial. When the dean of Edinburgh attempted to read the new service at St Giles’ Cathedral on 23 July 1637, a woman named Jenny Geddes is said to have thrown her stool at the pulpit, sparking a full-scale riot. The National Covenant was signed in February 1638, binding the Scots to resist the innovations. A general assembly abolished episcopacy. War followed; and the financial necessity of suppressing the Scottish rebellion forced Charles to summon the Short Parliament (1640) and then the Long Parliament — which would turn on Laud and Strafford with deadly determination.

Impeachment, Imprisonment, and Trial
The Long Parliament met in November 1640 in a fury against the policies of the Personal Rule. Pym and the popular leaders moved quickly. On 18 December 1640, after a deliberation of scarcely half an hour, the Commons voted an impeachment of high treason against the Archbishop. Laud, sequestered from Parliament and committed to the custody of the gentleman usher of the black rod, was sent to the Tower of London. Burnet records that when the news came, Laud’s secretary was busy for three hours destroying papers from his closet, including — it is believed — the original Magna Carta.
Laud remained in the Tower for nearly four years while the Commons, engaged in the greater enterprises of war, found no leisure to finish his impeachment. Finally, after the alliance with the Scottish Covenanters revived the spirit of Puritan vengeance, he was brought to trial. Hume writes that after examining over 150 witnesses, the Commons found so little likelihood of obtaining a judicial sentence that they “were obliged to have recourse to their legislative authority, and to pass an ordinance for taking away the life of this aged prelate.” The peers, threatened by the London mob, passed the bill of attainder by a vote of only seven — the rest absenting themselves from shame or fear.

Execution (10 January 1645)
Laud was brought to the scaffold on Tower Hill on 10 January 1645. He had behaved during his trial with spirit and vigour, and he met his death with composure. Though he had often professed a fear of violent death, Hume records that “he found all his fears to be dissipated before that superior courage by which he was animated.” On the scaffold, he was harassed by Sir John Clotworthy, a Puritan zealot, who attempted to trepan him into confessing that he trusted for salvation to good works rather than the death of the Redeemer. Having extricated himself from these theological toils, he laid his head on the block, and it was severed at one blow.
Burnet notes that the manner of his death, so unjust and violent, “raised his character, and established all his notions as standards, by which judgments are to be made of men whether they are true to the church or not.” Hume observes that the execution of this old and inoffensive prisoner “can be ascribed to nothing but vengeance and bigotry in those severe religionists, by whom the parliament was entirely governed.”

Character and Legacy
Laud’s character was the subject of fierce dispute in his own time and ever since. Hume’s portrait is unsparing: zealous, efficient, and utterly convinced of his own rectitude, Laud “overlooked every human consideration” in pursuit of his holy purposes, “the heat and indiscretion of his temper made him neglect the views of prudence and rules of good manners.” His enemies were, in his own eyes, the enemies of God and the king; every exercise of his anger became in his eyes a merit and a virtue.
Burnet offers a more measured assessment: Laud was “a learned, sincere and zealous man, regular in his own life,” but one who “eagerly pursued some matters that were either very inconsiderable or mischievous” — the position of the communion table, bowing to the altar, suppressing lectures, encouraging Sunday sports. “All the zeal and heat of that time was laid out on these.”
By imposing a high ceremonialism on a nation that had been raised on Calvinist austerity, by persecuting the Puritan gentry who dominated the House of Commons, and by pressing liturgical uniformity on the Scots, Laud united against the crown the very forces that would destroy it. He was, in Hume’s phrase, the man “who acquired so great an ascendancy over Charles, and who led him, by the facility of his temper, into a conduct which proved so fatal to himself and to his kingdoms.”

entities/bank-of-england.title: Bank of England
entities/bank-of-england.content:
Bank of England
Summary
The Bank of England was incorporated by Act of Parliament in 1694, under the name “The Governor and Company of the Bank of England.” It was a society of about 1,300 persons who subscribed L1,200,000 to the government, in return for which they received a Royal Charter and the right to conduct banking business. The Bank was governed by a Governor, Deputy-Governor, and 24 Directors elected annually.
Foundation
The Bank was established by an Act of Parliament grounded upon a loan of L1,200,000 to the government. Commissioners were appointed to take voluntary subscriptions from “any Person or Persons, Natives or Foreigners, Bodies Politic or Corporate.” The subscription was to be completed by 1 August 1694; if the full L1,200,000 was not subscribed by that date, the power of making the incorporation would cease and the money would be paid into the Exchequer.
The subscription was filled. The Bank then advanced the money to the government at 8 per cent interest, with an additional allowance of L4,000 per annum for management.
Constitution
The Bank was governed by a Governor, a Deputy-Governor, and 24 Directors, all elected annually by the shareholders. Directors could not serve more than one year without a break — “Provision so wise and effectual to prevent Fraud in some, to the prejudice of the rest, that it hardly leaves room for any doubt of that nature.”
The Bank was permitted to issue notes — paper currency backed by its capital — which circulated as money. It could discount bills of exchange, accept deposits, deal in bullion, and lend money on securities.
Effects
The pamphlets defending the Bank claimed several effects:
Lowering of interest. Before the Bank, government tallies on various funds sold at substantial discounts — 12, 14, 15, and as high as 30 per cent above the public interest on some funds. Even the Land Tax, “which is counted the best of all the Funds,” was frequently sold at 1 or 2 per cent premium for payment in 3 or 4 months. After the Bank was established, the interest on government borrowing was reduced. The Bank itself lent at 8 per cent, and the competition forced down rates on all public securities.
Raising money for the war. The Bank raised L1,200,000 for the war “cheaper than it could otherwise have been done,” at a time when the government was fighting the Nine Years’ War against France.
Increasing trade and credit. The Bank’s notes circulated as readily as gold. Merchants could discount bills at the Bank, which “has always given as great a Reputation, and increased its value, the more they serve the Interest of the Nation.”
Tying the people to the government. The pamphlets argued the Bank “tying the People faster to the Government” — creating a class of creditors whose financial interest was bound up with the stability of the post-Revolution regime.
The Goldsmith-Bankers
The Bank’s greatest opponents were the goldsmith-bankers of London, who had previously acted as the crown’s financiers. Before the Bank, the goldsmiths discounted Exchequer tallies at rates from 12 to 30 per cent. The pamphlet A Short Account of the Bank of England argues that “they who have made these Advantages by the Publick are prevented of the like for the future” by the Bank, and “will be more ready to Lend Money on Private Securities, or to Purchase Lands.”
The Engrafting Crisis (1696-1697)
At the General Court of the Bank held on Monday the Third of January, a proposal was debated to “engraft” Tallies upon Parliamentary Funds, together with one third part or more in Bank-Notes, Bills, or Money, into the Bank’s stock. A pamphlet written by a Bank insider, in the form of a letter to a friend with a large fortune in the Bank, records the arguments for and against this proposal.
The case for engrafting. Proponents argued that the Bank would be thereby made capable to serve the Publick, and that it would be for the Interest and Advantage of the Bank. They urged that the great advantages made by the buying of Tallies hindered every man that hath Money both from lending it to the Government and also from employing it in Trade; that while Tallies are sold at vast discount, no Body will lend their Money to the King, and few will employ it in Trade. They said these evils would infallibly be remedied if all Tallies on Parliamentary Funds were sunk or lodged in the Bank of England, because then there would be no Tallies to be sold, and people not having such opportunities to lay out their Monies in Tallies would necessarily lend it to the Government or employ it in Trade.
The author’s answer against. The author replied that if the Bank of England were in a condition to take in all those Tallies at par and give the Owners Money for them, it would have the same effect supposed. But the method proposed gave the Owners no Money, nor anything they could use instead of Money, only a proportionable Share of Bank-Stock; so they would be as bare of Money as before they parted with their Tallies. The real cause why men sold their Tallies at so great a loss was the want of Money or Bank-Notes to pay their Debts or carry on their Trades, not because they believed those Tallies would never be paid. Changing Tallies into Bank-Stock would neither supply nor lessen their occasions for Money, but increase them, for they must then be forced to sell their Bank-Stock at any rate as before they sold their Tallies. Moreover, the requirement that subscribers pay in one third part in Bank-Bills or Notes would unavoidably occasion a much greater want of Money, Bank-Bills, or Notes. The author concluded that this intended Engrafting was not advisable to be attempted, because if the Bank were Engrafted upon it would neither procure Loans to the King, Credit to the Nation, nor bring any more Money into Trade.
The six arguments for compulsion reported from the General Court. Six propositions were put forward in favour of the engrafting:
First, that all their Bills and Notes would be brought in with the Tallies, and so at once help them out of Debt.
Secondly, that as a natural consequence, their Bills and Notes would become at par or equal to Money for the Payment of Debts or Bills of Exchange.
Thirdly, that being once out of Debt and their Bills or Notes equal with Money, they might begin to establish a new and lasting Credit.
Fourthly, that the Bank could not otherwise recover their Credit in many Years, and that until their Bills or Notes went current again at par with Money, the present Proprietors could not expect any Dividend either of Profit or Interest.
Fifthly, that the Parliament would grant them more and greater Privileges than the present Bank enjoyed by its old Establishment.
Sixthly and lastly, that in case they refused to be Engrafted upon, the Parliament would not show them any Favour at all, but leave them to the Mercy of their Creditors and the Severity and Extremity of Law and Justice; so that their Refusal would expose them to an immediate, unavoidable, and irrecoverable Destruction.
The author’s replies to the six arguments. To the first, the author granted that if all Tallies were brought in and cancelled, the Bank would certainly be out of Debt. To the second, he granted it upon supposition of the first, but noted that how long their Bills and Notes would continue at par depended much on the Management of the Bank. To the third, he observed that the Bank had formerly possessed the highest credit — until May last, Bank of England Notes were not only esteemed equal to Money but preferred much before it, and every one endeavoured to contract for Payment in Bank-Notes rather than in Money — yet it had fallen into discredit notwithstanding all the good qualities of its Managers and the Security of its Funds, so there was reason to fear the same misfortune might happen again. To the fourth, he argued by examining the Bank’s accounts that it owed one Million nine hundred seventy five thousand Pounds as of the Tenth of November last, but was owed the same sum and above one hundred twenty five thousand Pounds over; and that the Bank could bring its Notes to par within less than a Year without new Subscriptions. To the fifth, he said he could not foretell what the Parliament would do, but believed that in consideration of the Bank’s eminent Services to the Government, the Parliament would grant such Privileges as might restore the Bank’s Credit. To the sixth, he treated the threat as groundless — the Parliament had given all possible demonstration of their Zeal and Affection to His Majesty, and the Bank had sacrificed its own Safety and Interest to the Publick Service, lending money when the Commissioners of the Treasury could not otherwise supply the King’s urgent occasions, accepting Tallies in lieu of Money and thereby bringing itself into its present difficulties.
Outcome. Notwithstanding these objections, the engrafting scheme was eventually implemented by Parliament under the Bank Act of 1697, enlarging the Bank’s capital by the subscription of Tallies and new money into Bank stock.
The Land Bank Alternative
Hugh Chamberlen, a physician, promoted a competing proposal: a Land Bank whose credit would be founded on landed security rather than on a subscription of cash. Chamberlen argued that “Land hath a greater value than Gold and Silver” and that land security was “better than Personal, or Goods pledged.” He cited the example of the Venetians and Hamburghers as successful bank models. This scheme was tried on a smaller scale in 1696 and did not succeed.
Burnet’s Account
Bishop Burnet, in his History of His Own Time, records the establishment of the Bank as one of the significant events of William III’s reign. Burnet notes the political division over the Bank: the Tories and Country party opposed it as a Whig project. He records that “the Bank of England and the new East-India Company, being in the hands of Whigs, they would have the command of all the Money, and by consequence, of all the Trade of England.” Burnet also records that during the recoinage crisis of 1696, “the credit of the Bank of England was much shaken” before being restored by parliamentary support.

entities/buckingham.title: George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham
entities/buckingham.content:
George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham (1592–1628)
Summary
George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham, was the most powerful royal favourite of early Stuart England — the glittering, capricious, and catastrophically inept minister who dominated the courts of both James I and Charles I from 1615 until his assassination in 1628. Rising from modest gentry to the highest offices in the kingdom through the king’s personal affection, Buckingham became Lord High Admiral, the architect of a disastrous foreign policy, and the most hated man in England. His handsome appearance, charm, and personal courage were undone by a headstrong temperament, a complete want of political or military judgment, and an arrogance that alienated both parliament and people. His assassination by John Felton at Portsmouth was greeted with public rejoicing.
Rise as Favourite (1615–1618)
Buckingham first appeared at court in 1614, introduced by a faction seeking to displace the reigning favourite, Robert Carr, Earl of Somerset. James I, who formed intense attachments to handsome young men, was immediately captivated by Villiers’s beauty, grace, and athletic prowess. With the fall of Somerset after the Overbury murder scandal in 1615, Villiers rose with astonishing speed. James created him successively Viscount Villiers, Earl, Marquis, and finally Duke of Buckingham — the first non-royal duke created in decades. He was made Knight of the Garter, Master of the Horse, Chief Justice in Eyre, Warden of the Cinque Ports, Master of the King’s Bench Office, Steward of Westminster, Constable of Windsor, and Lord High Admiral of England. His mother was created Countess of Buckingham; his brother was made Viscount Purbeck; and a train of needy relations were pushed up into credit and authority. Hume observes that James, “while he meant to play the tutor to his favourite, and to train him up in the rules of prudence and politics, took an infallible method, by loading him with premature and exorbitant honours, to render him, for ever, rash, precipitate, and insolent.”
Character
Hume’s character sketch of Buckingham is devastating. “Some accomplishments of a courtier he possessed; of every talent of a minister he was utterly destitute. Headstrong in his passions, and incapable equally of prudence and of dissimulation: sincere from violence rather than candour; expensive from profusion more than generosity: a warm friend, a furious enemy; but without any choice or discernment in either.” He partook at once of the insolence that attends a fortune newly acquired and the impetuosity that belongs to persons born in high stations. His behaviour in Spain — composed of English familiarity and French vivacity, sallies of passion, indecent freedoms with the prince, dissolute pleasures, and an arrogant, impetuous temper — made him the object of peculiar aversion at the Spanish court. The Condé Duke of Olivarez, the Spanish minister, was personally insulted by Buckingham’s frank declaration of enmity. Yet Buckingham was capable of personal courage and loyalty; Charles I loved him as a friend and never wholly ceased to mourn him.
The Spanish Match Adventure (1623)
Buckingham’s most dramatic exploit was the scheme, hatched with Prince Charles, to travel incognito to Madrid to woo the Infanta Maria in person. Buckingham persuaded Charles that a romantic journey would win the princess’s heart and break the diplomatic deadlock. James, after agonised hesitation and a famous scene in which he called Charles “baby Charles” and Buckingham “Stenny,” gave his reluctant consent. The two travelled disguised through France — even attending a court ball in Paris, where Charles first saw Henrietta Maria, whom he would later marry. They arrived in Madrid in March 1623, to universal astonishment.
The Spanish court treated Charles with elaborate courtesy, but the romance was a fiasco. The Spanish demanded strict religious conditions — the education of the children by the Infanta until the age of ten, the suspension of penal laws against Catholics — and the Pope delayed the dispensation. Meanwhile Buckingham’s arrogance antagonised the entire Spanish court. He returned to England in October 1623, humiliated and furious, his former enthusiasm for the Spanish alliance transformed into a thirst for war. The adventure, which had been meant to secure peace, instead drove England into a ruinous conflict with Spain.
Lord High Admiral and the Impeachment Attempts
Buckingham was appointed Lord High Admiral in 1619, an office for which he had no qualification whatsoever. Under his administration, the English navy declined in efficiency and morale. The expedition against Cadiz in 1625, intended to intercept the Spanish treasure fleet, ended in farce: the troops landed, got drunk on captured wine, and were re-embarked in disorder.
The parliaments of 1625 and 1626, summoned by the newly crowned Charles I, demanded Buckingham’s impeachment for corruption, mismanagement, and the abuse of royal favour. Charles, who regarded any attack on Buckingham as an attack on his own authority, responded by imprisoning Sir Dudley Digges and Sir John Eliot, the managers of the impeachment. The Lords refused to proceed, but the Commons would not grant supply, and Charles dissolved both parliaments without obtaining the funds he needed. The Duke was also chosen Chancellor of the University of Cambridge while under impeachment — a deliberate affront to the Commons.
The Isle of Rhé Expedition (1627)
Buckingham’s most catastrophic venture was the expedition to the Isle of Rhé, undertaken in 1627 to relieve the Huguenot stronghold of La Rochelle, then besieged by Cardinal Richelieu. A fleet of a hundred sail and an army of seven thousand men were placed under his command, though he was “altogether unacquainted both with land and sea-service.”
The operation was a masterpiece of incompetence. Buckingham landed on the island but allowed the French governor five days’ respite, during which the citadel of St Martin was victualled and prepared for siege. He neglected to take the small fort of Prie, which could have been captured without resistance. He guarded the sea negligently, allowing provisions to reach the besieged. He attacked the citadel without making a breach, rashly throwing away the lives of his soldiers. When a French army crossed in small boats and landed at the very fort he had overlooked, he was forced to retreat — and conducted the retreat so unskilfully that it amounted to a total rout. He was the last of the army to embark, having lost two-thirds of his land forces. “Scarce an illustrious family but mourned the loss of a son or brother,” Hume records. The disaster discredited Buckingham utterly, though his personal courage in the retreat was widely acknowledged.
Unpopularity
By 1628, Buckingham was the most detested man in England. The nation ascribed to him the failure of the Spanish war, the collapse of commerce, the forced loans and arbitrary imprisonments, and the extraordinary calamities of the Rhé expedition. Hume writes that the people considered themselves “the victim of the frivolous gallantry of a favourite, and of his boyish caprices.” The Commons’ remonstrance of 1628 declared Buckingham an enemy to the kingdom — a document that would have fatal consequences.
Assassination (23 August 1628)
While at Portsmouth preparing a new fleet to relieve La Rochelle, Buckingham was stabbed to death by John Felton, a disgruntled army lieutenant who had served in the Rhé expedition. Felton’s captain had been killed in the retreat, and when he applied for the company and was refused, he threw up his commission in discontent. Brooding on his private grievance, he heard the nation resound with complaints against the duke, and found in the Commons’ remonstrance a justification for murder. Religious fanaticism inflamed his purpose: he fancied he should do Heaven acceptable service.
On the morning of 23 August, as Buckingham passed through a crowded room after conversing with Soubize and other French gentlemen, Felton struck him in the breast with a knife. The duke pulled out the knife, uttered “the villain has killed me,” and died instantly. In the confusion, the French gentlemen were almost lynched. Felton was discovered walking calmly before the door, without a hat; inside the hat was sewn a paper containing lines from the Commons’ remonstrance declaring Buckingham an enemy to the kingdom, with a short ejaculation resembling a prayer. He offered his breast to the drawn swords of the crowd, saying he was willing to die. Charles received the news with an unmoved countenance, but was deeply grieved and retained affection for Buckingham’s friends for the rest of his life. He urged that Felton be put to the question — tortured — but the judges declared the practice illegal. The nation, by contrast, rejoiced.
Legacy
Buckingham left no positive achievement behind him. He had governed England for thirteen years without a single successful policy, military venture, or diplomatic triumph to his name. His sole legacy was the alienation of parliament from the crown, the impoverishment of the treasury by wasteful expenditure, and the deepening of the distrust between the Stuart monarchy and its subjects that would culminate in civil war. His personal courage, loyalty to his friends, and devotion to Charles I were genuine, but they were qualities that served only to make his incompetence more dangerous. Hume’s verdict — that by heaping premature honours upon him, James ensured he would be “for ever, rash, precipitate, and insolent” — is the just epitaph of a man who broke everything he touched.

entities/charles-i.title: Charles I of England
entities/charles-i.content:
Charles I of England
Summary
Charles I (r. 1625–1649), the second Stuart monarch of England, is one of the most consequential and tragic figures in English history. His reign was defined by an escalating conflict between royal prerogative and parliamentary authority, culminating in the English Civil War (1642–1649), his defeat, trial, and public execution on 30 January 1649. He was the first English sovereign to be tried and executed by his own subjects — an event that shook monarchies across Europe and established, for a time, a republican commonwealth in England.
Charles was a man of high personal virtue — a devoted husband, a patron of the arts, a sincere Anglican, and a brave soldier — but his political inflexibility, his reliance on controversial ministers (Buckingham, Strafford, Laud), and his willingness to govern without parliament for eleven years proved fatal. The Caroline era (from Carolus, Latin for Charles) saw the flowering of English portrait painting (Van Dyck) and architecture (Inigo Jones), but also the collapse of the Stuart monarchy into civil war and regicide.

Accession and the First Parliaments (1625–1626)
Charles succeeded his father James I on 27 March 1625. He was twenty-four years old, inexperienced, and deeply influenced by George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham — the favourite who had dominated the latter part of James’s reign and whom Charles regarded not merely as a minister but as a friend. Within weeks of his accession, Charles summoned his first parliament, eager to prove his trust in the Commons and to secure the supply necessary for the war with Spain that the previous parliament had demanded.
The Commons responded by granting a meagre two subsidies (about 112,000 pounds) — far below the king’s needs. Hume records that Charles, expecting the dutiful generosity of his subjects, was cruelly disappointed. The parliament was swiftly adjourned to Oxford to escape plague, but the Commons there grew more hostile, turning their attack upon Buckingham, whose conduct of affairs they deemed ruinous. When the Commons hesitated to grant supply, Charles dissolved the first parliament (August 1625) without having obtained the funds he required.
A second parliament met in February 1626. The Commons immediately moved to impeach Buckingham for corruption and mismanagement. Charles, who regarded any attack on Buckingham as an attack on his own authority, responded by imprisoning two members — Sir Dudley Digges and Sir John Eliot — who had spoken against the favourite. The Lords refused to proceed with impeachment, but the Commons would not grant supply. Charles dissolved the second parliament in June 1626, having received nothing but grievances.

The Cadiz Expedition and the Isle of Rhé
Meanwhile, Charles had committed English arms to two disastrous expeditions, both planned under Buckingham’s direction. The first, an attack on Cadiz (October 1625), was intended to intercept the Spanish treasure fleet but was mismanaged from the start. The troops landed, became drunk on captured wine, and were re-embarked in disorder. The expedition returned home in humiliation.
The second and more ruinous venture was the expedition to the Isle of Rhé (July–November 1627), intended to relieve the Huguenot stronghold of La Rochelle, then besieged by Cardinal Richelieu. Buckingham personally commanded the landing force, but the siege of the citadel of St Martin was incompetently conducted, the French received reinforcements, and the English were forced to retreat with heavy losses. Hume writes that scarce an illustrious family but mourned the loss of a son or brother. The disaster discredited both Buckingham and the king’s foreign policy.

The Petition of Right and Buckingham’s Assassination (1628)
By 1628, Charles was desperate for supply. Forced loans, arbitrary imprisonment, and the billeting of soldiers had inflamed the nation. Preparations for a third parliament were made with trepidation on both sides.
The third parliament met in March 1628. The Commons, led by Sir Edward Coke, Sir John Eliot, and Sir Thomas Wentworth (the future Earl of Strafford), resolved to secure the liberties of the subject before granting supply. They framed the Petition of Right, a landmark constitutional document that declared:

No forced loans or taxes without parliamentary consent
No imprisonment without cause shown (habeas corpus)
No billeting of soldiers in private houses
No martial law in peacetime

Charles, needing money to continue the war, gave a reluctant and ambiguous royal assent (7 June 1628). The Commons, satisfied, voted five subsidies. But Charles never fully accepted the Petition of Right as a binding limitation on his prerogative, and the ambiguity of his assent poisoned trust between crown and parliament for the remainder of his reign.
On 23 August 1628, Buckingham was stabbed to death in Portsmouth by John Felton, a disgruntled army officer who had been passed over for promotion. Felton, who had served in the disastrous Rhé expedition and nursed a grievance at being denied a captaincy, struck the duke with a knife as he passed through a crowded room. The assassination was greeted with public rejoicing. Charles, however, was deeply grieved; he wore mourning for his friend and insisted that Felton be put to torture (the judges refused, as it was contrary to law). With Buckingham’s death, Charles became his own minister and never again reposed such unlimited confidence in any single subject.

The Personal Rule (1629–1640)
The third parliament was dissolved in March 1629 after a tumultuous session in which the Speaker was held down in his chair while the Commons passed resolutions against Arminianism and the levying of tonnage and poundage without consent. Charles, disgusted with parliaments, resolved to govern without them. There would be no parliament for eleven years — a period often called the Personal Rule or the Eleven Years’ Tyranny.
Finance and Ship Money
Without parliamentary supply, Charles raised revenue through a variety of expedients. Ancient feudal dues were revived, monopolies were sold, forest boundaries were extended, and fines were imposed on landowners who had encroached on royal forests. The most controversial measure was Ship Money — an ancient tax on maritime counties for the defence of the coast, which Charles in 1635 extended to inland counties. The writs claimed that the king, as guardian of the realm, could levy this tax in times of danger without parliamentary consent.
John Hampden, a Buckinghamshire gentleman, refused to pay the 20-shilling assessment. His case was tried before the Court of Exchequer in 1637–1638. The judges, by a narrow majority of seven to five, found for the crown. But the trial became a national cause célèbre, and the narrowness of the verdict was seen as a moral victory for the opposition. Hampden was celebrated as a patriot, and the Crown’s legal position, though technically upheld, was fatally weakened in public opinion.
Laud and Religious Innovation
William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1633, was the dominant ecclesiastical figure of the Personal Rule. A high-church Arminian, Laud sought to impose uniformity in worship — restoring the communion table to the east end of churches, railing it in, and calling it an altar; requiring bowing at the name of Jesus; and enforcing the wearing of surplices and copes. These innovations, which Hume describes as reviving the superstitions of the fourth and fifth centuries, were deeply offensive to the Puritan majority. Many Englishmen suspected that Laud aimed to lead the Church of England back to Rome.
The enforcement of Laud’s reforms through the Court of High Commission and the Star Chamber was severe. Three Puritan pamphleteers — William Prynne, Henry Burton, and John Bastwick — were pilloried, branded, and had their ears cropped for seditious libel. The cruelty of their punishment excited widespread sympathy and further discredited the regime.
Strafford in Ireland
Thomas Wentworth, created Earl of Strafford in 1640, governed Ireland from 1633 with a ruthless efficiency that made him the most capable — and most feared — of Charles’s ministers. He increased the Irish revenue, built up a standing army (which Charles hoped to use for his own purposes), and enforced order with severity. Strafford’s policy was “Thorough” — an unflinching assertion of royal authority against all opposition. He made enemies on all sides, and his enemies in England would destroy him at the first opportunity.

The Bishops’ Wars and the Collapse of Personal Rule (1637–1640)
The trigger for the collapse of Charles’s Personal Rule came not from England but from Scotland. In 1637, Charles and Laud attempted to impose a new Prayer Book — based on the English Book of Common Prayer — on the Scottish Kirk. When the Dean of Edinburgh attempted to read the new liturgy at St Giles’ Cathedral on 23 July 1637, a riot erupted. A market-woman named Jenny Geddes is said to have thrown her stool at the Dean, crying “Darest thou say mass in my lug?”
The Scots responded by organising a National Covenant (February 1638) — a mass petition pledging resistance to the religious innovations. When Charles attempted to enforce his authority, the Scots raised an army under Alexander Leslie, veterans of the Thirty Years’ War.
The First Bishops’ War (1639) was a standoff: Charles assembled an English army near Berwick, but his troops were poorly equipped and reluctant to fight their northern neighbours. A truce was signed without a battle.
The Second Bishops’ War (1640) was a disaster. The Scots invaded England, routed a hastily assembled English force at Newburn (August 1640), and occupied Newcastle. Charles, humiliated and without money, was forced to call first the Short Parliament (April–May 1640), which refused supply and was dissolved after three weeks, and then the Long Parliament.

The Long Parliament (1640–1642)
The Long Parliament met in November 1640 and, in what Hume calls “the most memorable parliament of English history,” proceeded to dismantle the apparatus of Personal Rule. Led by John Pym, the parliamentary opposition:

Impeached Strafford, who was tried for high treason, attainted by bill, and executed on Tower Hill (12 May 1641) — Charles, after agonised hesitation, signed the death warrant, a decision that haunted him for the rest of his life
Impeached Laud, who was imprisoned (executed in 1645)
Abolished the Star Chamber and the Court of High Commission (July 1641)
Passed the Triennial Act, requiring parliament to be summoned at least every three years
Forced Charles to dismiss his unpopular ministers

In November 1641, the Commons passed the Grand Remonstrance — a comprehensive catalogue of grievances against Charles’s government, passed by a narrow majority of 159 to 148. The king’s response was disastrous. In January 1642, he marched into the House of Commons with several hundred armed men to arrest Pym, Hampden, and three other opposition leaders — the Five Members. They had been warned and had fled. The breach of parliamentary privilege was irreparable. Charles left London, which was now in open opposition to him, and established his court at York.

The Civil War (1642–1649)
The First Campaign
On 22 August 1642, Charles raised his standard at Nottingham, formally committing himself to war. The nation divided: roughly half supported the king (Cavaliers), half supported parliament (Roundheads). London, the eastern counties, and the navy supported parliament; the north and west supported the king. Both sides expected a short war.
The first major engagement was the Battle of Edgehill (23 October 1642), a confused and inconclusive fight in which neither side gained a decisive advantage. Prince Rupert of the Rhine, Charles’s dashing nephew, led the royalist cavalry to initial success but failed to press the advantage. Both armies settled into a winter of manoeuvre and negotiation.
The war swung back and forth through 1643. The royalists won a series of victories in the west — at Stratton, Lansdown, and Roundway Down — and captured Bristol, the second city of the kingdom. But the parliamentarian cause was saved by the political and military skill of John Hampden (mortally wounded at Chalgrove Field, June 1643), and by the alliance with Scotland: parliament agreed to the Solemn League and Covenant with the Scottish Covenanters, who sent an army into England in exchange for the promise of Presbyterian uniformity.
Marston Moor (1644)
The most important battle of the first civil war was Marston Moor (2 July 1644), near York. A combined parliamentarian and Scottish army, including Oliver Cromwell’s Ironsides cavalry, routed the royalist army under Prince Rupert. Yorkshire was lost to the king. The battle was a turning point: the north of England fell under parliamentarian control, and the reputation of Cromwell and his disciplined cavalry was established.
Naseby (1645)
Parliament reorganised its forces into the New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax and Cromwell, with the Self-Denying Ordinance removing members of parliament (except Cromwell) from military commands. At Naseby (14 June 1645), the New Model Army destroyed the main royalist army. The king’s private papers were captured, revealing his negotiations with the Irish Catholics and his determination not to yield to parliament — disclosures that fatally damaged his reputation.
Thereafter, the royalist cause collapsed. Fairfax swept through the west, capturing Bristol and routing the remaining royalist forces. Charles, his army gone, surrendered to the Scots at Newark (May 1646). The Scots, after protracted negotiation, handed him over to the English parliament in January 1647.

Captivity, Negotiations, and the Second Civil War
Charles was held at Holdenby House while parliamentary factions — Presbyterians and Independents — debated the future settlement. Charles, with characteristic obstinacy, refused to accept the terms offered, hoping to exploit the divisions between parliament and the army. In June 1647, Cornet George Joyce seized the king from parliamentary custody on the army’s orders, and Charles was taken to the army’s headquarters at Newmarket.
Negotiations dragged on through 1647 and 1648. Charles negotiated simultaneously with the Scots, the English Presbyterians, and even the Irish Catholics — agreeing to preserve the Presbyterian church in Scotland for three years — in exchange for a Scottish invasion of England. This triggered the Second Civil War (1648), a series of desperate royalist risings accompanied by a Scottish invasion under the Duke of Hamilton. Cromwell crushed the Scots at Preston (August 1648) and the other risings were suppressed.

Trial and Execution (January 1649)
The army, now radicalised and led by Cromwell and his son-in-law Henry Ireton, determined that the king must be eliminated. On 6 December 1648, Colonel Thomas Pride purged the Long Parliament of members who favoured a negotiated settlement — Pride’s Purge. The remaining Rump of the Commons, about sixty members, voted to try the king for treason.
The High Court of Justice was established — 135 commissioners (though fewer than seventy ever sat). Charles was brought to Westminster Hall on 20 January 1649. When the charge was read, he refused to recognise the authority of the court. “I would know by what power I am called hither,” he said. “I would know by what authority — I mean lawful authority — the House of Commons — for I have heard of a king, and not of a House of Commons — but where are the Lords?”
Three times he was brought before the court; three times he declined to plead. The court pronounced sentence on 27 January: death by beheading.
On the morning of 30 January 1649, Charles was led from St James’s Palace to the Banqueting House in Whitehall. The scaffold had been erected outside. He wore two shirts against the cold, lest the shivering be mistaken for fear. His last words, addressed to Bishop Juxon, affirmed his innocence and his forgiveness of his enemies. He declared that he died “a Christian according to the profession of the Church of England, as I found it left me by my father.” He laid his neck on the block and, at one blow, the executioner severed his head.
A great groan rose from the crowd. Within days, the Rump Parliament abolished the monarchy and the House of Lords, and England became a commonwealth.

Character and Legacy
Hume’s character sketch of Charles I is one of the finest in English historical literature. The king was, Hume writes, “a good rather than a great man,” whose virtues predominated “extremely above his vices, or more properly speaking, his imperfections.” His dignity was free from pride, his humanity from weakness, his bravery from rashness, his temperance from austerity, his frugality from avarice. He was a devoted husband, an indulgent father, a patron of the arts — Van Dyck’s portraits of him have defined the image of Caroline kingship for posterity.
But Charles lacked the suppleness and dexterity necessary to navigate the constitutional crisis of his age. He believed deeply in the divine right of kings and could not bring himself to accept the diminution of his authority that parliament demanded. His political inflexibility, his tendency to choose the wrong advisers, and his ingrained distrust of compromise drove him into collision with forces he could neither control nor defeat. As Hume observes, “Exposed without revenue, without arms, to the assault of furious, implacable, and bigoted factions, it was never permitted him, but with the most fatal consequences, to commit the smallest mistake; a condition too rigorous to be imposed on the greatest human capacity.”
The accusation of insincerity often levelled at Charles is questioned by Hume. In every treaty, Charles refused to make concessions he could not in conscience maintain. The violations of the Petition of Right are ascribed by Hume “more to the necessity of his situation, and to the lofty ideas of royal prerogative which, from former established precedents, he had imbibed, than to any failure in the integrity of his principles.”
The legacy of Charles I is double. In defeat and death, he became a martyr — his Eikon Basilike (“The Royal Image”), purportedly his own meditations, became the most published book of the seventeenth century, fixing in the popular imagination the image of the saintly monarch betrayed by fanatics. At the same time, his reign demonstrated that the English constitution could not function without trust between crown and parliament, and that a king who would not govern with his people could not govern at all. The Restoration of 1660 would restore the monarchy, but it would never restore the untrammelled prerogative that Charles had claimed as his birthright.
