entities/charles-ii.title: Charles II of England
entities/charles-ii.content:
Charles II of England
Summary
Charles II (r. 1660–1685), the eldest son of Charles I, was restored to the throne in 1660 after eleven years of republican government. His reign — the Restoration — was a period of profound contradiction: cultural renaissance and constitutional conflict, commercial expansion and military humiliation, an insatiable royal appetite for pleasure alongside a secret ambition to restore Catholicism and absolutism. The Merry Monarch who walked his spaniels in St James’s Park and fathered a dozen illegitimate children was also, as Hume describes him, a prince who “never said a foolish thing nor ever did a wise one.” By his death in 1685, Charles had outmanoeuvred his parliamentary opponents, crushed the Exclusion movement, and restored the vigour of the crown — but at the cost of a secret dependence on French subsidies, a ruined reputation for honesty, and a legacy of bitter partisan division between Whig and Tory that would define English politics for generations.

Exile and the Road to Restoration (1649–1660)
Upon the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649, the Scots proclaimed his son King Charles II at Edinburgh. The young prince, then not yet nineteen, spent the next eleven years in exile — a wandering education in poverty, dependence, and dissimulation. He made a desperate gamble in 1650 by landing in Scotland and accepting the Presbyterian Covenant, but the Scottish army was crushed by Cromwell at Worcester (3 September 1651). Charles famously hid in an oak tree at Boscobel House before escaping to France after six weeks of fugitive wandering.
His exile was spent in the courts of France, the Spanish Netherlands, and the Dutch Republic — dependent on the charity of foreign princes, surrounded by a threadbare court of loyalists, and learning the arts of intrigue and patience. The death of Oliver Cromwell in September 1658 and the collapse of Richard Cromwell’s protectorate opened the door. General George Monck, commander of the English army in Scotland, marched south, restored the Rump Parliament, and then — crucially — declared for a free parliament. Monck opened secret communications with Charles through Sir John Granville and the Devonshire gentleman Morrice. Charles, following Monck’s advice that he leave Spanish territory to avoid arrest, escaped to Breda.
From Breda, Charles issued the Declaration of Breda (April 1660), promising a general pardon (excepting those to be named by parliament), liberty of conscience, the satisfaction of army arrears, and the confirmation of property settlements. The Convention Parliament, elected in a surge of royalist sentiment, voted unanimously to restore the king. Charles landed at Dover on 25 May 1660, entered London on his thirtieth birthday (29 May), and was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661. Burnet records that “a spirit of extravagant joy spread over the Nation, that brought on with it the throwing off the very professions of virtue and piety.” The Restoration was greeted with bonfires, the roasting of rumps in effigy, and a national determination to forget two decades of civil war.

The Clarendon Ministry (1660–1667)
The first years of Charles’s reign were dominated by Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon — the king’s lord chancellor and, in many respects, the architect of the Restoration settlement. Clarendon, a veteran of the Long Parliament and Charles I’s counsellor, was a man of great learning and magisterial temper. Burnet describes him as “an absolute favourite, and the chief or the only Minister, but with too magisterial a way.” He was “indefatigable in business” and a good chancellor, “only a little too rough, but very impartial in the administration of justice.”
The Convention Parliament (1660) enacted the Indemnity and Oblivion Act, which pardoned all crimes committed during the civil wars and interregnum — excepting only the regicides. Ten of the fifty-nine men who had signed Charles I’s death warrant were executed; the rest either fled or were imprisoned. The lands confiscated by the Commonwealth were restored to their original owners, and the Church of England was re-established with the Book of Common Prayer, episcopal government, and the Act of Uniformity (1662). Some two thousand Presbyterian ministers were ejected from their livings for refusing to conform — the Great Ejection — and the Clarendon Code of penal laws (the Corporation Act, Conventicle Act, Five Mile Act) was enacted to suppress Nonconformist worship.
The Cavalier Parliament, elected in 1661 and destined to sit for eighteen years, was overwhelmingly royalist and Anglican. It granted Charles a generous but inadequate revenue — about 1.2 million pounds per annum from customs and excise — far short of what was needed to govern without parliamentary supply. Charles married Catherine of Braganza, a Portuguese princess, in 1662, receiving as dowry the city of Tangier, the island of Bombay, and 300,000 pounds. The queen proved barren, producing no surviving heir, which cast a long shadow over the succession.

The Second Dutch War and National Disasters (1665–1667)
The commercial rivalry between England and the Dutch Republic, exacerbated by colonial conflicts in Guinea and North America, erupted into open war in 1665. The English fleet, under the command of the Duke of York (the king’s Catholic brother), defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Lowestoft (3 June 1665) — a victory that might have decided the war had the English pressed their advantage. But the year 1665 also brought the Great Plague of London, which killed an estimated 70,000 people. The court fled to Oxford, and commerce ground to a halt.
The war continued through 1666 with the epic Four Days’ Battle (1–4 June 1666), the longest naval engagement in the age of sail, in which the English under Prince Rupert and the Duke of Albemarle fought the Dutch under De Ruyter to a costly draw. The English lost some twenty ships and 5,000 men; the Dutch losses were comparable. In August, the English won a victory at St James’s Day Battle, but the war had exhausted both sides.
On 2 September 1666, the Great Fire of London broke out in a baker’s shop in Pudding Lane and raged for four days, destroying 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches, St Paul’s Cathedral, and most of the City within the walls. Charles and his brother James personally directed firefighting efforts. The fire was widely — and falsely — blamed on Catholic conspirators.
The financial strain of war, plague, and fire was unbearable. In June 1667, the Dutch delivered the final humiliation. De Ruyter’s fleet sailed up the River Medway, broke through the defensive chain at Chatham, and burned three capital ships of the English navy — including the Royal Charles, the very ship that had brought Charles back to England in 1660. Campbell’s naval history calls this “the most dishonourable to the English nation that perhaps ever happened in any reign.” The shock was profound. The Peace of Breda (July 1667) ended the war on largely status quo terms, but the damage to English prestige — and to Clarendon’s position — was irreparable.

The Fall of Clarendon and the Cabal Ministry (1667–1672)
Clarendon had long been unpopular — with the court for his moralising, with the Commons for his perceived arrogance, with the people for his defence of royal prerogative. The disasters of the Dutch War and the Medway humiliation proved fatal. Parliament impeached him; Charles, whose affection for his old chancellor had cooled, refused to save him. Clarendon fled to France in November 1667, where he lived in exile until his death in 1674, writing his great History of the Rebellion. Burnet observes that Charles, who had submitted entirely to Clarendon’s advice in the early years, had come to resent his minister’s “positive way.”
The ministry that succeeded Clarendon was known, from the initials of its five leading members, as the Cabal: Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley (later Earl of Shaftesbury), and Lauderdale. It was a ministry of factions, not a coherent government. Hume writes that “if we consider the projects of the famous cabal, it will appear hard to determine, whether the end which those ministers pursued were more blamable and pernicious, or the means by which they were to effect it more impolitic and imprudent.”
The Cabal’s most notorious achievement was the Secret Treaty of Dover (1670), by which Charles agreed to join Louis XIV in war against the Dutch and, crucially, to declare himself a Catholic — in exchange for French subsidies of 200,000 pounds per year and the promise of 6,000 French troops to suppress any English rebellion. The treaty was negotiated in deepest secrecy by Charles, his sister Henrietta (the Duchess of Orleans), and four Catholic counsellors: Arlington, Arundel, Clifford, and Sir Richard Bellings. A sham treaty, omitting the religious clauses, was shown to the Protestant members of the Cabal — Buckingham, Ashley, and Lauderdale — to secure their participation in the war.

The Third Dutch War and the Test Act (1672–1674)
Charles launched the Third Dutch War in March 1672, in concert with France. The English fleet under the Duke of York fought the Dutch at Solebay (28 May 1672), a bloody and indecisive battle in which Lord Sandwich, the English admiral, was killed and his ship blown up. The war was deeply unpopular in England: the Dutch were fellow Protestants, the French were Catholic and absolutist, and the conflict was widely seen as a conspiracy to destroy English liberty.
In the same month, Charles issued the Declaration of Indulgence, suspending the penal laws against both Catholics and Nonconformists. Parliament, outraged, forced Charles to withdraw the Declaration and to assent to the Test Act (1673), which required all civil and military office-holders to receive the Anglican sacrament and to swear that they did not believe in transubstantiation. The Duke of York — a confessed Catholic — resigned his command of the Admiralty. The Cabal disintegrated: Clifford, a Catholic, resigned rather than take the test; Shaftesbury was dismissed and went into opposition; Buckingham fell from favour.
Charles made a separate peace with the Dutch at the Treaty of Westminster (1674), abandoned his French alliance for a time, and brought Sir William Temple and the Earl of Danby into government. Danby’s policy was to manage parliament through bribery and patronage, and to pursue a more Protestant foreign policy — including the marriage of Charles’s niece Mary to the Dutch Stadtholder, William of Orange (1677). But the king’s secret appetite for French money persisted, and he continued a covert correspondence with Louis XIV.

The Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis (1678–1681)
In 1678, the kingdom was convulsed by the Popish Plot — a fabrication by Titus Oates, a former Anglican clergyman turned Jesuit novice, who alleged a vast Catholic conspiracy to assassinate the king, burn London, and impose popery by French arms. Oates was, in Hume’s portrait, a man of “profligate character, mean birth, and infamous profession” — but his lurid accusations found ready believers in a nation already steeped in anti-Catholic paranoia.
The murder of Sir Edmund Bury Godfrey, the magistrate before whom Oates had sworn his deposition, was discovered in October 1678. Godfrey’s body was found in a ditch at Primrose Hill, run through with his own sword. Hume observes that “the dead body of Godfrey was regarded as the seal of the plot.” A wave of hysterical terror swept the nation. Fifteen innocent Catholics were executed on Oates’s perjured evidence. The Duke of York was forced into temporary exile in Brussels.
Shaftesbury, now leading the opposition in parliament, exploited the panic to launch the Exclusion Crisis — a concerted campaign to exclude the Catholic Duke of York from the succession. Three Exclusion Parliaments met between 1679 and 1681. The first passed an Exclusion Bill through the Commons, but it was defeated in the Lords. Charles dissolved parliament and called another; the bill passed the Commons again, only to be rejected once more. During this period, Charles created a new Privy Council under Sir William Temple’s scheme, including Shaftesbury as its president — but the arrangement lasted only months before Shaftesbury returned to open opposition.
The Habeas Corpus Act (1679) was passed in the midst of the crisis, strengthening the legal protection against arbitrary imprisonment. Charles gave reluctant assent, and it became one of the great constitutional foundations of English liberty. Meanwhile, the king’s natural son, the Duke of Monmouth — a handsome, popular Protestant — was put forward by the Exclusionists as a rival claimant. Monmouth made a triumphal progress through the west of England in 1680, collecting addresses from adoring crowds.
Charles outmanoeuvred his opponents by summoning a fourth parliament at Oxford in March 1681 — in the royalist heartland, away from the mob of London. When the Commons again pressed for exclusion, Charles dissolved parliament after only one week. He never called another.

The Tory Reaction and the Rye House Plot (1681–1685)
The dissolution of the Oxford Parliament marked the triumph of the royalist cause. A great wave of loyalist addresses poured in from the counties; the newly named Tories (as the court party was now called) routed the Whigs in the municipal elections of 1682; and the crown used quo warranto proceedings to strip London and other boroughs of their charters, remodelling their corporations in a loyalist interest. Charles, as Hume puts it, “was enabled to govern altogether without one” parliament.
The defeated Whigs, despairing of legal means, turned to conspiracy. The Rye House Plot (1683) was a scheme to assassinate Charles and his brother at the gate of a farmhouse called the Rye House in Hertfordshire, as they returned from the Newmarket races. The plot was discovered, and the government struck back ruthlessly. Lord William Russell, a popular Whig leader, was tried for high treason and executed in Lincoln’s Inn Fields (21 July 1683). Algernon Sidney, the republican theorist, was executed on 7 December 1683, convicted on the basis of his unpublished Discourses Concerning Government — an infamous abuse of the law of constructive treason. The Earl of Essex, arrested for complicity, cut his own throat in the Tower.
Hume judges that “the severities exercised during this part of the present reign were much contrary to the usual tenor of the king’s conduct.” Charles, in his last years, governed with a confidence he had never shown before. Monmouth, after a humiliating submission and recantation, was banished. The king received secret subsidies from Louis XIV, refused to call a parliament, and ruled through a Tory ministry dominated by the Earls of Halifax, Rochester, and Sunderland.

Death and Character
In February 1685, Charles was struck by a sudden apoplectic fit. He lingered for a few days, receiving Anglican clergymen with indifference — and then Catholic priests in secret, to whom he made his confession and received the last rites of the Roman Church. Two papers found in his cabinet, written in his own hand, contained arguments for the Catholic faith. He died on 6 February 1685, aged fifty-four, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign, and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
Hume’s character of Charles II is one of the great portraits of historical literature. As a companion, Charles was “the most amiable and engaging of men” — his wit “a plain, gaining, well-bred, recommending kind of wit,” his affability such that men “always went away contented both with him and with themselves.” As a sovereign, however, his record was darker: “Negligent of the interests of the nation, careless of its glory, averse to its religion, jealous of its liberty, lavish of its treasure, sparing only of its blood.” Hume attributes these failings chiefly to “the indolence of his temper — a fault which, however unfortunate in a monarch, it is impossible for us to regard with great severity.”
Burnet’s portrait is sharper. Charles had “a very good understanding” and “knew well the state of affairs both at home and abroad,” but was “liberal to excess” with fair promises “because he intended nothing by them.” He “seemed to have no sense of religion.” He hated business, delivering himself up “to a mad range of pleasure.” His first and longest mistress, Barbara Villiers (later Duchess of Cleveland), was “a woman of great beauty, but most enormously vitious and ravenous.” The ruin of his reign was “occasioned chiefly by his delivering himself up at his first coming over to a mad range of pleasure.”
Burnet records that Charles once told him he was no atheist, but “could not think God would make a man miserable only for taking a little pleasure out of the way.” He admired the French system of government and “thought a King who might be checkt, or have his Ministers called to an account by a Parliament, was but a King in name.” Yet he was a man of genuine intellectual curiosity: he understood mechanics, physics, and chemistry; was a good chemist “much set on several preparations of Mercury”; understood navigation and “the architecture of ships so perfectly, that in that respect he was exact rather more than became a Prince.”

Legacy
Charles II left an ambiguous inheritance. He restored the monarchy, the Church of England, and the social order that the civil wars had shattered. He presided over a cultural renaissance — the foundation of the Royal Society (1662), the flowering of Restoration drama (Dryden, Congreve, Wycherley), the architecture of Sir Christopher Wren, and the birth of the English navy as a permanent professional force. The Navigation Acts and the growth of colonial trade laid the foundations for England’s eighteenth-century commercial empire.
But he also left a poisoned constitution. His secret subsidy from France, his attempts to introduce Catholic toleration by prerogative, and his evasion of parliamentary government deepened the distrust between crown and Commons. The partisan categories forged in his reign — Whig and Tory, exclusionist and loyalist — would dominate English politics for two centuries. His brother James II inherited a throne vastly strengthened in power and prestige, but the religious and constitutional questions that Charles had suppressed rather than resolved would explode in the Glorious Revolution of 1688 within three years of his death.

entities/clarendon.title: Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon
entities/clarendon.content:
Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon
Summary
Edward Hyde (1609-1674), 1st Earl of Clarendon, was Lord Chancellor of England and the chief architect of the Restoration settlement of 1660. A constitutional royalist, moderate statesman, and historian of the English Civil Wars, Clarendon dominated the first seven years of Charles II’s reign before falling prey to the ingratitude of the king he had served and the hatred of the factions he had disappointed. Burnet describes him as “an absolute favourite, and the chief or the only Minister, but with too magisterial a way” — a man “indefatigable in business” and “a good Chancellour, only a little too rough, but very impartial in the administration of justice.” His great literary monument, the History of the Rebellion, remains the most authoritative contemporary account of the Civil Wars from the royalist perspective. Hume judged him “always a friend to the liberty and constitution of his country,” whose real crime was “his frequent opposition to exorbitant grants.”

Early Career and the Long Parliament (1609-1642)
Edward Hyde was born at Dinton in Wiltshire in 1609, the son of a substantial Wiltshire gentleman. He was educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford, and entered the Middle Temple, where he was called to the bar. His father, on his deathbed, exhorted him — according to the story preserved by Hume — to shun the common practice of straining every point in favour of prerogative, and perverting the law to the oppression of liberty. The old man was seized with an apoplexy in the midst of these counsels and expired in his son’s presence, an event that gave lasting weight to the principles he inculcated.
Hyde was returned to the Short Parliament (1640) as member for Wootton Bassett, and to the Long Parliament as member for Saltash in Cornwall. He soon distinguished himself in the House of Commons by his learning, his moderation, and his eloquence. Burnet records that he “distinguished himself so in the House of Commons, that he became considerable.” At this stage he aligned with the constitutional opposition to Charles I’s innovations but drew back when the parliamentary leadership turned to radical measures and armed resistance. His was the temper of the constitutional royalist: loyal to the crown, attached to the church, but no friend to arbitrary power.

The Civil War and Exile (1642-1660)
When the Civil War broke out in 1642, Hyde joined the king at Oxford, where he was “much trusted all the while the King was at Oxford.” He served as a councillor and drafter of royal declarations, giving the king’s cause the benefit of his legal learning and his moderate and persuasive pen. After the king’s defeat and execution, Hyde followed the Prince of Wales (the future Charles II) into exile. He was one of the prince’s most trusted counsellors during the long wandering through France, the Spanish Netherlands, and the Dutch Republic.
For eleven years he shared all the fortunes and directed many of the counsels of the young king, cementing a relationship of mutual dependence and trust. By 1660 he was, with General Monck and the Earl of Southampton, among the handful of men who negotiated the terms of the Restoration. He was the principal author of the Declaration of Breda (April 1660), which promised a general pardon, liberty of conscience, the satisfaction of army arrears, and the confirmation of property settlements — the foundation of the Restoration settlement.

The Clarendon Ministry (1660-1667)
At the Restoration, Hyde was created Earl of Clarendon (April 1661) and appointed Lord Chancellor. Hume describes him as, with the Duke of Ormond, the Earl of Southampton, and Sir Edward Nicholas, one of the ministers who “united together in friendship, and combined in the same laudable inclinations, supported each other’s credit, and pursued the interests of the public.” For the first seven years of the reign, Clarendon was prime minister in all but name.
He was the principal architect of the Restoration settlement, guiding through parliament the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion (a general pardon, sparing all but the regicides themselves), the settlement of the king’s revenue (1,200,000 pounds a year voted, though the funds assigned fell short of that sum), and the restoration of episcopal church government. The Corporation Act (1661) and the Act of Uniformity (1662) — which ejected some two thousand Puritan ministers — were part of the so-called Clarendon Code, though Clarendon’s personal responsibility for their more intolerant provisions has been questioned by historians. He presided over the trial and execution of the regicides, and over the king’s marriage to Catherine of Braganza of Portugal (1662), a union that brought Tangier and Bombay to the English crown as dowry.
In 1662, Clarendon consented to the sale of Dunkirk to France for 400,000 pounds — a measure forced by the king’s financial necessities, which the parliament’s over-frugal grants had produced. This sale was later one of the heaviest charges against him. Hume notes that “a mistake in judgment, allowing it to be such, where there appear no symptoms of corruption or bad intentions, it would be very hard to impute as a crime to any minister.”

Character and Conduct
Burnet’s character of Clarendon is the most vivid that survives. He was “bred to the Law” and might have grown eminent in his profession had the wars not intervened. As chancellor he was “good… only a little too rough, but very impartial in the administration of justice.” He “never seemed to understand foreign affairs well: And yet he meddled too much in them.” He “had too much levity in his wit, and did not always observe the decorum of his post. He was high, and was apt to reject those who addressed themselves to him with too much contempt.” He was “indefatigable in business, though the gout did often disable him from waiting on the King: Yet, during his credit, the King came constantly to him when he was laid up by it.”
Clarendon’s greatest weakness as a minister was his pride and his inflexible dignity. Amidst the dissolute manners of the Restoration court, he maintained an austere and magisterial bearing that alienated the king’s favourites and mistresses. He was a constant check on Charles’s pleasures and his extravagance. The Duke of Buckingham, a man of profligate morals and brilliant wit, “still made him the object of his raillery, and gradually lessened in the king that regard which he bore to his minister.”

Fall, Impeachment, and Exile (1667-1674)
By 1667, Clarendon was hated by every party. The sectaries regarded him as their determined enemy. The Catholics knew that while he held power they could expect no favour. The royalists, disappointed in their hopes of preferment, threw their envy on the man into whose hands the king had resigned the whole power of government. The sale of Dunkirk, the bad payment of the seamen, the disgrace at Chatham (where the Dutch burned the English fleet), and the unsuccessful conclusion of the Dutch War were all charged to his account. His magnificent new house in London was popularly called “Dunkirk House,” as if built with French gold.
The king, who had always more revered than loved him, abandoned him to his enemies. The Great Seal was taken from him and given to Sir Orlando Bridgeman (August 1667). The Commons voted his impeachment on seventeen articles, many of which Hume judges “either false or frivolous.” Clarendon, seeing that “the popular torrent, united to the violence of power, ran with impetuosity against him,” withdrew to Calais. Parliament passed a bill of banishment and incapacity, which received the royal assent. He was condemned to perpetual exile.
Clarendon survived his banishment six years, living privately in France. In 1674, a company of English soldiers quartered near him assaulted his house, broke open the doors, and gave him a dangerous wound on the head. He died later that year at Rouen. Hume observes that “the combination of king and subject to oppress so good a minister affords, to men of opposite dispositions, an equal occasion of inveighing against the ingratitude of princes, or ignorance of the people.”

The Historian: History of the Rebellion
In his exile, Clarendon employed his leisure in reducing into order the History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, for which he had collected materials over many years. It was published posthumously (1702-1704). Hume calls it “the most candid account of those times, composed by any contemporary author,” excepting only Whitlocke’s Memorials. Burnet, though critical of its courtly bias, acknowledges that it “gives a faithful representation of the beginnings of the troubles, though writ in favour of the Court, and full of the best excuses that such ill things were capable of.” The History remains a masterpiece of English historical writing: magisterial in its judgments, rich in character portraits, and infused with a profound sense of the tragedy that befall the three kingdoms.

entities/cloudesley-shovel.title: Sir Cloudesley Shovel
entities/cloudesley-shovel.content:
Sir Cloudesley Shovel
Summary
Sir Cloudesley Shovel (1650–1707) was one of the most respected English admirals of the late 17th and early 18th centuries, whose career spanned from the Third Dutch War through the War of the Spanish Succession. Rising from obscure beginnings — he is said to have begun at sea as a cabin boy — he attained the rank of rear-admiral of Great Britain and commanded in every major naval operation of his age. He was knighted by King William III, served as one of three joint commanders of the fleet in 1693, presided over the court-martial of the captains who deserted Admiral Benbow, and was joint flag-officer in the capture of Gibraltar and Barcelona. He perished in one of the worst maritime disasters in English history: the wreck of HMS Association and three other ships on the rocks of the Scilly Isles on the night of 22 October 1707, drowning with over 1,400 men.

Early Career
Cloudesley Shovel was born in 1650 at Cley-next-the-Sea in Norfolk, of a modest family long settled on the coast. Local tradition holds that he went to sea as a cabin boy and worked his way up through the ranks — a classic “tarpaulin” officer who earned his commission by experience rather than patronage. The first certain record places him as a lieutenant serving under Sir John Narborough in the Mediterranean, where he distinguished himself in the war against the Barbary corsairs. In one notable action, Narborough blocked the port of Tripoli at night and sent Lieutenant Shovel with the ship’s boats into the harbour, where he seized the guard-ship and burned the entire Tripoline shipping lying at anchor. Campbell’s Naval History records this exploit as having been performed by “Lieutenant Shovel, afterwards Sir Cloudesley, the famous admiral.”
He was promoted to captain in the 1670s, commanding successively the Sapphire and the James galley. In September 1681, in company with another English man-of-war, Captain Shovel fell in with and captured a large Algerine corsair called the Half-Moon, carrying thirty-two guns and three hundred and eighty men — a significant victory against the Barbary pirates that marked him as a rising officer.

Service Under James II and the Glorious Revolution
Shovel continued to serve through the reign of James II, and was given command of the Edgar, one of the largest ships in the navy. When William of Orange landed at Torbay in November 1688, Shovel — like most of the naval establishment — declared for the Prince and was continued in his command after the Revolution. He served throughout the campaign to reduce Ireland, conveying troops to Carrickfergus in 1690 under the escort of his squadron, and was present at the council of war called by the Dutch admirals at Plymouth to decide how best to secure the fleet against the French threat in the Channel.

The Battle of Barfleur and La Hogue
When the grand allied fleet assembled in May 1692 to meet the French invasion threat, Shovel — now Sir Cloudesley, knighted by King William — commanded as rear-admiral of the blue squadron under Admiral Edward Russell. The blue squadron was commanded by Henry Killigrew as admiral, Sir Ralph Delaval as vice-admiral, and Sir Cloudesley Shovel as rear-admiral. During the six-day engagement from 19 to 24 May 1692, Shovel handled his division with distinction in the bitter fighting off Barfleur, and was present for the pursuit and destruction of the French fleet in the bays of La Hogue and Cherbourg. William III, who went down to Portsmouth in person to honour the fleet, knighted Shovel on the spot — together with Captain John Ashby — and gave a bounty of ten shillings to every seaman who had fought in the action.

Joint Command of the Fleet
In 1693, after the dismissal of Admiral Russell, King William III placed the fleet under three joint commanders-in-chief: Henry Killigrew, Sir Ralph Delaval, and Sir Cloudesley Shovel. Burnet records that Killigrew and Delaval were suspected of Jacobite sympathies, and that Shovel was included as the one man of unquestioned loyalty — “no exception lay against Shovel,” Burnet writes, though he adds that Shovel was “only put with the other two, to give some reputation to the commission, and that he was one against two; so that he could neither hinder nor do any thing.” The arrangement proved disastrous: the combined fleet failed to intercept the French at Lagos Bay, where the Smyrna convoy was destroyed, and the experiment of joint command was never repeated.
Shovel returned to independent command later in the war. He was stationed with a squadron in the Soundings off Scilly for much of 1694 and 1695, and served on the Irish station. He was promoted through the successive ranks of rear-admiral of the red, vice-admiral, and ultimately admiral of the white.

The War of the Spanish Succession
On the outbreak of the War of the Spanish Succession, Sir Cloudesley Shovel was one of the most senior officers in the navy. In July 1702, he presided as president of the court-martial held aboard HMS Queen at Spithead, which tried the captains who had deserted Admiral Benbow in his action against Du Casse off the Spanish Main. The court condemned Captains Kirby and Wade to be shot, and cashiered others — a verdict that reflected Shovel’s own exacting standards of duty.
Later that year, he commanded a strong squadron fitted out to intercept the Spanish galleons returning from the West Indies. When the news of the victory at Vigo Bay arrived, Shovel was sent with reinforcements to assist Sir George Rooke. In 1703, he was sent with a considerable force to block the French squadron at Brest, and later that year commanded the fleet in the Mediterranean. Burnet relates that Shovel was ordered to sail for Leghorn with instructions that limited his freedom of action so severely that nothing of consequence could be accomplished; Shovel himself represented this to the ministry, but obeyed his orders nonetheless.

Gibraltar and Barcelona
In 1704, Shovel served as joint flag-officer with Sir George Rooke in the expedition that captured Gibraltar. The combined Anglo-Dutch fleet forced the harbour and landed the marines who scaled the Rock; the fortress surrendered on 4 August 1704. Shovel’s squadron covered the landing and provided the naval fire that suppressed the Spanish batteries. He was also present at the subsequent Battle of Malaga (24 August 1704), where the combined fleet under Rooke fought the French under the Comte de Toulouse to a standstill.
The following year, Shovel commanded the fleet that supported the capture of Barcelona by the Earl of Peterborough and the Archduke Charles (the Hapsburg claimant to the Spanish throne). The fleet landed the allied army, blockaded the port, and bombarded the city into submission. Barcelona fell on 9 October 1705, securing Catalonia for the Allied cause.

Wreck of the Association on the Scilly Isles
In the autumn of 1707, Sir Cloudesley Shovel commanded the Mediterranean fleet returning to England. The fleet consisted of twenty-one ships of the line, but navigational errors in heavy weather proved fatal. On the night of 22 October 1707, in thick fog and a rising gale, the flagship HMS Association (90 guns) struck the rocks of the Western Rocks of the Scilly Isles and sank almost instantly. Three other ships — the Eagle, the Romney, and the Firebrand — were also wrecked on the same rocks. Over 1,400 men drowned, including Sir Cloudesley Shovel himself.
The disaster caused profound shock throughout England. Queen Anne is said to have wept at the news. A court of inquiry was held in Portsmouth harbour on 10 October 1707 — even as the fleet was still believed at sea — to examine the conduct of the pilots, but no one was convicted; the proceedings were laid before the Queen in council, where “nothing appeared which could any way impeach” any officer. The post of rear-admiral of Great Britain, left vacant by Shovel’s death, was bestowed by Queen Anne on Sir John Leake with the remark “that she was put in mind of it, by the voice of the people.”
Shovel’s body was washed ashore on the island of St Mary’s a week later, recognised by a distinguishing mark. It was carried to Plymouth, embalmed, and buried in Westminster Abbey in December 1707 — where his monument, a grand marble structure by Grinling Gibbons, still stands.

Character and Legacy
Campbell’s Naval History ranks Shovel alongside the greatest seamen of the age — Hopson, Benbow, and Munden — and Burnet, though critical of the joint-command arrangement, never impugns Shovel’s personal honour or ability. He was the archetype of the English “tarpaulin” officer: a man who rose by merit through the harsh school of fighting sail, and who commanded the respect of both seamen and sovereign. His death on the Scilly rocks was a national tragedy that led, within a decade, to the passing of the Longitude Act of 1714, offering a public reward for a method of determining longitude at sea — the very problem that had cost Shovel his life. His monument in Westminster Abbey is a lasting symbol both of his service and of the perils of the sea.

entities/east-india-company.title: East India Company
entities/east-india-company.content:
East India Company
The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies, chartered by Queen Elizabeth on 31 December 1600, was by the late 17th century the most powerful chartered trading company in England. The company’s late-Stuart history was marked by scandal, political polarisation, a rival company, and a final merger that produced a single joint-stock corporation uniting the two interests.
Restoration and Charles II
Under Charles II the company reached the height of its power. Hume records that Charles II revived and supported the company’s charter, while Campbell notes that the East India Company were exceedingly favoured and protected under Charles II, especially at the start of his reign. The king’s support was critical: the company’s charter gave it monopoly rights over English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, and royal favour protected it against the attacks of interlopers and free-trade advocates.
By the 1680s the company’s stock was already large, and its Governor, Sir Josiah Child, was one of the wealthiest merchants in London. Child himself records that the company could take up whatever money it pleased at four per cent interest — a mark of the enormous credit it commanded in the City. Yet even at this height, the foundations of the company’s political position were fragile: its monopoly depended on the Crown’s goodwill, and every change in the political wind threatened its privileges.
The Monied Company of the Whig Interest
By the 1690s the East India Company had become a deeply political institution. Its stock was held by City of London merchants and financiers aligned with the Whig interest, alongside the Bank of England, and the two were often spoken of together as the pillars of the new financial order. Burnet records that opponents of the King’s ministry argued that the Bank of England and the new East-India Company, being in Whig hands, would command all the money and trade of England. The company’s connection to the court and the Whig ministry made it both powerful and vulnerable: every attack on the ministry was also an attack on the company, and every company scandal was ammunition for the Tories.
The company was governed by a Governor, Deputy Governor, and Court of Directors, elected by the freemen of the company. Sir Josiah Child, the leading economic writer of the age, served as Governor and was the company’s most able public defender. In his Discourse of Trade (1698), Child argued that a joint-stock company was essential for long-distance, high-risk trades that required years to return a profit, and that without the company the trade itself would not exist. He noted that any Englishman could buy into the company by purchasing an action for a modest five-pound admission fee — a far more open structure than the company’s earlier practice of charging a fifty-pound fine for admission.
The Bribery Scandal of 1695
In 1695, a parliamentary inquiry into the East India Company revealed a systematic programme of secret payments to Members of Parliament. Burnet writes that the company’s books recorded 170,000 pounds paid for secret services, most of which was believed to have gone to members of the House of Commons. For the two preceding winters there had been attempts to break the company and open a free trade to the Indies, and the company appears to have used bribes to defeat these efforts. Burnet observes that some of the fiercest opponents of the company insensibly fell off from that opposition and turned to serve it — notably Sir Edward Seymour, who was said to have received 12,000 pounds under the pretext of a bargain for their saltpetre.
The scandal widened when it emerged that the company had also attempted to bribe the Lord President (the Duke of Leeds) to procure a new charter. One Firebras, a merchant employed by the company, had treated with a certain Bates, a friend of the Marquess of Caermarthen, and Bates was to have five thousand guineas for procuring a new charter. Bates later swore he had offered the money to the Lord President, who refused it but advised him to keep it. The House of Commons voted an impeachment for misdemeanour against the Lord President, who saved himself by a speech before the House.
The scandal gave the company’s enemies powerful ammunition. The King, upon an address from the Commons, granted the old company a new charter — but with a condition that they take in a new subscription of 700,000 pounds to increase their stock and trade, and with a clause reserving to the Crown the power to dissolve them upon three years’ notice.
The New East India Company (1698)
The great crisis came in 1698. The government, desperate for funds to pay the arrears of the army and the navy, received a proposition for constituting a new East-India Company that would trade with a joint stock while admitting others in a determinate proportion to a separate trade. The projectors of the new company offered two million pounds at eight per cent interest, on the security of a good fund. The old company opposed this and offered a sum of their own — but far short of what the public occasions required.
Burnet describes how the old company belatedly offered the whole sum, but the party was already formed and they came too late. The proceeding was denounced as rigorous, if not unjust, and threw the old company into the hands of the Tories, making a great breach in the City of London.
The Act for the new company was carried, though the King himself was very indifferent in the matter at first. A new corporation was erected — the English Company Trading to the East Indies — which immediately began to trade in competition with the old company. The result was a decade of ruinous rivalry: two English companies simultaneously operating factories in India, undercutting each other’s prices, and confusing both the Mughal authorities and English merchants.
Electoral Corruption and Parliamentary Inquiries (1701)
The rivalry between the two companies poisoned English politics. In the general election of 1701, reports were brought of elections scandalously purchased by the new East-India Company. Instead of the drinking and entertainments by which elections were formerly managed, a new practice of buying votes appeared, with electors subscribing to choose a blank person before knowing the candidate’s name.
Burnet contrasts the methods: the old company had driven a course of corruption within doors with little shame, while the new company bought elections themselves rather than buying the persons already elected. Several elections were declared void, and some of the persons so chosen were imprisoned and expelled the House — though Burnet notes great partiality appeared in which cases were prosecuted.
When the new parliament met, some of its members tried to shake the Act made in favour of the new East-India Company. Burnet denounces this as contrary to the fundamental maxims of the constitution: money raised by parliament on bargains that were performed gave those who advanced it a sacred purchase on those acts; to overturn it would destroy all credit.
Trade and Economics
Gregory King’s trade statistics for the 1680s give the fullest picture of the East India trade’s scale and structure.





































MeasureValue (annual)Original exports (money or wares)500,000 poundsRe-exports of European/African/plantation goods20,000Total exports520,000Imports in gross1,700,000General increase (excess of imports over exports)1,260,000Freight costs (at 62.5%)780,000National profit after freight480,000
The trade was generating between double and treble its exports in gross profit. But the East India trade was extraordinarily expensive to conduct: freight consumed 62.5 per cent of the general increase, compared to only 12-13 per cent for European, African and Levant trades, and 26-30 per cent for the plantation trade. After freight, the national profit on the East India trade was roughly equal to the value of exports — whereas the plantation trade returned almost double, and the European trades four to five times their exports.
For comparison across trade branches:

Exports to East Indies + plantations: barely one-fourth of European/African/Levant exports
Imports from East Indies + plantations: two-thirds as large as European/African/Levant imports

The ratio of imports to exports shifted drastically with distance. In the infancy of the East India trade (1613), England had re-exported 200,000 pounds in pepper alone. By King’s time (circa 1688), re-exports from India in pepper, saltpetre, calicoes, silks, drugs, diamonds, and pearls reached 800,000 pounds annually.
Child, in his defence of the company, acknowledged the charge that the East-India Company imported much more than it exported, and carried out quantities of gold and silver annually to pay for its purchases — the classic mercantilist objection to the East India trade. His answer was that the Dutch esteemed the East India trade more profitable than the mines of gold and silver in America to the King of Spain. The real measure of a trade was not the immediate balance of bullion but the ultimate increase in national wealth through re-export and the stimulation of shipping, insurance, and ancillary industries.
The company also provided critical services to the Crown beyond its commercial functions. In 1699, when pirates in the Indian seas — mostly English — robbed ships of the Mughal and risked reprisals against the company’s factories, the East-India Company having represented the danger of the Mogul’s taking reprisals the government authorised an expedition to destroy the pirates’ bases in Madagascar. Captain Kidd was commissioned for this service, though the expedition was funded by private subscription rather than public money.
The Company and the Darien Scheme
The East India Company’s monopoly was a direct cause of the Darien disaster. When the Company of Scotland (the Darien Company) was projected, its establishment was seen in England as a threat to the East India Company’s exclusive trade. Dalrymple records that the houses of lords and commons on 13 December 1695 concurred in a joint address against the establishment of the Darien company, as detrimental to the East India company’s interest. The Commons even impeached some of their own countrymen for being instrumental in erecting the Scottish company — arraigning the subjects of another country for making use of the laws of their own.
Campbell, writing later and more dispassionately, describes the episode from the Scottish perspective. The Revolution of 1688 had brought back to Scotland several worthy patriots who procured an act in 1693 for the encouragement of foreign commerce, and another in 1695 for setting up a Scottish East India Company. Subscriptions were taken not only in Scotland but also at London, Hamburg, and Amsterdam, in which they were sufficiently supported by both the royal and legislative authority However, the English and Dutch East India Companies took umbrage and used their influence with their respective governments to obstruct the subscriptions. This forced King William into an impossible position: he was king of Scotland, which had sanctioned the company, but also king of England and Stadtholder of Holland, both of which opposed it. The affair forced him to dismiss two able ministers — the Marquis of Tweedale and Secretary Johnston — for having given the royal assent to the act establishing the company.
This English hostility, driven in part by the East India Company’s influence, was a major cause of the Darien Scheme’s failure and of the deep Scottish resentment that paved the way for the Union of 1707.
The Rival Companies in India
The creation of the new East India Company in 1698 did not merely create competition in London — it extended to India itself. The new company sent Sir William Norris as ambassador to the Great Mogul to promote its interests and obtain trading privileges. But the old company, being already in possession of the forts and factories in the East Indies, prepossessed the Mogul and other princes against the new company, so that the ambassador was indifferently received and the affair miscarried. The old company’s established presence on the ground — its factories at Surat, Madras, Bombay, and Hugli — proved an insuperable advantage.
Dalrymple, in a panegyric to Charles Montague inserted in his narrative, records that Montague was the man who erected the Bank of England, gave wings to public credit, established the East India Company on a firm basis, and settled the House of Hanover on the throne. The connection between the three great Whig achievements — the Bank, the re-founded East India Company, and the Protestant succession — was explicit in the minds of contemporaries.
The Union of the Companies
Under Queen Anne, the two rival companies were eventually merged into a single corporation — the United Company of Merchants of England Trading to the East Indies. The index to Burnet’s second volume records that the companies joined — a reference to the Act of Union of the two East India Companies passed in 1702 and finally implemented in 1709, the same year the Bank’s fund was enlarged. The merged company took the form that would endure for the next century and a half, with a single joint-stock, a unified Court of Directors, and a charter that confirmed its exclusive right to trade east of the Cape of Good Hope.
The union resolved the ruinous competition and restored the company’s credit, but the political divisions of the 1698 split had lasting consequences. Burnet’s reflection on the episode captures the transformation: the new financial institutions — the Bank, the East India Company, and the national debt — had engaged all those concerned in them to be, upon the account of their own interest, zealous for maintaining the Government. The East India Company, once a mere commercial venture, had become one of the pillars of the post-Revolution fiscal-military state.

entities/george-rooke.title: Sir George Rooke
entities/george-rooke.content:
Sir George Rooke
Summary
Sir George Rooke (1650–1709) was an English admiral whose career spanned the Nine Years’ War and the War of the Spanish Succession. He commanded the boat attack that burned the French ships at La Hogue in 1692, endured the disastrous Smyrna convoy of 1693, and later captured Gibraltar — the most celebrated naval achievement of Queen Anne’s reign — and fought the hard-fought Battle of Málaga in 1704. A capable and conscientious officer, Rooke was repeatedly the subject of political attack; his natural caution, which Burnet read as timidity, Campbell defended as prudent seamanship. He was knighted, served as a commissioner of the Admiralty, and died in retirement.

Early Career under Charles II and James II
George Rooke was born near Canterbury in 1650, the son of Sir William Rooke, a Kentish gentleman of moderate estate. He entered the navy in the reign of Charles II and rose steadily through the ranks in the merchant-service and the king’s ships. Under James II he received his first command and saw active service in the Mediterranean and the Channel. His early career, though not marked by any single celebrated action, gave him a thorough grounding in seamanship and convoy management that would serve him in the years to come. He was still a relatively junior captain at the Revolution of 1688, but he adhered promptly to William of Orange, as did the great majority of the English fleet.

The Nine Years’ War: Bantry Bay and La Hogue
Service in the Irish Campaign, 1689–1690
In the spring of 1689, Rooke was appointed commodore of a squadron sent to the coast of Ireland, where James II had landed with French support to reclaim his throne. Rooke’s squadron blockaded the Jacobite ports and prevented any communication between the Irish army and the Scottish Jacobites. He co-operated closely with Major-General Kirke in the relief of Londonderry in July 1689, assisting in the landing of troops on the Inch and the eventual breaking of the boom across the Foyle. Campbell records that he performed “all that could be expected from him” in these operations. He was at the Battle of Bantry Bay on 1 May 1689, where Admiral Herbert engaged the French fleet — the first naval action of the war — and Rooke commanded a ship in the English line.
The Battle of La Hogue, 1692
Rooke’s finest hour came in the great victory of May 1692. On 23 May, after Admiral Edward Russell had driven the French fleet into confusion off Barfleur, a number of French ships took shelter in the Bay of La Hogue on the Norman coast. Russell ordered Sir George Rooke, then rear-admiral of the red, into the bay with several men-of-war, fire-ships, and all the boats of the fleet to destroy them. Rooke found thirteen sail run up so high that only the smaller frigates could approach; but he resolved to execute his orders nonetheless. Manning the boats, he went in person to encourage the attack and, under a prodigious fire from the enemy’s batteries on shore and within sight of the Irish camp, burned six French ships that night and the remaining seven the next morning, together with a great number of transports and vessels laden with ammunition. This action, the climax of the battle, was performed with the loss of only ten men. Campbell calls it “by much the greatest service that happened during the whole affair.”

The Smyrna Convoy and Command in the Channel, 1693–1699
By 1693 Rooke was vice-admiral of the blue. In June of that year he was detached from the main fleet with a strong squadron of twenty-three men-of-war to convoy the annual Mediterranean merchant fleet — nearly four hundred sail of English, Dutch, Danish, Swedish, and Hamburg vessels — through the Straits of Gibraltar. The grand fleet left him on 6 June without certain intelligence of the French squadrons. Unknown to Rooke or the Admiralty, the French Brest fleet under Tourville, reinforced by the Toulon squadron, had already reached the coast of Portugal with seventy-one ships of the line. On 17 June Rooke discovered that he was facing eighty sail of French men-of-war. A council of war, overruling his own judgment, refused to lie by for better intelligence; he brought to and stood off, sending the smaller ships into nearby Spanish ports. The French fell upon the scattered merchantmen. About ninety ships were taken or destroyed — the worst English commercial loss of the war. Though Rooke himself escaped with most of his men-of-war, the disaster was laid at his door by political enemies, and he was strongly censured in parliament. Campbell defends his conduct, noting that he had been left without intelligence and that he showed “great presence of mind” in providing for the safety of as many vessels as possible.
Despite the Smyrna disaster, Rooke retained the confidence of the crown. In 1694 he served under Lord Berkeley in the bombardment of St Malo and other French Channel ports, and in 1695 he was knighted. He served as a commissioner of the Admiralty from 1694, and in 1700 he commanded the Anglo-Dutch fleet sent to the Baltic to support the interests of Sweden and the maritime powers during the Northern War. His handling of this delicate mission was characteristically cautious: when Charles XII of Sweden complained that the English bombs had overshot the Danish fleet, Rooke answered calmly, “Sir, I was sent hither to serve your Majesty, but not to ruin the king of Denmark.” The Danish government thanked Queen Anne for entrusting the commission to so prudent an officer. He entered parliament as a Tory and served again at the Admiralty board.

The War of the Spanish Succession: Cadiz, Gibraltar, and Málaga
The Cadiz Expedition, 1702
On the accession of Queen Anne and the outbreak of the War of the Spanish Succession, Rooke was appointed admiral of the fleet and lieutenant of the Admiralty of England — effectively the highest operational command in the navy. In June 1702 he sailed with the grand fleet of thirty English and twenty Dutch ships of the line, carrying nearly fourteen thousand troops under the Duke of Ormond, to seize Cadiz. The expedition was a failure. The admiral and the general differed on strategy: Ormond wished to assault the town swiftly; Rooke, mindful of his instructions to conciliate the Spaniards and treat them as friends, counselled a more deliberate approach. The troops landed at Port St Mary’s but discipline broke down, and the plundering of churches and houses so enraged the Spanish that the country rose against the allied cause. Rooke was blamed for the miscarriage, though Campbell inclines to the view that the instructions themselves — to be friends and enemies at the same moment — made success impossible.
The Capture of Gibraltar, July 1704
After the failure at Cadiz, Rooke’s fleet wintered at home. In 1703 he co-operated with Sir Cloudesley Shovel in covering the Mediterranean trade, and in early 1704 he sailed again. After an unsuccessful attempt on Barcelona in May, the fleet held a council of war in the Bay of Gibraltar on 21 July 1704. It was resolved to make a sudden and vigorous attempt upon Gibraltar for three reasons: the place, in its present condition, might be taken; its possession was of infinite importance to the war; and the capture would give lustre to the queen’s arms. The fleet anchored in the bay that same day. Eighteen hundred marines, English and Dutch, were landed under the Prince of Hesse on the isthmus to cut off communication with the mainland. On the morning of 22 July, Rooke gave the signal for a bombardment. Fifteen thousand shot were spent in five hours; the Spanish guns were driven from the fortifications at the South Mole. Rooke ordered Captain Whitaker to arm all the boats and seize the mole. Captain Hicks and Captain Jumper pushed on shore with their pinnaces and seized the works before the rest could come up. The Spanish governor capitulated on 24 July, and the Prince of Hesse took possession. Campbell observes that the design was “contrived by the admirals” and “executed entirely by the seamen,” and that the fortifications could have been held by fifty men against thousands. The Rock was taken in three days — the most brilliant stroke of the war and the foundation of Britain’s Mediterranean empire.
The Battle of Málaga, 13 August 1704
Rooke had no sooner garrisoned Gibraltar than he learned that the French fleet under the Count of Toulouse — fifty-two ships of the line and twenty-four galleys — was at sea. The allied fleet, fifty-three sail, sailed from Tetuan on 9 August and sighted the French on the 13th. The French had the advantage in every particular: larger ships, including seventeen three-deckers to Rooke’s seven; six hundred more guns; clean hulls freshly out of port; and the assistance of galleys that could tow disabled ships out of the line and replenish their complements. The allied fleet had been long at sea and some ships were so short of powder that they could not fire a single broadside. Despite these odds, Rooke bore down in order of battle and fought from ten in the morning until nightfall. Sir Cloudesley Shovel commanded the van, Rooke the centre, and the Dutch vice-admiral Callemberg the rear. The French van gave way, and though the Count of Toulouse claimed the victory, the French declined to renew the engagement on the two following days and thereafter avoided battle for the remainder of the war. Campbell argues that Málaga “decided the empire of the sea” and secured Gibraltar permanently in allied hands.

Retirement and Death
Rooke returned home covered in honour for Gibraltar but again the target of political attack. The failure at Cadiz was revived; his Tory connections made him a mark for the Whig ministry that came to power in 1705. Though he was continued in the Admiralty commission, his active command was not renewed. He withdrew from public life in 1705, suffering from the gout and from the accumulated strains of a harsh career at sea. He died at his estate in Kent on 24 January 1709, aged about fifty-nine.

Character
Rooke’s reputation has suffered from the partisanship of his own age. Burnet, a Whig historian, paints him as reluctant to fight and cold toward the Dutch — a view that Campbell, himself no friend to Burnet, rebuts in detail. The evidence of Rooke’s actions supports Campbell’s judgment: he burned the French ships at La Hogue under a close and heavy fire, he fought Málaga against a superior enemy when he might have declined, and he captured Gibraltar with a speed and decisiveness that no previous English admiral had matched. What his critics called timidity was in truth a professional caution born of hard experience, especially the trauma of the Smyrna disaster, where he had been let down by faulty intelligence and divided counsels. He was a Tory by conviction, a gentleman by birth, and a thorough seaman by training.

entities/james-i.title: James I of England (James VI of Scotland)
entities/james-i.content:
James I of England (James VI of Scotland)
Summary
James I (r. 1603–1625), the first Stuart monarch of England, united the crowns of England and Scotland in the person of one sovereign — a dynastic achievement known as the Union of the Crowns. He was the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, and had ruled Scotland as James VI from infancy since 1567. His English reign, often called the Jacobean era, was marked by a pronounced pacifism in foreign affairs, a deepening constitutional struggle with parliament over finance and prerogative, and the flowering of English culture in the persons of Shakespeare, Jonson, and the translators of the King James Bible.
Though an able scholar and a sincere advocate of peace, James left the crown financially weakened, the Commons newly assertive, and a legacy of unresolved tensions that his son Charles I would inherit to catastrophic effect. His reign stands as the hinge between Tudor supremacy and Stuart catastrophe — a period of peace abroad and growing conflict at home.
Accession and the Union of the Crowns (1603)
Upon the death of Elizabeth I on 24 March 1603, the English throne passed with remarkable tranquillity from the Tudor to the Stuart line. James was the great-grandson of Margaret Tudor, elder daughter of Henry VII, and his hereditary claim, long anticipated, encountered no serious obstacle. Elizabeth herself, with her dying breath, had recognised his title. The smooth transition Hume describes as “never transmitted from father to son with greater tranquillity” — no army marched, no faction contested the succession, and James was proclaimed king in London within hours of Elizabeth’s death.
James journeyed from Edinburgh to London in April 1603, greeted along the way by crowds of his new subjects. His temper, however, was ill-suited to the pageantry of royal progress. Disliking the bustle of a mixed multitude, he issued a proclamation forbidding further resort of people on pretence of scarcity of provisions. Once in London, he dispensed honours with a liberality that contrasted sharply with Elizabeth’s frugality: in six weeks he bestowed knighthood on 237 persons, a profusion that cheapened the honour and drew immediate satire. A pasquinade affixed to St Paul’s promised to teach an art “very necessary to assist frail memories in retaining the names of the new nobility.”
He retained most of Elizabeth’s ministers, among them Secretary Robert Cecil (later Earl of Salisbury), who had maintained a secret correspondence with James during the queen’s final years and thereby secured his own influence. Sir Walter Raleigh, Lord Cobham, and Lord Grey — all of whom had opposed Cecil’s faction — were discountenanced from the start. James also brought with him many Scottish courtiers, including the Duke of Lenox, the Earl of Marre, and Sir George Hume (whom he created Earl of Dunbar), whose sudden elevation and insolence bred resentment among the English nobility. Nevertheless, he left almost all the chief offices in the hands of Elizabeth’s former ministers, and Cecil remained his prime counsellor throughout the first decade of the reign.
Early Reign — Hampton Court Conference, Peace with Spain, and Raleigh’s Conspiracy
James’s first years were dominated by three notable events: the Hampton Court Conference, the peace with Spain, and the conspiracy that brought down Raleigh.
Hampton Court Conference (1604). The new king called a conference of divines at Hampton Court to address Puritan grievances, which had been presented in the Millenary Petition (so called for its reputed 750 clerical signatories). James, educated in Presbyterian Scotland and bearing a deep aversion to the Presbyterian clergy — whom he accused of republicanism and insubordination — had no sympathy for the Puritan cause. He told the assembled bishops and Puritan leaders that he would make them conform, “or else I will harry them out of the land.” Yet the conference produced one of the great cultural monuments of English history: the authorisation of a new translation of the Bible, published in 1611 as the King James Version.
Peace with Spain (1604). The nineteen-year Anglo-Spanish war, which had defined Elizabeth’s later years, was brought to a close by the Treaty of London. Trade was restored, prisoners exchanged, and James, whose love of peace was his ruling passion, secured what he considered a diplomatic triumph. The peace was deeply unpopular among those who saw Spain as the champion of Catholic tyranny, but it spared England the cost of continental war. The French ambassador, the Marquis of Rosni (later the Duke of Sully), had proposed a grand league against the House of Austria, but James’s genius was not equal to such vast enterprises. He confined himself to a secret subsidy for the United Provinces and a defensive alliance with France; the wider scheme came to nothing.
Raleigh’s Conspiracy (1603). Almost immediately on James’s accession, a conspiracy was discovered — or, as some suspected, manufactured — to depose the king and place Arbella Stuart on the throne. The so-called Main Plot and Bye Plot involved a strange coalition of Catholic priests, a Puritan lord (Grey), and Sir Walter Raleigh. The evidence against Raleigh was thin: a single accusation by Lord Cobham, a man of no honour or understanding, unsupported by any concurring circumstance.
Raleigh was nevertheless convicted in a notorious trial in which Attorney-General Sir Edward Coke heaped upon him the abuse of “traitor, monster, viper, and spider of hell.” Raleigh was reprieved but remained imprisoned in the Tower for the next thirteen years. The trial, in which the accused was not confronted with his accuser and the sole evidence was the contradictory testimony of a single disreputable witness, remains a landmark in the history of English criminal injustice.
Middle Reign — Gunpowder Plot, the Great Contract, and the Overbury Scandal
The Gunpowder Plot (1605). The most dramatic event of James’s reign, and one of the most famous in English history, was the conspiracy of a small group of Catholic gentry to blow up the king, the royal family, and both houses of parliament at the state opening. Led by Robert Catesby, the plotters — among them Guy Fawkes, Thomas Winter, and Thomas Percy — rented a cellar beneath the House of Lords and stockpiled thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. The plot was betrayed by an anonymous letter to Lord Monteagle; Fawkes was discovered in the cellar on the night of 4 November. The conspirators were pursued, killed or captured, and the surviving plotters, along with Henry Garnet, the Jesuit superior, were tried and executed. Hume describes the Gunpowder Treason as “one of the most memorable that history has conveyed to posterity, containing at once a singular proof both of the strength and weakness of the human mind.” The aftermath saw harsh recusancy laws imposed on English Catholics, though James himself was by nature more tolerant than the penal code suggests.
Parliament and the Great Contract (1610). James’s first parliament sat for seven years (1604–1610) and produced a series of constitutional frictions. The king’s claim to impose customs duties by prerogative, the dispute over the Buckinghamshire election (Goodwin v. Fortescue), and the Commons’ growing insistence on its own privileges set a pattern that would define the Stuart century. In 1610, Lord Treasurer Salisbury proposed the Great Contract: the king would surrender the feudal rights of wardship and purveyance in exchange for a permanent annual revenue of 200,000 pounds. The Commons, however, demanded the redress of grievances before supply, negotiations collapsed, and James dissolved the parliament in ignominy — left without either the Contract or adequate supply.
The Overbury Scandal and the Rise of Somerset. The death of Prince Henry (November 1612), the brilliant and martial heir who had seemed to embody the nation’s hopes, was a grievous blow to the king and the kingdom. Princess Elizabeth married Frederick V, the Elector Palatine, in 1613 — a match that would draw England into the maelstrom of the Thirty Years’ War.
Meanwhile, Robert Carr, Earl of Somerset, rose as the king’s favourite. Carr’s marriage to Frances Howard — divorced from the Earl of Essex in a sensational nullity proceeding — was followed by the mysterious poisoning of Sir Thomas Overbury in the Tower, who had opposed the match. When the murder was discovered, Somerset fell from favour and was succeeded by the dazzling George Villiers, later Duke of Buckingham, who would dominate the remainder of the reign and that of Charles I.
Late Reign — The Spanish Match, Prince Charles in Madrid, and Decline
James’s foreign policy throughout the 1610s and early 1620s was dominated by the catastrophe of the Thirty Years’ War and his obsessive pursuit of a Spanish marriage for his son Charles. When Frederick V accepted the crown of Bohemia in 1619 — in defiance of James’s advice — and was swiftly crushed at the Battle of the White Mountain (1620), the Palatinate was overrun by Spanish and Imperial forces. James’s daughter and grandchildren were driven into exile, yet the king refused to go to war. He believed that his moderation and justice, together with the prospect of a Spanish marriage, would persuade Philip IV to restore the Palatinate through diplomacy.
In 1623, Prince Charles and Buckingham made their rash and romantic journey to Madrid in disguise, hoping to conclude the marriage with the Infanta Maria in person. The adventure was a fiasco: the Spanish court was unimpressed, the religious conditions were impossible, and Charles returned to England in October 1623, humiliated and now eager for war with Spain. The marriage treaty was broken, and Charles and Buckingham — suddenly popular — pressed James into summoning a parliament (1624) that voted supplies for war.
James’s health was failing, and he withdrew increasingly from the direction of affairs, leaving Buckingham to manage both the king and the prince. The old king, who had dreamed of a peaceful settlement through dynastic marriage, saw his entire foreign policy collapse around him.
The Mansfeldt expedition of 1624–1625, an ill-conceived attempt to recover the Palatinate with English troops under the German mercenary Count Mansfeldt, ended in disaster. The army, cooped up in ships at Dover and then stranded at Calais without orders or provisions, was ravaged by disease. Half the men died on board. It was, as Hume notes, the only disaster to befall England during the “prosperous and pacific reign of James.”
Foreign Policy — Pacifism, the Thirty Years’ War, and the Palatinate
James’s foreign policy was defined by a consistent and principled aversion to war. He refused to join Henry IV of France in a grand league against the House of Austria in 1603, declined to intervene in the Dutch Revolt except through covert subsidies, and mediated the Twelve Years’ Truce between Spain and the United Provinces (1609). When the Thirty Years’ War erupted, he refused to support his own son-in-law’s rebellion against the Emperor, holding that subjects must never oppose their lawful sovereign. He sought to recover the Palatinate through negotiation, not arms, and pinned his hopes on a Spanish marriage alliance that never materialised. His pacifism, though genuine and defensible on grounds of national interest, was widely seen as pusillanimity, and it earned England the contempt of both Spain and the Protestant powers. The Commons grew ever more frustrated with a king who would neither fight for his daughter’s inheritance nor listen to their counsels. By the end of his reign, James had managed the singular feat of displeasing every faction in Europe — the Catholics because he would not tolerate them, the Protestants because he would not fight for them, and the Spanish because he could not be relied upon to keep his own people in check.
Death and Legacy
James died at Theobalds on 27 March 1625, after a short illness (a tertian ague), and was buried in Westminster Abbey. He was fifty-eight years old and had reigned over England for twenty-two years and some days; his reign over Scotland had begun in infancy and was almost of equal duration with his life. When encouraged by his courtiers with the common proverb that a tertian ague in spring was health for a king, he replied wryly that the proverb was meant of a young king. He sent for the prince, exhorted him to bear a tender affection for his wife, to preserve constancy in religion, to protect the Church of England, and to extend his care towards the unhappy family of the Palatine. With decency and courage he prepared himself for the end.
Hume’s character sketch captures the ambivalence of James’s reputation: “Many virtues he was possessed of, but scarce any of them pure, or free from the contagion of the neighbouring vices. His generosity bordered on profusion, his learning on pedantry, his pacific disposition on pusillanimity, his wisdom on cunning, his friendship on light fancy and boyish fondness.” He was awkward in person, undiscriminating in affection, and destitute of political courage — yet he was also humane, learned, and sincerely devoted to peace.
James’s reign is difficult to assess because it was transitional. He inherited from Elizabeth a nation prosperous, respected, and solvent; he bequeathed to Charles a crown in debt, a parliament estranged, and a foreign policy in disarray. The constitutional struggles that erupted under his son — over impositions, forced loans, parliamentary privilege, and the control of religion — all had their roots in James’s failure to resolve the tension between royal prerogative and the Commons’ growing sense of its own authority. The King James Bible and the Union of the Crowns are enduring achievements; the fissures that led to civil war are the enduring tragedy of his reign. Historians have long debated whether James was the architect of his own misfortunes or merely the unlucky monarch who happened to preside over an inevitable constitutional crisis. What is beyond dispute is that no English sovereign between the Conquest and the Revolution governed with so little war, yet left his successor so ill-prepared for the conflicts that were to come.
