entities/james-ii.title: James II of England (James VII of Scotland)
entities/james-ii.content:
James II of England (James VII of Scotland)
Summary
James II (r. 1685–1688), the younger son of Charles I and younger brother of Charles II, was the last Catholic monarch to reign over England, Scotland, and Ireland. His brief reign was a study in self-destructive zeal: a prince of undoubted personal honour, industry, and courage, he was consumed by a bigotry so absolute and a conception of royal authority so exalted that within three years he had squandered the most loyal parliament, the most devoted church party, and the most obedient army any Stuart had ever commanded. Hume judged him “more unfortunate than criminal” — a king whose virtues, wanting only a due regard for the religion and constitution of his country, became dangerous and pernicious. His flight to France in December 1688 and the subsequent Convention Parliament’s declaration that he had “abdicated the government” completed the Glorious Revolution, established William III and Mary II on the throne, and settled the Protestant succession in England for centuries.

As Duke of York (1633–1685)
James, born 14 October 1633, was created Duke of York at the age of nine. During the Civil War he was taken prisoner by parliamentary forces but escaped to the continent in 1648, where he served with distinction in the French and Spanish armies, acquiring a reputation for personal courage and an inflexible temper. At the Restoration, Charles II appointed him Lord High Admiral, a post he held with notable competence. He commanded the English fleet at the Battle of Lowestoft (1665), the first great naval engagement of the Second Dutch War, and took an active and capable hand in naval administration. Campbell’s naval history records his diligent application to the business of the fleet.
James’s conversion to Catholicism — the decisive fact of his life — occurred sometime in the late 1660s or early 1670s. He ceased attending Anglican services, received the sacrament according to the Roman rite, and became an increasingly open and zealous Catholic. When Parliament passed the Test Act in 1673, requiring all office-holders to receive the Anglican communion and swear against transubstantiation, James resigned his command of the Admiralty rather than comply. Burnet records the scene: the Duke carried all his commissions to the King and wept as he delivered them up — but Charles showed no concern at all.
The revelation of James’s Catholicism ignited the Exclusion Crisis (1679–1681), in which the Earl of Shaftesbury and the Whig party attempted to bar him from the succession. Three Exclusion Bills passed the Commons and were defeated in the Lords. Charles II, fighting for his brother’s inheritance, dissolved parliament, rejected exclusion, and governed without one for the last four years of his reign. James was twice sent into temporary exile — to Brussels (1679) and to Scotland (1680–1682) — where he governed as Lord High Commissioner and pursued a harsh policy against Presbyterian conventiclers. The Rye House Plot (1683), a conspiracy to assassinate both brothers, further strengthened the Tory reaction and secured James’s eventual succession.

Accession and the Parliament of 1685
Charles II died on 6 February 1685, and James succeeded without opposition. His first act was to assemble the Privy Council, where he declared his resolution to maintain the established government in church and state. “We have now the word of a king,” men said, “and a word never yet broken.” The new king was universally regarded as a man of great sincerity and honour. Addresses of the most servile adulation poured in from every quarter.
Yet James’s first exercise of authority revealed his conception of royal power. He issued a proclamation ordering the customs and excise — revenue that had legally expired with his brother’s death — to be paid as before, refusing even the gesture of deferring collection until Parliament could authorise it. He went openly to mass with all the ensigns of his dignity, an illegal meeting that displayed at once his arbitrary disposition and his bigotry. Hume remarks that these were the two great characteristics of his reign and the bane of his administration.
The Parliament that met on 19 May 1685 was the most loyal imaginable: packed by the remodelled corporations, overwhelmingly Tory and Anglican, and eager to please. The king demanded a revenue for life. After debate, the Commons voted unanimously to settle on him all the revenue enjoyed by the late king at his demise, together with additional duties on wines, vinegar, tobacco, and sugar amounting to some 600,000 pounds a year. The Speaker, presenting the bill, reminded the king of the Commons’ trust in his repeated declarations to support the Church of England — but could not extort from James a single word in favour of that religion. Soon after, Titus Oates was tried for perjury on overwhelming evidence, convicted, and sentenced to savage whipping and perpetual imprisonment.

Monmouth Rebellion and Sedgemoor
The parliamentary proceedings were interrupted in June 1685 by news that the Duke of Monmouth had landed at Lyme Regis in Dorsetshire with three ships from Holland. Monmouth, the illegitimate son of Charles II and a Protestant champion, had been pushed by his followers into a premature attempt on the crown. Parliament voted 400,000 pounds to suppress the rebellion and passed a bill of attainder against him.
Monmouth’s following swelled rapidly among the common people of the West Country. At Taunton he was presented with colours worked by twenty young maids of some rank, and was persuaded to take the title of king. His numbers reached six thousand, but they were poorly armed and undisciplined. The king’s forces, commanded by the Earl of Feversham with John Churchill as second-in-command, marched to intercept him. On the night of 5 July 1685, Monmouth attacked the royal camp at Sedgemoor near Bridgewater. The rebel infantry fought with desperate courage, throwing the veteran forces into disorder and driving them from their ground; but Monmouth’s own indecision and the cowardice of Lord Gray, who commanded the horse, prevented victory. After three hours the rebels gave way, and some fifteen hundred were slaughtered in the pursuit.
Monmouth fled twenty miles, disguised as a peasant, and was discovered lying in a ditch covered with fern. He wrote James the most submissive letters, conjuring him to spare the life of his brother’s son. James admitted him to his presence, hoping to extort a discovery of his accomplices, but Monmouth refused to purchase life by infamy. He was executed on 15 July 1685 on Tower Hill. The executioner, unnerved by Monmouth’s warning to strike cleanly, struck five feeble blows before the head was severed. Hume’s portrait of Monmouth’s end is among the most affecting passages in his history.

The Bloody Assizes
The victory at Sedgemoor might have strengthened the crown had it been managed with prudence. Instead, the cruelty with which it was prosecuted became a principal cause of James’s ruin. Colonel Percy Kirke, commanding at Tangier veterans hardened by service among the Moors, hanged nineteen prisoners at Bridgewater without trial, using executions as entertainment while his regiment drank the king’s health. His “lambs,” as he called them, became a byword for terror in the West Country.
Chief Justice Jefferies followed with the judicial massacre known as the Bloody Assizes. Opening his commission at Dorchester, he ordered twenty-nine convicted rebels to immediate execution. Terrified, most of the remaining prisoners pleaded guilty. At Dorchester alone, two hundred and ninety-two received sentence and eighty were executed; at Exeter, two hundred and forty-three were tried. In total, some two hundred and fifty-one persons were executed by the hand of justice, besides those butchered by the military. The whole country was strewed with the heads and limbs of traitors. The most infamous cases were those of Lady Lisle, a widow of seventy, executed for harbouring a fugitive; and Mrs. Gaunt, an Anabaptist benefactress, burned alive for sheltering a rebel who then betrayed her. Jefferies was rewarded with a peerage and the Lord Chancellorship.

The Dispensing Power and Catholic Appointments
Elated by his easy victory over Monmouth and by the servility of his Parliament, James pressed forward with the Catholicising project that defined his reign. In his speech to Parliament in November 1685, he plainly declared that he had employed Catholic officers and dispensed with the Test Act in their favour, and that he was determined to continue doing so. When the Commons voted an address against the dispensing power, James answered with a flat denial uttered with great warmth. The House was so daunted that they sent one of their own members, Coke of Derby, to the Tower for saying “I hope we are all Englishmen, and not to be frightened with a few hard words.” They then submissively voted the supply.
The Lords, led by the Bishop of London, also showed some resistance. But James prorogued Parliament and never called it again — dissolving it after a year and a half of prorogations. He had resolved to govern without parliaments.
The dispensing power was tested in the collusive case of Sir Edward Hales (1686), a Catholic convert who had accepted a colonel’s commission. His coachman was directed to prosecute him for the statutory penalty. The judges, obedient to the crown, upheld the dispensing power. Thus fortified, James proceeded to pack the state with Catholics. Catholic peers were admitted to the Privy Council. Four Catholic lords — Powis, Arundel, Bellasis, and Tyrone — were placed in high office. A Catholic, Sir Richard Talbot, was created Earl of Tyrconnel and placed at the head of the Irish administration, where he systematically replaced Protestant officers and magistrates with Catholics. Obadiah Walker, a Catholic, was installed as master of University College, Oxford. A Benedictine monk was recommended for a degree at Cambridge. The papal nuncio, Ferdinando d’Adda, was received at court with full honours — the first papal representative in England since the Reformation.

The Ecclesiastical Commission and Magdalen College
In 1686 James created a Court of Ecclesiastical Commission, modelled on the High Commission that Charles I had used and Parliament had abolished. Its first act was to suspend Henry Compton, Bishop of London, for refusing to discipline a Protestant clergyman who had preached against popery. The commission was given power over all clergy, colleges, and schools.
The most notorious attack on the established church was the assault on Magdalen College, Oxford. When the college’s president died in 1687, James recommended that the fellows elect Anthony Farmer, a Catholic convert of scandalous character. The fellows, bound by their statutes and their oaths, elected instead John Hough, a man of unexceptionable character. James summoned them before the Ecclesiastical Commission; when they refused to submit, he expelled the president and all the fellows except two who complied, and installed the Catholic bishop Samuel Parker in his place. Upon Parker’s death, he nominated John Gifford, a titular bishop of the Sorbonne. Hume calls this act “perhaps the most illegal and arbitrary” of James’s entire reign — a direct attack on private property, college statutes, and sworn oaths. The universities, the nurseries of the Anglican clergy, were now plainly threatened.

The Declaration of Indulgence and the Seven Bishops
In April 1687 James issued a Declaration of Indulgence, suspending all penal laws against Catholics and Dissenters. When the Anglican clergy refused to cooperate, he issued a second declaration in April 1688, ordering it to be read in all churches. The Archbishop of Canterbury, William Sancroft, and six bishops — Lloyd of St. Asaph, Ken of Bath and Wells, Turner of Ely, Lake of Chichester, White of Peterborough, and Trelawney of Bristol — met privately and drew up a petition to the king, humbly beseeching him not to insist on their reading a declaration founded on a dispensing power that Parliament had declared illegal.
James, incapable of yielding to the slightest contradiction, summoned the bishops before the council. When they acknowledged the petition, he committed them to the Tower. The spectacle of the seven prelates being conveyed by barge to the Tower drew crowds of prostrate spectators; soldiers knelt for their blessing. At their trial in Westminster Hall, the jury acquitted them after several hours’ deliberation. The news was received with extraordinary rejoicing throughout the kingdom. The soldiers on Hounslow Heath, whom the king had reviewed that very day, broke into such tumultuary joy that James, hearing the commotion, was told by Feversham that it was only the soldiers rejoicing at the acquittal of the bishops. “Do you call that nothing?” James replied. “But so much the worse for them.”

Birth of the Prince of Wales
A few days before the acquittal, on 10 June 1688, Queen Mary of Modena was delivered of a son — James Francis Edward Stuart, the Prince of Wales. For James and the Catholics, this was an answer to prayer: the king was past middle age, and without a male heir the succession would pass to the Protestant Princess Mary and her husband William of Orange. Pilgrimages had been made; the Duchess of Modena had journeyed to Loretto. But for the Protestant nation, the birth was a disaster. A Catholic heir would perpetuate the peril indefinitely.
A calumny spread across the kingdom: that the child was supposititious, smuggled into the queen’s bed in a warming-pan. James, from an ill-timed haughtiness, disdained to answer the rumour, saying he would not satisfy those who could deem him capable of so base an action. The calumny was wholly unfounded, but it was widely believed, and it gave William of Orange a pretext for his intervention. The prince declared that one of his objects was to examine the proofs of the prince’s legitimacy.

William’s Invasion and James’s Flight
William of Orange, long the centre of European resistance to Louis XIV, had been in secret correspondence with English grandees for two years. The birth of the Prince of Wales transformed hesitation into action. In October 1688, William issued his declaration, enumerating the grievances of the nation; on 5 November — the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot — he landed at Torbay with a fleet of nearly five hundred vessels and an army of fourteen thousand men.
The response was extraordinary. The whole nation rose against the king. Lord Cornbury deserted with three regiments. John Churchill, who owed his entire fortune to James’s favour, went over to the prince, carrying the Duke of Grafton and Colonel Berkeley. Prince George of Denmark, James’s son-in-law, deserted him at Andover. The Princess Anne fled to Nottingham. James, at Salisbury, received these blows with increasing despair. “God help me,” he cried when he heard of Anne’s desertion, “my own children have forsaken me!” He retreated to London and made some last-minute concessions — restoring the charters, annulling the Ecclesiastical Commission, reinstating the fellows of Magdalen College — but they were regarded as symptoms of fear, not repentance.
On the night of 12 December, James sent the queen and the infant prince to France under the conduct of Count Lauzun. He himself disappeared the same night, throwing the Great Seal into the Thames as he went. He was seized by fishermen at Faversham and roughly handled before being recognised; he was brought back to London, where the populace received him with unexpected acclamation. But the prince of Orange, having no intention of allowing James to remain, ordered him to leave Whitehall. James retired to Rochester, and on 23 December, urged by letters from the queen, he privately embarked for France. He arrived at Ambleteuse in Picardy and hastened to the palace of St. Germains, where Louis XIV received him with the highest generosity and sympathy.

Death in Exile
James spent the remainder of his life at the French court of St. Germains-en-Laye. He made one attempt to recover his throne, landing in Ireland in March 1689 with French support. His Irish Parliament at Dublin enacted a programme of Catholic ascendancy and forfeiture of Protestant estates; but his cause was destroyed by William’s victory at the Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690. James fled the field, returning to France in disgrace — a conduct that confirmed the Irish in their contempt and the French in their diminishing regard. He withdrew to the monastery of La Trappe for periods of religious retreat and devoted himself increasingly to piety. He died at St. Germains on 16 September 1701, of a cerebral haemorrhage, and was buried in the Church of the English Benedictines in Paris. Louis XIV, on hearing the news, ordered a mourning of the whole court, and James’s son, James Francis Edward — the “Old Pretender” — was proclaimed King James III of England and James VIII of Scotland by the Jacobite court.

Character
Hume’s character of James II is one of the most measured in his history. In domestic life his conduct was irreproachable: severe but open in his enmities, steady in his counsels, diligent in his schemes, brave in his enterprises, faithful, sincere, and honourable in his dealings with all men. His frugality of public money was remarkable, his industry exemplary, his application to naval affairs successful, his encouragement of trade judicious, his jealousy of national honour laudable. What was wanting to make him an excellent sovereign? “A due regard and affection to the religion and constitution of his country.” When that was wanting, every excellency he possessed became dangerous and pernicious.
James valued himself highly on his sincerity. Yet his reign was almost one continued invasion of the liberties and religion he had promised to preserve. Hume allows that James may have sincerely believed he never meant to subvert the laws — but his idea of legal authority was so lofty that it left his subjects little right to liberty but what was dependent on his sovereign will; and his zeal for proselytism plainly stopped at nothing short of full Catholic establishment. “On the whole,” concludes Hume, “allowing this king to have possessed good qualities and good intentions, his conduct serves only, on that very account, as a stronger proof how dangerous it is to allow any prince, infected with the Catholic superstition, to wear the crown of these kingdoms.”
Burnet’s judgment is less generous. He describes James as a prince of “a very different nature” from his brother — without Charles’s indolent good humour or cynical flexibility. James was open, sincere, and honourable in private, but his understanding was narrow, his temper inflexible, and his zeal for his religion so absolute that it overrode every consideration of policy, prudence, or constitutional obligation. His reign confirmed Burnet in the conviction that a Catholic monarch could never govern a Protestant nation without either betraying his faith or subverting the laws.

Legacy
The reign of James II lasted only three years, yet it transformed the English constitution. The Glorious Revolution established parliamentary supremacy over the crown, enacted the Bill of Rights (1689), which declared the dispensing and suspending power illegal, and secured the Protestant succession through the Act of Settlement (1701). James’s flight was deemed by the Convention Parliament to constitute abdication; the throne was declared vacant and offered jointly to William III and Mary II. Thomas Macaulay, two centuries later, would call the Revolution of 1688 the “preserving revolution” — the last successful invasion of England and the foundation of its limited monarchy.
James himself became the focus of Jacobite hopes for the next sixty years — a dynasty in exile that twice (in 1715 and 1745) raised the Highlands in arms. But the revolution he provoked had answered the question that had haunted English politics since the Reformation: the crown could not lawfully be worn by a Catholic. The price of James II’s reign, for the Stuarts, was the permanent loss of the throne they had held for three centuries.

entities/john-benbow.title: Admiral John Benbow
entities/john-benbow.content:
Admiral John Benbow
Summary
Admiral John Benbow (1653–1702) was an English naval commander whose career rose from a merchant seaman to vice-admiral of the blue. He was the most popular seaman of King William III’s navy — a blunt, honest, and courageous officer whose name became a byword for British tenacity. His last action, a five-day running fight against the French admiral Du Casse off the Spanish Main in August 1702, is one of the most dramatic and controversial episodes in naval history: abandoned by most of his captains, his leg shattered by chain-shot, Benbow fought on from a cradle on the quarter-deck until his squadron’s cowardice forced him back to Jamaica, where he died of his wounds. The subsequent court-martial condemned two of his captains to be shot. Du Casse himself wrote demanding that the defaulters be hanged.

Early Life and Merchant Service
John Benbow was born in 1653, the son of Colonel John Benbow, a Shropshire gentleman of good family who had fought and suffered for Charles I and Charles II in the Civil Wars and at Worcester. The family’s fortunes were ruined by their royalism; the elder Benbow died of joy when Charles II recognised him in the Tower and promised to provide for him, and John, then about fifteen, was left to make his own way.
He was bred to the sea and by the reign of Charles II had risen to be owner and commander of a merchant ship called the Benbow Frigate. He was well known among the London merchants as a bold, brave, and active commander who kept strict discipline but took care of his men, and was therefore cheerfully obeyed. No man on the Exchange was better known or more esteemed than Captain Benbow.
In 1686, while bound for Cadiz, his ship was attacked by a Salee rover. Though outnumbered, Benbow defended himself with such vigour that the Moors boarded him and were beaten off, leaving thirteen men dead. Benbow ordered their heads cut off and packed in a tub of pork pickle. At Cadiz, the Spanish customs officers insisted on inspecting the tub; Benbow sternly ordered his servant to throw the heads on the table, saying “if you like them, they are at your service.” The story reached the court of Madrid, and King Charles II of Spain was so pleased that he wrote to King James II on Benbow’s behalf. James gave him a ship — his introduction to the Royal Navy.

Service in the Nine Years’ War
After the Glorious Revolution, Benbow served King William III with the same energy he had shown as a merchant captain. He was employed at the request of the merchants themselves to cruise in the Channel against French privateers, and he combined this duty with close reconnaissance of French ports, gaining intelligence and forming schemes to disturb French commerce. He was repeatedly chosen to command the squadrons that bombarded the French Channel ports — Granville, St Malo, Havre de Grace, and Dunkirk — and on those occasions was always present in his boat under a prodigious fire, enforcing his commands by his example. During the Dunkirk operation in September 1694, he went in and sounded the western channel under a heavy cannonade from the ships and citadel.
Promoted to rear-admiral, Benbow was given command of a small squadron in May 1696 with orders to prevent the famous French privateer Du Bart from escaping Dunkirk. Though Du Bart gave him the slip in hazy weather and fell upon the Dutch Baltic fleet, Benbow pursued him, then convoyed the northern-bound fleet to Gothenburgh and Hamburg. His diligence was such that when political libels flew against almost every flag officer, he escaped the slightest censure.
The seamen regarded Benbow as their greatest patron. He was consulted more than once by the king on the proper balance between promoting “tarpaulins” (plain seamen) and gentlemen, and always advised employing both, judging a man by his actions at sea rather than the company he kept ashore.

First West Indies Command, 1698–1700
In November 1698, Rear-admiral Benbow was sent to the West Indies with a small squadron of three fourth-rates, charged with protecting trade, observing the Spanish ports, and keeping fair with the governors. He arrived at Barbadoes in February 1699 and proceeded to the Leeward Islands. Finding that the Spanish at Carthagena had seized two English ships for use against the Scots at Darien, Benbow stood over to the Spanish coast and demanded their return with characteristic bluntness. When the governor trifled, Benbow sent word that if the ships were not delivered in twenty-four hours, he would come and fetch them. The ships were released.
He performed a similar service at Porto Bello, where the admiral of the Spanish Barlovento fleet had seized English slave-trade vessels. Benbow’s plain speaking, backed by the threat of force, secured their restoration. He also sailed in search of the pirate Captain Kidd. He returned home with authentic testimonies from the merchants and planters that he had done them all the service they could desire. The king granted him an augmentation of arms — adding arrows to the three bent bows his family bore.

Return to the West Indies and the Action Against Du Casse, 1702
King William was reluctant to send Benbow back to the West Indies so soon, saying he had met with nothing but difficulties there and it was fair another officer should take his turn. But others excused themselves, and the king said merrily, “Well then, I find we must spare our beaus, and send honest Benbow.” When asked if he was willing to go, Benbow answered that he did not understand such compliments, that he had no right to choose his station, and that he would cheerfully execute his orders wherever sent.
He sailed in September 1701 with ten ships — two third-rates and eight fourth-rates — with instructions to engage the Spanish governors to disown the French candidate for the Spanish throne, or to seize the galleons. After a winter in the West Indies during which he frustrated all French designs against Jamaica and the Leeward Islands, he sailed from Jamaica on 11 July 1702 to intercept the French squadron under M. Du Casse.
On Wednesday 19 August, Benbow came up with Du Casse off the coast of Santa Martha and engaged. The fight lasted five days. From the first, several of his captains showed a strange backwardness: the Defiance (Captain Kirby), the Windsor (Captain Constable), the Greenwich (Captain Wade), and others repeatedly fell out of gun-shot, disobeyed signals, and left the admiral to bear the whole weight of the enemy. Only Captain Fog of the Breda (Benbow’s own ship) and Captain Walton of the Ruby supported him. On 24 August, a chain-shot shattered Benbow’s right leg. He had his cradle brought to the quarter-deck and continued the fight till daybreak. His ships were now in such confusion that Du Casse’s disabled ship was towed away under the noses of the English captains, who made no attempt to prevent it.
Captain Kirby came aboard and told the admiral he had better desist — that there was nothing to be made of it. Benbow, seeing that even with the fairest opportunity that had yet offered he could expect no support from his captains, most unwillingly consented to return to Jamaica. Du Casse himself, after safely reaching Carthagena, wrote Benbow a letter: “I had little hopes on Monday last but to have supped in your cabin, but it pleased God to order it otherwise. As for those cowardly captains who deserted you, hang them up, for by God they deserve it.”

Court-Martial and Death
Benbow arrived at Jamaica suffering from a fever induced by his wounds. His leg was amputated, but he never recovered. On 6 October 1702, he issued a commission to Rear-admiral Whetstone and several captains to hold a court-martial. Kirby and Wade were condemned to death for cowardice, breach of orders, and neglect of duty; it was proved that Kirby, after two or three broadsides, kept always out of gun-shot and threatened to kill his boatswain for repeating the admiral’s command to fire. Constable was cashiered and imprisoned. Captain Hudson died before his trial could take place — his conduct was judged to have been exactly as bad as Kirby’s and Wade’s. Captains Vincent and Fog were suspended for signing a paper, at Kirby’s persuasion, obliging themselves not to fight.
Benbow died on 4 November 1702. His last weeks were spent giving orders for the protection of trade and writing to his wife, showing more anxiety for the nation than for his own family. He is said to have replied to a lieutenant who expressed sorrow for the loss of his leg: “I am sorry for it too, but I had rather have lost them both than have seen this dishonour brought upon the English nation. But do you hear — if another shot should take me off, behave like brave men, and fight it out.”
Queen Anne spoke of his loss with great regret. His picture was hung in the town hall of Shrewsbury, where it still remains.

Character
Benbow was an honest, rough seaman — brave, blunt, and utterly devoted to duty. Campbell writes that “he had a probity that was never questioned, and a knowledge of men and things which always procured him credit in whatever station he appeared.” His strict discipline at Jamaica, where he treated the gentlemen-captains briskly when they were not ready to obey, likely provoked the conspiracy that destroyed him. His rugged honesty baffled them, but the anxiety of the affair brought on the melancholy that hastened his death. He was no mere fighting seaman: his scheme for intercepting Du Casse while keeping the Spanish settlements in check shows a judicious and capable command. The tragedy of his last battle was not his own want of courage — which was never in question — but the fact that no English admiral was ever more shamefully betrayed by those who should have supported him.

entities/marlborough.title: John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough
entities/marlborough.content:
John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough
Summary
John Churchill (1650–1722), 1st Duke of Marlborough, was the greatest English general of his age and one of the foremost military commanders in European history. His career spanned the reigns of five monarchs — Charles II, James II, William III, Anne, and George I — and his four great victories in the War of the Spanish Succession (Blenheim, Ramillies, Oudenarde, and Malplaquet) shattered the military supremacy of Louis XIV and established England as a first-rate continental power. Yet his character was as complex as his achievements were brilliant: a man of graceful bearing and unfailing courtesy, he was also acquisitive, secretive, and capable of a cold ingratitude that shocked even his contemporaries. Burnet judged him “one of the greatest men the age has produced” while acknowledging that his hunger for fortune was never fully shaken off, even in his highest elevation. His 17th-century career — service under Turenne, the Tangier garrison, the victory at Sedgemoor, the defection to William of Orange, the Irish campaign, and the long years of disgrace — was the foundation on which his later fame was built.

Early Career under Charles II and James II
John Churchill was born about 1650 into a family of minor Devonshire gentry ruined by the Civil War. His father, Sir Winston Churchill, was a Cavalier who had fought for Charles I and suffered sequestration. The young Churchill was placed as a page in the household of the Duke of York (the future James II) and began his military education in earnest by serving as a volunteer in the French army under the great Marshal Turenne. Hume records that during the campaign of 1675, at the Battle of Consarbruck and the retreat after Turenne’s death, “the Duke of Marlborough, then captain Churchill, here learned the rudiments of that art which he afterward practised with such fatal success against France.” He distinguished himself by his coolness under fire and was promoted by Turenne himself — an early mark of the military genius that would later humble France.
Returning to England, Churchill was given a commission in the English forces sent to garrison Tangier, the Moroccan possession acquired through Charles II’s marriage to Catherine of Braganza. The Tangier service — among the veterans who later became known as the “Tangerines” — was a hard school: the garrison fought constant skirmishes with Moorish forces in a pestilential climate. Churchill’s conduct there brought him to the notice of the Duke of York, who advanced him through a succession of commands. By 1683 he was a colonel and had been raised to the Scottish peerage as Lord Churchill of Eyemouth.
When Charles II died in February 1685 and James II succeeded, Churchill was one of the few men in whom the new king reposed entire confidence. James had known him since boyhood and had promoted him steadily; Churchill had repaid that confidence with conspicuous loyalty during the succession crisis. When the Duke of Monmouth landed at Lyme Regis in June 1685 to claim the crown, Churchill was sent as second-in-command to the Earl of Feversham to suppress the rebellion. At the Battle of Sedgemoor (5 July 1685), the rebel infantry attacked the royal camp by night and threw the veteran forces into disorder; but Churchill’s steady handling of the cavalry, combined with Monmouth’s own indecision and Lord Gray’s cowardice, turned the tide. After three hours the rebels gave way, and some fifteen hundred were slaughtered in the pursuit. Churchill emerged from the campaign with his reputation enhanced, though the savagery of the Bloody Assizes that followed was the work of Kirke and Jefferies, not of the young general.

Defection to William of Orange
The contradiction at the heart of Churchill’s character — his capacity for profound ingratitude to a master who had raised him from nothing — was revealed in the crisis of 1688. James II’s campaign to Catholicise the army and the state had driven even his most loyal servants to despair. Churchill, according to Burnet, had told the Earl of Gallway as early as James’s accession that “if the King was ever prevailed on to alter our religion, he would serve him no longer, but withdraw from him.” He was no party to the King’s violent measures, and he was profoundly doubtful of the legitimacy of the Prince of Wales born in June 1688 — the so-called “warming-pan baby” that the Whigs insisted was a supposititious child smuggled into the Queen’s bed.
Churchill quietly committed himself to the Prince of Orange’s enterprise. He undertook that Prince George of Denmark and the Princess Anne would leave the Court and join the Prince as soon as possible. When William landed at Torbay in November 1688, Churchill was with the royal army at Salisbury. On the night of 24 November, he rode out of the camp at Axminster with the Duke of Grafton and Colonel Berkeley, taking several troops of dragoons with him, and joined the Prince. Hume writes that Churchill “had been raised from the rank of a page, had been invested with a high command in the army, had been created a peer, and had owed his whole fortune to the king’s favour: yet even he could resolve, during the present extremity, to desert his unhappy master, who had ever reposed entire confidence in him.” The blow broke James’s spirit. His daughter Anne, guided by Lady Churchill, fled London that same night, and within days the King had lost all heart for resistance and was in flight for France.

Service under William III: The Irish Campaign
William III, though he could never entirely trust a man who had deserted his former master, recognised Churchill’s military talents. In 1689 Churchill was created Earl of Marlborough and sent to Flanders to command the English contingent of the Grand Alliance. His first independent command of note came in 1690, when William, then engaged in Ireland, authorised Marlborough to undertake an amphibious expedition against the southern Irish ports held by the Jacobites.
Marlborough proposed to strike at Cork and Kinsale, which commanded the communications between France and the Irish Jacobites. Contrary winds delayed his departure until October, a dangerously late season for campaigning. He took Cork by storm with impressive speed: four thousand prisoners fell into his hands, though the assault cost the life of the Duke of Grafton, who received a mortal wound. From Cork he marched to Kinsale, where he found the two forts that commanded the port far stronger than the intelligence reports had indicated. Burnet records that Marlborough told him “if he had known their true strength, he had never undertaken the expedition, in a season so far advanced.” Yet within a few days the place capitulated. The reduction of these two ports cut off the quick communication between France and Ireland and contributed materially to the eventual Jacobite defeat at Limerick. It was a model campaign — bold in conception, rapid in execution, and economical in blood.

Disgrace and Imprisonment
Despite his Irish success, Marlborough’s position under William was precarious. The King suspected him — not without reason — of maintaining secret correspondence with the exiled James II at St. Germains. In January 1692, William dismissed Marlborough from all his employments. Burnet notes that Admiral Russell “almost upbraided the King with the Earl of Marlborough’s Services, who, as he said, had set the Crown on his head.” Russell’s intercession availed nothing. Worse followed: in May 1692, as a French invasion fleet prepared to land James II in England, Marlborough was sent to the Tower of London on a charge of high treason. The accusation, Dalrymple records, was “a forged accusation” by profligate creatures who “fancied that forgeries and false swearing would be as acceptable, and as well rewarded, in this Reign, as they had been formerly.” The conspiracy was eventually detected and the forgers whipped and pilloried, but Marlborough was held in the Tower for several weeks and released only on bail.
The causes of his disgrace were complex. His wife Sarah’s intimacy with Princess Anne had made the Marlboroughs objects of Queen Mary’s jealousy. And there was some truth to the rumours of Jacobite correspondence: Marlborough, ever the trimmer, appears to have maintained a line of communication with St. Germains as insurance against a Stuart restoration. Yet Dalrymple suggests that King William himself may have tacitly authorised such contacts as a channel of intelligence. At a later period, William restored Marlborough to his rank and employed him in great services — partly from “that indulgence for recent prejudices, to which he yielded more than most of his subjects, and partly because he found his business done better by that Lord than by any other person.” Marlborough was made governor to the young Duke of Gloucester, Princess Anne’s sole surviving child, and was gradually readmitted to military employment in the closing years of William’s reign.

Rise under Queen Anne
The death of William III in March 1702 and the accession of Queen Anne transformed Marlborough’s fortunes. Anne had been the intimate friend of his wife Sarah Churchill since childhood, and the queen’s affection for “Mrs. Freeman” — the pet name by which Sarah was known in their correspondence — gave the Marlboroughs an ascendancy at Court such as no subject had enjoyed since Buckingham. Within a week of her accession, Anne sent Marlborough to Holland to assure the Dutch States-General of her commitment to the war against France. He was appointed Captain-General of the English forces, and the States gave him effective command of the allied army. In December 1702, after a successful first campaign that saw the capture of Venlo, Ruremond, Stevenswaert, and Liege, Anne raised him to a dukedom — the Duke of Marlborough — and both Houses of Parliament sent their formal thanks.
The years that followed were the summit of Marlborough’s career and of England’s military glory. His strategy was founded on two principles: the destruction of the Franco-Bavarian alliance that threatened Vienna, and the bold offensive that the cautious Dutch generals were always reluctant to authorise. In 1703 he took Bonn and Huy; in 1704 he conceived a design of breathtaking audacity.

Blenheim (1704)
In the spring of 1704, Vienna was in mortal peril. The Elector of Bavaria had joined Louis XIV, and a combined Franco-Bavarian army under Marshal Tallard and the Elector threatened to take the Imperial capital. Marlborough resolved on a march that contemporaries regarded as madness: he would move the allied army from the Low Countries to the Danube, a distance of some 250 miles, across the lines of communication of the enemy, without losing a man to desertion or enemy action. He accomplished this feat with such secrecy and discipline that the French had no idea of his true destination until he was already in Germany. At Schellenberg he stormed the heights overlooking Donauwörth in a ferocious assault that cleared the passage to Bavaria.
On 13 August 1704, Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy — the imperial general who became his close collaborator — faced the combined Franco-Bavarian army at the village of Blenheim on the Danube. The French were strongly posted, with the Danube on one flank and a marshy rivulet in front. Marlborough and Eugene attacked nonetheless. Burnet, who received Marlborough’s own account of the battle, writes that the Duke told him “he never saw more evident Characters of a special Providence” than that day. A cannonball struck the ground so near him that he was “some time quite covered with the Cloud of Dust and Earth that it raised about him.” The battle was decided by Marlborough’s cavalry, which broke through the French centre after the infantry had pinned the enemy in place. Tallard was taken prisoner, and twelve thousand French infantry — trapped in the village of Blenheim — laid down their arms. The French and Bavarians lost some forty thousand men killed, wounded, and taken; the allies about twelve thousand. Vienna was saved, Bavaria was conquered, and the myth of French invincibility was shattered. The Emperor created Marlborough a Prince of the Empire, with the principality of Mindelheim assigned to him.

Ramillies, Oudenarde, and Malplaquet
The victories continued. At Ramillies (23 May 1706), Marlborough destroyed a French army under Marshal Villeroy in what many military historians consider his most perfect battle. He feinted at the French left, drew Villeroy into reinforcing it, then struck the weakened centre with overwhelming force. The French army disintegrated; Marlborough captured almost the whole of the Spanish Netherlands — including Brussels, Ghent, Bruges, Antwerp, and Ostend — in a single whirlwind campaign. The French lost some fifteen thousand men; the allies fewer than four thousand.
At Oudenarde (11 July 1708), Marlborough and Eugene caught a French army under the Duke of Vendome and the Duke of Burgundy in the midst of crossing the Scheldt and attacked before the enemy could deploy. The battle was a confused, six-hour melee in which Marlborough’s tactical genius and his power of personal command on the field turned a potential stand-off into a decisive victory. The French were driven back into Ghent in disorder.
The bloodiest of Marlborough’s victories came at Malplaquet (11 September 1709). The French, now commanded by Marshal Villars, had fortified their position with elaborate fieldworks — a foretaste of the entrenchments that would dominate eighteenth-century warfare. Marlborough and Eugene, overruling Dutch caution, attacked the entrenchments in a series of frontal assaults. The slaughter was terrible: the allies lost some twenty-four thousand killed and wounded to the French fifteen thousand. Yet the French army retreated in good order, and Villars declared that he had lost the field, not the honour. Malplaquet was the most pyrrhic of Marlborough’s victories, and it marked the beginning of the war-weariness that would eventually undo him.

Fall from Power, Exile, and Return
Marlborough’s political position rested on the favour of Queen Anne and the partnership of Lord Godolphin, the Lord Treasurer, in what the Tories called the “duumvirate.” But the war had become increasingly unpopular as its costs mounted. The Battle of Malplaquet, with its dreadful casualty list, and the failure to achieve a decisive peace weakened Marlborough’s hold on the public. His wife Sarah, once the Queen’s dearest friend, had become overbearing and quarrelsome; Anne had transferred her affections to a new favourite, Abigail Masham, a cousin of Robert Harley, who led the Tory opposition.
In 1710, the Tories swept to power in a general election. Harley became Chancellor of the Exchequer and effectively prime minister. In January 1711, Anne, under pressure from Harley and the Tories, dismissed Sarah from her posts at Court. Marlborough himself was accused of peculation — of having taken bribes from the army contractor Medina and of having enriched himself at public expense. The charges were genuine enough in their substance if inflated in their presentation; Marlborough, ever acquisitive, had indeed taken a percentage on the bread and transport contracts of the allied army.
In December 1711, Anne dismissed Marlborough from all his employments. The Captain-General who had saved Europe from French domination was stripped of his commands, and the Duke of Ormond was sent to replace him in Flanders. Marlborough went into voluntary exile on the Continent, where he remained until the death of Queen Anne in August 1714. The accession of George I restored him to favour: he was reappointed Captain-General and given command of the army, but his health was broken and he took no further active part in military affairs. He suffered a series of strokes, and died at Windsor on 16 June 1722.

Character and Legacy
Burnet’s character of Churchill, written before his greatest battles, remains the most penetrating portrait. He was “a man of a noble and graceful appearance, bred up in the Court with no literature: But he had a solid and clear understanding, with a constant presence of mind. He knew the arts of living in a Court beyond any man in it. He caressed all people with a soft and obliging deportment, and was always ready to do good offices. He had no fortune to set up on. This put him on all the methods of acquiring one. And that went so far into him, that he did not shake it off, when he was in a much higher elevation.”
The 17th-century foundation of his career — the years as a page in James’s household, the service under Turenne, the Tangier garrison, the victory at Sedgemoor, the defection to William, the Irish campaign, the Tower — was essential to everything that followed. It forged the soldier who would never lose a battle, the courtier who could navigate the treacherous waters of Stuart and Hanoverian politics, and the statesman who, for a decade, was the most powerful man in England after the Queen. He was laid to rest in Westminster Abbey, and his memory is preserved in Blenheim Palace, the vast Oxfordshire house that a grateful Queen Anne had begun to build for him before their friendship soured — a monument in stone to the greatest captain of his age.

entities/mary-ii.title: Mary II of England
entities/mary-ii.content:
Mary II of England
Summary
Mary II (r. 1689–1694), elder daughter of James II and Anne Hyde, reigned jointly with her husband William III after the Glorious Revolution. She was the most popular figure of the reign — gracious, charitable, and devout — and her death from smallpox at thirty-two was mourned as a national calamity. Burnet, who attended her in her final illness, calls her “the most universally lamented Princess, and deserved the best to be so, of any in our Age, or in our History.”

Birth, Education, and Marriage (1662–1677)
Mary was born at St. James’s Palace on 30 April 1662, the eldest surviving child of James, Duke of York (later James II) and his first wife, Anne Hyde. Charles II had obliged his brother to allow the two princesses — Mary and her younger sister Anne — to be educated in the Protestant faith, and Mary was raised in the Church of England under the guidance of her grandmother, the Dowager Queen Henrietta Maria, and later under the care of the Earl and Countess of Clarendon. She received a thorough grounding in religion, languages, and music, and was noted from her youth for a sweetness of temper and a serious piety that distinguished her from the fashionable libertinism of the Restoration court.
The marriage of the fifteen-year-old princess to her first cousin, William Henry of Orange, was concluded in the autumn of 1677. Charles II, alarmed by the growing power of France and the distrust of his Parliament, saw the match as a means of reassuring Protestant opinion. Hume records that the king “entertained proposals for marrying the prince of Orange to the lady Mary, the elder princess, and heir apparent to the crown.” William, who had never met his cousin, insisted on seeing her first. He was introduced to the princess at Newmarket and found her “in the bloom of youth, and extremely amiable both in her person and her behaviour.” The marriage was celebrated at St. James’s Palace on 4 November 1677 — William’s twenty-seventh birthday — and gave universal satisfaction: “All parties strove who should most applaud it.”
Mary accompanied her husband to Holland, where she adapted herself to the sober manners of the Dutch court with remarkable grace. She learned the language, embraced the Reformed religion with genuine warmth, and won the hearts of the Dutch people by her unaffected piety and her steady devotion to her husband. The marriage, though initially a political arrangement, ripened into a deep and genuine partnership.

The Glorious Revolution (1688–1689)
The birth of a son to James II and Mary of Modena in June 1688 — the Prince of Wales, a Catholic heir — threatened to displace Mary and William from the succession and tipped the crisis into revolution. William invaded England in November 1688, and James’s cause collapsed within weeks. Mary remained in Holland during the invasion, but her role in the constitutional settlement that followed was decisive.
In the debates of the Convention Parliament, it was by no means certain that William would accept the crown on any terms other than as king in his own right, not merely as the husband of a queen regnant. Burnet records a private conversation he had with the princess at The Hague in 1686, years before the Revolution, that settled the matter. When he asked Mary what she intended William’s status to be if she came to the throne, she at first assumed her husband would share her authority by right of marriage. Burnet explained the precedents of Henry VII and Queen Mary’s marriage to Philip of Spain, and warned that a “titular Kingship” would be unacceptable to a man of William’s temper. Mary answered without hesitation: she took no time to consider it. She would give William the real authority as soon as it came into her hands. She promised him “he should always bear rule,” and asked only that he obey the commandment “husbands love your wives” as she would obey “wives be obedient to your husbands.”
This understanding was honoured in the settlement of February 1689. The Convention Parliament declared that James had abdicated and that the throne was vacant, and on 13 February 1689 William and Mary were offered the crown jointly. William was to exercise the regal power in his own name; Mary was to be queen, but her authority was vested in her husband during his lifetime. They were crowned together at Westminster Abbey on 11 April 1689.

Joint Reign and Regency (1689–1694)
Mary’s role during her six-year reign was primarily that of regent during William’s prolonged absences on campaign. The king could not conduct the war against France from Whitehall; he needed to command his armies in Ireland and Flanders in person, and the constitution required that the government continue to function in his absence. Mary was left as regent, governing through a council of ministers, and she performed these duties with an efficiency and dignity that earned her the confidence of both Parliament and people.
In the summer of 1690, while William fought at the Boyne, Mary remained in London as regent — the French fleet under Tourville had just defeated the English and Dutch at Beachy Head, and the threat of invasion was real. She managed the crisis with composure, overseeing the defence of the kingdom and maintaining the unity of the administration. In subsequent years, when William campaigned in Flanders, she proved herself a capable and conscientious ruler, diligently applying herself to the business of state.
Mary was the most popular figure of the reign. Where William’s cold reserve and Dutch bluntness alienated many, Mary’s warmth, charity, and personal piety made her universally beloved. Burnet dwells on her “pious care” in the disposition of bishoprics, recording how she personally investigated the character of a bishop recommended for an Irish see and, discovering he laboured under an ill fame, withdrew her consent. She was a zealous patron of the Church of England and took a particular interest in the propagation of the Gospel in the colonies: it was through her advocacy that the College of William and Mary was founded in Virginia, a project she “espoused with a particular zeal.”
She was deeply affected by the death of Archbishop Tillotson in 1694, speaking of him “in the tenderest manner, and not without tears.” She pressed the king earnestly for Stillingfleet to succeed him, before yielding to the general wish for Tenison.

Piety and Character
Burnet, who knew Mary as well as any man, presents her as a woman of extraordinary piety and unimpeachable integrity. She rose early for private devotions, read the Scriptures daily, and was scrupulous in her religious duties without the least tincture of ostentation. Her household was a model of order and sobriety in an age of lax morals. She was generous to the poor, charitable in her judgments, and utterly devoid of personal ambition. When Burnet broached the subject of the crown with her in 1686, she had not even considered the question of her own authority — a naivety that speaks as much to her modesty as to her inexperience.
She wrote extensively — letters, meditations, and prayers — and Burnet himself wrote a book on her character, in which he claimed to have said “nothing but that which I knew to be strictly true, without the enlargement of Figure or Rhetorick.” Her letters to William during his absences, preserved by Dalrymple, reveal a woman of acute intelligence and deep emotional dependence on her husband, written in a vein of affectionate solicitude that stands in marked contrast to the formal stiffness of most royal correspondence.

Death from Smallpox (1694)
In December 1694, smallpox raged in London. Mary had never had the disease, and apprehensions were great. Burnet records her final illness in the most moving passages of his History:
She was taken ill, but the next day the symptoms seemed to abate. Burnet had the honour to spend half an hour with her that day, and she complained of nothing. The following day she went abroad, but her illness returned with such severity “that she could disguise it no longer.” She shut herself up in her closet that night, burnt many papers, and put the rest in order. Within two days the smallpox appeared with very bad symptoms. The physicians’ conduct was universally condemned: Dr. Ratcliffe was chiefly relied upon, and other physicians were not called until it was too late.
William was “struck with this beyond expression.” He came on the second day of her illness to pass the Triennial Bill, which otherwise might never have become law. The next day he called Burnet into his closet and “gave a free vent to a most tender passion,” bursting into tears and crying that “there was no hope of the Queen; and that, from being the happiest, he was now going to be the miserablest creature upon Earth.” He told Burnet that during the whole course of their marriage he had never known one single fault in her.
Archbishop Tenison, when the desperate condition was beyond doubt, told the king he could not do his duty faithfully unless he acquainted the queen with her danger. William approved. When the Archbishop prepared her with some address, “she presently apprehended his drift, but shewed no fear nor disorder upon it. She said, she thanked God she had always carried this in her mind, that nothing was to be left to the last hour.” She received the Sacrament on the day before she died, with all the attending bishops receiving it with her. “We were, God knows, a sorrowful Company; for we were losing her, who was our chief hope and glory on Earth.”
She died on 28 December 1694, about one in the morning, in the thirty-third year of her age and the sixth of her reign.

Aftermath and Legacy
The universal sorrow that followed her death was without precedent. Both Houses of Parliament walked in procession before the chariot that carried her body to Westminster Abbey, where they sat in form while the Archbishop preached the funeral sermon — an honour never before paid to any sovereign, since the death of a monarch had always dissolved Parliament. An act passed early in her reign, vesting the administration entirely in the king even after the queen’s death, prevented any constitutional crisis.
William’s grief was as great as it was just — greater, Burnet writes, “than those who knew him best thought his temper capable of.” He fainted often during her sickness, and after her death “his Spirits sunk so low, that there was great reason to apprehend that he was following her.” For weeks he was incapable of business or company. He turned himself to religion and secret prayer; Tenison was often and long with him. He would never marry again.
Mary II was the first queen regnant of England since Mary I to rule in her own right, and the first to share the throne with a husband who was king in fact as well as in name. Her constitutional position — a queen whose authority was exercised by her husband — was a unique settlement that satisfied the requirements of the Revolution without diminishing William’s capacity to wage war. She was the most genuinely beloved of the Stuarts, and her early death removed from the throne the one figure who might have softened the partisan divisions that marked the remainder of William’s reign. Her legacy survived in the institutions she fostered — the College of William and Mary, the Triennial Act, and the memory of a piety that Burnet held up as a model for Christian princes.

entities/monk-albemarle.title: George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle
entities/monk-albemarle.content:
George Monck, 1st Duke of Albemarle
Summary
George Monck (1608–1670), 1st Duke of Albemarle, was the most enigmatic figure of the English Revolution. A soldier who fought for the king, then for the parliament, then for the Protectorate, then single-handedly restored the monarchy — Monck’s career was a study in pragmatic loyalty. He commanded Cromwell’s army in Scotland, held the nation together after the Protector’s death, marched his Coldstream troops to London in 1660, and orchestrated the Restoration of Charles II with a minimum of bloodshed. Hume, who thought him a man of parts “more solid than shining,” observed that his decisive intervention “fortune, united to prudence, had enabled him to perform.” Created Duke of Albemarle, he went on to command the English fleet in the epic Four Days’ Battle of 1666 against the Dutch, an old soldier learning the sea at fifty-eight and fighting De Ruyter to a standstill. He died in 1670, leaving his reputation to the verdict of a grateful — and puzzled — nation.

Early Life and Military Apprenticeship
George Monck was born on 6 December 1608 at Potheridge, near Great Torrington in Devon, the second son of Sir Thomas Monck, a gentleman of ancient but reduced family. Lacking a settled estate, he sought his fortune by the sword — the common resource of younger sons in an age of incessant war. At sixteen he enlisted as a volunteer in the expedition to Cadiz (1625), and saw his first service in the disastrous descent upon the Spanish coast. He then served under Sir Richard Grenville and Lord Wimbledon in the Low Countries, where the Dutch war with Spain provided a harsh schooling in military discipline. In the Dutch service he fought at the famous Siege of Breda (1637) and rose to the rank of captain, learning the trade of war under the eyes of the finest soldiers in Europe.
Returning to England in 1638, he obtained a commission in the army being raised by Charles I against the Scots in the First Bishops’ War. His conduct in the sorry campaign of 1639 brought him to the notice of the Earl of Strafford, who appointed him lieutenant-colonel of a regiment in the Irish army.

The Civil War: Royalist, Prisoner, Parliamentarian
When the Civil War broke out in 1642, Monck naturally adhered to the king. He fought with the royalist forces in Ireland, where the rebellion of 1641 had already plunged the kingdom into confusion. But the king’s Irish army, cut off from reinforcement and command, was defeated by the parliamentary forces at Nantwich in January 1644. Monck was taken prisoner and sent to the Tower of London.
His imprisonment was not severe, and the parliament was eager to recruit capable officers. Monck, whose loyalty was to the profession of arms rather than to any party, accepted a commission in the parliamentary army. He served under General Fairfax with distinction, commanding a regiment of foot at the storming of Naseby (1645) and in the reduction of the west country. His military competence, discipline, and total lack of political enthusiasm marked him as a useful instrument — one who would obey orders without question.

Cromwell’s Commander in Scotland
In 1650, Cromwell appointed Monck as his lieutenant-general in Scotland, with the rank of colonel of foot in the New Model Army. He commanded a brigade at the Battle of Dunbar (3 September 1650), where Cromwell’s crushing victory over the Scots established the Commonwealth’s authority north of the border. After Cromwell departed for England, Monck remained as commander-in-chief in Scotland, reducing the remaining strongholds. He laid siege to Stirling Castle, which surrendered with all the records of the kingdom, and forced the submission of the Earl of Leven and other royalist lords. Hume records that “the successes which attended Monk in Scotland were no less decisive” than those of Cromwell himself. By 1654 he had completed the subjugation of the Highlands, building a chain of forts and governing the kingdom with a firm but not brutal hand.
His command in Scotland lasted nearly a decade. During those years he kept his army disciplined, his administration orderly, and his opinions opaque. He impressed no political character upon his soldiers — a remarkable feat in an army that had become a debating society for republicans, Fifth Monarchists, and Levellers. To all appearances, he was Cromwell’s most reliable subordinate.

The Protectorate Collapse and the March to London
When Oliver Cromwell died in September 1658, Monck immediately proclaimed Richard Cromwell as Protector and held Scotland quiet. But the new Protector’s regime collapsed within months, and the Rump Parliament was restored in May 1659. The army in England, faction-ridden and mutinous, expelled the Rump in October, and a Committee of Safety seized power. Monck, in Scotland, watched and waited.
From his headquarters at Coldstream on the Scottish border, Monck began his march south in November 1659. He declared for the parliament against the army’s Committee of Safety, and the country — exhausted by years of military rule — rallied to his standard. Lambert, sent north with a superior army to intercept him, found his own troops melting away; Monck’s discipline and reputation for fair dealing had preceded him.
He crossed the Tweed at Coldstream on New Year’s Day 1660 — the origin of the Coldstream Guards, the oldest continuously serving regiment in the British army — and marched slowly towards London. The Rump, restored to power by his advance, received him with fulsome thanks. But Monck had his own purposes. On 6 February 1660 he entered London and quartered his army at Westminster. The Rump, desperate to retain power, ordered him to suppress the City of London — to break down its gates and portcullises, and arrest its leading citizens. Monck obeyed in a rough show of force, then turned on his masters.

The Restoration of the Monarchy
On 11 February 1660, Monck wrote a letter to the parliament demanding writs for a new and free parliament within a week. He marched into the City and, at Guildhall, swore union with the citizens for the settlement of the commonwealth. The joy, Hume records, was universal: “The prospect of peace, concord, liberty, justice, broke forth at once from amidst the deepest darkness.” City bonfires roasted rumps in effigy; the long parliament was, in the popular mind, buried.
On 21 February, Monck readmitted the secluded members — those Presbyterians and moderate parliamentarians whom Pride’s Purge had expelled in 1648. They dissolved the Long Parliament for good and issued writs for a Convention Parliament. Monck, through his kinsman Morrice and Sir John Granville, opened a secret correspondence with Charles II in exile at Breda. The king issued the Declaration of Breda (April 1660), promising a general pardon, liberty of conscience, and satisfaction of army arrears. The Convention Parliament, overwhelmingly royalist, voted unanimously to restore the monarchy.
Charles landed at Dover on 25 May 1660. Monck met him on the beach. The king created him Duke of Albemarle, Knight of the Garter, and granted him extensive lands and offices. Hume notes that Monck, alone among the great men of the Revolution, was never suspected of aiming at the crown for himself: “His caution, reserve, and consummate prudence in the most critical junctures, were the qualities that most signalised his character.”

Naval Command and the Second Dutch War
In the Second Dutch War (1665–1667), the old soldier was called to a new element. On 23 April 1666, Albemarle went on board the fleet as joint commander with Prince Rupert. It was an extraordinary appointment: Monck was fifty-eight years old, had never commanded at sea, and was setting out to fight the greatest admiral of the age — Michiel de Ruyter.
Campbell records that Albemarle, like Blake before him, “thought that fighting was, almost on any terms, preferable to running away.” When intelligence arrived that the French fleet was sailing from Toulon to join the Dutch, Albemarle insisted on detaching Prince Rupert with twenty ships to intercept them. Sir George Ayscue protested against the temerity of fighting the Dutch with only sixty sail, but Albemarle’s authority prevailed.
The Four Days’ Battle (1–4 June 1666) followed — the longest naval engagement of the age of sail. The English had sixty ships against ninety-one Dutch, carrying 4,716 guns and 22,460 men. On the first day, Albemarle attacked before the Dutch could weigh anchor, and both fleets fought until nightfall. The second day saw Van Tromp surrounded and De Ruyter himself in desperate straits. On the third day, Albemarle was forced to retreat, burning three disabled ships and conducting the withdrawal with, in Campbell’s words, “wonderful courage and conduct.” He burnt the ships that were disabled, sailed before with those most torn, and brought up the rear with twenty-eight men-of-war. On the fourth day, with Prince Rupert rejoined, the fleets fought again until both were crippled. The outcome was a costly draw: the English lost sixteen ships, the Dutch fifteen.
Hume calls it “one of the most memorable battles that we read of in story,” and judges that Albemarle “made here some atonement by his valour for the rashness of the attempt.” The Dutch Pensioner De Witte said that “if the English were beat, their defeat did them more honour than all their former victories.”
On 25 July 1666, Albemarle and Rupert fought the St James’s Day Fight, a clear English victory. De Ruyter’s squadron was battered and forced to retreat; Admirals Evertz, De Vries, and Koenders were killed. The battle restored English prestige after the Four Days’ Battle, though the war as a whole ended in humiliation when De Ruyter broke the chain at Chatham and burned the fleet in the Medway (June 1667).

Death and Character
George Monck, Duke of Albemarle, died on 3 January 1670 at New Hall in Essex, aged sixty-one. He was buried in Westminster Abbey — a singular honour for a man who had fought against the king’s father, commanded the republic’s army, and then restored the monarchy. His death occasioned no controversy; he had outlived his enemies and kept his friends.
His character resists easy summary. He was not a man of brilliant intellect — Hume thought his capacity “not extensive” and that he appeared “unfit for the court, a scene of life to which he had never been accustomed.” But his judgment in the critical hour was unerring. He understood the one thing that no other commander in the revolutionary wars understood: that the army could not govern England, and that the only settlement the nation would accept was the return of the king. He had the patience to wait for that hour, the nerve to act when it came, and the modesty to step aside afterwards.
Campbell, who wrote his naval Memoirs with admiration, says simply that Albemarle was of the same spirit as Blake — a man who believed that the reputation of a maritime nation depended on fighting. Hume calls him “a man of plain sense, great integrity, and invincible firmness.” His political philosophy, if he had one, was fidelity to the established order — first to the king, then to the parliament, then to the Protector, and finally back to the king. He served every master faithfully while they governed, and abandoned them only when they had ceased to be the government.
Monck’s greatest achievement was the Restoration itself: a bloodless counter-revolution carried out by an army that could have turned England into a military dictatorship. That he did not seize the crown, that he restored it instead, is the measure of the man. He was — to borrow his own phrase — the instrument of providence; but he was also, in an age of fanatics and ideologues, a practical man who knew what England needed and had the courage to give it to her.
