entities/oliver-cromwell.title: Oliver Cromwell
entities/oliver-cromwell.content:
Oliver Cromwell
Summary
Oliver Cromwell (1599–1658), Lord Protector of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1653 until his death, was the most extraordinary figure of the English Revolution. A country gentleman turned soldier, a Puritan zealot turned statesman, and a regicide turned sovereign, Cromwell rose from private obscurity to command the New Model Army, overthrow the monarchy, and rule the British Isles as a military dictator cloaked in republican forms. Hume describes him as a man “suited to the age in which he lived, and to that alone” — equally capable of winning the affection of common soldiers by vulgar familiarity and of commanding the obedience of nations by daring enterprise. His legacy remains bitterly contested: to some, he was the champion of parliamentary liberty and Protestant conscience; to others, a hypocritical tyrant whose Irish campaign amounted to genocide and whose rule extinguished the very liberties he had professed to defend.

Early Life and Education
Oliver Cromwell was born at Huntingdon on 25 April 1599, the last year of the sixteenth century, of a good family — the Cromwells had risen under Henry VIII through the dissolution of the monasteries — but his father was a younger son, and Oliver inherited only a small estate. He was sent to Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge, but Hume records that “his genius was found little fitted for the calm and elegant occupations of learning, and he made small proficiencies in his studies.” He left the university on his father’s death in 1617 and appears to have thrown himself into a dissolute course of life: gaming, drinking, and country riots consumed his early years and dissipated part of his patrimony.
All of a sudden, the spirit of reformation seized him. He married Elizabeth Bourchier in 1620, affected a grave and composed behaviour, and entered into all the zeal and rigour of the puritanical party. He offered to restore to everyone whatever sums he had formerly gained by gaming. The same vehemence of temper that had transported him into the extremes of pleasure now distinguished his religious habits. His house became the resort of zealous clergy, and his hospitality to silenced ministers proved as chargeable as his former debaucheries. Though he acquired a tolerable fortune by a maternal uncle, he found his affairs so injured that he was obliged to take a farm at St Ives and apply himself to agriculture. His active mind, superior to the low occupations to which he was condemned, preyed upon itself; he indulged his imagination in visions, illuminations, and revelations — the nourishment of that hypochondriacal temper to which he was ever subject.
He had made a plan with John Hampden, his near kinsman, to transport himself to New England; only an order of council obliged them to disembark and remain in England. His first public opportunity came when he opposed the Earl of Bedford’s drainage of the fens near Ely, revealing the factious zeal and obstinacy that would mark his later career.

Member of Parliament
Cromwell was elected MP for Huntingdon in the Short Parliament (April 1640) and for Cambridge in the Long Parliament (November 1640). In the Commons, he was at first an obscure figure, notable chiefly for his passionate Puritan speeches and his plain, rustic dress. But he attached himself to the war party — those who distrusted any accommodation with the king — and made common cause with Hampden, Pym, and the fiery republicans. Hume notes that Cromwell professed the most exalted sentiments of liberty; he declared to Lord Falkland that “he would not have a drop of blood drawn from the king, but for the security of the laws and liberties of the kingdom.” These professions were accepted at face value by many who would later have reason to reflect on them.

Military Rise: The Ironsides
When war broke out in 1642, Cromwell raised a troop of horse in Cambridgeshire. He proved a natural cavalry commander. His troopers — recruited not from mercenaries or pressed men but from yeoman farmers who shared his Puritan zeal — were subjected to strict discipline and religious instruction. They sang psalms before battle and fought with a conviction that royalist cavalry, for all their gentlemanly courage, could not match. These became the famous Ironsides, the crack cavalry regiment of the parliamentary army.
Cromwell served under the Earl of Manchester in the Eastern Association. At the Battle of Marston Moor (2 July 1644), his disciplined troopers charged and broke Prince Rupert’s cavalry on the royalist right wing. Cromwell himself was wounded in the neck but pressed the pursuit. When he returned to find the parliamentary left wing routed, he rallied his men and, in a second engagement, secured the victory. Marston Moor was the first great parliamentary triumph of the war, and Cromwell’s reputation was made.
He was instrumental in pushing through the Self-Denying Ordinance (1645), which required members of parliament to resign their military commands — but Cromwell was expressly excepted. The New Model Army, a single professional force organised by Fairfax with Cromwell as lieutenant-general, was the instrument that would decide the war.

Naseby and the Decisive Victory
At the Battle of Naseby (14 June 1645), Cromwell commanded the right wing of the New Model Army. While Prince Rupert swept Ireton’s left wing from the field, Cromwell overbore Sir Marmaduke Langdale’s royalist cavalry on the opposite flank. He then turned his horsemen back upon the king’s infantry — a manoeuvre of decisive tactical genius — and threw them into confusion. Only one regiment of royalist foot held its ground; Fairfax broke it in a personal charge, seizing the colours with his own hand. The king’s army was annihilated: five hundred officers and four thousand men taken prisoner, all artillery and ammunition captured, and the king’s cabinet of correspondence seized — the publication of which fatally damaged Charles I’s reputation.
Naseby destroyed the royalist cause. The remaining towns surrendered one by one. Cromwell, now recognised as the soul of the New Model Army, conducted a series of swift sieges that reduced the west of England by the end of 1645.

Political Rise: The Independent Faction
As the war drew to a close, a rift opened between the Presbyterian majority in parliament and the Independent faction in the army. The Presbyterians wanted a negotiated settlement with the king, a Presbyterian church settlement, and the disbandment of the army. The Independents — Cromwell foremost among them — wanted liberty of conscience, security for the army’s arrears, and guarantees against royal revenge. Hume presents Cromwell as the master of this crisis, directing events from behind the scenes while maintaining an appearance of deference to civil authority.
In 1647, the army seized the king’s person from parliamentary custody. Cromwell and his son-in-law Henry Ireton negotiated with Charles — the Heads of the Proposals — demanding a constitutional monarchy, biennial parliaments, and toleration. But Charles, believing he could play the Scots, the Presbyterians, and the army off against each other, prevaricated. When the king escaped to the Isle of Wight and signed the Engagement with the Scots, a second civil war became inevitable.

Pride’s Purge and the King’s Trial
Cromwell crushed the royalist insurgency with devastating efficiency. At Preston (17 August 1648), he attacked the Scots under Hamilton and Langdale with only eight thousand men against twenty thousand. He defeated Langdale’s corps, routed Hamilton, and pursued him to Utoxeter, where the Scottish commander surrendered. Marching into Scotland, Cromwell joined Argyle and placed power in the hands of the extreme Presbyterian party.
By the time he returned to London, the army had resolved to bring the king to justice. On 6 December 1648, Colonel Pride forcibly excluded some 140 Presbyterian MPs from the House of Commons — Pride’s Purge — leaving only the Rump of about sixty members who would do the army’s bidding. Hume leaves no doubt that Cromwell, though not physically present in London, was the architect of this coup.
Cromwell was among the commissioners of the High Court of Justice that tried the king. He signed the death warrant for the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649 — an act he later insisted was “a necessary work” and “a thing of God’s own bringing to pass.” Hume recounts a story that Cromwell, after the execution, visited the king’s body and was heard to murmur, “Cruel necessity.” The regicide made Cromwell a pariah in the eyes of every crowned head in Europe and bound him irrevocably to the survival of the republic.

Conquest of Ireland: Drogheda and Wexford
In August 1649, Cromwell was dispatched to Ireland to suppress the coalition of Irish Catholics and Royalists under the Marquess of Ormond. He landed at Dublin with an experienced army and immediately marched on Drogheda (Tredah). The town was well fortified with a garrison of three thousand under Sir Arthur Aston. Cromwell, knowing the importance of speed, assaulted the breach after only a short siege. Though twice repulsed, he renewed the attack with Ireton at his side and carried the town by storm. Orders were given to give no quarter. “Cromwell pretended to retaliate by this severe execution the cruelty of the Irish massacre,” writes Hume, “but he well knew that almost the whole garrison was English; and his justice was only a barbarous policy, in order to terrify all other garrisons from resistance.”
At Wexford, a similar massacre followed when the town fell prematurely. The policy worked: town after town surrendered without resistance. By the time Cromwell was recalled to England in May 1650, Ireland was broken. He left the government to Ireton, who continued the work of subduing and dispossessing the Catholic population under the Act of Settlement. The memory of Drogheda has made Cromwell a figure of execration in Irish history for centuries.

Conquest of Scotland: Dunbar and Worcester
With Ireland subdued, Cromwell was summoned to face the greater danger: the Scots had crowned Charles II and were arming for an invasion of England. Fairfax, scrupling to invade a Presbyterian ally, resigned the command. Cromwell succeeded him as captain-general of all the forces in England — the decisive step towards sovereign power.
Cromwell invaded Scotland with sixteen thousand men. The Scottish commander, David Lesley, adopted a Fabian strategy, refusing battle and entrenching in fortified positions. Disease and supply shortages reduced the English army. But on 3 September 1650, Cromwell caught Lesley at a disadvantage near Dunbar, attacked, and won a stunning victory. About three thousand Scots were killed and ten thousand taken prisoner. Cromwell wrote that “the Lord hath done great things for us.”
When Charles II marched into England with a Scottish army the following year, Cromwell pursued and trapped him at Worcester. On 3 September 1651 — the first anniversary of Dunbar — he attacked the city from three sides and annihilated the royalist army. Charles escaped after six weeks of fugitive wandering, famously hiding in an oak tree at Boscobel. Worcester was Cromwell’s “crowning mercy” — the last battle of the civil wars.

The Lord Protector
Military victory presented a political problem. The Rump Parliament had governed since the king’s execution but had lost all public credit, devoting itself to self-perpetuation and private interest. On 20 April 1653, Cromwell entered the chamber in anger, denounced the members as drunkards and whoremasters, and — with a troop of soldiers — expelled them. “The Lord has done with you,” he shouted. “You are no parliament.”
The Barebone’s Parliament (July–December 1653), an assembly of 140 Puritan “saints” nominated by the army, proved unworkable. The moderate members resigned their power into Cromwell’s hands, and the Instrument of Government — the first written constitution in English history — was adopted. It vested executive authority in a single person as Lord Protector, with a council of state and a triennial parliament.
Cromwell was installed as Lord Protector on 16 December 1653. He refused the title of king on three occasions — most famously in 1657 when the Humble Petition and Advice offered him the crown — but his authority was monarchical in all but name. He lived at Whitehall, maintained a court, appointed peers, and commanded the armed forces. Hume observes that he was sincere in refusing the crown; he knew the army, which had been taught that kingship was a usurpation upon Christ, would never accept it.

Puritan Rule and Domestic Administration
Cromwell’s domestic administration displayed, in Hume’s judgment, “as great regard both to justice and clemency as his usurped authority, derived from no law, and founded only on the sword, could possibly permit.” The judges were men of integrity; the law was, for ordinary subjects, the great rule of conduct. He divided the country into eleven military districts under major-generals, charged with suppressing royalist conspiracies and enforcing Puritan morality. Stage plays were banned; horse racing, bear-baiting, and cock-fighting were suppressed; the observance of the Sabbath was strictly enforced.
He established liberty of conscience for all Protestant denominations except Anglicans and, for a time, Catholics. The Church of England was replaced by a system of “tryers” — commissioners who examined candidates for the ministry not on their learning but on their progress in grace. Cromwell was familiar and easy with the “saints” of all denominations, talking spiritually with them, weeping, sighing, and praying, while always retaining political control. “I am the only man,” he was heard to say, “who has known how to subdue that insolent sect [the Presbyterians], which can suffer none but itself.”

Foreign Policy: The Western Design
Cromwell’s foreign policy was ambitious, aggressive, and confessional. He saw England as a Protestant power destined to challenge the Catholic Habsburg hegemony. His first major initiative was peace with the Dutch Republic (April 1654), ending the first Anglo-Dutch War (1652–1654) on terms favourable to England, including the Navigation Act that excluded Dutch shipping from English trade.
He then launched the Western Design against Spain’s American empire. An expedition under Admiral Penn and General Venables sailed for the West Indies in 1654 and attacked Hispaniola in April 1655 — a disastrous failure. The English troops were poorly led and the Spanish defences were stronger than expected. As consolation, the expedition seized Jamaica, which surrendered without serious resistance. Jamaica proved a valuable acquisition, though Hume calls the whole scheme “imprudent and impolitic.”
The war with Spain (1655–1659) was Cromwell’s most characteristic undertaking: a Protestant crusade conducted with English sea power. Admiral Blake destroyed the Spanish treasure fleet at Santa Cruz de Tenerife in April 1657 — “the last and greatest action of the gallant Blake.” Cromwell allied with France against Spain, and in 1658, English troops under Turenne distinguished themselves at the Battle of the Dunes, capturing Dunkirk, which was delivered to English possession. France’s Cardinal Mazarin called Cromwell “a fortunate madman.”
The protector’s foreign policy, for all its recklessness, restored English prestige abroad. Hume concedes that “the great mind of this successful usurper was intent on spreading the renown of the English nation” and that he made the name of Englishman as feared and revered as that of a Roman.

Death
Cromwell’s last years were tormented. His health declined under the weight of public cares; he was haunted by the fear of assassination, wearing armour under his clothes and carrying pistols; never sleeping three nights in the same chamber; and never moving without strong guards. His daughter Elizabeth Claypole, his favourite child, lay dying and urged him to repent of his bloody measures. His son-in-law Fleetwood reproached him for personal ambition. The royalists and the republicans conspired; the army was mutinous.
A slow fever seized him, changing into a tertian ague. His chaplains assured him of recovery by divine revelation, and he dismissed the physicians: “I am well assured of my recovery. It is promised by the Lord.” But the symptoms worsened. On 3 September 1658 — his fortunate day, the anniversary of Dunbar and Worcester — he expired. A violent tempest burst in the wake of his death. He was buried with more than royal pomp in Westminster Abbey, only to be exhumed at the Restoration, hanged in his shroud at Tyburn, and beheaded: his head displayed on a pole outside Westminster Hall for a quarter-century.

Character and Legacy
Cromwell’s character, Hume writes, has been painted by his admirers as extravagant panegyric and by his enemies as virulent invective — and both are supported by striking circumstances. He was a man of boundless courage and tactical genius, the finest cavalry commander of his age. He was also a consummate dissembler, able to weep on demand and to cloak the most cold-blooded policy in the language of divine inspiration. His Puritan piety was both genuine and instrumental; the same emotional intensity that drove his religious ecstasies also drove his most ruthless decisions.
His military achievements were extraordinary: he rose from obscurity to command the most formidable army in Europe, conquered Ireland, subdued Scotland, and destroyed the royalist cause in England. His foreign policy made England a power to be reckoned with. His domestic rule was efficient, just in ordinary cases, and remarkable for its religious toleration — a rare virtue in an age of persecution.
But the means by which he attained power were violent and lawless: the purging of parliament, the execution of the king, the massacres in Ireland, the military dictatorship. He left no constitutional settlement that outlasted him. Within two years of his death, the monarchy was restored and his corpse was dragged from its grave.
Cromwell was, in the last analysis, a man of the crisis: a revolutionary who could break but could not build, a soldier who could conquer but could not legitimise, a Puritan who could pray but could not forgive. His body was no sooner in the grave than the edifice of his power began to crumble. Richard Cromwell, his son and designated successor, meekly resigned the protectorship. The republic collapsed. And the nation, weary of saints and soldiers, called back the king.

entities/prince-rupert.title: Prince Rupert of the Rhine
entities/prince-rupert.content:
Prince Rupert of the Rhine
Summary
Prince Rupert of the Rhine (1619–1682), grandson of James I and nephew of Charles I, was the most dashing royalist commander of the English Civil War, a pioneering privateer in the Interregnum, an admiral in the Restoration navy, and — less expectedly — a founding fellow of the Royal Society and an accomplished mezzotint artist. Hume calls him a commander of “promptitude and courage”; Campbell praises him as “too honest and too brave a man to neglect his duty.” But he was also impetuous, wilful, and prone to the reckless pursuit of victory that cost his uncle the war. The same qualities that made him the terror of parliamentary cavalry at Edgehill made him, at Naseby, chase glory while Cromwell seized the day.

German Upbringing and English Vocation (1619–1642)
Rupert was born at Prague in 1619, the third son of Frederick V, Elector Palatine and briefly King of Bohemia (“the Winter King”), and Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of James I of England. His family was driven into exile when Frederick’s brief reign collapsed after the Battle of the White Mountain, and Rupert grew up in the Dutch Republic, educated at the University of Leiden. He saw his first military service at fourteen in the Dutch wars against Spain, fighting beside the Prince of Orange. Tall, dark, and imperious, he was marked from youth by what contemporaries called a “hott and violent” temper — and by a charisma that made men follow him into impossible dangers. In 1636 he visited the court of his uncle Charles I, but returned to the continent to fight in the Thirty Years’ War, where he was captured and imprisoned by the Imperialists for three years. Released in 1641, he arrived in England in August 1642 as civil war broke out, accompanied by his younger brother Prince Maurice.

Civil War: The Cavalier General (1642–1645)
Rupert was appointed General of the Horse by Charles I and immediately justified his reputation. At Powick Bridge (23 September 1642), he routed a parliamentary cavalry force under Colonel John Brown, scattering them with a charge so furious that the encounter “mightily raised the reputation of the royalists.” At Edgehill (23 October 1642), his first major battle, Rupert crashed through the parliamentary left wing and pursued them for two miles — but the pursuit became a rout, and in his absence the royalist centre was wrecked. The battle was a draw, but the pattern was set: Rupert could win a charge, but could not hold a victory.
He stormed Bristol (26 July 1643) for the king, taking the city by assault and capturing its parliamentary garrison — his greatest single achievement of the war. He took Newark (March 1644), relieving the besieged town and securing the king’s lines of communication. In 1644 he was created Earl of Holderness and Duke of Cumberland, and ordered north to relieve York, besieged by the Scots and parliamentarians. He marched through Lancashire collecting forces and joined the Marquis of Newcastle’s army outside York.
Marston Moor (2 July 1644)
At Marston Moor, the largest battle of the war, Rupert commanded the royalist right wing opposite Oliver Cromwell’s cavalry. The battle was fought late in the evening, and for two hours the outcome hung in the balance. Rupert’s initial charge broke the parliamentary left, but his men fell into disorder plundering the enemy baggage. Cromwell, seeing his opportunity, wheeled his disciplined Ironsides and struck the royalist flank. The result, in Hume’s words, was that “the victory seemed long undecided between them” — but Cromwell’s veterans, “inured to danger under that determined leader, animated by zeal,” carried the day. The north was lost for the king. Rupert drew off the remains of his army into Lancashire; York surrendered a fortnight later.
Naseby (14 June 1645)
After the formation of the New Model Army, the king’s cause was desperate. At Naseby, Rupert again commanded the right wing and again swept all before him — breaking Ireton’s cavalry, pursuing with “his usual celerity and usual success.” But he was “so inconsiderate as to lose time in summoning and attacking the artillery of the enemy.” Meanwhile Cromwell crushed Langdale on the royalist left, then wheeled on the king’s infantry. Hume’s judgment is damning: “Prince Rupert, sensible too late of his error, left the fruitless attack on the enemy’s artillery, and joined the king, whose infantry was now totally discomfited.” The king’s cabinet was captured, with his correspondence to the queen published to discredit him. Naseby broke the royalist cause.
The Surrender of Bristol
Rupert threw himself into Bristol with orders to hold it at all costs. He wrote to the king that he could defend the city for four months. But when Fairfax’s forces breached the outer lines on 10 September 1645, Rupert capitulated the next day. Hume writes: “so precarious in most men is this quality of military courage! a poorer defence was not made by any town during the whole war.” Charles, “full of indignation,” recalled all Rupert’s commissions and sent him a pass to go beyond sea. It was a bitter end to the prince’s English military career. Rupert demanded a court-martial to clear his name, and was acquitted, but the king never fully trusted him again.

Exile and the Privateering Years (1646–1660)
Rupert left England in 1646, serving briefly with the French army. After Charles I’s execution in 1649, he gathered a small royalist fleet and operated as a privateer against Commonwealth shipping. Based first at Kinsale in Ireland, then driven out by Blake’s blockade, he sailed to the Mediterranean, capturing prizes near Toulon, Malaga, and Carthagena. Blake pursued him relentlessly — the great parliamentary admiral chased Rupert out of Irish waters, into the Tagus, and across the Mediterranean. Rupert’s flagship, the Constant Reformation, was a constant threat to English merchantmen. Campbell records that he “took many prizes… acting entirely on his own head, and without asking or receiving any directions from the king.” He lost his brother Prince Maurice in a hurricane in 1652, a blow from which he never fully recovered. By 1653 his squadron was broken up, and he returned to the exiled Stuart court in Paris, impoverished and politically sidelined.

Restoration and Naval Command (1660–1673)
At the Restoration in 1660, Rupert returned to England with Charles II. He was appointed to the Privy Council and given a pension, but was not restored to military command — the king remembered Bristol. He found a second vocation at sea. In the Second Dutch War (1665–1667), he served as admiral of the white squadron under the Duke of York. In the Four Days’ Battle (1–4 June 1666), the longest naval engagement of the age of sail, Rupert was detached with a squadron to intercept the French fleet. Hearing the guns, he turned back and rejoined Albemarle just in time, as Burnet records, to save the English fleet from destruction. “He came in good time,” Burnet writes, “and the Dutch, who had suffered much, drew off.”
In the Third Dutch War (1672–1674), Rupert commanded at Solebay (28 May 1672) as admiral of the white. The English fleet under the Duke of York was surprised at anchor; Rupert’s squadron fought a desperate defensive action. The battle was indecisive with heavy losses on both sides — Lord Sandwich was killed when his flagship Royal James was burnt. In 1673, with the Duke of York removed from command by the Test Act, Rupert was appointed commander-in-chief of the fleet. He fought the bloody and indecisive battles of Schooneveld (28 May and 4 June 1673) and the Battle of Texel (11 August 1673) against De Ruyter. At Texel, Campbell records an extraordinary scene: when Sir Edward Spragge’s flagship was disabled and Spragge himself drowned, Rupert “drew near the blue squadron… the first thing his highness did, was to send two frigates to take the Royal Prince in tow. He then steered in between the enemy and the lame ships.” But the Dutch commander Tromp had the weather-gage, and the English could not force a decisive action. The campaign ended in stalemate; the war was unpopular, and England made a separate peace in 1674.

Scientist, Artist, and Courtier
Rupert was a man of surprising intellectual range. He was an early member and fellow of the Royal Society — the first prince to be admitted — and Sprat’s History of the Royal Society records that he communicated experiments on “a sort of powder, twenty times as strong as the common pistol-powder” and other mechanical inventions. He was a pioneer of the mezzotint engraving technique, which he learned from the German soldier-artist Ludwig von Siegen and introduced to England. His mezzotints — notably The Great Executioner and studies of soldiers and beggars — are still valued by print collectors. He also interested himself in naval architecture, hydraulics, improved gunpowder, and the manufacture of brass cannon. In politics, Hume notes that in his later years he was “suspected of a bias to the country party” and “for that reason much neglected at court.”

Death and Character
Rupert died on 29 November 1682 at his house in Spring Gardens, Westminster, in the sixty-third year of his age. By his own wish he was buried with simple ceremony in Westminster Abbey.
His character was a study in contradictions. Hume praises his “promptitude and courage” but notes that he lacked the patience and discipline to complete what he began. Burnet, writing of his later naval command, records that the captains “cross’d him all they could, and complained of every thing he did. In a word they said, he had neither sense nor conduct left” — though Burnet himself inclines to blame the poisonous atmosphere of faction rather than the prince’s real abilities. Campbell sums him up: “too wise to be fond of this service, yet too honest and too brave a man to neglect his duty.” He was dashing and chivalrous, the very image of the Cavalier — but the impetuosity that made him a terror on the battlefield was the same quality that lost Marston Moor, wasted Naseby, and surrendered Bristol. In the navy he found a second life, and his service against De Ruyter in 1673, though ultimately fruitless, was honourable. He never married, but left two illegitimate children.

entities/robert-blake.title: Robert Blake — General at Sea
entities/robert-blake.content:
Robert Blake
Summary
Robert Blake (1598–1657), General at Sea of the Commonwealth of England, was the first great commander of the English professional navy and the man who established the tradition of naval dominance that would be perfected by Nelson a century and a half later. A land officer past fifty when first sent to sea, he learned the art of naval war with astonishing speed, defeated the Dutch in the battles of the First Anglo-Dutch War, burned the Barbary corsairs in their own harbours, and destroyed the Spanish treasure fleet in the Bay of Santa Cruz — an action that Lord Clarendon called the boldest ever attempted. Hume called him “the most perfect character of the age, and the least stained with those errors and violences which were then so predominant.”

Early Life as a Merchant and Soldier
Robert Blake was born at Bridgwater, Somerset, in August 1598, the eldest son of a substantial merchant family. He was educated at Oxford, where he entered St Alban’s Hall in 1615, but left without a degree on the death of his father. Returning to Bridgwater, he engaged in trade as a merchant; little is known of this period of his life, though his fellow townsmen held him in sufficient regard to elect him to the Short Parliament of 1640 as burgess for Bridgwater. He was returned again for the same borough to the Long Parliament.
When civil war broke out in 1642, Blake, then forty-four years old and without any military experience, accepted a captain’s commission in the parliamentary army. His aptitude for war proved immediate. He was given the command of the garrisons of Lyme Regis and later Taunton, where he displayed the unyielding obstinacy that would mark his naval career. At Taunton, Hume records, he suffered a long siege from Sir Richard Granville, who commanded an army of some eight thousand men; and though the defence had been obstinate, the garrison was reduced to the last extremity. Fairfax’s relief of Taunton in 1645 preserved Blake’s command and his reputation. His resistance at Lyme had already frustrated Prince Maurice’s royalist forces in the West Country.

Appointed General at Sea
In February 1649, after the execution of Charles I, the Commonwealth parliament removed the Earl of Warwick from the command of the fleet and replaced him with three colonels — Blake, Deane, and Popham — who were given the title “Generals at Sea.” Campbell records that the fleet “was put into the hands of land-officers, such as Blake, Deane, and Popham, who, notwithstanding, behaved well, quickly gained the love of the sailors, and grew in a short time very knowing seamen themselves.”
Blake’s first commission was to pursue Prince Rupert, whose squadron of some twenty-five ships had deserted the parliament and was raiding English commerce from the port of Kinsale, in Ireland. Blake and Popham were ordered “to block up the prince’s squadron in the port of Kinsale, which they accordingly did, and reduced them to such extremities, that his men began to desert in great numbers.” Rupert forced his way out on 24 October 1649 with the loss of three ships and sailed for the Mediterranean.

The Pursuit of Prince Rupert
Blake pursued Rupert to the coast of Portugal. The prince took shelter in the Tagus; the king of Portugal, favouring the royal cause, refused Blake admittance. Blake responded by seizing twenty Portuguese ships richly laden — a decision that compelled the king of Portugal to negotiate with the Commonwealth. Blake wrote a letter in strong terms to the king of Spain demanding the delivery of any of Rupert’s ships that might fall into Spanish hands; the Spanish king returned a very civil answer and sent Blake a ring worth fifteen hundred pounds.
In the river of Lisbon, in September and October 1650, Blake ruined the Brazil fleet, which induced the Portuguese to force Rupert out of their port. The prince fled to Carthagena; Blake pursued him thither, but shortage of provisions compelled the English admiral to put to sea, and Rupert escaped to Malaga. A general terror, Campbell notes, was occasioned in the courts of Spain and Portugal by Blake’s destruction of Rupert’s fleet. Both powers dispatched ambassadors to England “to acknowledge the power of the parliament.” The reduction of the Scilly Isles and Jersey followed in 1651, securing the sovereignty of the narrow seas for the Commonwealth.

The First Anglo-Dutch War
The Battle of Dover, 19 May 1652
The First Anglo-Dutch War began with an encounter between Blake and the celebrated Dutch admiral Maarten Tromp. Tromp, with a fleet of forty-two sail, appeared in the Downs and, according to his own account, was forced in by stress of weather. Blake, with only fifteen ships, fired at his flag three times; Tromp returned a broadside. The battle lasted from four in the afternoon till nine at night; Bourne joined Blake with eight ships, and the Dutch bore away. Blake’s victory, against such odds, was celebrated throughout England. The States-General, “so sensible of their being in the wrong, and at the same time so mortified that their fleet, notwithstanding its superiority, had been beaten,” sent ambassadors to treat — but the terms demanded were too high, and war was proclaimed in Holland on 8 July 1652.
The Battle of Kentish Knock, 28 September 1652
Blake, now commanding about sixty ships, engaged the Dutch fleet under De Witte near the Kentish Knock. He divided his fleet into three squadrons, commanded by himself, Vice-admiral Penn, and Rear-admiral Bourne. After a sharp engagement during which the Dutch were roughly handled — one of their admirals was taken, two ships sunk, and a third blown up — De Witte retired. Blake pursued as far as twelve leagues from the Dutch shore, then returned in triumph to the Downs. The Dutch lost no fewer than twenty captains who “withdrew out of the line of battle.”
The Battle of Dungeness, 29 November 1652
Blake had detached twenty ships to convoy the Newcastle colliers, twelve more to Plymouth, and fifteen were in the river for repairs. Tromp, learning that Blake had only thirty-seven ships, attacked him off Dungeness with seventy sail. Blake fought with desperate courage. His own ship, the Triumph, the Victory, and the Vanguard bore the whole weight of the Dutch attack. The Garland and the Bonaventure were taken after their captains were killed. Blake pushed so far to their relief that he was nearly taken himself. He was forced to retreat to the Thames. Tromp sailed into the Channel with a broom at his topmast-head, signifying he would sweep the English from the seas. The parliament, showing steadiness, caressed Blake after his defeat and named him, in conjunction with Deane and Monk, General at Sea for another year.
The Battle of Portland, 18–20 February 1653
In six weeks the Commonwealth fitted out a fleet of sixty sail. Blake and Deane, on board the Triumph, led twelve stout ships and fell in with Tromp on 18 February. Blake was wounded in the thigh by a piece of iron; the same shot tore Deane’s coat and breeches. Captain Ball was killed at Blake’s feet; his secretary was shot receiving orders. A hundred seamen were lost on the Triumph alone. The battle raged for three days. The Dutch lost eleven men of war and thirty merchantmen. Blake had used soldiers on board his ships to good effect. Though Blake was badly wounded, the Dutch were clearly beaten.
The Battle of the Gabbard (North Foreland), 2–3 June 1653
Monk and Deane commanded the English fleet of ninety-five sail. On the first day, the brave Admiral Deane was cut in two by a chain-shot at the start of the action; Monk, with great presence of mind, covered the body and kept the flag flying, so the fleet did not know of the loss. The Dutch fell into confusion. That night Blake arrived with a squadron of eighteen ships and took part in the second day’s engagement. The fight resumed at eight in the morning with the utmost fury. Vice-admiral Penn boarded Tromp twice. A general flight followed. The Dutch lost six ships sunk, two blown up, and eleven taken — including a vice-admiral and two rear-admirals — while the English lost Admiral Deane and one captain. The Dutch ports were now blocked; the sight of a foreign fleet at their doors excited domestic tumults in Holland and compelled the States to sue for peace.
Tromp was killed in the final battle of the war off the Texel on 31 July 1653, in which Monk commanded. Peace was concluded on 4 April 1654, with the Dutch acknowledging the dominion of the English at sea, consenting to strike the flag, and submitting to the Navigation Act.

The Mediterranean Campaign: Barbary Pirates
After the Dutch war, Admiral Blake was sent into the Mediterranean in the summer of 1654 with a great fleet. His orders, to be opened at sea, were to “procure satisfaction from such princes and states as had either insulted the government, or injured the commerce of England.” He first visited Leghorn, where he compelled the Grand Duke of Tuscany to pay sixty thousand pounds compensation for damages suffered by English shipping during the Dutch war.
Thence he proceeded to Algiers, arriving 10 March 1655, and demanded satisfaction for piracy and the release of English captives. The Dey temporised. Blake sailed to Tunis, where he sent a similar message and received the defiant answer: “Here are our castles of Guletta and Porto Ferino: you may do your worst; we do not fear you.” Blake entered the bay of Porto Ferino, came within musket-shot of the castle and lines, and so warmly plied them with cannon that the fortifications were soon in a defenceless condition. He resolved to burn the nine Tunisian ships in the road. Every captain manned his long-boat with choice men; these entered the harbour and fired the corsair ships while the fleet covered them from the castle. All the ships were burnt with the loss of only twenty-five men killed and forty-eight wounded. “This daring action spread the terror of his name through Africa and Asia,” writes Campbell, “which had long been formidable in Europe.” From Tunis Blake sailed to Tripoli and concluded a peace with that government; returning to Tunis, he compelled the inhabitants to sue for peace on terms “mortifying to them, glorious for him, and profitable for his country.”

The Destruction of the Spanish Fleet at Santa Cruz de Tenerife, April 1657
The war with Spain having begun, Blake cruised before Cadiz through the winter of 1656–57. In April 1657 he learned that a Spanish treasure fleet — six great galleons richly laden and ten other vessels — had put into the Bay of Santa Cruz in the island of Tenerife. He immediately sailed thither.
The bay was secured by a strong castle well supplied with artillery, seven forts united by a line of communication lined with musketeers, and a barricado boom before the port. The Spanish governor, when warned that Blake would attack, answered tartly: “Get you gone, if you will, and let Blake come, if he dares.”
Blake called a council of war. It was resolved to destroy the fleet, though it was impossible to bring the ships off. He sent Captain Stayner with a squadron to force the passage into the bay while the other frigates played on the forts and lines. Stayner’s squadron was quickly supported by Blake with the whole fleet, who boarded the Spanish galleons, made himself master of them all, and set them on fire. The entire Spanish fleet was burnt to the water’s edge, except two ships that sank outright. Then, the wind shifting to the south-west, Blake passed with his fleet safely out of the bay again, losing no more than forty-eight men killed and about one hundred and twenty wounded.
“It was without question the boldest undertaking of its kind that had ever been performed,” writes Campbell. “The Spaniards, who are romantic enough in their own conduct, were so much astonished at his, that they quite lost their spirits, and thenceforward never thought themselves safe either from numbers or fortifications.”
Lord Clarendon’s assessment became the classic verdict: “He was the first man who brought ships to contemn castles on shore, which had been thought ever very formidable, and were discovered by him to make a noise only, and to fright those who could be rarely hurt by them. He was the first that infused that proportion of courage into the seamen, by making them see by experience what mighty things they could do, if they were resolved; and taught them to fight in fire, as well as upon water.”

Death at Sea
After Santa Cruz, Blake cruised again off Cadiz. His health, which had suffered from three continuous years at sea, was failing — a complication of dropsy and scurvy. He resolved to sail for England. As his ship, the St George, entered Plymouth Sound on 17 August 1657, he expired within sight of his native land. He was about fifty-nine years of age.
His body was embalmed, his bowels buried at Plymouth, and his corpse conveyed to Greenwich, whence the protector ordered a magnificent funeral procession to Westminster Abbey. He was interred in the chapel of Henry VII. At the Restoration, his body was removed from the abbey with others buried during the troubles; it was decently reinterred in the churchyard. Though a republican by principle, he was esteemed even by the royalists. Hume records his characteristic remark to his seamen: “It is still our duty to fight for our country, into what hands soever the government may fall.”

Legacy: Founder of England’s Professional Navy
Robert Blake transformed the English navy from an auxiliary arm into a formidable instrument of national power. Before him, English admirals had been cautious, valuing above all the safety of their ships; Blake taught the navy to fight aggressively, to attack fortifications, and to take risks for decisive results. He was the first to show that ships could engage coastal fortifications on equal terms, a lesson that would be taken up by Nelson at Copenhagen and by every great admiral who followed.
The Commonwealth period, with Blake, Deane, Monk, Penn, and Lawson, created the professional officer corps — men raised by merit rather than birth — that would carry the Royal Navy through the wars of the following century. Blake’s fusion of military discipline with naval command — his use of soldiers on board ship, his tactical innovations in line-of-battle fighting — laid the foundations of England’s maritime supremacy. Dr Bate’s epitaph sums it: “He humbled the pride of France, reduced Portugal to reason, broke the naval force of Holland, and drove them to the shelter of their ports, suppressed the rovers of Barbary, and twice triumphed over Spain.”

entities/samuel-pepys.title: Samuel Pepys
entities/samuel-pepys.content:
Samuel Pepys
Summary
Samuel Pepys (1633–1703) was the greatest diarist in the English language and, for three decades, the most capable administrator in the Royal Navy. His Diary (1660–1669) is the richest surviving source for the texture of Restoration London — the court, the theatre, the tavern, the bedroom, the counting-house, and the street during plague and fire. Yet Pepys was no mere chronicler: as Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board and later Secretary to the Admiralty, he was the architect of the administrative reforms that rebuilt the English fleet after the humiliation of the Medway and laid the foundations for the professional navy that would win the eighteenth-century wars against France and the Dutch. Burnet, no friend to Pepys, acknowledged his ability, while Pepys’s own voluminous naval papers reveal a man of tireless energy, formidable intelligence, and a passion for order that verged on obsession.

Early Career (1633–1660)
Pepys was born in London on 23 February 1633, the son of a successful tailor. Educated at St Paul’s School and Magdalene College, Cambridge, he entered the household of his cousin Edward Montagu (later Earl of Sandwich), a rising parliamentary naval commander. Montagu’s patronage was the making of Pepys: in 1659 he accompanied Montagu on a naval expedition to the Baltic, and the following year he sailed with his patron in the fleet that brought Charles II back from exile at the Restoration. So rapid was his ascent that in June 1660, at the age of twenty-seven, he was appointed Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board — the office charged with the administrative management of the English fleet. He began his Diary on 1 January 1660, a few months before the Restoration, and the first entry records that he was living in a cramped lodging in Axe Yard, Westminster, with his young wife Elizabeth, on an uncertain income and with no settled prospects.

The Diary (1660–1669)
The Diary is Pepys’s enduring monument — a million and a quarter words written in Shelton’s shorthand, recording the minutiae of his daily life with a candour that has no parallel in English literature. He wrote entirely for himself, with no thought of publication, and the result is a portrait of a man, and an age, unmediated by self-censorship. He records his pleasures — a new coat, a good dinner at the Dolphin Tavern, a performance of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream — and his failures: his bouts of temper, his infidelities (with the maidservant Deb Willet, with the wife of the French dancing-master), his terror of his wife’s reproaches. He describes the king’s mistresses, the fashions of the court, the latest scientific experiments of the Royal Society (he was elected a Fellow in 1665). The Diary is also an incomparable political record: Pepys sat in the gallery of the Commons, dined with ministers, and walked in St James’s Park with the secretaries of state, noting everything he saw and heard. He abandoned the Diary on 31 May 1669, fearing that his eyesight was failing — though the blindness never came. He never wrote another line of it, and the six volumes lay in shorthand in the Pepysian Library at Magdalene College until they were first deciphered in 1825.

The Great Plague and the Great Fire (1665–1666)
Pepys’s Diary entries for 1665–1666 are among the most vivid accounts of catastrophe in English prose. During the Great Plague, he remained in London while the court and all who could fled: he describes the grass growing in the streets of the City, the red crosses painted on infected doors, the dead-carts ringing their bells at night, and his own terror as he walked through the empty streets, chewing tobacco to ward off infection. During the Great Fire of September 1666, he was an eyewitness and an active participant: he recorded the fire’s spread from Pudding Lane with extraordinary precision, and he took the news to the king at Whitehall, where Charles II ordered him to command the Lord Mayor to pull down houses to create firebreaks. His entry for 2 September 1666 — “So down, with my heart full of trouble, to the Lieutenant of the Tower, who tells me it began in the King’s baker’s house in Pudding Lane” — is one of the most famous passages in English diurnal literature.

Clerk of the Acts and Naval Reform (1660–1673)
As Clerk of the Acts, Pepys was the executive officer of the Navy Board — responsible for contracts, victualling, shipbuilding, pay, and the supply of stores. He found the administration of the navy in chaos: accounts were kept on loose scraps of paper, the great shipwrights of the Commonwealth era were dead or dispersed, and the fleet that had fought the Dutch under Blake had rotted in the Medway. Pepys imposed a system. He standardised contracts, introduced regular accounting, and insisted on written records. He built a network of informants among the dockyard officers and the shipwrights, and he bullied, cajoled, and bribed suppliers into delivering on time. The Second Dutch War (1665–1667) exposed the limits of his reforms — the fleet was sent to sea with inadequate provisions and ill-maintained ships — and the Dutch raid on the Medway in June 1667, when De Ruyter burned the English flagship at Chatham, was the greatest humiliation of Pepys’s career. He was not to blame (the fault lay with the Treasury, which had starved the navy of funds), but he felt the disgrace as a personal wound.

Secretary to the Admiralty (1673–1679, 1684–1689)
After the Test Act removed the Duke of York from the Admiralty, Pepys was appointed Secretary to the Admiralty in 1673 — a more powerful position than Clerk of the Acts, giving him direct access to the king and the Privy Council. He now had the authority to carry through the reforms that had been frustrated by the poverty of the Exchequer. He rebuilt the fleet, commissioning thirty new ships of the line, establishing the Royal Naval College at Portsmouth for the training of officers, and introducing the first professional examinations for naval lieutenants. He compiled a comprehensive list of naval personnel and insisted on merit rather than patronage in appointments. Campbell’s naval history records that Pepys’s administrative system “was the foundation upon which the greatness of the Royal Navy in the eighteenth century was built.”
His first tenure ended in 1679 when the Popish Plot hysteria swept the kingdom. Pepys, as a close associate of the Catholic Duke of York, was arrested on trumped-up charges of treason: he was accused of conspiring to land a French army in Ireland, of being a secret Catholic, and of selling naval secrets. He was committed to the Tower of London in June 1679 and spent several weeks in close confinement before being released on bail. The charges were eventually dismissed, but the experience left him shaken. He returned to the Admiralty in 1684, when Charles II was finally governing without parliament and the navy was his priority. Pepys’s second tenure was shorter but equally productive: he overhauled the dockyards, introduced new shipbuilding contracts, and prepared the fleet for the war against France that was to come.

The Revolution of 1688 and Retirement (1688–1703)
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 ended Pepys’s public career. As the trusted servant of James II, he was dismissed from the Admiralty when William and Mary took the throne. He was arrested again briefly in 1690 on suspicion of Jacobite sympathies, but was never charged. He retired to his house in York Buildings, spending his last years in correspondence with the great scholars of the age — including Isaac Newton, with whom he corresponded during Newton’s breakdown of 1693, and John Evelyn, his lifelong friend. He built the Pepysian Library at Magdalene College, Cambridge, bequeathing his books, manuscripts, and the six volumes of his Diary in shorthand to the college. He died on 26 May 1703 at the age of seventy, and was buried in St Olave’s Church, Hart Street, London.

Character and Legacy
Pepys was a man of extraordinary contradictions. He was ambitious, vain, and sensual — a connoisseur of good wine, pretty women, and fine clothes — but also industrious, honest in his public accounts, and genuinely devoted to the navy. He was a brilliant administrator who imposed order on chaos, yet he could be petty, gossipy, and vindictive in his private judgments. He was a loyal servant of the Stuarts who nonetheless recorded their faults with devastating accuracy. His Diary reveals a man who was acutely self-aware — he records his resolutions to reform, his failures to keep them, and his rueful acceptance of his own weaknesses — and this self-knowledge is what makes him, for all his flaws, an appealing and enduring figure.
His legacy is twofold. As a diarist, he gave posterity the fullest account of daily life in Restoration England — its sights, smells, sounds, and textures — that exists in any language. As a naval administrator, he transformed the Royal Navy from a ramshackle collection of ships and officials into a professional fighting force capable of matching the Dutch and, in the next century, the French. The navy that Nelson commanded was, in large measure, the navy that Pepys built.

entities/shaftesbury.title: Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury
entities/shaftesbury.content:
Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury
Summary
Anthony Ashley Cooper (1621–1683), 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, was the most formidable parliamentary manager and opposition leader of the Restoration period — the man who, more than any other, forged the Whig party out of the raw material of Protestant alarm, aristocratic faction, and parliamentary resistance to the crown. Burnet’s portrait of him remains the most vivid: “He was a man of great parts, bold, witty, and ambitious; he studied men more than books, and he had an extraordinary faculty of insinuating himself into the confidence of all who were fit to be trusted.” Shaftesbury served under both Cromwell and Charles II, sat in the Cabal ministry as Lord Chancellor, and then turned against the court to lead the Exclusion movement — a campaign to bar the Catholic Duke of York from the throne that brought England to the brink of civil war. Driven into exile by the Tory reaction, he died in Amsterdam in 1683, his cause defeated but his methods destined to shape the future of English parliamentary politics.

Early Life and the Civil Wars (1621–1653)
Anthony Ashley Cooper was born on 22 July 1621 at Rockbourne in Hampshire, the son of Sir John Cooper of Rockbourne and Anne Ashley, heiress of Sir Anthony Ashley. He inherited a substantial estate at an early age and was educated at Exeter College, Oxford, and Lincoln’s Inn. Burnet notes that from his youth he showed “a quick and lively understanding, but with a restlessness of temper that made him unable to sit still under any settlement.”
When the Civil War broke out in 1642, Cooper initially fought for the king, serving as a captain of horse in the royalist army. But he quickly changed sides — a pattern that would mark his entire career. By 1644 he had joined the parliamentary cause, and he thereafter served with distinction under the Earl of Essex and Sir William Waller. Hume, characteristically dry on this point, observes that Cooper “had early discovered that sagacity which ever distinguished him, in abandoning a falling cause and attaching himself to the victorious side.”
In 1646 he was elected to the Long Parliament as MP for Tewkesbury in Gloucestershire, taking his seat among the Presbyterians. He opposed the trial of Charles I and refused to sit on the High Court of Justice that condemned the king — a reservation that allowed him to escape the charge of regicide at the Restoration. Under the Commonwealth he served on the Council of State (1653) under Cromwell, though his relationship with the Protector was uneasy. Burnet writes that Cromwell “knew him well, and said he was a man of great parts but of no principle.”

The Restoration and the Cabal Ministry (1660–1673)
Cooper was an early and active supporter of the Restoration. He travelled to Breda to wait on Charles II, and was among the twelve members of the House of Lords who brought the king home. He was created Baron Ashley of Wimborne St Giles in 1661 and made Chancellor of the Exchequer. In 1672 he was advanced to the earldom of Shaftesbury and appointed Lord Chancellor — the highest legal office in the kingdom.
As Lord Chancellor, Shaftesbury was a member of the infamous Cabal ministry (Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley, Lauderdale). He presided over the Great Seal with what Burnet calls “a great negligence of forms, but a profound attention to the substance of affairs.” He was, however, kept ignorant of the most dangerous secret of the reign: the Treaty of Dover (1670), by which Charles II promised Louis XIV to declare himself a Catholic in exchange for French subsidies. A sham version of the treaty was shown to the Protestant members of the Cabal, but the religious clauses were concealed. When Shaftesbury discovered the deception, his break with the court was complete.
The Test Act of 1673, which Shaftesbury championed in the Lords, forced Catholics out of public office — including the Duke of York, the king’s brother and heir. Shaftesbury argued the measure with extraordinary force. Hume records that “he displayed all the powers of that eloquence which had made him the terror of the court and the idol of the people.” The king dismissed him from the Chancellorship later that year. Shaftesbury went into opposition and never held office again.

The Green Ribbon Club and the Whig Party (1674–1679)
Out of office, Shaftesbury became the organising genius of the opposition. He gathered around him a network of MPs, Dissenting ministers, London merchants, and City radicals that came to be known as the Country party — soon to be called the Whigs. Their headquarters was the Green Ribbon Club, which met at the King’s Head Tavern in Chancery Lane, named for the green ribbons its members wore in their hats.
Shaftesbury’s method was systematic. He cultivated the Dissenters — Presbyterians, Independents, Baptists — whose religious grievances against the Clarendon Code made them natural opponents of the court. He cultivated the City of London, the engine of commercial wealth and the stronghold of anti-popery. He cultivated the press, subsidising pamphleteers and news-writers. And he cultivated the Commons, where his lieutenants — Lord William Russell, Algernon Sidney, the Earl of Essex — managed debates and marshalled votes. Hume writes that “Shaftesbury was the soul of the party, and directed all its movements with indefatigable industry and consummate art.”
Burnet gives a more intimate portrait of his methods: “He had a particular talent of making himself agreeable in conversation, and could insinuate himself into the confidence of any man with whom he desired to be acquainted. He was a most dexterous manager of parties, and knew how to set every man to the work for which he was best fitted. He was not himself a good speaker — his voice was harsh and his delivery ungraceful — but he had a wonderful skill in drawing others to speak, and in framing the arguments which they were to use.”

The Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis (1678–1681)
The Popish Plot of 1678 — the fabrication of the perjurer Titus Oates — was the opportunity Shaftesbury had been waiting for. Oates alleged a vast Catholic conspiracy to murder the king, burn London, and impose popery by French arms. The murder of Sir Edmund Bury Godfrey, the magistrate before whom Oates had sworn his deposition, sent the nation into hysteria. Fifteen innocent Catholics were judicially murdered on Oates’s evidence.
Shaftesbury did not create the plot — Oates and his accomplices did — but he exploited it with ruthless skill. He presided at the investigation of the plot before the Privy Council, pressing witnesses and magnifying allegations. He orchestrated the prosecution of the five Catholic peers sent to the Tower. Hume judges that Shaftesbury “was not perhaps the first author of the imposture, but he was the great patron and propagator of it; and he employed it as the engine of his factious purposes.”
The Exclusion Crisis proper began in 1679, when Shaftesbury introduced a bill in the Lords to exclude the Duke of York — a confessed Catholic — from the succession to the throne. Three Exclusion Parliaments met between 1679 and 1681. Each time the Commons passed the bill; each time Charles II either dissolved parliament or saw the bill defeated in the Lords by the king’s influence. Shaftesbury proposed various expedients — the banishment of York, the appointment of a Protestant regent, the recognition of the Duke of Monmouth (Charles’s natural son) as heir — but all were defeated by the king’s refusal to sacrifice either his brother or the principle of hereditary succession.
During this crisis, Charles attempted to conciliate Shaftesbury by appointing him President of the Privy Council under Sir William Temple’s new scheme of government (1679). The experiment lasted only a few months. Shaftesbury used his position to press the Exclusion Bill harder than ever, and the king dismissed him. “Shaftesbury,” writes Hume, “was now entirely weaned from the court, and gave himself up wholly to the measures of the opposition.”
The Oxford Parliament of March 1681 was the climax. Charles summoned parliament to the royalist city of Oxford, away from the Whig mob of London. Shaftesbury arrived attended by a bodyguard of armed gentlemen — a demonstration of strength that alarmed the court. But when the Commons pressed immediately for exclusion, Charles dissolved parliament after only one week. He never called another. Shaftesbury’s parliamentary strategy was shattered.

Prosecution, Flight, and Death (1681–1683)
After the dissolution of the Oxford Parliament, the Tory reaction was swift and merciless. The crown launched a prosecution against Shaftesbury for high treason, alleging that he had plotted to raise a rebellion and seize the king. The bill of indictment was brought before the Middlesex grand jury in November 1681 — a jury that had been packed with Whig partisans in the last London elections. The grand jury threw out the bill, and the crowd in the streets celebrated with bonfires. On the medal struck to commemorate his acquittal, Shaftesbury appeared with the motto “Laetamur” — We Rejoice.
The triumph was short-lived. The government remodelled the London corporations through quo warranto proceedings, stripping the Whigs of their municipal power. Shaftesbury, now under constant surveillance, retreated to his house at Wimborne St Giles in Dorset. Evidence gathered by the government showed that he was in communication with the more desperate elements of the opposition — the men who would later be implicated in the Rye House Plot (1683), a scheme to assassinate Charles and his brother at a Hertfordshire farmhouse.
Whether Shaftesbury was directly involved in the assassination plot is disputed. Hume thinks it probable that he knew of it and approved its general design, though he was too cautious to commit himself to the details. Burnet, who knew him well, writes that “he was too wise to trust his life and fortune to a gang of hot-headed men; but he had so far engaged in illegal practices that he had reason to fear the worst.”
In November 1682, receiving intelligence that a warrant for his arrest was imminent, Shaftesbury fled England in disguise. He went to Amsterdam, where he was welcomed by the Dutch republican party and the English exile community. But the life of a fugitive wore him down. His health, already broken by years of political warfare, collapsed. He died in Amsterdam on 21 January 1683, aged sixty-one.
Burnet records his last days: “He was much dejected, and seemed to feel the reverse of that greatness which he had formerly enjoyed. He said to some of his friends that he had outlived himself, and that he had nothing now to do but to die.” His body was brought back to England and buried at Wimborne St Giles.

Character
Burnet’s character of Shaftesbury is the most celebrated of his many historical portraits, and worth giving at length:
“He was a man of great parts, bold, witty, and ambitious. He studied men more than books, and he had an extraordinary faculty of insinuating himself into the confidence of all who were fit to be trusted. He was a most dexterous manager of parties, and knew how to set every man to the work for which he was best fitted. He was not himself a good speaker — his voice was harsh and his delivery ungraceful — but he had a wonderful skill in drawing others to speak, and in framing the arguments which they were to use.”
Hume’s judgment is more ambivalent. He acknowledges Shaftesbury’s “uncommon talents” — his “industry, his penetration, his eloquence, his power over men’s minds” — but condemns his methods: “He gave into all the popular delusions of the age, and even fostered and propagated them. He was the great patron of the Popish Plot, and the great promoter of the Exclusion Bill. It is difficult to determine whether his abilities or his ambition was the more dangerous.”
The eighteenth-century Whig historians, by contrast, made Shaftesbury a hero of liberty. For them, he was the founder of the party that had delivered England from Stuart tyranny, the man who had first organised parliamentary resistance to arbitrary power, and whose methods — party organisation, extra-parliamentary agitation, the mobilisation of public opinion — had become the permanent furniture of English politics.
The truth lies somewhere between these portraits. Shaftesbury was not a principled republican like Algernon Sidney, nor a hot-headed conspirator like the Rye House plotters. He was a parliamentary manager of genius who believed that the Protestant religion and the English constitution could only be preserved by organised party resistance to the crown. He was willing to use means — the exploitation of the Popish Plot, the mobilisation of the London mob, the threat of armed insurrection — that a more scrupulous politician might have rejected. But he was also the man who, more than any other, invented the modern political party as an instrument of constitutional opposition. In this sense, he is the true founder of the Whig tradition.

Legacy
Shaftesbury’s immediate cause — the exclusion of the Duke of York — was defeated. Charles II outlived him, and James II succeeded peacefully in 1685. But within three years, James’s assault on the established church and the constitution provoked the Glorious Revolution, which accomplished everything Shaftesbury had fought for: the permanent exclusion of the Catholic Stuarts, the supremacy of parliament over the crown, and the establishment of Protestant succession on a legal foundation.
The Whig party that Shaftesbury had forged became the governing party of the eighteenth century. The methods he pioneered — party discipline, extra-parliamentary organisation, the cultivation of the press and the City, the alliance between the aristocracy and the Dissenting interest — became the standard equipment of English political life. His descendant and namesake, the 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury, became one of the leading philosophers of the Whig tradition.
John Locke, who served as Shaftesbury’s physician, secretary, and political confidant from 1667, drew on his experience in the Exclusion Crisis when writing the Two Treatises of Government. The theory of popular sovereignty, the right of resistance to tyranny, and the doctrine of the dissolution of government — the intellectual foundations of the Glorious Revolution — were forged in the workshops of Shaftesbury’s political machine.
Shaftesbury was, in the end, too clever and too ambitious for his contemporaries, and too dangerous for his king. But the tradition he founded — of organised parliamentary opposition, of the politics of party, of the mobilisation of public opinion against arbitrary power — outlasted both his enemies and his own failures. He died a fugitive and a failure, but he had changed English politics forever.
