entities/strafford.title: Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford
entities/strafford.content:
Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford
Summary
Thomas Wentworth, 1st Earl of Strafford (1593–1641), was the most able and most tragic of Charles I’s ministers — a man of commanding talents who began his public career as a parliamentary opponent of the crown and ended it as the king’s chief counsellor, executed by bill of attainder on the accusation of his former allies. Hume describes him as “one of the most eminent personages that has appeared in England,” whose character was “stately and austere: more fitted to procure esteem than love.” His administration of Ireland under the policy of “Thorough” was a model of efficient, if unpopular, colonial governance. His trial and execution in May 1641 were the decisive rupture between Charles I and his parliament, and the first great act of political violence that preceded the Civil War. Burnet records that Strafford’s death “raised his character, and cast a lasting odium on that way of proceeding” — making him both a royalist martyr and a cautionary example of the perils of constructive treason.

Early Career and Parliamentary Opposition
Thomas Wentworth was born in London on 13 April 1593, the eldest son of Sir William Wentworth of Wentworth Woodhouse in Yorkshire. He was educated at St John’s College, Cambridge, and studied law at the Inner Temple. The Wentworths were an ancient and wealthy Yorkshire family, and Thomas inherited an ample estate upon his father’s death in 1614.
He entered Parliament in 1614 as MP for Yorkshire, but made no notable impression. By the first parliament of Charles I in 1625, however, he had emerged as one of the leading figures of the opposition. Hume lists him among “a set of men of the most uncommon capacity, and the largest views” — alongside Sir Edward Coke, Sir John Eliot, John Pym, and John Selden — who were “animated with a warm regard to liberty” and resolved to use the king’s financial necessities to reduce the prerogative within reasonable bounds.
In the parliament of 1626, Charles attempted to silence the opposition by appointing Wentworth and three other popular leaders as sheriffs of their counties — an expedient that the king believed would incapacitate them from being elected as MPs. The tactic failed; enough patriots remained to keep up the ill-humour of the house. Wentworth was nevertheless prevented from sitting, and his influence during that session was limited.

Defection to the Court (1628)
The turning point in Wentworth’s career came in 1628. In the parliament that produced the Petition of Right, Wentworth was again elected and at first joined the opposition in demanding the king’s assent to that great charter of English liberties. But shortly thereafter, he was won over to the court. The precise reasons remain debated: Hume writes that his virtue “seems not to have been entirely pure, but to have been susceptible of strong impressions from private interest and ambition.” Others have suggested that Wentworth was genuinely alarmed by the growing extremism of the Puritan faction and concluded that only a strong monarchy could preserve order.
Whatever his motives, the defection was absolute and irrevocable. Hume observes that the leaders whom the king gained “lost from that moment all interest with their party, and were even pursued as traitors with implacable hatred and resentment.” Charles raised Wentworth through the peerage in rapid succession — first Baron Wentworth, then Viscount Wentworth, and finally Earl of Strafford — appointed him President of the Council of the North, and later Lord Deputy of Ireland. He became, next to Archbishop Laud, the king’s most trusted minister.

President of the Council of the North
As President of the Council of the North (1628–1633), Strafford governed the northern counties with efficiency and firmness. The council had been erected by Henry VIII after the Pilgrimage of Grace, originally as a criminal court. Charles extended its powers to include a large civil jurisdiction, and Strafford enforced this authority vigorously. Hume notes that “some irregular acts of that council were complained of,” and that the extension of its powers effectively put “all the northern counties out of the protection of ordinary law, and subjecting them to an authority somewhat arbitrary.”
Nevertheless, Strafford brought order to a region long troubled by lawlessness. His administration was marked by rigorous discipline, suppression of local faction, and careful attention to the crown’s revenues. He never once sat as president after receiving the expanded instructions — a fact that he later used in his defence — but the reputation he built in the north commended him for higher service.

Lord Deputy of Ireland: The Policy of Thorough
In 1633, Strafford was appointed Lord Deputy of Ireland, where he remained for eight years, governing with what he called the policy of “Thorough” — a systematic programme to strengthen royal authority, increase revenue, impose religious uniformity, and reduce Ireland to a profitable dependency of the English crown. Hume records that he governed “with great vigilance, activity, and prudence, but with very little popularity.”
His achievements in Ireland were substantial. A large debt was paid off, and a considerable sum was left in the exchequer. The revenue, which had never before met the charges of government, was raised to equality with them. A small standing army was augmented and brought under exact discipline. Industry and the arts of peace were introduced among a rude people: shipping increased a hundred-fold, customs tripled on the same rates, exports doubled in value over imports. The linen manufacture was introduced and promoted. Agriculture advanced through English and Scottish plantations. The Protestant religion was encouraged without the persecution or discontent of Catholics.
He managed the Irish parliament with such skill that it voted whatever was necessary for the payment of the army and for the support of the king’s authority. At the same time, he exercised discretionary powers — holding courts-martial, billeting soldiers, deciding causes upon paper-petitions before the council — that were usual enough in England but carried much further in Ireland, where a rude and barely subdued people required, in his judgment, a sterner hand.

Earl of Strafford and Recalled to England
Strafford was created Earl of Strafford in January 1640, at the height of his power. He was recalled from Ireland in the autumn of 1639, when the crisis with Scotland began to demand his presence. The Scots had risen in rebellion against Laud’s liturgical innovations, and Charles needed his ablest counsellor. Strafford was appointed lieutenant-general of the army that marched against the Scottish Covenanters.
The Second Bishops’ War (1640) was a disaster. The English army, poorly supplied and unwilling to fight, was routed at Newburn by the Scots, who then occupied Newcastle and a large part of northern England. Strafford urged the king to call a parliament to raise funds — the Short Parliament — but when it refused supply and was dissolved, the situation only worsened. The Long Parliament was summoned in November 1640, and Strafford’s fate was sealed.

Impeachment, Trial, and Bill of Attainder
The Long Parliament moved against Strafford immediately. He was impeached for high treason on 11 November 1640, the very day after the parliament opened. Pym, his old colleague in the opposition, led the prosecution. Strafford was sequestered from parliament and committed to the Tower. A committee of thirteen was chosen to prepare the charge against him.
His trial began on 22 March 1641 in Westminster Hall, before both houses of parliament, with the king and queen watching from a close gallery. The articles of impeachment were twenty-eight in number, covering his conduct in the north, in Ireland, and as counsellor in England. Hume writes that “such were the capacity, genius, presence of mind, displayed by this magnanimous statesman, that, while argument and reason and law had any place, he obtained an undisputed victory.” The charge of treason could not be sustained; his conduct, exposed to the most severe scrutiny, was “innocent, and even laudable.”
The decisive blow came from a different quarter. Sir Henry Vane, the secretary of state, produced notes of a council meeting at which Strafford had reportedly said that the king, having tried all other means, “was absolved from all rules of government” and might use the Irish army to reduce “this kingdom” — the meaning of which phrase was bitterly contested: whether it meant Scotland (where the army was intended to go) or England. On this single, ambiguous, and disputed piece of evidence, the commons abandoned the impeachment and proceeded by bill of attainder — a legislative act of condemnation that required no proof of a specific crime.
The bill passed the commons by a vote of 204 to 59. The lords, surrounded by a mob of six thousand armed citizens crying for justice, passed it by only 26 to 19. Charles, torn between his conscience and his fear of the mob, hesitated. Strafford himself wrote a letter releasing the king from his promise of protection, urging him to sacrifice one life for the peace of the kingdom — a letter that Hume treats with scepticism, noting it may have been a forgery of the popular leaders. Charles at last gave his assent by commission. “Put not your trust in princes,” Strafford said when he heard the news, quoting Scripture, “nor in the sons of men: for in them there is no salvation.”

Execution and Aftermath
Strafford was executed on Tower Hill on 12 May 1641. On his way to the scaffold, he stopped under the window of Archbishop Laud, his old friend and fellow minister, who was himself imprisoned in the Tower and would be executed four years later. The aged primate, dissolved in tears, pronounced a blessing on his departing friend. Strafford, “still superior to his fate, moved on with an elated countenance, and with an air even of greater dignity than what usually attended him.”
His speech on the scaffold was full of decency and courage. He feared, he said, “that the omen was bad for the intended reformation of the state, that it commenced with the shedding of innocent blood.” He declared himself “nowise afraid of death” and laid down his head on the block “as cheerfully as ever I did when going to repose.” With one blow, the executioner ended his life in the forty-ninth year of his age.
Hume pronounces the judgment of history: “Though his death was loudly demanded as a satisfaction to justice, and an atonement for the many violations of the constitution, it may safely be affirmed, that the sentence by which he fell was an enormity greater than the worst of those which his implacable enemies prosecuted with so much cruel industry.” The first parliament after the Restoration reversed the bill of attainder. Even the Long Parliament itself, within weeks of his execution, remitted the more severe consequences of his sentence to his children, “as if conscious of the violence with which the prosecution had been conducted.”
Burnet records that Strafford’s death “made all his former errors be forgotten: it raised his character, and cast a lasting odium on that way of proceeding; whereas he had sunk in his credit by any censure lower than death.”

Character and Legacy
Strafford was, in Hume’s judgment, a man of eminent talents whose abilities merited all the confidence his master reposed in him. His character was austere, commanding, and proud — a man who could inspire respect but rarely affection. As an administrator, he was efficient, tireless, and systematic: the policy of Thorough, however harsh, brought order to Ireland and the north of England at a time when both were troubled and disordered. As a parliamentary politician, he was a formidable debater and a master of management.
His great political sin, in the eyes of his contemporaries, was his defection. The leaders of the popular party never forgave him for crossing from opposition to the court. To them, he was the betrayer who had sold the liberties of England for a peerage. To the royalists, he became a martyr — the king’s most faithful servant abandoned by the king under the pressure of mob violence.
His trial established a dangerous precedent: the doctrine of constructive treason, by which a man could be condemned for words spoken in council that could be construed (however remotely) as tending to the subversion of the constitution. Burnet’s history repeatedly returns to the injustice of “attainting a man upon so remote a presumption” as that used against Strafford. The memory of Strafford’s fate hung over the Long Parliament, the Civil War, and the Restoration, serving as a warning to ministers and a reproach to parliaments.

entities/william-iii.title: William III of England (William of Orange)
entities/william-iii.content:
William III of England (William of Orange)
Summary
William III (r. 1689–1702), Prince of Orange and Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic before his English kingship, was the dominant figure of the late seventeenth century in Europe. Born to a nation fighting for its existence against Louis XIV, he became the lifelong champion of Protestant Europe against French hegemony. His invasion of England in 1688 — the last successful invasion of the island — overthrew James II and established a constitutional monarchy on foundations that endure to this day. Burnet, who sailed with him and knew him intimately, called him a prince of “great qualities” whose cold exterior concealed a profound dedication to the liberties of Europe. Macaulay, two centuries later, would rank him among the greatest of English sovereigns.

Youth and the Stadtholderate (1650–1672)
William Henry of Orange was born on 4 November 1650, a posthumous child: his father, William II of Orange, had died of smallpox eight days before the birth. His mother was Mary Stuart, eldest daughter of Charles I of England. The infant prince was born into a republic that had abolished the Stadtholderate after his father’s death, and he was raised under the guardianship of his mother and his grandmother, Amalia of Solms, in a household riven by political faction.
The education of the young prince was entrusted to Johan de Witt, the Grand Pensionary who had guided the Dutch Republic through the First and Second Anglo-Dutch Wars. De Witt, a republican who mistrusted the House of Orange as a threat to the States’ sovereignty, ensured that William’s upbringing was careful but restricted. The prince was taught mathematics, history, and the art of war, and showed early signs of that tenacity and reserve that would mark his mature character. He was a pale, asthmatic child, slight of frame but indomitable of spirit.
The year 1672 — the “Year of Disaster” — transformed his fortunes. Louis XIV, with Charles II of England as his ally, launched a devastating invasion of the Dutch Republic. The French army crossed the Rhine and swept through the provinces; three of the seven provinces were overrun. The Dutch people, in a panic, rose against the De Witt administration. Johan de Witt and his brother Cornelius were torn to pieces by an Hague mob. In the midst of this national crisis, the States General appointed the twenty-two-year-old Prince of Orange Stadtholder and Captain-General of the Union. Hume records that William was then in the twenty-second year of his age and already gave “strong indications of those great qualities by which his life was afterwards distinguished.”
The prince saved the republic by opening the dikes and flooding the Water Line — the great Dutch defence — and by conducting a dogged defensive campaign that convinced both France and England that the republic could not be conquered. By 1674 England had made a separate peace; by 1678 the war ended with the Treaty of Nimeguen, and William’s reputation as the foremost Protestant prince in Europe was established.

Marriage to Mary (1677)
William’s marriage to his cousin Mary, elder daughter of the Duke of York (the future James II), was a matter of high policy as much as personal attachment. Charles II, needing to reassure a parliament that distrusted his French and Catholic leanings, consented to the match, and the marriage was celebrated at St. James’s Palace on 4 November 1677 — William’s twenty-seventh birthday. Burnet, who was present, describes the princess as a woman of exemplary piety, beauty, and sweetness of temper. She was devoted to her husband from the first, and though the marriage was initially a political arrangement, it ripened into a genuine partnership that would carry them through the greatest crisis of the age.
The marriage had a double significance: it bound the House of Orange to the Stuart dynasty, and it placed William next in the English succession after James’s children. The birth of a son to James and Mary of Modena in June 1688 — the Prince of Wales — threatened to displace Mary and William from that succession and precipitated the crisis that followed.

The Invitation and the Invasion (1687–1688)
By 1687, James II’s Catholicising project had alienated every class of his subjects. The trial and acquittal of the Seven Bishops in June 1688 demonstrated the breadth of the opposition. The birth of the Prince of Wales transformed discontent into action. On 30 June 1688 — the very day the bishops were acquitted — seven men, known to history as the Immortal Seven, dispatched a formal invitation to William of Orange to intervene. The signatories included the Earl of Devonshire, the Earl of Danby, the Earl of Shrewsbury, Lord Lumley, the Bishop of London (Compton), Edward Russell, and Henry Sidney. They assured William that the army and nation were ready to rise.
William had been in communication with English malcontents for two years, but the invitation and the birth of the prince made delay impossible. He obtained the approval of the States General for an expedition of unprecedented scale: a fleet of nearly five hundred vessels, carrying an army of some fourteen thousand men, together with a train of artillery, horses, and stores. The States, Burnet writes, “fitted out a Fleet” that was “as great a one as had ever been set out by the Republic.”
The enterprise was hazardous in the extreme. Twice the fleet put to sea and was driven back by storms. A third attempt succeeded when a strong easterly wind — the “Protestant wind” — carried the armada down the English Channel and at the same time kept the English fleet bottled up in the Thames and the Downs. The Dutch ships passed the Straits of Dover in a great procession that took two days. On 5 November 1688 — the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot — the fleet entered Torbay in Devon. Burnet, who sailed in the prince’s own ship, records that the landing was effected without opposition and that the whole coast of Devonshire declared for the prince within hours.

The Revolution and the Settlement (1688–1689)
William’s advance was a triumphal progress. The gentry and nobility flocked to his standard. The first great defection was that of Lord Cornbury with three regiments of dragoons. Then came John Churchill — the future Duke of Marlborough — who abandoned the king to whom he owed everything, carrying with him the Duke of Grafton and Colonel Berkeley. Prince George of Denmark, James’s son-in-law, deserted at Andover. On 25 November, Princess Anne fled London for Nottingham in the company of Lady Churchill, an act that broke James’s spirit. “God help me,” he cried, “my own children have forsaken me!”
James made a series of panicked concessions — dismissing the Ecclesiastical Commission, restoring the charters of London and the corporations, reinstating the fellows of Magdalen College — but they were received as signs of terror, not repentance. On 11 December he attempted flight, throwing the Great Seal into the Thames as he went. He was caught by fishermen at Faversham and brought back to London, where the populace unexpectedly cheered him; but William, who had no intention of allowing James to remain, ordered him to leave Whitehall. On 23 December 1688, James embarked for France, where Louis XIV received him with the utmost generosity at St. Germains.
William summoned a Convention Parliament, which met on 22 January 1689. After heated debate — especially over the word “abdication” versus “desertion” and the question of whether the throne was vacant — the Convention declared that James, having endeavoured to subvert the constitution and having withdrawn from the kingdom, had abdicated the government, and that the throne was thereby vacant. On 13 February 1689, William and Mary were offered the crown jointly, in accordance with the Declaration of Rights. William insisted on being king in his own right, not merely a regent or consort. Mary, with characteristic deference, made it known that she would accept no authority but from and through her husband. They were crowned together on 11 April 1689. The Declaration of Rights was later enacted as the Bill of Rights, which declared the dispensing and suspending power illegal, prohibited standing armies in peacetime without parliamentary consent, and settled the succession.

The War of the Grand Alliance and the Boyne (1689–1691)
The Revolution immediately involved England in the Nine Years’ War (1688–1697) against France. William, as Stadtholder, had been the soul of the Grand Alliance from the moment Louis XIV’s aggression had threatened the Dutch Republic; as King of England he commanded the resources of a second great power. His first and most urgent military task was Ireland, where James II had landed in March 1689 with French support and had summoned a Catholic parliament at Dublin.
William himself took command in Ireland in June 1690. Burnet records that he had 36,000 men in excellent condition, “full of heart and zeal.” He advanced from Belfast to the River Boyne near Drogheda in six days. King James had posted his Irish and French army — some 26,000 men — on the south side of the river. On 1 July 1690 (Old Style), William forced the passage. He was wounded by a cannonball on the eve of battle, but the injury was slight and he used it to rally his troops. The battle was a decisive victory: the Irish army was routed, James fled the field precipitately and returned to France, and Dublin fell without further resistance. The Boyne secured the Protestant ascendancy in Ireland for a century and confirmed William’s reputation as a soldier-king.
On the day before the Boyne, the English and Dutch fleets under the Earl of Torrington suffered a severe defeat at the Battle of Beachy Head. The French admiral Tourville exploited Torrington’s hesitation and the Dutch squadron’s bravery to inflict heavy losses. Torrington was court-martialled but acquitted — though he was never employed again. The defeat left the Channel temporarily open to French incursion, but the danger passed when Tourville failed to press his advantage.

La Hogue and the Naval War (1692–1694)
In 1692 the French prepared a full-scale invasion of England. A Jacobite army was assembled at La Hogue under the command of James II in person, with transports for 30,000 men. Admiral Tourville put to sea with a powerful fleet of 44 ships of the line. But the English and Dutch had now joined their forces under Admiral Edward Russell, who commanded a fleet of 99 sail.
The two fleets met off Cape Barfleur on 19 May 1692. After a fierce engagement, the French were forced to retreat through the Race of Alderney. While at anchor, their ships were attacked by English fireships, and twelve of the finest vessels in the French navy were burned or taken — six at La Hogue, five at Cherbourg, and others in the bay. Burnet records the rejoicing: “This victory seemed to fix the King more firmly on his throne, to the terror of all his enemies.” Campbell’s naval history gives the credit to Russell, whose “prudence, courage, and good conduct” had saved the kingdom. The Battle of La Hogue (or Barfleur) removed any serious French naval threat for the remainder of the war.

The Financial Revolution and the Bank of England (1694)
The cost of the war — with armies in Flanders, Ireland, and at sea — pressed heavily on the English Treasury. The old methods of parliamentary supply were inadequate. In 1694, William gave his assent to the bill creating the Governor and Company of the Bank of England — a private corporation that advanced 1.2 million pounds to the government at 8 percent interest, funded by a perpetual annual charge on certain taxes. The Bank became the engine of the financial revolution: it provided a permanent source of credit, stabilised the currency, and established the national debt on a solid foundation. Burnet notes that the Bank “quickly recovered its Credit so entirely, that there was no discount upon the Notes.” Though the Land Bank scheme that followed failed, the Bank of England proved one of the most durable institutions created in William’s reign, and it transformed England’s capacity to wage war.

Death of Queen Mary (1694)
On 28 December 1694, Queen Mary died of smallpox at Kensington Palace. She was thirty-two years old. Burnet, who attended her in her final illness, describes her death as a scene of extraordinary piety and composure. She had been the most popular figure of the reign — gracious, charitable, and devout — and her loss was felt throughout the kingdom. William was inconsolable. His grief was so profound that those who knew him wondered whether he would survive her. He shut himself up for weeks, refusing to see anyone. The asthmatic and consumptive state of his own health, which had long given uneasiness, became a source of general anxiety. Burnet observes that the King’s cold reserve and long hours in his closet were considerably worsened by the Queen’s death, which “seemed to break his spirit” and left him more solitary and withdrawn than ever. He would never marry again.

The Peace of Ryswick (1697)
The war dragged on for three more years after Mary’s death, with campaigns in Flanders that were costly and indecisive. William, despite his ill health, commanded the allied armies in person in each campaign. By 1696 both sides were exhausted. Negotiations opened at Ryswick, a palace near The Hague, and on 20 September 1697 a peace was signed. Louis XIV recognised William III as rightful King of England, agreed to provide no further assistance to James II, and restored most of the conquests he had made since the Treaty of Nimeguen. The peace was received in England with immense relief and rejoicing. For the first time in nine years, William could command the reduction of the army to a peace establishment — a step the Commons demanded and he reluctantly accepted.

The Act of Settlement (1701)
The great constitutional work of William’s reign was concluded in his last years. The death in 1700 of Princess Anne’s last surviving child, the Duke of Gloucester, threw the succession into peril. William pressed Parliament to settle the Protestant succession beyond all dispute. The result was the Act of Settlement of 1701, which provided that the crown should pass, after Anne, to the Electress Sophia of Hanover — a granddaughter of James I — and her Protestant descendants. The Act excluded Catholics and those who married Catholics from the throne, required future monarchs to join in communion with the Church of England, and placed important restrictions on the royal prerogative. Burnet records that William himself instructed him to propose the naming of the “Dutchess of Hanover and her Posterity” in the House of Lords, and that the King “signified his pleasure in this also to the Ministers.” The Act of Settlement remains, alongside Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights, one of the fundamental statutes of the British constitution.

Death and Character
William III died at Kensington Palace on 8 March 1702. His health had been declining for years: he suffered from asthma, dropsy, and a persistent cough. On 20 February 1702, his horse Sorrel stumbled on a molehill in Hampton Court Park and threw the King, fracturing his collarbone. The injury was not thought serious at first, but his constitution was too broken to recover. He rallied briefly, then sank into a fever and died in the arms of his physician. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.
The character of William III, as drawn by those who knew him, is a study in contrasts. Burnet, who had every opportunity of observing him at close quarters, paints him as a prince of profound abilities but a “cold and reserved temper” that kept even his closest servants at a distance. He was apt to be “peevish,” and his long hours in his closet, combined with his constitutional reserve, gave him an air of melancholy that was often mistaken for pride. He valued secrecy and was slow to confide his plans to anyone, but once he had taken a resolution, he adhered to it with immovable firmness. In the field he was brave to the point of recklessness, sharing the hardships of his soldiers and exposing himself freely to enemy fire. He had little of the graces of a court — he spoke slowly and with difficulty, disliked ceremony, and was indifferent to the arts — but he had an unerring sense of the great forces at work in European politics and the patience to wait for his opportunities. His whole life was a single-minded struggle against the ambition of Louis XIV. “He seemed to have nothing else in his view,” Burnet writes, “but to check the growing greatness of France and to secure the liberties of Europe.”
Hume’s judgment, though briefer, is no less measured. He notes that William’s reign established the revolution settlement on a foundation of law, that his wars laid the basis for England’s emergence as a European great power, and that his financial innovations gave the monarchy the resources it needed without the arbitrary methods of his predecessors. The cost was a war debt that burdened the nation for generations, but the achievement was the preservation of a free constitution and a Protestant succession against the most formidable monarchy in Europe.

Legacy
William III transformed the English state. The Bill of Rights, the Toleration Act, the Bank of England, the national debt, the Act of Settlement, and the standing army all date from his reign. He gave England the constitutional framework within which parliamentary government would develop in the eighteenth century, and he placed the kingdom at the head of the European coalition that finally checked the power of Louis XIV. The Glorious Revolution that he led — bloodless in England, costly in Ireland — became the central myth of Whig constitutionalism: the justification for limited monarchy, the rule of law, and the Protestant succession. For the Jacobites he was “the usurper,” the little Dutchman who stole a crown; for posterity he was the king who saved English liberty from the fate that awaited it under James II. His name is remembered in the annual celebration of the Orange Order, in the institutions he founded, and in the constitution he established. He was the last successful invader of England, and by that invasion he shaped the history of Britain and Europe for centuries to come.

events/battle-of-beachy-head.title: Battle of Beachy Head
events/battle-of-beachy-head.content:
Battle of Beachy Head (10 July 1690)
Summary
The Battle of Beachy Head, fought on 10 July 1690 (30 June Old Style) in the English Channel off the Sussex coast, was a decisive naval victory for the French over the combined Anglo-Dutch fleet. The Comte de Tourville, commanding some eighty-two ships of the line, defeated Lord Torrington’s allied fleet of approximately fifty-six sail after Queen Mary II had sent peremptory orders to engage. The Dutch squadron bore the brunt of the fighting and was virtually destroyed; the English fleet withdrew in good order. The defeat threw England into panic, exposed the south coast to French depredation, and dealt a severe blow to English naval prestige. Torrington was subsequently court-martialled and acquitted, but never served at sea again.

Context: Louis XIV’s Naval Strategy and James II in Ireland
The battle must be understood within the twin pressures of the Nine Years’ War (1688–1697). In Ireland, James II, deposed in the Glorious Revolution, had landed at Kinsale in March 1689 with French officers, French arms, and French money, hoping to recover his throne. William III had taken personal command of the Irish campaign and sailed for Belfast on 11 June 1690, leaving Queen Mary as regent in England with a restive kingdom and rumours of Jacobite insurrection.
Louis XIV saw an opportunity to strike at the heart of the Revolution settlement. A French fleet under the Comte de Tourville — the finest admiral France had produced — was ordered to clear the Channel, cover a landing of James’s supporters, and cut William’s communications with Ireland. Dalrymple records that the Marquis de Seignelai, son of the great Colbert, added twenty-two fire-ships and numerous frigates to the fleet with a scheme to burn English ports one by one after the naval battle was won. Tourville sailed from Brest with seventy-eight great ships of war and posted himself off Plymouth within eight days of William’s departure.

The Allied Fleet: Torrington vs. Tourville
Lord Torrington — Arthur Herbert — was at St. Helen’s with no more than forty ships when news of the French arrival reached him. He had been instrumental in bringing William over in 1688, but his command now suffered from the dispersal of English naval strength: part of the fleet had sailed to Spain and the Mediterranean; the squadron attending the King was still in Ireland; and only a portion of the Dutch contingent had joined. Sir Cloudesley Shovel’s Plymouth squadron had not yet arrived.
Torrington put to sea on Midsummer Day with such ships as he had, and was joined over the following days by Admiral Evertzen with seven Dutch men-of-war. His whole force now amounted to twenty-two Dutch ships and about thirty-four English — fifty-six sail in total, against Tourville’s eighty-two. At a council of war it was unanimously resolved not to risk an engagement. Torrington shadowed the French as they passed eastward through the Channel, keeping between them and the coast, hoping to preserve his fleet.
But the political situation in London was desperate. Queen Mary’s council, alarmed by reports of a planned Jacobite insurrection coordinated with the French arrival, consulted Admiral Edward Russell — the only sea officer in the cabinet. Russell, whom Dalrymple suggests may have been motivated either by contempt for French naval prowess or by ambition to supplant Torrington, gave his opinion that the fleet was strong enough to fight. The Queen sent positive orders: Torrington was to engage at all events.

The Dutch Squadron Sacrificed
The order reached Torrington off Beachy Head. He had no choice but to obey. On the morning of 10 July (N.S.), he bore down upon the French fleet, which awaited him in order of battle. The Dutch squadron under Admiral Evertzen held the van, as was the custom; Torrington commanded the main body of English ships.
Dalrymple’s narrative captures the fatal misalignment. Evertzen, burning to distinguish himself, pressed forward eagerly and out-sailed the English main body. He passed part of the French van without firing a shot and plunged into the middle of the enemy line. This created a dangerous gap between the Dutch and the English. The French instantly filled it with a mass of their ships, cutting off the van from the main body. Part of the French fleet made head against Torrington, while the rest closed upon Evertzen’s squadron on one side, and the portion of the van he had rashly passed turned and surrounded it on the other.
The Dutch fought with desperate valour. Campbell’s Naval History records that the engagement lasted from nine in the morning until five in the evening with incredible fury. A calm that fell about one o’clock prevented the Dutch from pursuing their initial advantage and left them exposed. The French poured their whole force against the isolated Dutch squadron, which fought against overwhelming odds. Rear-Admiral Jan Dick and Rear-Admiral Brakel were killed; Captain Nordel perished with them. Three Dutch ships were sunk in the fight, and the Friezland, having lost all her masts, was taken. Admiral Evertzen’s own account testifies that there was not a single officer or seaman who did not exactly perform his duty — twenty-two Dutch ships had fought against eighty-two French.

The English Withdrawal
Torrington, seeing the destruction of his allies and conscious of his own inferiority, made it his object to save what he could. He worked his way between the Dutch cripples and the French main body — by his own account, ordering the English squadron to anchor so that the tide would carry them between the disabled Dutch ships and the enemy. After about five hours of effort, he succeeded in interposing the English red squadron. The French, having neglected to anchor, were carried away from the scene by the tide, and the combatants drifted apart.
In the retreat to the Thames, the Dutch were forced to burn three more of their disabled ships on the Sussex coast; the English burnt one — the Anne, a seventy-gun ship that had lost all her masts and was run ashore near Winchelsea. In total the Dutch lost six ships of the line, while English losses were comparatively light: about two ships and 350 men. The French fleet pursued as far as Rye Bay, then stood off. Seignelai’s scheme for burning English ports miscarried, partly because he fell ill just as the fleet sailed and had not communicated the details to Tourville, and partly because Torrington had given orders to remove the buoys along the coast.

The Political Aftermath: Torrington’s Court-Martial and Acquittal
News of the defeat threw England into consternation. The loss of the Boyne — which William had won on the very same day the fleets were fighting off Beachy Head — was for several days unknown, and the double French victory at Fleurus (on land in Flanders) compounded the alarm. London prepared for invasion; the militia was raised; the city offered to raise six auxiliary regiments at its own expense. Queen Mary ordered the arrest of known Jacobite sympathisers and sent Mr. Harbord to the States-General to express her concern at the sacrifice of the Dutch squadron and to promise that the Dutch ships would be refitted at England’s cost.
Torrington was examined before the Privy Council, where he defended himself with great presence of mind. He argued that he had saved the English fleet and that to have fought longer would have sacrificed the last hope of defending the kingdom. Nevertheless, he was committed to the Tower. The Dutch clamoured for justice.
The question of how to try him became a constitutional point. The king insisted on a court-martial; Torrington’s friends maintained he ought to be tried by his peers. A new act of parliament was passed to settle the power of the Admiralty commissioners, and on 10 December 1690 a court-martial convened on board the Kent frigate at Sheerness, presided over by Sir Ralph Delaval. The charge was that Torrington, through treachery or cowardice, had misbehaved in his office, drawn dishonour on the English nation, and sacrificed the Dutch allies.
Torrington’s defence was masterly: the council of war had unanimously opposed an engagement; the Queen’s express order had forced them to fight against their own judgment; the French fleet of eighty-two ships had faced only fifty-six allies; the Dutch had been destroyed by their own rashness, not by English betrayal; and he had saved the English fleet, which was his first duty. After a full hearing the court unanimously acquitted him. William III took away his commission the next day, and Torrington never commanded again. Edward Russell succeeded him as admiral and commander-in-chief — a post he would justify triumphantly at La Hogue two years later.

Strategic Significance
Beachy Head was the greatest naval defeat suffered by the Anglo-Dutch alliance during the Nine Years’ War, and the most conspicuous French naval victory of the age. French writers celebrated it in extravagant terms; the Marquis de Quincy and Father Daniel both produced inflated accounts that Campbell later refuted point by point. For England, the loss of prestige was severe — the vaunted superiority of English seamanship had been exposed, and the Dutch had been sacrificed in plain view of the English fleet.
Yet the defeat was not fatal. The French failed to press their advantage: Tourville did not enter the Thames, did not land an invasion force, and did not destroy the English fleet entirely. The Jacobite insurrection that was to have accompanied the French arrival never materialised, partly because of the Queen’s prompt arrests and partly because the French themselves were uncertain how to proceed. Seignelai’s ambitious plan for burning English ports died with his own illness.
The most profound consequence may have been psychological. The humiliation of Beachy Head stiffened English resolution. Parliament voted vigorous measures for rebuilding the fleet; the Dutch, with astonishing speed, ordered fourteen new men-of-war built and launched within as many days. When the French again put to sea in force in 1692 — under the same Tourville, with the same invasion plan — they were annihilated at Barfleur and La Hogue. Beachy Head was avenged, and English naval supremacy in the Channel was restored for the remainder of the war.

events/battle-of-boyne.title: Battle of the Boyne
events/battle-of-boyne.content:
Battle of the Boyne (1 July 1690)
Summary
The Battle of the Boyne, fought on 1 July 1690 (Old Style) on the banks of the River Boyne near Drogheda, was the decisive engagement of the Williamite War in Ireland. King William III, commanding a multinational army of some 36,000 men, defeated the forces of the deposed King James II, who fielded approximately 26,000 troops including a contingent of French regulars. The battle secured the Protestant interest in Ireland, confirmed the Glorious Revolution settlement, and sent James fleeing back to France. It has been commemorated in Irish Protestant folk memory — under the anomalous date of 12 July — as the foundational victory of the Orange tradition.

The Williamite War in Ireland
When James II fled England in December 1688, Ireland remained his best hope of recovering the throne. The Lord Deputy, the Earl of Tyrconnel, had systematically purged the Irish administration and army of Protestants and replaced them with Catholics. By the spring of 1689, James’s viceroy held all of Ireland except the Protestant strongholds of Derry and Enniskillen. James himself arrived at Kinsale in March 1689 with French money, French arms, and a corps of French officers, and summoned a Jacobite parliament in Dublin that reversed the Cromwellian land settlement and vested the property of absent Protestants in the crown.
The relief of Derry in July 1689 and Marshal Schomberg’s subsequent campaign in Ulster had checked the Jacobite advance but produced no decisive result. Through the winter of 1689–1690 the two armies faced each other across a wasted countryside, disease taking a heavier toll than combat. It became clear that only the presence of William himself could galvanise the war to a conclusion.

William’s Expedition
William resolved to take personal command of the Irish campaign in the spring of 1690. He assembled an army of some 36,000 men, drawn from English, Dutch, Danish, Brandenburg, and Huguenot regiments — the most formidable force ever sent to Ireland from England. On 11 June 1690 he embarked at Chester with his forces on board 288 transports, escorted by a squadron of six men-of-war under Sir Cloudesley Shovel. Campbell’s Naval History records that William landed at Carrickfergus on 14 June and dismissed Admiral Shovel with orders to join the grand fleet.
William advanced rapidly south from Belfast. He covered in six days a march that had taken Schomberg weeks the previous summer. The Jacobites abandoned the strong passes of Newry and Dundalk without a fight, falling back to the line of the Boyne. Burnet notes that James and his court had been so buoyed by news of political distractions in England that they flattered themselves William would never dare leave England at all — and that James remained ignorant of William’s landing for six days after it occurred.

The Armies
William’s army, encamped on the north bank of the Boyne near Drogheda, numbered about 36,000 men: English, Scots, Dutch, Danes, Brandenburgers, and Huguenot refugees — the latter burning to avenge themselves on the French troops serving under James. The army was well-provisioned, in good spirits, and confident in its commander.
James’s army, on the south bank, numbered about 26,000. His cavalry was good, and he had 5,000 French regulars under the Count of Lauzun, sent by Louis XIV in exchange for 5,000 Irish recruits shipped to France. The Irish infantry were numerous but poorly armed and untrained; their officers were divided by faction and jealousy. The French professionals held the Irish in contempt, and the Irish resented the French.

The Council of War
James held councils of war on 29–30 June. The unanimous advice of both his French and Irish officers was to avoid a general engagement. They urged him to strengthen the garrisons, fall back behind the Shannon, and draw William away from his fleet and supplies, protracting the war until the French navy could cut William’s communications with England. Lauzun’s officers, in particular, argued that the French fleet would soon destroy William’s transports in the Irish Sea, trapping his army in a hostile country.
James overruled them all. He was positive that he must stand and defend the Boyne. To abandon Dublin without a battle, he argued, would lose him all reputation, dishearten his friends in England, and cause the Irish people to capitulate. Burnet records that James seemed almost pleased at the prospect of a decisive battle for his crown: many about him suspected he was weary of the struggle and longed to see an end of it at any rate.

The Ground
The River Boyne at the fords near Drogheda was deep and rose high with the tide. On the south bank, where James’s army lay, the ground rose from the river through a series of defensive positions: first a broken bank lined with old houses and hedges, then a range of small hills, and finally the village of Dunore on a height commanding the whole field. On James’s left, a bog made the ground impassable; on his right, downstream, lay Drogheda itself, held by his garrison. Three miles above the Jacobite camp stood the bridge of Slains, the only crossing beyond the fords. The position was naturally strong, and James had thrown up breastworks at the principal fords.

William’s Wounding
On the afternoon of 30 June, William rode along the north bank to reconnoitre the fords. He stopped for some time in one place to observe the ground. The Jacobites spotted him, brought down two field-pieces concealed behind a hedge, and fired. A ball struck William on the right shoulder, tearing his clothes and about a hand’s-breadth of the skin.
Burnet, who gives a first-hand account, writes that about a spoonful of blood came from the wound and that was all the harm it did. But the terror it struck into those around him was immense. William declared it was nothing, allowed it to be washed and plastered, and immediately remounted. He rode about all the posts of his army — remaining nineteen hours on horseback that day — to dispel the alarm. A deserter carried news of the wound to the Jacobites, and from there it reached France, where it was taken for granted that William could not survive. Paris erupted in rejoicing: the guns of the Bastille were fired, the city was illuminated, and public rejoicings exceeded those for any victory. The French court was later covered in confusion when they learned William was still alive.

The Battle: 1 July 1690
William’s plan, which he communicated to his generals only in written orders late on the night of 30 June, involved a three-pronged assault. Count Schomberg, son of the Marshal, was to march upstream at daybreak with the right wing of about 10,000 men (mostly cavalry), cross at the fords below Slains bridge, and push for the pass of Duleek behind the Jacobite position, cutting off any retreat. Some hours later, once Count Schomberg was known to be across, the centre under the old Duke of Schomberg was to force the fords directly between the two camps. William himself, commanding the left wing, would cross downstream near Drogheda and fall on the Jacobite flank.
The Right Wing: Count Schomberg
Count Schomberg’s column marched off at six in the morning. James, seeing this movement, mistook it for a general advance and sent successive bodies of troops to oppose it, weakening his centre. The Count found little opposition at the crossing, and though the bog on the far side slowed his infantry, his boldness dismayed the enemy, who fell back towards Duleek.
The Centre: The Duke of Schomberg
When William received word that Count Schomberg was across, he ordered the centre to advance. The Dutch Blue Guards entered the river first, followed by the Brandenburghers, prompted by national rivalry. The sudden resistance of so many men swelled the river; the infantry crossed breast-high, holding their arms above their heads, while the horses swam.
The Irish troops fled from the breastworks and hedges after firing only confused, ill-aimed volleys. But as the Williamite infantry emerged into the open ground, General Hamilton — who had commanded James’s cavalry and had previously deserted from William — launched a furious countercharge. He had distributed brandy to his dragoons and led them with a rage that was more frantic than brave. At the same time the French regiments, who had been hidden among the hills, rose up and added their fire.
The double shock threw William’s centre into disorder. The Dutch stopped; the Huguenots were broken through; the Danes turned and fled back across the river. Marshal Schomberg, seeing the crisis, rode into the river to rally the French Protestants, crying out, “Voila, Messieurs, vos persécuteurs!” (“There, gentlemen, are your persecutors!”). In the confusion of the melee, Schomberg was wounded and then killed — most likely by the fire of his own men in the swirling action. Burnet compares his fall to that of Epaminondas, dying on the day of his side’s triumph.
William’s Crossing
William himself had crossed downstream with his cavalry. With his wounded arm freed from its sling and his sword drawn, he appeared on the flank of the Jacobite position at the critical moment. The Jacobites fell back to the strong station of Dunore, where the battle raged for another half-hour with various success. In the heat of the action, one of William’s own dragoons mistook him and clapped a pistol to his head. The King turned it aside and said calmly, “What, do you not know your friends?”
The Rout
The Irish infantry at length gave way. Hamilton’s cavalry attempted one more charge and almost succeeded, but Hamilton himself was taken prisoner. James, who had watched the entire battle from a safe distance at the church of Dunore, seeing that all was lost and that Count Schomberg was still advancing towards Duleek, abandoned his post while the armies were still fighting. He left orders for the army to fall back to the Shannon and fled himself.
Burnet’s account is blunt: James was the first that ran for it and reached Dublin before the action was quite over. He rode that same day from Dublin to Duncannon Fort, and from there boarded a French ship that had been prepared for him by his special direction to Sir Patrick Trant. He sailed for France, never to return to Ireland.

Aftermath and Significance
The Jacobite army lost about 2,000 killed; William’s losses were under 500. William declined a hot pursuit, judging that his cavalry were exhausted and that the pursuit of a broken army would be mere butchery — a thing he had always abhorred. The Irish army, abandoned by its officers, dispersed; many of them reassembled later under the walls of Limerick, where the war would drag on for another year.
The strategic significance of the Boyne was decisive. It secured Dublin and the eastern provinces; it shattered the myth of Jacobite invincibility; it confirmed the Protestant succession in Ireland. For William, the victory justified his bold strategy of leaving England at a moment when political discontent was high and the French fleet dominated the Channel. Burnet notes that the victory was almost wholly attributed to the King’s courage and conduct.

Irish Cultural Memory
The Battle of the Boyne acquired a symbolic resonance far exceeding its military importance. In Irish Protestant folk memory, it became the central episode of the Williamite deliverance — the triumph of Protestant liberty over Catholic tyranny. The date of the battle, 1 July 1690 under the Old Style Julian calendar then in use, translates to 11 July under the New Style Gregorian calendar. But the commemorative celebrations were moved to 12 July after the calendar reform of 1752, giving rise to “Orangement’s Day” or “the Twelfth.” The Orange Order, founded in 1795 to uphold the Protestant ascendancy, took the Boyne as its foundational myth. To this day, the Twelfth of July is marked by parades, bonfires, and marching bands across Northern Ireland — a living, and often contentious, link to the events of 1690.

Contemporary Accounts
Burnet, the Whig bishop, is the most valuable first-hand witness among the sources listed. He does not claim to have been on the field — he was in England at the time — but he wrote his account from conversations with the King and with officers who fought, and he supplies details that appear in no other narrative: the size of the armies, the tenor of James’s council of war, the manner of William’s wounding, and the King’s movements on the battlefield. Dalrymple’s Memoirs draws on original documents and on Story’s contemporary history of the Williamite war, and provides the most detailed tactical account of the battle. Campbell’s Naval History supplies the maritime context — the transport of the army and the naval operations in the Irish Sea that made William’s campaign possible.

events/battle-of-la-hogue.title: Battle of La Hogue (Barfleur)
events/battle-of-la-hogue.content:
Battle of La Hogue (Barfleur), 19–24 May 1692
Summary
The Battle of La Hogue, also known as the Battle of Barfleur, was the decisive naval engagement of the Nine Years’ War. Fought over six days from 19 to 24 May 1692 (Old Style) in the English Channel and along the coast of Normandy, it pitted the combined English and Dutch fleets — some 99 ships of the line under Admiral Edward Russell — against the French Brest fleet of about 44 ships under the Comte de Tourville. The battle shattered Louis XIV’s planned invasion of England in favour of the deposed James II, destroyed the flagship Soleil Royal and fifteen other French men-of-war, and ended French naval power for the remainder of the war. Dalrymple calls it one of the most important events in the annals of England; Campbell’s Naval History reckons it the greatest victory at sea since the Armada.

The French Invasion Plan
The reduction of Ireland in 1691, and the prospect of William III launching an invasion of France from the English coast, convinced Louis XIV that he must stake everything on a single blow: a full-scale invasion of England in concert with Jacobite conspirators. Dalrymple records that the French assembled twenty thousand men — fourteen battalions of English and Irish troops plus nine thousand French regulars under Marshal Bellefonde — together with three hundred transports at the Norman ports. The Comte de Tourville was ordered to bring the grand fleet from Brest to clear the Channel, while the Comte d’Estrees was to sail from Toulon with a reinforcement of twelve ships. The timing was fixed for the middle of March, before the English and Dutch squadrons could unite.
The plan rested on intelligence from a network of Jacobite agents reaching deep into William’s own government. Dalrymple, drawing on documents since lost, relates that Lord Marlborough, Lord Godolphin, Lord Shrewsbury, and even Admiral Russell himself had all, at various points, opened correspondence with James. Russell in particular proposed either to delay the invasion until winter or, if it proceeded immediately, to draw the English fleet away on a descent at St. Malo, leaving the Channel clear. Yet Russell added a warning that baffled James: as an officer and an Englishman, he would fire on the first French ship he met, even if James himself stood on the quarterdeck.

The English and Dutch Fleets
William III had left England at the beginning of March with instructions to Russell to use all imaginable diligence in getting the fleet to sea. The Queen — Mary II — acted with equal resolution. Alarmed by reports that many officers of the fleet were disaffected, she sent word through Secretary Nottingham that she would not remove a single commander; she reposed entire confidence in their fidelity. The flag-officers and captains, assembled on board the Britannia at St. Helen’s on 15 May, drew up a loyal address vowing to die in her cause. Russell himself did not sign it — whether from accident or from consciousness of his ambiguous correspondence with James, Dalrymple cannot determine.
By the third week of May the allied fleet stood complete: ninety-nine ships of the line carrying over 7,000 guns and 40,000 men — the greatest navy that had ever covered the ocean. The Dutch, under Admiral Allemonde, formed the van; the English red squadron, under Russell in the Britannia, held the centre; the blue squadron, under Sir John Ashby, brought up the rear. Russell’s second in command was Sir Ralph Delaval, with Sir Cloudesley Shovel as rear-admiral. Sir George Rooke served as rear-admiral of the blue.

The Battle off Barfleur, 19 May
On the evening of 18 May the allied fleet stood over for Cape La Hogue. At three o’clock on the morning of the 19th, scouts to the westward fired swivel-guns; by four, the fog lifting, the French were seen standing southward about seven leagues from Cape Barfleur. Tourville had only forty-four ships under his command — d’Estrees had not yet arrived from Toulon, and contrary winds had delayed the Brest squadron’s departure. His orders from Louis were explicit: to fight the English whether strong or weak. He called a council of war the night before; his officers unanimously counselled avoiding action, but Tourville produced the king’s written orders and they resolved to obey.
The French bore down with great resolution. Tourville, in the Royal Sun — the finest ship in Europe, carrying 104 guns — singled out Russell’s flagship and brought to within three-quarters musket-shot at half-past eleven. He plied his guns warmly for an hour and a half, but Russell’s men fired faster, and Tourville was soon seen in great disorder, his rigging and sails shot to pieces, his boats towing him to windward. Five fresh ships of the French blue squadron closed in ahead and astern of their admiral and continued the fight till past three o’clock.
A thick fog at four o’clock separated the fleets. When it cleared, Tourville was discovered towing away northward. Russell ordered a general chase. In the running fight that followed, Rear-Admiral Carter of the blue squadron fell mortally wounded; his last words were to fight his ship as long as she could swim — a death that, as Campbell observes, effectually confuted the base reports that he had taken bribes to fire only powder.

The Pursuit: Cherbourg and La Hogue, 20–24 May
The 20th and 21st were thick and foggy. The French fled westward along their own coast, the English and Dutch in relentless pursuit. On the 22nd, Tourville’s Royal Sun, together with the Conquerant and the Admirable, ran ashore near Cherbourg. The main body of eighteen French ships hauled in for the bay of La Hogue.
Russell detached Sir Ralph Delaval to destroy the ships at Cherbourg. Delaval, sounding the shoals in his own boats and hoisting his flag in a small frigate, sent in fire-ships on the morning of 22 May. Captain Heath of the fire-ship burnt the Royal Sun — the most difficult service, as Delaval’s letter records; Captain Greenway burnt the Conquerant, and the Admirable was set ablaze by the boats. Of the three three-deckers that had taken refuge, not one escaped.
Russell himself anchored in the bay of La Hogue on the night of the 21st. On the 23rd he sent Vice-Admiral Sir George Rooke, with several men-of-war, fire-ships, and all the boats of the fleet, to destroy the remaining thirteen French ships. The French had hauled them as far up the shallows as the tide would permit, covered by the forts of Lisset and La Hogue, with platforms raised on shore and planted with the artillery of the army. King James himself, the Duke of Berwick, Marshal Bellefonde, and Tourville stood on the heights to watch the action.
James had advised putting regiments aboard the grounded ships — they could have fought as steadily as in land castles — but his advice was overruled. Rooke found that neither his men-of-war nor his frigates could get within range. The whole service fell to the boats. The seamen, striving with each other whose barge should be foremost, pulled in with oars alone, gave three huzzas, and scrambled up the sides of the French ships with cutlasses. Six were burnt the first evening, the remaining seven the following morning, together with a great number of transports and ammunition vessels. The whole destruction of fifteen capital ships was accomplished with the loss of only ten men.

The Burning of the Soleil Royal
The Soleil Royal was Tourville’s flagship, the pride of the French navy. Campbell provides the full list of ships destroyed: Soleil Royal (104 guns), L’Ambitieux (104), L’Admirable (90), La Magnifique (76), Le St. Philip (76), Le Conquerant (76), Le Triumphant (74), L’Etonant (80), Le Terrible (80), L’Aimable (68), Le Fier (68), Le Glorieux (60), Le Serieux (60), Le Trident (56), and others. Sixteen ships of consequence in total, besides transports. The French fleet that had escaped through the hazardous Race of Alderney took refuge in St. Malo, effectively neutralised for the remainder of the campaign.

Strategic Significance
The battle ended the immediate threat of invasion. James returned slowly and sadly to St. Germains, and, according to Dalrymple, retired to bury the remembrance of his greatness in the convent of La Trappe. His observation as the English seamen swarmed up the sides of the French ships — “Ah! none but my brave English could do so brave an action!” — was carried through the French camp, creating equal offence and respect.
More profoundly, La Hogue ended French naval power for the duration of the Nine Years’ War. The French navy never recovered the capacity to challenge the combined English and Dutch fleets in a line-of-battle engagement for the remainder of the conflict. The victory secured William’s throne, confirmed the Revolution settlement, and established that the maritime powers — not France — held dominion over the Channel. As Campbell writes, had the English squadron that pursued the French through the Race of Alderney reached St. Malo, the victory would have put an end to French naval power entirely; as it was, it remained the most signal feat at sea since the defeat of the Armada.
Politically, the victory came at a moment of profound internal danger. Dalrymple’s narrative reveals the extraordinary web of Jacobite intrigue that had entangled Marlborough, Godolphin, Shrewsbury, and Russell himself. The Queen’s decision to trust her officers — and their answering loyalty — was vindicated by the victory. William, returning from Flanders, used the intelligence he had gathered of the conspiracy to bind Godolphin to him for ever, and to put Marlborough in the Tower. The victory at La Hogue, in short, secured not only the coast of England but the fabric of the post-Revolution state.

events/battle-of-marston-moor.title: Battle of Marston Moor
events/battle-of-marston-moor.content:
Battle of Marston Moor (2 July 1644)
Summary
The Battle of Marston Moor, fought on 2 July 1644 on a broad expanse of heath west of York, was the largest single engagement of the English Civil War. Some 50,000 British troops were led to mutual slaughter — the most numerous armies that met during the whole course of those wars. The combined Parliamentarian and Scottish forces under the Earl of Leven, Lord Fairfax, and the Earl of Manchester — with Oliver Cromwell commanding the cavalry — defeated the Royalist army of Prince Rupert and the Marquis of Newcastle. The victory broke Royalist power in the north of England, cost the king the city of York and the entire northern counties, and drove the Marquis of Newcastle into permanent exile. It was the first great battlefield triumph of Cromwell’s cavalry, and it established the military reputation that would carry him to the head of the Parliamentarian cause.

The Siege of York
By the spring of 1644 the north of England had become the decisive theatre of the war. The Scots had invaded in January, crossing the Tyne on 22 February under the Earl of Leven, and though the Marquis of Newcastle contained them for a time with an army of some 14,000 men, events in Yorkshire overturned his position. Colonel Bellasis, Newcastle’s lieutenant in the county, was routed at Selby on 11 April by Sir Thomas Fairfax, returning from Cheshire with his victorious forces. Afraid of being caught between the Scottish army and Fairfax, Newcastle retreated into York. Leven joined Fairfax, and together they sat down before that great city.
The Parliamentarian and Scottish forces were not numerous enough to invest the whole of York, a large town divided by a river, and for some weeks they contented themselves with a loose blockade. Affairs hung in suspense. The besiegers suffered losses and fatigues but flattered themselves that the important conquest would soon crown their labours.

The Approach of Prince Rupert
Prince Rupert, the King’s nephew and most aggressive cavalry commander, had been active in Lancashire and Cheshire, collecting a considerable army. He joined Sir Charles Lucas, who commanded Newcastle’s horse, and hastened toward York with an army of 20,000 men. The allied generals raised the siege at once and drew up on Marston Moor, intending to give battle. But Rupert approached the town by another quarter, interposed the River Ouse between himself and the enemy, and safely joined his forces to those of Newcastle.
The Marquis of Newcastle urged Rupert to be content with having successfully relieved the city. The enemy, he argued, was diminished by losses and discouraged by ill-success; their mutual dissensions had already begun to appear; it was wiser to let them dissolve of their own accord. Rupert, whose martial disposition was not sufficiently tempered with prudence, pretended to have positive orders from the king. Without deigning to consult Newcastle — whose merits and services deserved better treatment — he immediately issued orders for battle and led out the army to Marston Moor on 2 July.

The Armies
The two armies were not much different in number, and together they represented the largest concentration of armed force seen in the British Isles during the war. On the Parliamentarian side: the Earl of Leven’s Scottish army, Lord Fairfax’s Yorkshire regiments, and the Earl of Manchester’s Eastern Association army, in which Oliver Cromwell commanded the cavalry — the “choice troops of the parliament, inured to danger under that determined leader, animated by zeal, and confirmed by the most rigid discipline.” On the Royalist side: Prince Rupert’s collected forces from Lancashire and Cheshire, Sir Charles Lucas’s horse, and Newcastle’s own northern regiments — among them the famous “Whitecoats,” Newcastle’s own regiment, resolute to conquer or to perish.

The Battle
The action was obstinately disputed between the most numerous armies that were engaged during the course of these wars. Prince Rupert commanded the Royalist right wing, opposed directly to Cromwell on the Parliamentarian left. After a short combat, the Royalist cavalry gave way before Cromwell’s charge, and such of the infantry as stood next them were likewise borne down and put to flight. Only Newcastle’s regiment — the Whitecoats — obstinately kept their ground, maintaining by their dead bodies the same order in which they had first been ranged.
On the other wing, Sir Thomas Fairfax and Colonel Lambert, with some troops, broke through the Royalists and, transported by the ardour of pursuit, soon reached their victorious friends who were also engaged in pursuit of the enemy. But Lucas, who commanded the Royalists in that wing, restored order to his broken forces, made a furious attack on the Parliamentarian cavalry, threw them into disorder, pushed them upon their own infantry, and put that whole wing to rout. Lucas was ready to seize on the enemy’s carriages and baggage when he perceived Cromwell, now returned from pursuit of the other wing.
Both sides were not a little surprised to find they must renew the combat for a victory each thought already won. The front of the battle was now exactly counterchanged: each army occupied the ground the enemy had held at the beginning of the day. This second battle was as furious and desperate as the first, but after the utmost efforts of courage by both parties, victory turned wholly to the Parliament. Prince Rupert’s train of artillery was taken, and his whole army was pushed off the field.

The Death of Newcastle’s Marquis
The Marquis of Newcastle was entirely lost to the royal cause by this battle — not by death on the field, but by a kind of political death. That nobleman, the ornament of the court and of his order, had been drawn into military command against the natural bent of his disposition, merely by a high sense of honour and personal regard to his master. Munificent and generous, polite and elegant, courteous and humane — his inclinations were secretly drawn to the soft arts of peace: poetry, music, and conversation. He had chosen Sir William Davenant, an ingenious poet, for his lieutenant-general, and the companions of his camp were more the instruments of his refined pleasures than the support of discipline.
When Prince Rupert, contrary to his advice, resolved on battle and issued all orders without communicating his intentions, Newcastle took the field but only as a volunteer. Enraged to find that all his successful labours were rendered abortive by one act of fatal temerity, and terrified at the prospect of renewing his pains and fatigue, he resolved to abandon the cause. Next morning he sent word to the prince that he was instantly leaving the kingdom, went to Scarborough, found a vessel, and carried himself beyond sea. He lived abroad in great necessity until the Restoration, his opulent fortune sequestered by the usurping government; but he disdained by submission to show obeisance to their authority.

Aftermath and Significance
Prince Rupert, with equal precipitation, drew off the remains of his army and retired into Lancashire. Sir Thomas Glenham, the Royalist governor of York, surrendered the city on 16 July, marching out his garrison with all the honours of war. Lord Fairfax remained in the city, established his government over the whole county, and sent a thousand horse to join the Parliamentarian forces pursuing Rupert. The Scottish army marched northward to receive reinforcements and reduce the town of Newcastle, which they took by storm. The Earl of Manchester, with Cromwell — to whom the fame of this great victory was chiefly ascribed, and who was wounded in the action — returned to the Eastern Association to recruit his army.
The strategic significance of Marston Moor was decisive and irreversible. It lost the King the entire north of England: York surrendered, Newcastle fell, and the Royalist grip on the northern counties was broken forever. The victory demonstrated the superiority of Cromwell’s disciplined cavalry — the Ironsides — over the more impetuous but less controlled Royalist horse. It marked the emergence of Cromwell as the paramount military figure on the Parliamentarian side, a reputation that would carry him through the New Model Army to Naseby, the defeat of the King, and ultimately to the Protectorate. For Charles I, the loss of the north meant that he could never again draw on the resources of England’s richest counties; from Marston Moor onward, he fought on the defensive, waiting for a deliverance that never came.
