events/battle-of-naseby.title: Battle of Naseby
events/battle-of-naseby.content:
Battle of Naseby (14 June 1645)
Summary
The Battle of Naseby, fought on 14 June 1645 in the rolling fields of Northamptonshire, was the decisive engagement of the First English Civil War. The newly formed New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax — with Oliver Cromwell commanding the cavalry on the right wing — met and destroyed the principal field army of King Charles I, commanded by the King himself with Prince Rupert leading the horse. The victory broke the military power of the Royalist cause, and the subsequent capture of the King’s cabinet, containing his private correspondence, fatally damaged his political standing. Naseby effectively ended the First Civil War and sealed the fate of the Stuart monarchy.

The New Model Army
The Parliamentarian army that took the field at Naseby bore little resemblance to the county levies and locally raised regiments that had fought at Edgehill and Marston Moor. By the Self-Denying Ordinance of April 1645, members of both Houses of Parliament were compelled to resign their military commands. This removed the Earl of Manchester and the Earl of Essex — men of rank but uncertain zeal — and opened the way for a unified, professional force under Sir Thomas Fairfax as Lord General. The New Model Army was a national army, paid from a central treasury, clothed in the famous red coats, and subjected to a discipline unknown in any previous English force. Its infantry was commanded by Major-General Philip Skippon, a veteran of continental wars; its cavalry was entrusted to Oliver Cromwell, whose “Ironsides” had already proved their superiority at Marston Moor. Lieutenant-General Henry Ireton, Cromwell’s son-in-law, commanded the left wing of horse.

The Royalist Army
King Charles I, having taken Leicester by storm on 31 May 1645, marched south with the intention of relieving the siege of Oxford. His army was numerically inferior to Fairfax’s, but it contained the flower of the Royalist nobility and gentry, men who had staked their fortunes on the King’s cause. Prince Rupert commanded the Royalist right wing, with his accustomed fiery energy; Sir Marmaduke Langdale led the left. The King himself, wearing a black armour and mounted on a white horse, took command of the main body of infantry. The army was full of impatient spirits, eager for action and confident that one decisive victory could undo the work of the Self-Denying Ordinance. Goring had written to the King urging him to avoid a general action until the western forces could join him, but that letter fell into Fairfax’s hands. The King’s council of war, pushed forward by the boiling ardour of the Prince, resolved to give battle.

The Battle
The two armies met on a broad ridge near the village of Naseby. Fairfax placed himself in the centre with Skippon; Cromwell commanded the right wing; Ireton the left. The Prince began the battle with his characteristic celerity. He charged Ireton’s wing with such fury that, despite Ireton’s stout resistance — he was run through the thigh with a pike and taken prisoner — the whole Parliamentarian left was broken and pursued headlong from the field. Rupert, however, committed a fatal error: instead of wheeling upon the enemy’s centre, he wasted precious time attacking the Parliamentarian baggage train and artillery, which had been left with a strong guard.
In the centre, the King led his infantry with conspicuous valour. He displayed the conduct of a prudent general and the courage of a stout soldier. Fairfax and Skippon met him with equal resolution. Skippon, dangerously wounded, was urged by Fairfax to leave the field, but declared he would remain as long as one man maintained his ground. The Parliamentarian infantry was broken and pressed back, until Fairfax brought up the reserve with great presence of mind and renewed the combat.
On the right, Cromwell had meanwhile led his troops against Langdale’s wing. He overbore the Royalist horse by the force of his charge, and improved that advantage by his prudence. Having pursued the enemy about a quarter of a mile, he detached troops to prevent their rallying and turned back upon the King’s infantry, throwing them into utter confusion. One regiment alone preserved its order unbroken, though twice desperately assailed by Fairfax. That General, excited by so steady a resistance, ordered Captain Doyley of his life-guard to charge them in front while he himself attacked them in the rear. Fairfax killed the enemy’s ensign with his own hand, seized the colours, and gave them to a soldier to keep. When the soldier later boasted of having won the trophy, Doyley reproved him; but Fairfax said, “Let him retain that honour; I have to-day acquired enough besides.”
Prince Rupert, now sensible too late of his error, abandoned his fruitless attack on the artillery and joined the King. Charles exhorted the rallied cavalry not to despair, crying, “One charge more, and we recover the day.” But the disadvantages were too evident, and they could by no means be induced to renew the combat. The King was obliged to quit the field, leaving the victory to the enemy.

The Capture of the King’s Cabinet
Among the spoils of Naseby was seized the King’s cabinet, containing copies of his private correspondence with Queen Henrietta Maria. The Parliament ordered these letters published, choosing such extracts as would reflect dishonour upon him. The letters revealed the King’s negotiations with Irish Catholics, his efforts to bring foreign troops into England, and his private determination to yield nothing of substance to his antagonists. The propaganda effect was devastating: it confirmed the worst suspicions of the parliamentary party and persuaded many moderates that no accommodation with Charles was possible. Hume, in his narrative, observes that the letters are “written with delicacy and tenderness, and give an advantageous idea both of the king’s genius and morals” — but the political damage was irreparable.

The Pursuit
The Royalist army was shattered. Fairfax made five hundred officers prisoners and four thousand private men; he took all the King’s artillery, ammunition, and baggage. The King himself retreated with the remnant of his horse, first to Hereford and then into Wales, hoping in vain to raise a new body of infantry. Fairfax retook Leicester on 17 June, then marched westward against the only remaining Royalist field force, that of Lord Goring. Never again would Charles command an army capable of meeting the New Model in open battle.

Strategic Significance
Naseby was the decisive battle of the First Civil War. It destroyed the principal Royalist field army, captured the King’s artillery train, and shattered the political credibility of the King through the publication of his intercepted letters. The war continued for another year — the sieges of Bristol, the campaigns in the west, the last stand at Oxford — but the strategic initiative passed irrevocably to Parliament. The New Model Army, forged at Naseby, became the dominant military institution in the kingdom; Cromwell, already the most formidable cavalry commander in England, was confirmed as the indispensable man of the Parliamentarian cause. Within a year the King would surrender himself to the Scots at Newark. Within four years the scaffold would be erected at Whitehall.

events/sedgemoor.title: Monmouth's Rebellion and the Battle of Sedgemoor
events/sedgemoor.content:
Monmouth’s Rebellion and the Battle of Sedgemoor (6 July 1685)
Summary
The Monmouth Rebellion, also known as the “Pitchfork Rebellion,” was an attempt by James Scott, Duke of Monmouth, the illegitimate son of Charles II, to seize the throne from his Catholic uncle, James II. Landing at Lyme Regis in Dorsetshire on 11 June 1685 with just three ships and fewer than a hundred followers, Monmouth raised the Protestant West Country in arms. Within four days he had assembled over two thousand men. The rebellion culminated in a desperate night attack on the royal army at Sedgemoor in the early hours of 6 July 1685 — the last pitched battle fought on English soil. Monmouth’s defeat, his botched execution on Tower Hill, and the subsequent Bloody Assizes under Lord Chief Justice Jefferies, in which over 250 rebels were executed and hundreds more transported, became a byword for Stuart vengeance and did much to prepare the ground for the Glorious Revolution three years later.

The Duke of Monmouth
James Scott, Duke of Monmouth (1649–1685), was the eldest of Charles II’s many illegitimate children, born to Lucy Walters during the king’s exile on the Continent. Handsome, charming, and militarily brave — he had distinguished himself at the siege of Maastricht in 1673 and commanded the English contingent in the French service — Monmouth became the darling of the Protestant faction during the Exclusion Crisis of 1679–1681. The Earl of Shaftesbury and the Whig party promoted the fiction that Charles had secretly married Lucy Walters, the proof of which was supposedly kept in a mysterious black box. Charles himself, pressed by his brother James, issued a declaration in council denying any such marriage and affirming Monmouth’s illegitimacy. After the failure of the Rye House Plot in 1683, in which Monmouth was implicated, he fled into exile in Holland and later Brussels. Upon James’s accession in February 1685, Monmouth was persuaded against his better judgment to mount a desperate invasion of England.

The Landing at Lyme Regis
Monmouth sailed from Holland with three small ships, accompanied by a handful of exiled Whig gentlemen including Lord Grey of Warke and the Scottish republican Fletcher of Salton. He landed at Lyme Regis in Dorsetshire on 11 June 1685 with scarcely a hundred followers. His manifesto, drafted by the republican theorist Robert Ferguson, denounced James II — referred to throughout as the “Duke of York” — as a traitor, a tyrant, an assassin, and a popish usurper, imputing to him the Fire of London, the murder of Sir Edmund Bury Godfrey, and even the poisoning of Charles II.
The response in the West Country was immediate and fervent. Within four days Monmouth had assembled over two thousand men, mostly clothworkers, farmers, artisans, and Dissenters — “the lowest of the people,” in Hume’s dismissive phrase, but men with strong Protestant convictions and old scores against the Stuart court. The Duke of Albemarle, son of the man who had restored Charles II, assembled the Devonshire militia at Axminster, but finding his troops bore a marked affection for Monmouth, prudently retired.

The Rising in the West
Monmouth advanced through the West Country, passing through Taunton, which received him with open arms. Twenty young women of some rank presented him with a pair of silk colours of their own making, together with a Bible. It was at Taunton that Monmouth was persuaded — reluctantly, according to some accounts — to assume the title of king and to assert the legitimacy of his birth. His army swelled to some six thousand men, though many had to be dismissed for want of arms.
The rebellion was not, however, joined by any man of substantial rank or property. The gentry held aloof. The city of London, where a simultaneous rising had been projected, failed to stir. And from Scotland came news that the Earl of Argyll, Monmouth’s confederate, had already been defeated and captured. Monmouth sank into despondency, at one point resolving to abandon his followers; it was the West Countrymen themselves who urged him on.

The Royal Army
James II acted with energy and decision. Parliament voted a bill of attainder against Monmouth and a supply of 400,000 pounds. Six regiments of British troops were recalled from the Dutch service and dispatched to the West Country under the command of Louis de Duras, Earl of Feversham, a French-born Huguenot of limited military ability, and his second-in-command, Colonel John Churchill — the future Duke of Marlborough, whose later desertion of James would prove decisive in the Glorious Revolution. The royal army, numbering some three thousand regulars, took up a position on Sedgemoor, a flat, marshy plain about three miles south-east of Bridgewater.

The Night March and the Battle of Sedgemoor
On the evening of 5 July, Monmouth climbed the tower of St Mary’s Church in Bridgewater and, with the aid of a spyglass, observed the royal camp at Sedgemoor. The horse and foot lay at some distance from each other, carelessly encamped in overconfidence. Monmouth resolved on a night attack.
His plan was bold but simple: he would lead the infantry against Feversham’s foot, while Lord Grey, with the cavalry, would make a circuit to attack the royal horse in a village to the rear and set it ablaze. The rebels marched out in the dead of night, guided by a local man. But the plan unravelled. A Captain Hucker fired a pistol prematurely, alerting the royal camp, though the royalists were at first uncertain what the alarm meant. The rebels found a ditch — the Bussex Rhine — before the royal lines that they had not anticipated, but forced their way across it.
What followed was an extraordinary three-hour contest in the dark. Monmouth’s irregulars — armed with scythes, pitchforks, and a motley collection of firearms — drove the veteran troops back, fighting with a courage that astonished both sides. Hume writes that they “threw the veteran forces into disorder; drove them from their ground; continued the fight till their ammunition failed them; and would at last have obtained a victory, had not the misconduct of Monmouth and the cowardice of Gray prevented it.” Dalrymple’s account describes how the rebels formed into a solid body, “laying their shoulders close to each other,” advancing, stopping, fighting, and dying together. For three hours they sustained the attack.
But Lord Grey’s cavalry charge failed utterly; Grey fled almost at once. Without cavalry support, and with Feversham’s cannon brought to bear on the densely-packed rebel ranks, the advantage turned. The royal horse, having driven off Grey, returned and fell on the rebel rear. When their ammunition ran out, the rebels finally broke. About fifteen hundred fell in the battle and pursuit.

The Capture and Execution of Monmouth
Monmouth fled the field, riding twenty miles until his horse foundered. He exchanged clothes with a peasant and attempted to hide, but was discovered two days later near Ringwood in Dorsetshire, lying in a ditch covered with fern. In his pockets were found some green peas — all that had sustained him — and his George of diamonds. When seized, Hume records, he burst into tears.
He wrote abject letters to James, begging for an audience and hinting at secrets of great importance. James admitted him to his presence, hoping to extract a confession of his accomplices, but Monmouth would not name names. He offered to change his religion; James was unmoved. On 15 July 1685, Monmouth was beheaded on Tower Hill. The execution was a horror: he warned the executioner not to botch the job as had been done with Lord Russell. The warning unnerved the axeman, who struck feebly. Monmouth raised his head from the block and looked reproachfully at him. It took five blows to sever the head. The crowd, which had loved him, dissolved in weeping.

The Bloody Assizes
The vengeance that followed was calculated to terrify. Colonel Percy Kirke, whose regiment — known as “Kirke’s Lambs” — had served at Tangiers, hanged nineteen prisoners without trial at Bridgewater, often while he and his officers drank the king’s health. Feversham hanged another twenty. The country was strewn with the heads and limbs of the executed.
But the worst was yet to come. Lord Chief Justice George Jefferies, the most feared judge in England, was sent on a judicial progress through the West Country — the “Bloody Assizes.” At Dorchester, he exhorted thirty prisoners to confess, and when twenty-nine were found guilty, ordered them to immediate execution. At Exeter, two hundred and forty-three were tried; at Taunton and Wells, more still. Jefferies bullied juries, browbeat witnesses, and harangued the accused with drunken fury. In all, some two hundred and fifty-one men and women were executed by judicial sentence, and hundreds more were transported to the plantations in the West Indies.
The most notorious cases were those of two women: Lady Alice Lisle, the elderly widow of a regicide, condemned for harbouring two rebels the day after Sedgemoor and beheaded at Winchester; and Elizabeth Gaunt, an Anabaptist who had sheltered a rebel, who was burned alive at Tyburn after the man she had saved betrayed her to save his own skin.

Aftermath and Significance
The rebellion, though brief and ill-conducted, had far-reaching consequences. James II, emboldened by his easy victory and by the compliant parliament that had supported him, now believed he could impose his Catholicising policies without resistance. The Bloody Assizes had terrorised the nation but also disgusted it; the executions alienated the very classes — the Protestant gentry and the Dissenting interest — whose support James would desperately need three years later when William of Orange landed at Torbay. As Hume observes, “This victory, obtained by the king in the commencement of his reign, would naturally, had it been managed with prudence, have tended much to increase his power and authority. But by reason of the cruelty with which it was prosecuted, and of the temerity with which it afterward inspired him, it was a principal cause of his sudden ruin and downfal.”
The Battle of Sedgemoor holds a unique place in English history: it was the last pitched battle fought on English soil. It also provided an early display of the military talents of John Churchill, who would go on to become the greatest general of his age. For the common people of the West Country, the rebellion became a folk memory of courage and betrayal — a lost cause in which the scythe and the pitchfork had almost, but not quite, overcome the king’s redcoats.

Contemporary Accounts
Hume’s History of England (vol. 8) provides the most comprehensive narrative of the rebellion, the battle, and the Bloody Assizes, with vivid descriptions of the atrocities committed by Kirke and Jefferies. Dalrymple’s Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland (vol. 1) adds important tactical detail on the battle of Sedgemoor itself, drawn from the original papers in the state paper office, including Monmouth’s movements in the West and his council of war at Bridgewater. Burnet’s History of His Own Time (vol. 1) offers the Whig perspective, with particular attention to the character of Jefferies and the political consequences of the rebellion.

sources/bank-england-arguments-engraftin.title: The Arguments and Reason for the Acceptance of Engrafting upon the Bank of England (1697)
sources/bank-england-arguments-engraftin.content:
The Arguments and Reason for the Acceptance of Engrafting upon the Bank of England (1697)
Anonymous — The Arguments and Reason for the Acceptance of Engrafting upon the Bank of England. As they were Debated at the General Court of the said Bank. In a Letter to a Friend. — London, 1697.
A pamphlet written in the form of a letter to a friend who has “the greatest part of your Fortune in the Bank of England” and asks for advice on whether the proposed “engrafting” of tallies into Bank stock will serve the government and the Bank’s proprietors.
Content Summary
The pamphlet addresses the proposal to “engraft” outstanding government tallies (credit instruments drawn on parliamentary funds) into Bank of England stock. Under the plan, the Bank would take in all tallies on parliamentary funds, along with Bank-notes, bills, or money, and convert them into shares of Bank stock.
The case for engrafting (presented by proponents):

The Bank will be enabled to serve the public more effectively
It will be for the interest and advantage of the Bank itself
The great discounts on tallies (sold at heavy losses) harm trade and government credit — “while Tallies are sold at this vast Discount, no Body will lend their Money to the King; and but few will employ it in Trade”
If all tallies are lodged in the Bank, there will be no tallies to sell on the discount market, forcing money back into trade and government loans

The author’s arguments against:
The author responds point by point. The core objection: the proposal gives tallies-holders no money or cash-equivalent in exchange — only a proportionate share of Bank stock. Since they were selling tallies because they needed ready money, “they will be then as bare of Money as they were before they parted with their Tallies.”
The author further argues that the Bank’s present credit was founded on:

The security of its parliamentary fund
The reputation of its managers
The confidence of the public that it would not lend beyond secure funds

He questions whether an “engrafted” Bank would maintain this credit, observing that the Bank itself had fallen into discredit despite the good qualities of its managers. He warns that “if the present Bank of England, from a flourishing State, be fallen into Discredit, and rendered incapable of discharging its Debts,” the same could happen after engrafting.
The six arguments for compulsion (as reported from the General Court):
The proponents also argued six reasons why the Bank must accept: (1) all outstanding Bank bills and notes would be brought in and cancelled, leaving the Bank debt-free; (2) its notes would then trade at par; (3) its credit would increase; (4) it would have more time to call in loans; (5) Parliament would grant further privileges; (6) if they refused, Parliament would leave them “to the Mercy of their Creditors and the Severity and Extreamity of Law and Justice.” “the credit of the Bank of England was much shaken” in 1696, and the engrafting scheme was part of the parliamentary rescue that restored it. The scheme was eventually implemented under the Bank Act of 1697.
OCR Quality
Fair. The first pages contain heavy OCR noise from black-letter type and decorative elements, but the main text (from approximately line 40 onward) is readable in substance. The 18th-century typography (long-s, archaic spellings) is preserved, and the author’s arguments are clearly intelligible despite occasional garbled characters and page-break artifacts.

sources/bank-of-england-1694-account.title: A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England (1694)
sources/bank-of-england-1694-account.content:
A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England (1694)
Anonymous — A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England. — Printed by Randal Taylor, near Stationers-Hall, London, 1694.
A contemporary pamphlet published in the year the Bank of England was founded (1694). It presents the case for establishing a national bank, addresses objections, and explains how the Bank would operate. It is a primary source for the Financial Revolution — the creation of modern public credit institutions that transformed English state finance.
The source was downloaded from the Internet Archive as OCR text from a DjVu scan. It is 720 lines (~21 KB).
Content Summary
The pamphlet is a defence of the Bank of England proposal against its critics. Written during the Nine Years’ War (1689–1697) , when William III’s government was desperate for new methods of raising funds, the pamphlet addresses both the practical and political objections to a national bank.
The author begins by noting that the want of a public bank has caused “much unnecessary Credit, to the loss of several Millions” and that the height of interest rates in England compared to “our Rival Neighbors” (the Dutch) has damaged trade.
The main objections answered:


“The King will become Absolute” — Critics argue the Bank will make the king a master of it, and that moneyed men are naturally timid and would comply with the king. The author rejects this, arguing the Bank’s constitution provides security.


“Banks only exist in Republics” — The old Whig objection that a bank requires a Commonwealth form of government. The author dismisses this with the example of other monarchies (implicitly referencing the successful Dutch and Venetian models).


“It will raise the price of Land and ruin Trade” — Critics claim that making real securities current through the bank will destroy personal credit. The author counters that the Bank will actually stimulate both land values and trade by making credit more available.


“All Money will run into Trade” — A strange objection — critics argued that the Bank would be so profitable that all money would leave land purchases. The author treats this as self-refuting.


The positive case:
The author then explains the Bank’s intended structure:

Subscriptions from the public creating a permanent fund
The fund to be managed by a Governor, Deputy-Governor, and Directors
The Bank to issue notes that circulate as money
The Bank to handle government borrowing (the “Exchequer Bills” model)
The Bank to discount merchants’ bills and facilitate trade

The benefits claimed:

Lower interest rates (bringing English rates down to Dutch levels)
Increased trade and commerce
Secure and convenient payments
Support for the government’s war finances
The revival of national virtue and prosperity — the pamphlet ends on a note of patriotic hope: that the Bank will enable the nation “to revive, recover, and transmit to Posterity, the Virtue, Lustre, and wonted Glory, of their Renowned Ancestors.”

This pamphlet represents the pro-Bank side of the public debate. It appeared in the same year the Bank was chartered (July 1694). The pamphlets against the Bank (by the Tory interest, the goldsmith-bankers who saw their monopoly threatened, and the Country party who feared court influence) were numerous and fierce.
OCR Quality
Poor to moderate. The DjVu OCR from the 1694 pamphlet uses old-tyle black-letter type, long-s, and ligatures, resulting in frequent garbled characters, inserted page-artefacts, and broken words. The text is readable with effort — the structure and arguments are clear, but individual words are often corrupted. Some passages (title page decorations, page breaks) produce binary garbage in the extraction. The full content is present and comprehensible, making this a usable source for research purposes.

sources/bank-of-england-short-account.title: A Short Account of the Bank of England (c. 1694)
sources/bank-of-england-short-account.content:
A Short Account of the Bank of England (c. 1694)
Originally by Michael Goddard — A Short Account of the Bank of England. — Heretofore Published by Michael Goddard, and now Reprinted. London, c. 1694–1700.
A pamphlet defending the Bank of England, written in the early years of its existence. The text identifies itself as a reprint of an earlier work by Michael Goddard, a merchant and early director of the Bank. It provides a detailed description of the Bank’s constitution, the subscription process, the benefits to trade, and a refutation of its critics.
The source was downloaded from the Internet Archive as OCR text from a DjVu scan. It is 1,756 lines (~50 KB).
Content Summary
The pamphlet is structured as a defence of the Bank against its opponents, whom the author divides into three groups: those averse to the government (Jacobites), those acting from prejudice, and those acting from self-interest (the goldsmith-bankers whose monopoly was threatened).
The Constitution of the Bank:

The Bank is a society of about 1,300 persons, incorporated by Act of Parliament under the name “The Governor and Company of the Bank of England”
The original subscription was £1,200,000 (the entire sum lent to the government)
Subscriptions were taken by commissioners appointed by Parliament, open to “any Person or Persons, Natives or Foreigners”
If the full £1,200,000 was not subscribed by 1 August (1694), the charter would lapse
The Bank is governed by a Governor, Deputy-Governor, and 24 Directors, elected annually
Directors cannot serve more than one year without a break (to prevent fraud)

Advantages claimed for the Bank:

Raised £1,200,000 for the war cheaper than could otherwise have been done
Ties the people faster to the government (the Whig argument: the Bank creates stakeholders in the regime)
Lowers the interest of money — the central claim. Before the Bank, government loans carried rates of 12%, 14%, up to 30%. The Bank’s existence forced down rates. The author argues this benefits trade and land values
Raises the value of land — lower interest makes land purchases more attractive
Increases trade — accessible credit stimulates commerce
The Bank’s own credit has become so strong that its notes circulate as readily as gold

The goldsmith-bankers:
The pamphlet’s most revealing passages concern the struggle with the goldsmiths, who had previously monopolised public credit. Before the Bank, the goldsmiths discounted Exchequer tallies at ruinous rates. The author claims that on some funds, tallies traded at 25–30% discount above the public interest. The Bank’s competition forced these rates down.
Comparison with other funds:
The author compares the Bank’s terms (8% interest) with the cost of other contemporary funds: the Million Lottery and Annuities were costing the nation 14% over 16 years, amounting to vastly greater long-term burdens.
The final argument:
The Bank, the author concludes, rests on the credit of Parliament and the broader national interest. Only if “the public good be postponed to private interest, and a small number of oppressors be too hard for the nobility, gentry, and traders of England in general” could the Bank be subverted. The benefits already seen “in its infancy” are a good earnest of future advantages.
Michael Goddard was a merchant and a subscriber to the original Bank stock — one of the “monied men” of the Whig interest. His pamphlet was considered important enough to be reprinted (probably in the early 1700s), suggesting it had lasting value as a statement of the Bank’s case.
OCR Quality
Poor. The DjVu OCR from the old typeface produces heavily garbled text, especially in the first half. The text becomes somewhat more readable in the later pages. Mathematical comparisons and financial figures are frequently corrupted. However, the argument and structure are clear, and enough readable passages survive to make this a usable source.

sources/brewster-life-newton.title: Brewster — The Life of Sir Isaac Newton
sources/brewster-life-newton.content:
Brewster — The Life of Sir Isaac Newton
Sir David Brewster (1781–1868) — The Life of Sir Isaac Newton. — Harper & Brothers, New York, 1838 (stereotyped edition).
A comprehensive biography of Isaac Newton (1642–1727) by the Scottish physicist and biographer Sir David Brewster. Brewster was himself a distinguished scientist (known for the Brewster angle in optics) and had access to Newton’s manuscripts and correspondence that earlier biographers lacked.
The volume contains 334 page-files, extracted as 13,183 lines (~0.3 MB) of plain text.
Relevance for the 17th-century wiki: Newton’s life spans the entire second half of the 17th century (born 1642, the year of the Civil War’s outbreak). His major discoveries — the prism experiments (1666), the reflecting telescope (1668), the theory of gravity (1684–1687), and the Principia (1687) — were all 17th-century achievements. Chapters I–XIII cover his life within the 17th century.
Contents
CHAPTER I — Birth and Early Life (p. 1)
Newton’s birth at Woolsthorpe, Lincolnshire (Christmas Day 1642, O.S.). His parentage — his father died before he was born. His early education at Grantham School. His mechanical pursuits as a boy: constructing a working windmill, a water-clock, a self-moving cart, and sundials. His preparation for university.
CHAPTER II — Cambridge (p. 17)
Newton enters Trinity College, Cambridge (1661). The origin of his propensity for mathematics. He studies Descartes’s geometry unaided. He purchases a prism. He attends Dr. Barrow’s optical lectures. Barrow’s opinion of Newton’s abilities. Newton takes his degrees and is elected a Fellow of Trinity. He succeeds Barrow as Lucasian Professor of Mathematics (1669).
CHAPTER III — The Prism Experiments (p. 30)
The annus mirabilis (1666). Newton’s first experiments with the prism during the plague years at Woolsthorpe. He discovers the composition of white light and the different refrangibility of light rays — the foundation of modern optics. He abandons attempts to improve refracting telescopes and constructs the first reflecting telescope (1668). The telescope examined by the Royal Society and shown to the King. Brewster traces the subsequent history of the reflecting telescope (Hadley, Short, Herschel, Ramsden, Lord Oxmantown).
CHAPTER IV — Optical Discoveries and Controversies (p. 47)
Newton delivers his optical lectures at Cambridge. He is elected a Fellow of the Royal Society (1672). He communicates his discoveries on the nature of light. Popular account of them. His disputes with Pardies, Linus, Lucas, Dr. Hooke, and Huygens — the first of the great Newton controversies. The effect of these disputes on Newton’s character — his aversion to publication.
CHAPTER V — The Achromatic Telescope (p. 63)
Newton’s mistake in supposing that the improvement of refracting telescopes was hopeless. Mr. Hall invents the achromatic lens. It is reinvented by Dollond. Brewster discusses modern improvements in the aplanatic telescope and corrections to Newton’s spectral analysis.
CHAPTER VI–IX — Further Optical Work (p. 75–110)
Newton’s work on the colours of thin plates (Boyle’s and Hooke’s rings), the theory of fits of easy reflection and transmission, the colours of natural bodies, the diffraction of light, double refraction, and the polarization of light. Brewster discusses the subsequent history of each discovery — Young’s interference principle, Fresnel’s wave theory, etc.
CHAPTER X — Astronomical Discoveries (p. 110)
The necessity of combined effort in great discoveries. A sketch of the history of astronomy before Newton: Copernicus (1473–1543), Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), Kepler (1571–1630), Galileo (1564–1642). The state of astronomical knowledge that Newton inherited.
CHAPTER XI — Gravity and the Principia (p. 140)
The most famous chapter. The first idea of gravity occurs to Newton in 1666 (the apple story). His early speculations and their interruption by his optical work. He resumes the subject after a discussion with Dr. Hooke (1679–1684). He discovers the law of universal gravitation and the cause of planetary motions. Dr. Halley urges him to publish. The Principia is published in 1687. A general account of its contents and the discoveries it contains. The opposition to Newtonian philosophy from Cartesianism. The reception and establishment of Newtonianism in England and abroad.
CHAPTER XII — Fluxions and the Calculus (p. 168)
Newton discovers the binomial theorem and the method of fluxions (calculus) in 1666 — predating Leibniz. His manuscript work communicated to friends. The technical works: Treatise on Fluxions, Universal Arithmetic, Methodus Differentialis, Geometria Analytica. The Bernouilli and Leibniz problems. The great calculus priority dispute. The Commercium Epistolicum and the Royal Society’s report.
CHAPTER XIII — Newton and Politics; His Illness (p. 200)
James II attacks the privileges of Cambridge University (1687). Newton is chosen one of the delegates to resist this encroachment — his first public role. He is elected to the Convention Parliament (1689) that settled the crown on William and Mary. The burning of his manuscript (suspected chemical/alchemical papers). His supposed mental derangement (1693) — Brewster devotes extensive space to refuting the story, using the correspondence with Pepys and Locke to show it was a temporary illness, not insanity.
CHAPTER XIV — The Mint and Knighthood (p. 223)
Covers 1695–1705. The lack of national gratitude for Newton. His friendship with Charles Montague (Earl of Halifax) . Montague becomes Chancellor of the Exchequer and resolves on a recoinage. Newton appointed Warden of the Mint (1695) and later Master of the Mint (1699) — his administrative career. He is elected an Associate of the Academy of Sciences (1699), MP for Cambridge (1701), President of the Royal Society (1703) . Queen Anne knights him (1705). The second edition of the Principia (edited by Roger Cotes). Newton’s conduct regarding Ditton’s method for finding the longitude.
CHAPTER XV — Chronology Controversy (p. 234)
Newton at the court of George I. The Princess of Wales delights in his conversation. Leibniz tries to prejudice her against Newton and Locke. The controversy over Newton’s chronological system — his attempt to date ancient events using astronomical calculations. The Abbé Conti copies and publishes the manuscript. Freret’s refutation. Halley’s defence.
CHAPTER XVI — Theological Studies (p. 242)
Newton’s extensive theological researches — his work on biblical prophecy, his Lexicon Propheticum, his observations on the book of Daniel and Revelation. Letters to Dr. Bentley. Brewster argues that Newton’s theological work was serious and orthodox, contrary to claims that he was a sceptic or Unitarian.
CHAPTER XVII — Minor Discoveries (p. 265)
Newton’s researches on heat, fire and flame, elective attraction, the structure of bodies. His supposed attachment to alchemy. His hypothesis of an ether as the cause of light and gravity. His inventions: the reflecting sextant (before 1700), the reflecting microscope, the prismatic reflector, the method of varying the magnifying power of Newtonian telescopes. His experiments on retinal impressions.
CHAPTER XVIII — Final Years (p. 284)
His illness (attended the Royal Society in failing health). His death on 20 March 1727. His body lies in state in the Jerusalem Chamber. His funeral in Westminster Abbey. The monument and epitaph. A medal struck in his honour. Roubiliac’s full-length statue at Cambridge. His property and successors.
CHAPTER XIX — Character and Reputation (p. 292)
Brewster’s concluding assessment. The permanence of Newton’s reputation. His method of investigation compared to Galileo’s. Brewster disputes the claim that Newton followed Bacon’s method. Newton’s modesty, simplicity, and religious character. His hospitality and mode of life. His personal appearance. The statues and pictures of him. Memorials.
APPENDIXES

No. I — Observations on the Newton family
No. II — Newton’s letter to Francis Aston on travelling advice
No. III — A remarkable conversation between Newton and Mr. Conduit

OCR Quality
Good. The 1838 stereotype edition uses clean modern typography. The OCR is near-perfect. Footnotes and marginal references are partially preserved.

sources/burnet-history-of-his-own-time-v.title: Burnet — History of His Own Time, Vol. I
sources/burnet-history-of-his-own-time-v.content:
Burnet — History of His Own Time, Vol. I
Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury — Bishop Burnet’s History of His Own Time. Vol. I. From the Restoration of King Charles II to the Settlement of King William and Queen Mary at the Revolution. To which is prefix’d a Summary Recapitulation of Affairs in Church and State from King James I to the Restoration in the Year 1660. — Printed for Thomas Ward, London, 1724.
This is Volume I of Burnet’s classic contemporary history, published posthumously in 1724. Burnet was a Scottish bishop, a close associate of William of Orange, and a central figure in the Glorious Revolution. He wrote from personal knowledge, having lived through the entire period, and his history is one of the most frequently cited primary-source accounts for the Restoration and Revolution.
The volume contains 866 page-files (from the 1724 first edition), extracted as 46,853 lines (~1.2 MB) of plain text. The text uses 18th-century typography (long-s, etc.) which OCR renders mostly accurately.
Scope: Covers the Restoration (1660) through the Revolution (1688–1689) , with a preliminary Book I summarising events from James I (1603) through the Civil War and Commonwealth. This is a contemporary firsthand account — Burnet was an eyewitness to many of the events he describes.
Structure









































BookTopicLinesEraBOOK ISummary Recapitulation: Scotland & England from James I to the Restoration1,6191603–1660 (summary)BOOK IIThe first twelve years of Charles II’s reign5,9761660–1673BOOK IIIThe rest of Charles II’s reign18,9921673–1685BOOK IVThe reign of James II33,2671685–1689—Table of Contents & Index44,952—
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK I — Summary Recapitulation (line 1,619)
A retrospective summary of events from James I’s minority through the Civil War, Commonwealth, and Protectorate, up to the Restoration in 1660. Key topics:

The distractions of James I’s minority in Scotland
The practices of the House of Guise and Catholic influence
The Gunpowder Plot
Prince Henry’s death (suspected poisoning)
The Elector Palatine’s marriage and the loss of the Palatinate
Buckingham’s rise and the Spanish Match
Charles I’s early reign and the grievances that led to civil war
Strafford and Laud — their characters and fate
The Covenanters, the Bishops’ Wars
The Long Parliament, the Civil War
Cromwell’s rise, the Commonwealth, the Protectorate
Cromwell’s death, the collapse of the Protectorate
Monk and the Restoration

This book is Burnet’s Scottish perspective — he discusses events in Scotland with more depth than most English historians. The characters of the Covenanters, the role of the Scottish nobility, and the ecclesiastical disputes are covered in particular detail.
BOOK II — Charles II, 1660–1673 (line 5,976)
The first twelve years of the Restoration. Key topics:

The Restoration settlement — the king’s return, the Convention Parliament
The execution of the regicides
The settlement of the revenue
The Savoy Conference and the failure of comprehension
The Act of Uniformity (1662) and the Great Ejection
The Corporation Act
The king’s marriage to Catherine of Braganza
The trial and execution of Sir Henry Vane
The sale of Dunkirk to the French
The first Dutch War (Second Anglo-Dutch War, 1665–1667)
The Great Plague (1665) and the Great Fire of London (1666)
The Dutch raid on the Medway (1667)
The fall of Clarendon
The rise of the Cabal ministry
Affairs in Scotland: the restoration of episcopacy, the persecution of Covenanters
Burnet’s own early career and observations

Burnet was in Scotland during much of this period and provides detailed accounts of Scottish ecclesiastical politics — the repressive policies of the Duke of Lauderdale, the synod of Glasgow, and the state of the Scottish church.
BOOK III — Charles II, 1673–1685 (line 18,992)
The later years of Charles II’s reign. Key topics:

The Test Act (1673) and the Duke of York’s resignation of the Admiralty
The king’s Declaration of Indulgence — withdrawn under parliamentary pressure
The cabal’s schemes exposed
The secret Treaty of Dover (1670) — Burnet discusses the rumours of Catholic conspiracy
The marriage of William of Orange to Princess Mary (1677)
The Popish Plot (1678) — Titus Oates, Godfrey’s murder, the terror
The trials and executions of the Catholic peers (Lord Stafford, etc.)
The Exclusion Crisis — Shaftesbury, Monmouth, the Whig movement
The Oxford Parliament (1681) and the Tory reaction
The Rye House Plot (1683) — Lord Russell and Algernon Sidney executed
The deaths of Shaftesbury and the decline of the Whig party
The death of Charles II (1685)

Burnet was closely involved with the Protestant and Whig circles. His account of the Popish Plot is notably sceptical — he regards Oates as a monstrous fabricator, though he acknowledges the genuine fear that gripped the nation. He also provides intimate portraits of the leading figures: Shaftesbury (“bold, witty, and ambitious”), Halifax (“the wisest and most virtuous man of the age”), and Monmouth (“brave but weak”).
BOOK IV — James II, 1685–1689 (line 33,267)
The climax of the volume. Key topics:

The accession of James II (Feb 1685)
Monmouth’s Rebellion and Sedgemoor (1685)
The Bloody Assizes under Judge Jeffreys
James’s Catholicising policy: the dispensing power, Catholic appointments
The case of Godden v. Hales and the legal validation of the dispensing power
The Ecclesiastical Commission
The attack on Magdalen College, Oxford
The trial and acquittal of the Seven Bishops (June 1688)
The birth of the Prince of Wales (June 1688)
The invitation to William of Orange
William’s preparations, the Dutch fleet, the landing at Torbay (Nov 1688)
The defection of Churchill and other officers
James’s flight, his capture, his second escape to France
The Convention Parliament
The offer of the crown to William and Mary
The Revolution settlement, the Bill of Rights

Burnet was himself a participant in the Revolution. He accompanied William of Orange on the invasion fleet (he was nearly shipwrecked on the first attempt), and his account of the voyage, the landing at Torbay, and the negotiations in London is a firsthand report. He was appointed Bishop of Salisbury (the “whig bishop”) as a reward and was a key figure in the post-Revolution church settlement.
OCR Quality
Moderate. The 1724 edition uses 18th-century typography: long-s (ſ), v/u interchange, and abundant ligatures. The OCR renders most of this correctly, though occasional characters are garbled. Subscriber lists occupy substantial early pages but are not part of the history proper. The Table of Contents at the end is a useful finding aid.

sources/burnet-history-of-his-own-time-v.title: Burnet — History of His Own Time, Vol. II
sources/burnet-history-of-his-own-time-v.content:
Burnet — History of His Own Time, Vol. II
Gilbert Burnet (1643–1715), Bishop of Salisbury — Bishop Burnet’s History of His Own Time. Vol. II. From the Revolution to the Conclusion of the Treaty of Peace at Utrecht, in the Reign of Queen Anne. To which is added, The Author’s Life, by the Editor. — Printed for the Editor by Joseph Downing and Henry Woodfall, London, 1734.
This is Volume II of Burnet’s contemporary history, published posthumously in 1734. It continues directly from Vol. I (which ended with the Revolution of 1688–1689) and covers the reigns of William & Mary, William III alone, and Queen Anne — from the Revolution settlement to the Treaty of Utrecht (1713).
The volume contains 810 page-files from the 1734 first edition (New York Public Library copy), extracted as 47,271 lines (~1.2 MB) of plain text.
Scope note for the 17th-century wiki: Only Books V and VI (covering William & Mary and William III, 1689–1702) fall within the 17th century — roughly the first half of the volume. Book VII (Queen Anne, 1702–1713) is early 18th century.
Structure









































BookTopicLinesEra—Subscriber lists (extensive)11734BOOK VReign of King William & Queen Mary2,4501689–1694BOOK VIReign of King William III (alone)9,5711695–1702BOOK VIIReign of Queen Anne18,2691702–1713—Table of Contents40,965—
Book-by-Book Summary
BOOK V — William & Mary (line 2,450)
Covers 1689–1694. Burnet begins writing on 1 May 1705, looking back on the reign. Key topics:

The Revolution settlement — the Convention Parliament, the Declaration of Rights, the offer of the crown
The establishment of William and Mary
The first parliament under the new sovereigns — the Bill of Rights, the Toleration Act, the Mutiny Act
The Jacobite resistance — the first Jacobite rising (1689–1690): Dundee’s rising in Scotland, Killiecrankie, the defence of Londonderry, the siege of Enniskillen
The War of the Grand Alliance (Nine Years’ War) begins — England joins the coalition against Louis XIV
The Battle of the Boyne (1690) — William’s victory in Ireland, James II’s flight to France
The Battle of Beachy Head (1690) — the Anglo-Dutch naval defeat by the French
The Battle of La Hougue / Barfleur (1692) — the decisive Anglo-Dutch naval victory, the destruction of French naval power
The Massacre of Glencoe (1692) — Burnet’s account of the Scottish tragedy
The establishment of the Bank of England (1694) and the financial revolution
The death of Queen Mary (Dec 1694) — Burnet’s poignant account of her final illness and her reputation
Burnet’s own role: appointed Bishop of Salisbury, his involvement in ecclesiastical affairs, his relations with the court

Burnet was a close confidant of both William and Mary. His account of Mary’s death is particularly moving — he attended her in her final hours. He also provides detailed insider accounts of the ecclesiastical settlement, the disputes between High Church and Low Church parties, and the negotiations with the Nonjurors (clergy who refused to swear allegiance to William and Mary).
BOOK VI — William III (line 9,571)
Covers 1695–1702. The period after Mary’s death, with William ruling alone. Key topics:

The funeral of Queen Mary — the unprecedented attendance of both Houses of Parliament
The parliamentary inquiry into naval miscarriages (1695)
The recoinage crisis — the reform of the currency under Somers and Montagu
The Treason Trials Act (1696) — reform of treason procedure
The Assassination Plot (1696) — a Jacobite conspiracy to kill William, the discovery and trials
The Peace of Ryswick (1697) — the end of the Nine Years’ War, the terms, Louis XIV’s recognition of William as king
The first Partition Treaty (1698) and the question of the Spanish succession
The standing army controversy — the parliament’s demand to disband the army in peacetime
The Second Partition Treaty (1700) and the death of Charles II of Spain
The death of the Duke of Gloucester (1700) — the last surviving child of Princess Anne, precipitating the succession crisis
The Act of Settlement (1701) — the Hanoverian succession established, the limitations on the crown
The exiled Jacobite court at St Germain and James II’s death (1701)
The Grand Alliance renewed (1701) — the War of the Spanish Succession begins
The death of William III (March 1702) — his last illness, his character

Burnet’s account of the Partition Treaties and the Spanish succession negotiations is particularly valuable — he was involved in the diplomatic discussions. His portrait of William III in old age, the king’s declining health, his lonely determination, and his final days is drawn from personal observation.
BOOK VII — Queen Anne (line 18,269)
Covers 1702–1713. The reign of Anne and the War of the Spanish Succession. Key topics:

The accession of Anne (March 1702) — her first speech, her promise to follow William’s footsteps
The beginning of the War of the Spanish Succession — the Grand Alliance against France and Spain
The Duke of Marlborough’s campaigns — the great victories: Blenheim (1704), Ramillies (1706), Oudenarde (1708), Malplaquet (1709)
The naval war — Sir George Rooke’s capture of Gibraltar (1704), the Battle of Málaga (1704), the capture of Barcelona (1705), the capture of Minorca (1708)
The Union of England and Scotland (1707) — Burnet was a Scottish bishop and gives a detailed account of the negotiations, the arguments for and against, and the final passage of the Act of Union
The party conflicts — the struggles between Whigs and Tories, the Godolphin ministry, the fall of the Whig junto
The Sacheverell trial (1710) — the high church狂热, the riots, the political fallout
The fall of Marlborough and the Harley-St John ministry (1710–1714)
The Peace of Utrecht (1713) — the terms: Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, the Asiento, the recognition of the Protestant succession
The Hanoverian succession — the arrival of the Electress Sophia’s son
The concluding reflections on the state of Britain

Burnet was a Whig bishop and his account of Queen Anne’s reign reflects Whig perspectives. He was deeply involved in the Union negotiations and provides one of the best contemporary accounts of how the Union was achieved — the bribery, the arguments, the Scottish resistance and eventual acquiescence. His account of the Sacheverell affair and the Tory reaction after 1710 has the quality of a participant watching his cause collapse.
OCR Quality
Moderate. The 1734 edition uses 18th-century typography (long-s, ligatures). The OCR handles it reasonably well. Extensive subscriber lists (lines 1–2,449) precede the main text. The “Life of the Author by the Editor” mentioned on the title page does not appear clearly in the OCR text.

sources/campbell-naval-history-vol2.title: Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. II
sources/campbell-naval-history-vol2.content:
Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. II
John Campbell (1708–1775) — The Naval History of Great Britain, Commencing with the Earliest Period of History, and Continued to the Expedition against Algiers, under the Command of Lord Exmouth, in 1816. Including the History and Lives of the British Admirals. — Volume II. Printed for Baldwyn and Co., London, 1818.
This is Volume II of an 8-volume set. It covers English naval history from the accession of Charles I (1625) through the Peace of Ryswick (1697) under William III — essentially the entire 17th century from the early Stuart period to the end of the Nine Years’ War. It is directly relevant to the England 17th Century wiki.
The volume contains 556 page-files (OCR’d from the Michigan State University library copy, stamped “V.2”), extracted as 23,637 lines (~1 MB) of plain text. Source: MSU barcode 31293027342389.
The volume ends with “END OF VOL. II” and printed by Joyce Gold, Shoe-lane, London.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. XIV — Charles I (line 162, pages 3–53)
Covers the full reign of Charles I (1625–1649). Opens with the accession and Charles’s marriage to Henrietta Maria of France. Major topics include:

The Cadiz expedition (1625) — the disastrous amphibious attack on Spain under Sir Edward Cecil, a failure of planning and logistics
The expedition to the Isle of Ré (1627) — Buckingham’s ill-fated support of the Huguenots of La Rochelle, the English defeat and the loss of thousands of men
Ship Money — Charles’s controversial levy to fund the navy, its legal and political consequences
John Felton’s assassination of Buckingham (1628) at Portsmouth
Tensions with the Dutch over fishing rights and the doctrine of British dominion of the seas
Colonial ventures: settlement of the Caribbean (Barbados, Providence Island), New England, and the beginnings of the Navigation Acts
The growth of English privateering against Spanish shipping
Memoirs of Sir Robert Mansel (Treasurer of the Navy) and Sir William Monson (naval commander and hydrographer)
The state of the navy at the outbreak of the Civil War — neglected, debt-ridden, divided in loyalty

CHAP. XV — Civil War to the Restoration (line 2395, pages 54–112)
Covers 1642–1660, arguably the most dramatic period in English naval history. Key topics:

The struggle between King and Parliament for control of the fleet — the Earl of Northumberland’s defection to Parliament brought most of the navy over
Prince Rupert’s royalist naval campaign, the “royalist privateering” from Continental ports
Robert Blake — the key figure of the chapter. His transformation from army colonel to the greatest English admiral of the century. Memoirs cover his entire career: the blockade of Rupert’s fleet at Kinsale, the destruction of Prince Rupert’s squadron at Cartagena (1650), the Battle of Portland (1653), the Battle of the Gabbard (1653)
The First Anglo-Dutch War (1652–1654) — full narrative including the Battles of Dover, Kentish Knock, Dungeness, Portland, the Gabbard, and Scheveningen (Texel)
Blake’s Mediterranean campaign against the Barbary corsairs (1655)
The War with Spain (1655–1660) — Blake’s destruction of the Spanish West India fleet at Santa Cruz de Tenerife (1657), Admiral Stayner’s capture of the silver fleet
The Western Design — Cromwell’s Caribbean expedition against Hispaniola and the capture of Jamaica (1655)
The navy under the Protectorate, Commonwealth naval administration
The Restoration of Charles II and the fleet’s role in bringing him back — Montague’s mission to the Hague

CHAP. XVI — Charles II (line 5769, pages 133–382)
The longest chapter (covering lines 5769–16581, ~10,800 lines). Covers 1660–1685. Major topics:

The Restoration settlement — Charles II’s return, the reorganisation of the navy under James, Duke of York (Lord High Admiral)
Expeditions against the Algerine corsairs (1662–1664) — the Earl of Sandwich’s campaign against the Barbary pirates
The Second Anglo-Dutch War (1665–1667) — the most detailed narrative in the chapter:

Battle of Lowestoft (1665) — English victory under James, Duke of York
The Four Days’ Battle (1666) — English defeat under Monck and Prince Rupert
St. James’s Day Battle (1666) — English victory
Holmes’s Bonfire (1666) — Sir Robert Holmes’s raid on the Dutch Vlie estuary, burning 140 merchant ships
The Dutch Raid on the Medway (1667) — de Ruyter’s stunning attack on Chatham, the destruction of English ships at anchor, the humiliation of the English fleet


The Third Anglo-Dutch War (1672–1674) — Solebay (1672), the Schooneveld battles (1673), and the Battle of Texel (1673)
Memoirs of the admirals: James, Duke of York (later James II); George Monck, Duke of Albemarle; Admiral Montague, Earl of Sandwich; Prince Rupert; Sir John Lawson; Sir John Kempthorne; Sir George Ayscue; Sir Edward Spragge; Sir Thomas Allen; Sir Robert Holmes; Sir Richard Stayner; Sir Thomas Tiddiman; James, Earl of Marlborough; Sir William Berkeley; Sir John Harman; Sir John Holmes; Sir Christopher Myngs; Sir John Narborough
The state of colonial trade and plantation development under Charles II
Pepys’s naval administration — the reforms of Samuel Pepys as Clerk of the Acts (though Campbell writes from a slightly earlier perspective, the administrative transformation is documented)

CHAP. XVII — James II (line 16582, pages 383–397)
Covers 1685–1688. A shorter chapter reflecting the brevity of James’s reign. Key topics:

James’s accession (Feb 1685) with general acclamation
His efforts to restore and improve the fleet after the neglect of the late Caroline period
Monmouth’s Rebellion (1685) and the fleet’s role in intercepting the rebel ships
James’s Catholicisation of the military and naval officer corps — replacing Protestant officers with Catholics
The growing tension with the Dutch and William of Orange
James’s failure to prevent the Dutch invasion of 1688 — the fleet’s inability to intercept William’s invasion armada due to weather, divided command, and James’s mistrust of his own officers
The defection of the fleet to William — Admiral Herbert’s (Lord Dartmouth) hesitation vs. the pro-Orange sentiment among captains
James’s flight and the collapse of Stuart naval power

CHAP. XVIII — William III (line 17271, pages 398–538)
Covers 1689–1697. The chapter title indicates coverage to the Peace of Ryswick (1697). Key topics:

The Nine Years’ War (1689–1697) — the naval war against Louis XIV
The Jacobite threat — French support for James II’s restoration, the Battle of the Boyne (1690) and naval logistics
The Battle of Beachy Head (1690) — English-Dutch defeat by the French under Tourville
The Battle of Barfleur-La Hougue (1692) — the decisive Anglo-Dutch naval victory that destroyed French naval ambitions for the war; Admiral Russell’s victory
The Smyrna convoy disaster (1693) — the loss of the Mediterranean trade convoy to the French at Lagos
The English bombardment of French ports — Dieppe, Le Havre, St Malo, Calais, Dunkirk
The campaign against French privateers and the convoy system
The struggle for control of the Mediterranean — the English occupation of Cadiz (as a winter base) and the Toulon campaign
Anglo-Dutch naval cooperation and its inherent frictions
Naval administration under William — the rebuilding of the fleet after the combined wars
Memoirs of Admiral Edward Russell (Earl of Orford) , Sir George Rooke, Sir Cloudesley Shovel, John Benbow, and other commanders
The Peace of Ryswick (1697) and the fleet’s reduction in peacetime

The volume ends with an account of the parliamentary inquiry into naval miscarriages in 1696, the votes for naval supply, and the state of the fleet at the close of William III’s active war participation.
OCR Quality
Good. The text is fully readable with minor OCR artifacts — occasional garbled page numbers, header debris, and some broken line-end words. The MSU library stamps and date-due slips appear at the beginning of the scan but do not affect the main text. Footnote markers are preserved, though the footnoted sources (Bishop Burnet, Reresby, etc.) are partially inline.

sources/campbell-naval-history-vol3.title: Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III
sources/campbell-naval-history-vol3.content:
Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. III
John Campbell (1708–1775) — The Naval History of Great Britain, Commencing with the Earliest Period of History, and Continued to the Expedition against Algiers, under the Command of Lord Exmouth, in 1816. Including the History and Lives of the British Admirals. — Volume III. Printed for Baldwyn and Co., London, 1818.
This is Volume III of an 8-volume set. It continues from where Vol. II left off (Chap. XVIII mid-stream) and covers from the closing years of William III’s reign through the entire reign of Queen Anne (1702–1714).
The volume contains 554 page-files (OCR’d from the Columbia University Library copy), extracted as 23,608 lines (~1 MB) of plain text. Source: Columbia barcode cu09367306.
Scope note for the 17th-century wiki: This volume is primarily 18th century (Queen Anne’s reign occupies the bulk of it). The 17th-century content is limited to the continuation of Chapter XVIII (William III, closing the Nine Years’ War) and Chapter XIX (William III’s remaining years, 1697–1702). Chapters XX–XXI cover the War of the Spanish Succession under Anne.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. XVIII (continued) — William III (line 152, pages 1–16)
Continues directly from Vol. II’s Chapter XVIII. Covers the tail end of the Nine Years’ War (1689–1697). Key topics:

Operations in the West Indies — the French attack on English colonies (Jamaica, Barbados), the defence of the plantations, naval engagements in the Caribbean theatre
The English capture of Port Royal (Acadia/Nova Scotia) under Sir William Phips
The Peace of Ryswick (1697) — terms affecting the colonies and the naval balance
The state of the fleet and colonies as the war concluded

CHAP. XIX — William III, Post-Ryswick (line 2598, pages 17–161)
Covers 1697–1702, the final years of William III’s reign after the Peace of Ryswick. Key topics:

The peacetime reduction of the fleet and the administrative challenges of maintaining naval readiness
English naval operations to counter the growing power of Louis XIV’s France in the Mediterranean
The Scottish Darien Scheme (1698–1700) — the disastrous colonial venture in Panama, the English refusal to support it, and its role in precipitating the Act of Union
The War of the Spanish Succession — the diplomatic prelude, the death of Charles II of Spain (1700), Louis XIV’s acceptance of the Spanish throne for his grandson
English naval preparations for the coming war
Memoirs of:

George Legge, Baron Dartmouth — James II’s admiral who failed to intercept William’s invasion fleet in 1688
Sir John Berry — naval commander in the Second and Third Anglo-Dutch Wars
Arthur Herbert, Baron Herbert of Tor Bay — the admiral who brought the fleet over to William of Orange
Anthony Hastings — captain and commissioner of the navy
John Neville — naval commander in the West Indies
Sir Francis Wheeler — commander in the Mediterranean campaign
Henry FitzRoy, Duke of Grafton — illegitimate son of Charles II, killed at the storming of Cork
Sir John Ashby — admiral at the Battle of Barfleur
Edward Russell, Earl of Orford — the victor of Barfleur-La Hougue, First Lord of the Admiralty



CHAP. XX — Queen Anne, Accession to the Union (line 7141, pages 162–302)
Covers 1702–1707. The opening of the War of the Spanish Succession (1702–1714). Key topics:

The accession of Queen Anne (March 1702) and the immediate declaration of war against France and Spain
Sir George Rooke’s expedition to Cadiz (1702) — the failure at Cadiz redeemed by the capture of the Spanish treasure fleet at Vigo Bay
The Battle of Vigo Bay (1702) — destruction of the French-Spanish fleet
The capture of Gibraltar (1704) — Rooke’s bold seizure of the Rock, perhaps the greatest prize of the war
The Battle of Málaga (1704) — the largest naval battle of the war, an Anglo-Dutch tactical draw against the French under Toulouse
The War in the Mediterranean — Sir Cloudesley Shovel’s campaigns, the Toulon blockade, support for the Austrian claimant to Spain (Charles III)
The capture of Barcelona (1705) — the English fleet’s role in the Mediterranean campaign under the Earl of Peterborough
English operations in the West Indies — defence of the colonies, capture of French islands
Naval administration and finance under Anne
The Union of England and Scotland (1707) — the naval implications: a unified British navy, Scottish access to English trade routes, and British naval dominance

CHAP. XXI — Queen Anne, Union to the End of her Reign (line 13432, pages 303–505)
Covers 1707–1714. The climax and conclusion of the War of the Spanish Succession. Key topics:

The disaster off the Scilly Isles (1707) — Sir Cloudesley Shovel’s flagship Association and three other ships wrecked, over 1,400 men lost, including Shovel himself
The Battle of Toulon (1707) — the failed Anglo-Dutch assault on the French Mediterranean base
Minorca captured (1708) — the British seizure of Port Mahon, establishing the Mediterranean naval base
Admiral Byng’s victory at Passaro (1718) — the destruction of the Spanish fleet (note: this may be covered later or as a coda)
The capture of Sardinia and Sicily — British Mediterranean dominance
The Peace of Utrecht (1713) — terms: Gibraltar and Minorca ceded to Britain, the Asiento (slave-trading monopoly), French recognition of the Protestant succession
The death of Queen Anne (1714) and the Hanoverian succession
Memoirs of Vice-admiral John Benbow — his controversial West Indies campaign against the French, the mutiny of his captains, his death from wounds (1702), and the subsequent court-martial of his cowardly captains

OCR Quality
Good. Text is fully readable. Columbia University Library stamps appear on early pages. Footnote markers are preserved inline.

sources/campbell-naval-history.title: Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. I
sources/campbell-naval-history.content:
Campbell — Naval History of Great Britain, Vol. I
John Campbell (1708–1775) — The Naval History of Great Britain, Commencing with the Earliest Period of History, and Continued to the Expedition against Algiers, under the Command of Lord Exmouth, in 1816. Including the History and Lives of the British Admirals. — Printed for Baldwyn and Co., London, 1818.
This is Volume I of an 8-volume set. It covers English naval history from the ancient Britons (pre-Roman period) through the death of King James I in 1625. The volume contains 618 page-files (OCR’d from the original scan), extracted as 24,529 lines (~1.1 MB) of plain text. The text is OCR output from a 19th-century printed book, so minor artifacts (scrambled characters, odd line breaks) are present but do not impede reading.
Scope note: Only Volume I has been acquired (covering antiquity–1625). Volumes II–VIII (1625–1816) are not yet available. For the 17th-century wiki, the most directly relevant chapter is Chapter XIII (James I, 1603–1625).
The book includes portrait plates of admirals and battle plan engravings, which were not extractable from the OCR’d text.
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. I — Naval History of the Ancient Britons (line 1713)
Covers the maritime activities of the Britons before the Roman invasion, during the Roman occupation of Britain, and in the post-Roman period up to the coming of the Saxons. Examines the evidence for early British sea power from Geoffrey of Monmouth and other early chronicles, discusses the Roman fleet in British waters, and the gradual decline of Roman naval presence. Draws on Camden, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and classical authors including Caesar and Tacitus. Spans approximately 1,740 years.
CHAP. II — Naval History of the Saxons (line 2822)
Traces the naval history of the Anglo-Saxons from their first settlement in Britain to their subjugation by the Danes. Includes extensive memoirs of King Alfred the Great, recognised as the founder of the English navy. Covers Alfred’s shipbuilding program, his naval battles against the Danes, and the organisation of the first standing fleet. Also details the reigns of Alfred’s successors and the deteriorating naval situation that allowed Danish incursions.
CHAP. III — Naval History of the Danes (line 3906)
From the peaceful accession of Canute (Cnut) to the English throne, through the restoration of the Saxon line under Edward the Confessor, to the death of King Harold at Hastings in 1066. Discusses Danish naval organisation, Canute’s empire spanning England, Denmark, and Norway, and the naval aspects of the Norman Conquest. Ends with the Battle of Hastings and the collapse of Anglo-Saxon naval power.
CHAP. IV — Naval History under the Norman Kings (line 4633)
Covers the reigns of William the Conqueror, William Rufus, Henry I (Beauclerk), and Stephen. Examines William’s use of naval power for the Conquest, the organisation of the Cinque Ports, naval administration under the Norman dynasty, and the maritime dimensions of the Anarchy under Stephen. Details ship types, naval taxation, and the beginnings of English naval administration.
CHAP. V — Naval History under the Early Plantagenets (line 5690)
A broad chapter covering the reigns from Henry II through Richard II (1154–1399). Discusses naval operations during the Crusades (especially Richard I’s voyages), King John’s loss of the fleet and the French invasion threat, Henry III’s naval rebuilding, the naval wars with France under Edward I, II, and III — including the Battle of Sluys (1340), the first great English naval victory of the Hundred Years’ War — and the naval decline under Richard II.
CHAP. VI — Naval History under the House of Lancaster (line 8935)
Covers the reigns of Henry IV, Henry V, and Henry VI (1399–1461). Focuses on Henry V’s naval buildup for the invasion of France (Agincourt campaign), the naval blockade of Harfleur, and the English fleet’s dominance in the Channel. Includes memoirs of Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick (“the Kingmaker”) and Sir Anthony Widville, Earl Rivers, discussing their roles as naval commanders during the Wars of the Roses. The chapter ends with the deterioration of English naval power amid the dynastic conflict.
CHAP. VII — Naval History under the House of York (line 9670)
Covers the brief reigns of Edward IV, Edward V, and Richard III (1461–1485). Examines Edward IV’s restoration of naval order after the Wars of the Roses, his encouragement of commerce, and the beginnings of English overseas trade expansion. Richard III’s naval preparations against the Tudor invasion are discussed, culminating in Henry Tudor’s landing at Milford Haven and the end of the Yorkist dynasty.
CHAP. VIII — Naval History under Henry VII (line 11276)
Covers 1485–1509. Henry VII’s establishment of a royal navy, including the construction of the Great Harry (the first English carrack). Chronicles the voyages of John Cabot (discovery of Newfoundland, 1497) and the beginning of English Atlantic exploration. Includes memoirs of Sir John Cabot and Sir Edward Howard, detailing early Tudor naval administration and the founding of the permanent royal dockyards at Portsmouth.
CHAP. IX — Naval History under Henry VIII (line 11920)
The longest chapter on a single reign to this point (1509–1547). Henry VIII’s massive naval expansion: the building of the Mary Rose, Great Harry, and dozens of other warships; the establishment of the Navy Board and the Admiralty; the construction of dockyards at Deptford and Woolwich; and the naval war with France and Scotland. Includes memoirs of Sir Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk (Lord Admiral) and Sir William Fitz-Williams, Earl of Southampton. The sinking of the Mary Rose in 1545 is covered.
CHAP. X — Naval History under Edward VI (line 13008)
Covers 1547–1553. The continuation of Henry VIII’s naval policies under the boy-king, including the voyage of Sebastian Cabot (who led an expedition seeking a Northeast Passage) and Sir Hugh Willoughby’s ill-fated Arctic expedition (1553), whose entire crew perished. Discusses the decline of naval readiness during the Somerset and Northumberland protectorates.
CHAP. XI — Naval History under Queen Mary (line 14165)
Covers 1553–1558. English naval involvement in the Spanish marriage, the war with France that resulted in the loss of Calais (1558), and the decay of the fleet under Mary’s pro-Spanish policies. Includes memoirs of Sir John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland, Charles Howard, Earl of Nottingham (later Lord Admiral under Elizabeth), Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex (naval commander against Spain), Sir Humphrey Gilbert (explorer and naval theorist), Sir John Hawkins (slave trader, naval treasurer, ship designer), Sir Francis Drake (circumnavigator and admiral), and Sir Martin Frobisher (Arctic explorer and naval commander against the Armada).
CHAP. XII — Naval History under Queen Elizabeth I (line 14907)
The most substantial chapter in the volume (covers lines 14907–20918, ~6,000 lines). Covers 1558–1603 in immense detail. Key topics:

The naval buildup in the 1570s–1580s in anticipation of war with Spain
The voyages of discovery: Thomas Cavendish (circumnavigation), Edward Fenton, George Clifford, Earl of Cumberland, Sir Robert Dudley
Sir Richard Grenville and the Revenge at the Azores (1591)
Sir Richard Hawkins’s South Sea voyage (1593)
Captain James Lancaster’s East India voyage (1591–1594)
Captain William Parker’s West Indian expeditions
The Spanish Armada (1588): full campaign narrative — fleet composition, battle tactics, the fireship attack at Gravelines, the disastrous return voyage around Scotland and Ireland
The Counter-Armada (1589) and the Portugal expedition
Privateering and commerce raiding as state policy
The establishment of the East India Company (1600)
Naval administration under Lord Admiral Howard and John Hawkins (as Treasurer)

CHAP. XIII — Naval History under King James I (line 20919)
Covers 1603–1625. This is the chapter most directly relevant to the 17th-century wiki. Key topics:

The peaceful accession of James VI of Scotland to the English throne and the political manoeuvring that secured the succession (Cecil’s secret correspondence with James, the Howards’ support)
The immediate proclamation of James and his journey to London
Naval security during the transition — the fleet kept on station off Spain to prevent disruption
The peace with Spain (1604) and its effect on the navy: decline of the fleet, sale of ships, decay of dockyards
The Gunpowder Plot (1605) and its naval connections
The Virginia Company and the founding of Jamestown (1607) — naval logistics of the colony
English exploration and colonisation under James: Newfoundland, the Somers Isles (Bermuda)
Sir Walter Raleigh’s expeditions to Guiana (1595, 1617) and his execution (1618)
The decline of English privateering after the peace with Spain
Naval administration under the Duke of Buckingham (Lord High Admiral from 1619)
The disastrous Cadiz expedition (1625 — promised in the next volume)
State of the navy at James’s death: corruption, neglected ships, unpaid seamen

The volume ends mid-sentence promising treatment of Buckingham’s management in the next volume.
OCR Quality
Good. The text is fully readable with occasional OCR artifacts (scrambled letters on decorative title-page text, stray punctuation, and some broken words at line-ends). Page numbers and running headers are preserved as OCR’d text and appear inline. A section of map/plan descriptions (Battle of Copenhagen, 1801; Cape St Vincent, 1797; Aboukir, 1798) appears to be from later volumes or endpaper plates and has been included in the extraction.

sources/chamberlen-reflections-bank-engl.title: Chamberlen — Some Useful Reflections upon the Intended Bank of England
sources/chamberlen-reflections-bank-engl.content:
Chamberlen — Some Useful Reflections upon the Intended Bank of England
Hugh Chamberlen (c. 1630–1720) — Some Useful Reflections upon a Pamphlet Call’d A Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England. — London, 1694.
A pamphlet responding to and defending against the anonymous Brief Account of the Intended Bank of England (also in this wiki). Chamberlen was a physician and projector — known for inventing the obstetrical forceps (kept secret by the Chamberlen family) and for promoting a land bank scheme as an alternative or complement to the Bank of England.
The source was downloaded from the Internet Archive as OCR text from a DjVu scan. It is 2,356 lines (~100 KB). The text is organised as a point-by-point refutation of the earlier pamphlet.
Content Summary
Chamberlen writes as a defender of the earlier Brief Account, which had been attacked by critics. His pamphlet takes the form of a line-by-line commentary on the earlier work, paragraph by paragraph, defending its claims and amplifying its arguments.
The Land Bank Alternative:
Chamberlen was the leading proponent of a Land Bank — a bank whose credit would be based on landed security rather than gold and silver. This was the competing proposal to the Bank of England (which was based on a subscription of cash lent to the government). Chamberlen argues throughout that a Land Bank would be superior: “Land hath a greater value than Gold and Silver,” he insists, and that “something else besides Gold and Silver will answer the uses of Money.”
Key arguments:

Banks are useful and interest rates are too high
The want of public funds is a cause of high interest and the loss of millions to trade
A Land Bank is more secure than a Money Bank because land is more permanent and valuable than precious metals
The objection that Banks only work in Republics is unfounded — England’s constitution is compatible with banking
The intended Bank of England will lower interest rates, increase trade, and raise land values
Chamberlen cites the examples of Venice and Hamburg as successful bank models
He defends the credit-based Fishery scheme (a project for financing the fishing industry through land-backed credit)

The Exchange of Objection and Answer:
The latter part of the pamphlet takes the form of direct question-and-answer, where Chamberlen lists objections to the Bank and provides his answers:

Whether land-security is sufficient for a national credit
Whether the Bank will make the king absolute
Whether it will ruin trade by drawing away money
Whether paper credit will disgrace the nation
Whether the Land Bank can survive the cancellation of its tallies/tickets

OCR Quality
Poor. The scan uses dense black-letter type and the OCR produces widespread noise, broken characters, and garbled lines. Readable passages emerge intermittently, particularly in the question-and-answer section at the end. The pamphlet is usable for research but requires effort to decipher.

sources/child-discourse-of-trade-1698.title: Child — A New Discourse of Trade (1698)
sources/child-discourse-of-trade-1698.content:
Child — A New Discourse of Trade (1698)
