Sir Josiah Child (1630–1699) — A New Discourse of Trade, Wherein is Recommended Several Weighty Points Relating to Companies of Merchants, the Act of Navigation, Naturalization of Strangers, and our Woollen Manufactures, the Ballance of Trade, and the Nature of Plantations, and their Consequences in Relation to the Kingdom, are Seriously Discussed. Methods for the Employment and Maintenance of the Poor are Proposed. The Reduction of Interest of Money to 4 per Centum, is Recommended. — Printed by T. Sowle, London, 1698.
Sir Josiah Child was a merchant, Governor of the East India Company, and one of the leading economic writers of late 17th-century England. This work collects essays on trade policy, interest rates, the poor, and colonies, written over several decades and revised for this edition.
The volume contains 304 page-files (Columbia University Library copy), extracted as 9,515 lines.
Contents
Preface (lines 83–1086)
Child opens by situating the work in the parliamentary debates of 1669–1670 over interest rates. He responds to critics of his earlier writings, particularly Thomas Manly’s Interest of Money Mistaken. The preface gives a broad comparison of English and Dutch economic practices. Child identifies fifteen specific causes of Dutch prosperity: their merchants sit in councils of state; the law of gavelkind equalises inheritances; exact packing of commodities maintains repute abroad; their great ships sail at one third the English charge; their thrifty living, with a merchant of £100,000 spending less than one of £1,500 in England; the education of both sexes in arithmetic and merchants’ accounts; low customs and high excise; careful employment of the poor; the use of banks, estimated to profit the public by at least a million a year; toleration of different religious opinions; law-merchants for swift dispute resolution; transferable bills of debt; public registers of lands and houses; and the lowness of interest. Of all these, Child argues, the last is the causa causans — the root cause that makes all the others possible.
Chap. I — A Short Reply to a Treatise, Entituled, Interest of Money Mistaken (line 1088+)
Child defends his central thesis: that reducing the legal rate of interest to 4 per cent would transform English commerce. The argument runs through the entire work rather than being confined to this single chapter. He traces English prosperity since the first interest law of 1545, claiming that the abatement of interest has increased English riches six-fold: “We have now almost One Hundred Coaches for one we had formerly; we with ease can pay a greater Tax now in One Year, than our Forefathers could in Twenty.” He cites the growth of London’s wharfs, the increase of merchants’ estates, the rise in land values from eight or ten years’ purchase to twenty, and the improvement of the country’s rents and customs. Interest reduction is the efficient cause of all this: low interest forces money out of idle lending into productive trade.
Chap. II — Concerning the Relief and Employment of the Poor (line 4125, p. 33)
Child examines the problem of poverty as an economic question. “This is a calm Subject, and thwarts no common or private Interest amongst men.” He argues the Dutch handle poverty better by national-level organisation rather than leaving it to each parish. He challenges the claim that English wages are too high: the Dutch pay generally higher wages to their manufacturers yet undersell the English, because their lower interest rates give them cheaper capital. The real cure for poverty, he insists, is not wage control but reducing interest — which would enable merchants to employ more hands. High interest “eats up” the profit of trade, reducing the capital available for employing the poor.
Chap. III — Concerning Companies of Merchants (p. 80)
A defence of chartered trading companies, particularly the East India Company. Child argues that for long-distance and high-risk trades, a joint-stock company is essential. Individual merchants lack the capital and the patience for trades that take years to return a profit. The regulated company provides stability, negotiation strength with foreign princes, and the capacity to maintain forts and factories abroad. He rebuts the charge that companies create monopolies harmful to the public: without the company, he contends, the trade itself would not exist, and the nation would be the poorer.
Chap. IV — Concerning the Act of Navigation (line 5185, p. 102)
“Though this Act be by most concluded a very Beneficial Act for this Kingdom,” Child writes, he argues it requires supplementary policies to be effective. The Navigation Acts reserving English trade to English shipping are valuable, but they do not of themselves cause prosperity. They must be combined with low interest, which would allow English merchants to build and operate ships as cheaply as the Dutch. Without low interest, the Navigation Acts merely raise freight costs, which ultimately fall on the English consumer and exporter. He recommends complementary policies to ensure the Acts achieve their intended effect.
Chap. V — Concerning Transferrence of Debts (line 5640, p. 125)
“The great Advantage that would accrue to this Kingdom, by a Law for Transference of Bills” is Child’s subject. He argues that making debts assignable by endorsement would revolutionise commerce. Under current English practice, a merchant who sells foreign goods must wait six, nine, or twelve months to recover payment, during which his capital is locked. With transferable bills, he could immediately dispose of his credit and recommence trading. Child estimates that this single reform would allow English merchants to “turn their Stocks twice or thrice in Trade, for once that we can in England” — effectively tripling the velocity of commercial capital.
Chap. VI — Concerning a Court Merchant (line 5821, p. 131)
Child proposes establishing specialised mercantile courts on the Dutch model, “by which all Controversies between Merchant and Tradesmen are decided in three or four days time, and that not at the fortieth part of the Charge they are with us.” He draws on “the late most Prudent and Charitable Institution” of such courts in London, arguing they should be extended. The current system of common-law litigation for commercial disputes is ruinously expensive and slow; a merchant’s court with expert judges and summary procedure would be a tremendous stimulus to trade.
Chap. VII — Concerning Naturalization (line 6111, p. 140)
“That an Act of Naturalization of Strangers would tend to the advancement of Trade, and encrease of the value of Lands.” Child argues England should follow the Dutch policy of welcoming foreign Protestants and granting them naturalisation. Immigrants bring skills, capital, and industry; they do not detract from the employment of natives but increase it by expanding the economy. He dismisses the objection that foreigners would take Englishmen’s jobs: it is better to have them add to the nation’s productive capacity than to see them take their skills to Holland or Brandenburg.
Chap. VIII — Concerning Wool and Woollen Manufactures (p. 145)
On the preservation and improvement of the wool trade, England’s greatest manufacturing export. Child discusses the causes of the decline in woollen cloth exports and proposes remedies. The discussion emphasises quality control: Dutch packing and finishing of cloth is superior, which allows them to command higher prices abroad. He recommends a return to strict regulation of manufacturing standards.
Chap. IX — Concerning the Ballance of Trade (line 6497, p. 152)
“That the greatness of this Kingdom depends upon Trade, is generally acknowledged.” Child examines England’s trade balance with various regions. He argues the balance is not inherently favourable — England imports more from the Baltic and other northern regions than she exports there — and must be managed by policy. He defends the principle that a nation should export more than it imports, with the difference coming in treasure. He discusses the mechanisms of trade and exchange, and how policy (rather than mere natural advantage) determines the balance.
Chap. X — Concerning Plantations (line 7425, p. 178)
“The Trade of our English Plantations in America, being now of as great Bulk, and Employing as much Shipping as most of the Trades of this Kingdom.” Child examines the English colonies in America and the West Indies. He compares them with Spanish and Portuguese plantations, arguing English plantations thrive because they allow “an Amsterdam Liberty” in religion, unlike the rigid uniformity enforced by Spain. He discusses the Newfoundland fishery in detail, noting the decline from 250 English fishing ships in 1605 to under 80 at the time of writing. He attributes this to the growth of French fishing, the liberty of eating flesh on fast days in Catholic countries, and the high cost of bottomry loans at 20 per cent. He closes with two principal conclusions: that English plantations may thrive beyond any others if well-regulated; and that it lies within the power of king and parliament to make sugar a securely English commodity, as herrings are Dutch.
A Small Treatise Against Usury (p. 217)
A shorter work appended to the main discourse. It argues against high interest on moral and economic grounds — that “biting Usury” corrodes trade, discourages industry, and enriches the idle lender at the expense of the productive borrower. Child maintains that the law of Moses, which the Jews were commanded to follow, allowed lending at interest only to strangers and not to brethren, which he interprets as a national economic policy rather than a universal moral prohibition.

sources/dalrymple-memoirs-great-britain-.title: Dalrymple — Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland, Vol. I
sources/dalrymple-memoirs-great-britain-.content:
Dalrymple — Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland, Vol. I
Sir John Dalrymple, Bart. (1726–1810) — Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland. From the Dissolution of the last Parliament of Charles II. until the Sea-Battle of La Hogue. Vol. I. — Printed by David Hay, Dublin, 1788.
Dalrymple’s Memoirs is a pioneering document-based history of the Restoration and Revolution period. Unlike Hume (who wrote a synthetic narrative) or Burnet (who wrote from personal recollection), Dalrymple worked from original state papers — he gained access to the French archives at Versailles, King William’s private cabinet at Kensington, and numerous private family collections. His work is particularly famous for exposing the secret Treaty of Dover (1670) and the clandestine diplomacy of Charles II.
This is Volume I of the Dublin edition (1788). It covers from the Dissolution of Charles II’s last Parliament (1681) through the Battle of La Hogue (1692).
The volume contains 604 page-files, extracted as 27,922 lines (~0.7 MB) of plain text.
Contents
The volume opens with an extensive introductory Review of the Political State of England — a sweeping essay tracing English liberty from the Saxons through the Restoration. This is a distinctive feature: Dalrymple argues that English freedom is ancient and continuous, and that the Stuarts’ innovations were the true novelty.
PART I — Charles II and James II (1681–1688)
Book I — The dissolution of the Oxford Parliament (1681). Dispositions of the people. Prosecutions of Whigs. The Duke of York’s administration in Scotland. The Prince of Orange’s visit. The secret French subsidy treaty. Monmouth’s progress through the West. The invasion of the charters (quo warranto). The Rye House Plot. Shaftesbury’s retreat and flight. Trials of Lord Russell and Algernon Sidney. Their characters and last hours.
Book II — Charles II’s last year. His fluctuation about Monmouth. The power of the King and Duke. Project for a Popish army in Ireland. Scotland remodelled. Sunderland’s intrigues against the Duke. The King’s death (1685).
Book III — James II’s accession. Temper of the nation. The King’s declaration. His first steps in the reign. New ministry. Coronation. James’s relations with the Prince of Orange. Argyle’s expedition to Scotland. Monmouth’s preparations in Holland, his manifesto, his landing, his defeats, his execution. The Bloody Assizes. The temper of Scotland. Cruelties of Kirke and Jeffreys.
Book IV — James’s prosperous condition. His speech to the second session of parliament. The parliament roused. The address of the Commons. The Lords prepare to imitate them. Parliament prorogued. The camp on Hounslow Heath. Sunderland’s promotion. The Cabal of Seven. The dispensing power asserted. Roman Catholics brought into offices. Scotland new-modelled. Ireland under Tyrconnell. The trial of Sharpe. Sunderland’s intrigues. Attempts on the possessions of the Church. The Declaration of Indulgence. The attempt on Magdalen College. The bishops’ petition and trial.
Book V — The nation turns to the Prince of Orange. His secret preparations in Holland. James kept in the dark. Offers of France. Officers cashiered for refusing Popish recruits. James advances to the Church. His negotiations with the States. Differences in the Prince’s English councils. The Prince’s declaration. The inquiry into the birth of the Prince of Wales. The Prince detained by contrary winds.
Book VI — The Prince takes his farewell of the States. The rendezvous at Helvoetfluys. The first sailing, driven back. The second sailing. The fleet’s movements. The landing at Torbay. James joins his army. His intention to send off the Prince of Wales disappointed. Councils in the camp. Insurrections. Flight of Prince George and Princess Anne. James’s terror and flight. His capture at Faversham. His return to London. The Dutch enter London. James goes to Rochester, then to France.
Book VII — The Prince calls together the members of Charles II’s last parliaments. Proceedings of the peers. The Convention meets. The Commons pass the vote of abdication. State of parties in the Lords. The conference between the Houses. The Prince opens his sentiments. The settlement of the government. The Claim of Rights. The arrival of the Princess Mary. The tender of the crown.
PART II — William & Mary (1689–1692)
Book I — The state of parties. The opposition in parliament. The Whigs attack the Tories. The King’s arts to remove opposition. Parliament hurts public credit. The King’s scheme for composing differences disappointed. His breach with the Church.
Book II — The state of the war in Ireland. The siege of Londonderry. The sea-fight of Bantry Bay. The cruelties of Marshal Rosen. The siege raised. The Irish parliament. James’s own conduct. Lord Dundee’s exploits. The Battle of Killiecrankie. The manners of the Highlanders.
Book III — Discontents in the House of Commons. Clamours of the merchants. Divisions between the Houses. The Whigs renew attacks on the Tories. Breach in the Royal Family (Anne and Mary). Discontents in Scotland. The King’s scheme for gaining the Scots disappointed.
Book IV — The King becomes unpopular. Preparations for the war in Ireland. Schomberg’s march to Dundalk. The miseries of his army. Heats in parliament. The Commons disapprove of the King’s measures. The King breaks with the Whigs and dissolves parliament.
Book V — The King’s strength in the new parliament. The first conspiracy against the government. The English fleet defeated at Beachy Head (1690). Emotions in England. The Battle of the Boyne. James’s flight to France. Louis drops the scheme of invasion. The siege of Limerick raised. Marlborough’s expedition against Cork and Kinsale. Torrington’s trial.
Book VI — The Congress at the Hague. Ginkell takes Athlone. The Battle of Aghrim. The siege of Limerick and its capitulation. Campaigns on the Continent. The Massacre of Glencoe. Severities against Episcopacy in Scotland.
Book VII — Causes which incited Louis XIV to a grand invasion. Intrigues of James in the English court. French preparations. Admiral Russell’s correspondence with James. The Battle of La Hogue / Barfleur (1692) — the decisive naval engagement, the destruction of the French fleet. The happy conclusion.
Dalrymple’s Method and Value
Dalrymple’s distinctive contribution is the documentary evidence woven into his narrative. Throughout the text, he inserts original letters, treaty drafts, and state papers — many published here for the first time. The secret Treaty of Dover, the correspondence between Charles II and Louis XIV, the letters of the French ambassadors — these are the raw materials of the story.
For the 17th-century wiki, this volume covers the political and diplomatic climax of the century: the collapse of the Stuart monarchy, the Glorious Revolution, and the establishment of the Williamite settlement. It’s a valuable complement to Hume (narrative) and Burnet (personal recollection) — Dalrymple gives you the documentary spine.
OCR Quality
Moderate. 18th-century typography (long-s) with some OCR artifacts. Footnotes and marginal notes are partially preserved.

sources/dalrymple-memoirs-great-britain-.title: Dalrymple — Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland, Vol. III
sources/dalrymple-memoirs-great-britain-.content:
Dalrymple — Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland, Vol. III
Sir John Dalrymple, Bart. (1726–1810) — Memoirs of Great Britain and Ireland. From the Dissolution of the last Parliament of Charles II. till the Capture of the French and Spanish Fleets at Vigo. A New Edition, in Three Volumes; With the Appendixes Complete. Vol. III. — Printed for A. Strahan and T. Cadell, London, 1790.
This is Volume III of a revised three-volume edition of Dalrymple’s Memoirs. While Vol. I (1788 edition) covered the narrative from 1681 to 1692, this edition reorganises the material into three volumes with expanded appendices, extending the coverage from 1690 through the Capture of Vigo (1702) .
The volume contains 746 page-files (New York Public Library copy), extracted as 29,676 lines (~0.8 MB) of plain text.
Scope for the 17th-century wiki: Parts II–III (1690–1700) are directly relevant. Part IV (Queen Anne, 1702) extends into the early 18th century. Note that Part II (Books V–VII) duplicates coverage of the Boyne, Beachy Head, and La Hogue already covered in Vol. I — this is the re-edited version with fuller documentary appendices.
Contents
PART II (continued) — William & Mary (1690–1691)
Book V — The King’s strength in the new parliament. The first conspiracy against the government. The English fleet defeated at Beachy Head. Emotions in England. The Battle of the Boyne. James’s flight. The siege of Limerick raised. Marlborough’s capture of Cork and Kinsale. Torrington’s trial.
Appendix to Book V — A full account of the conspiracy of William Earl of Annandale against the government. Letters from Lords Nottingham and Caermarthen.
Book VI — The Congress of the Hague. Ginkell takes Athlone. The Battle of Aghrim. The capture of Limerick. Campaigns on the Continent. The Massacre of Glencoe.
Appendix to Book VI — Letters on the state of England and the second conspiracy. Correspondence on the affair of Glencoe from Secretaries Stair, Melville, and others.
Book VII — Louis XIV’s grand invasion scheme. James’s intrigues in the English court. French preparations. Admiral Russell’s correspondence with James. The Battle of La Hogue / Barfleur (1692). The defeat and destruction of the French fleet.
Appendix to Book VII — Additional correspondence on the invasion and the naval campaign.
PART III — William III (1692–1700)
Book I — The state of the war on the Continent and at sea. The ministry reviewed. An intended descent on France. Russell removed from command. Sufferings of trade. The campaign and an attempt to assassinate the King. A regular opposition in parliament. Complaints about the commitment of three peers. Inquiry into miscarriages by sea. A Place Bill. The Triennial Bill.
Appendix to Book II — Two letters from Lord Capel on Irish affairs.
Book III — Treachery of the great in England. The attack on Brest betrayed (the Camaret Bay disaster). The French fleet blocked at Toulon. The turn in the scale of the war. The Triennial Bill passed. The impeachment of the Duke of Leeds. Queen Mary’s death (1694) and the King’s reconciliation with Princess Anne.
Book IV — Continued operations. William’s dealings with the Continent. The Peace of Ryswick (1697). The state of the nation.
Book V — William’s offers to the exiled family. The disbanding of the army.
Book VI — The Darien Scheme — the most detailed section of the volume. Paterson’s original intentions. The Darien Company erected. England’s opposition. Scotland’s support. The fate of the first colony. William recommends a Union of Kingdoms. The fate of the second colony. Paterson’s last plan. Reflections on the disaster.
Book VII — The Partition Treaties. The will of Charles II of Spain. Louis accepts the will. Reflections on the Partition Treaties. The Act of Resumption. The English fleet bombards Copenhagen and saves Sweden.
Book VIII — Continued diplomatic manoeuvrings.
Book IX — A new parliament. The King appoints a Tory ministry. His refined policy to bring parliament into the War of the Spanish Succession. The Whig lords impeached for the Partition Treaties and acquitted. The Protestant succession settled.
PART IV — Queen Anne (1702–1708)
Book I — The first steps of the new reign. The state of alliances in Europe. The Queen at home. The state of the English and French nations. The French King’s plan of war. The state of Scotland. The dispute concerning the Scottish union. The plan of war on the Continent.
Book II — The capture of Vigo Bay (1702) — the destruction of the French and Spanish treasure fleet by Sir George Rooke and the Duke of Ormonde. Reflections on the weakness of Spanish America and the opportunities for English commerce in the South Seas. The glory of the Duke of Marlborough begins. The end of the volume.
APPENDIXES
A series of documentary appendices attached to the various books, including:

Correspondence on the state of English and Scottish parties
Letters on the Darien Scheme and Paterson’s plans
Papers on the Partition Treaties
No. I: An account of an intended expedition into the South Seas by private persons
No. II: Letter on South Seas exploration
No. III: Project of an expedition to Yucatan and Honduras
No. IV: Account of the River La Plata
No. V: Comparative expense of white and black troops in hot climates

Dalrymple’s Value
This volume extends the documentary approach of Vol. I forward through the 1690s. The Darien section is particularly valuable — it draws on Scottish sources rarely seen in English-focused histories. The appendices contain original letters and state papers from the French and English archives.
For the 17th-century wiki: Part III (1692–1700) covers the middle years of William III’s reign, the Peace of Ryswick, the Darien disaster, and the Partition Treaties — all crucial for understanding the transition from the 17th-century Stuart world to the 18th-century Hanoverian one.
OCR Quality
Moderate. 18th-century typography, some broken footnotes and marginalia. The appendix sections contain French-language documents with mixed OCR quality.

sources/dampier-new-voyage-round-the-wor.title: Dampier — A New Voyage Round the World (1697)
sources/dampier-new-voyage-round-the-wor.content:
Dampier — A New Voyage Round the World (1697)
William Dampier (1651–1715) — A New Voyage Round the World. Describing particularly, The Isthmus of America, several Coasts and Islands in the West Indies, the Isles of Cape Verd, the Passage by Terra del Fuego, the South Sea Coasts of Chile, Peru, and Mexico; the Isle of Guam one of the Ladrones, Mindanao, and other Philippine and East India Islands near Cambodia, China, Formosa, Luconia, Celebes, &c. New Holland, Sumatra, Nicobar Isles; the Cape of Good Hope, and Santa Hellena. Their Soil, Rivers, Harbours, Plants, Fruits, Animals, and Inhabitants. Their Customs, Religion, Government, Trade, &c. — Printed for James Knapton, at the Crown in St Paul’s Churchyard, London, 1697.
Dampier’s New Voyage Round the World is one of the most influential travel narratives of the late 17th century. It combines the adventure of a buccaneer’s life with meticulous natural history, ethnographic observation, and practical seamanship. Dampier was the first Englishman to explore and describe parts of Australia (New Holland), and his detailed observations of winds, currents, tides, and navigation made the book a standard reference for later explorers — including Cook and Darwin.
The volume is dedicated to Charles Montague (later Earl of Halifax), the same statesman who oversaw the creation of the Bank of England and the re-foundation of the East India Company.
The raw text is extracted from a CIHM/ICMH microfiche scan (National Library of Canada copy), consisting of 41,066 lines (~1.2 MB) of OCR’d text. The quality is moderate — microfiche scanning produces significant OCR artifacts, particularly in marginalia, maps, and decorative initials.
Contents
Dedication and Preface
The book opens with a dedication to Charles Montague, President of the Royal Society and Lord Commissioner of the Treasury. Dampier presents himself as a plain seaman with a zeal for promoting useful knowledge. The Preface explains his method: he has been more concerned with truth and accuracy than with fine writing, and has chosen to be particularly detailed rather than elegantly brief. He notes the book includes several maps engraved for the purpose, and refers to a planned Appendix on winds and a chorographical description of the South Sea coast of America.
Introduction (line 1170+)
The author’s departure from England and the circumstances that led him to the South Seas. Dampier relates his early voyages to the West Indies and the Bay of Campeachy (where he cut logwood), his time among the buccaneers, and his travels through the Isthmus of Darien.
Chap. I — The Author’s Return out of the South Seas (line 1043)
His landing near Cape St. Lawrence in the Isthmus of Darien, with a description of the Moskito Indians.
Chap. II — (line 1110+)
Continued travels through the Darien region.
Chap. III — (line 1111+)
Further adventures among the Spanish settlements.
Chap. IV — His Departure for the South Seas again (line 1051)
Dampier’s second voyage into the South Seas. Describes the coast of Chile, the islands of Juan Fernandez, and encounters with the Spanish.
Chap. V — (line 1113+)
Coasting along Peru and Chile. Descriptions of Quibo and other islands.
Chap. VI — (line 1110+)
Further South Sea voyages, including the Galapagos Islands.
Chap. VII — (line 17330+)
Return to the American coast. Descriptions of the Mexican coast, including the port of Acapulco and the Manila Galleon.
Chap. VIII — (line 1110+)
The coast of Mexico and Central America continued.
Chap. IX — (line 1115+)
Departure from Cape Corrientes for the East Indies. Crossing the Pacific Ocean.
Chap. X — (line 1096)
Arrival at Guam, one of the Ladrone (Marianas) Islands.
Chap. XI — (line 1097)
Arrival at Mindanao, one of the Philippine Islands, and its natural state.
Chap. XII — (line 1098)
The political state of Mindanao.
Chap. XIII — (line 1099)
Occurrences during the author’s stay at Mindanao.
Chap. XIV — Departure towards Luconia (line 1096)
Travels through the Philippine Islands, including descriptions of Mindoro, Manila, and the Bay of Manila.
Chap. XV — (line 1118)
Arrival at Pulo Condor (Con Son Islands) on the coast of Cambodia.
Chap. XVI — (line 1120)
Coasting along Cambodia, China, and Formosa.
Chap. XVII — (line 1122)
Return to the East Indies and arrival at Sumatra.
Chap. XVIII — (line 36098)
At Sumatra and the Nicobar Islands. A detailed account of the Nicobar islanders.
Chap. XIX — (line 1126)
Departure from the Nicobars and arrival at the Cape of Good Hope.
Chap. XX — (line 1128)
Departure from the Cape of Good Hope to the island of Santa Hellena (St. Helena), and the return to England.
Dampier’s Coverage Areas
For the 17th-century England wiki, Dampier is valuable for:

The Darien region (Isthmus of Panama) — detailed descriptions of the very area the Scottish Darien Scheme attempted to settle a few years later. Dampier describes the Moskito Indians, the terrain, the harbours, and the Spanish presence.
The South Sea / Pacific — English buccaneer activity, Spanish colonial defences, the Manila Galleon route.
The East India trade — descriptions of Mindanao, the Philippines, Cambodia, Sumatra, and the routes between them. Includes observations on the Dutch East India Company’s presence in the Spice Islands.
New Holland (Australia) — Dampier was the first Englishman to describe the northwest coast of Australia (1688), including the flora, fauna, and Aboriginal inhabitants.
Natural history — detailed descriptions of plants, animals, fish, shells, and tropical fruits across three oceans.
Navigation — observations on winds, currents, and tides that made the book a standard reference for a century.

OCR Quality
Moderate. The text is from a microfiche scan of the original 1697 edition, with significant OCR artifacts from the scanning process. Pages with maps, illustrations, or decorative initials are particularly degraded. Long-s is preserved in the original spelling. Some pages have errata slips or damaged text.

sources/gregory-king-observations-1696.title: Gregory King — Natural and Political Observations (1696)
sources/gregory-king-observations-1696.content:
Gregory King — Natural and Political Observations (1696)
Gregory King (1648–1712) — Natural and Political Observations and Conclusions upon the State and Condition of England, 1696.
This file contains the 17th-century primary source material extracted from the modern book British Empiricism and Early Political Economy: Gregory King’s 1696 Estimates of National Wealth and Population by John A. Taylor (Praeger, 2005). Only the appendices containing King’s own writings are included — the modern analysis chapters (1–11) are excluded from use in wiki pages.
From the modern book, the following appendix content is included:

Appendix 1 (lines 1–700) — King’s Autobiography, written in his own hand
Appendix 2 (lines 701–1325) — King on the Naval Trade of England, his original data on shipping, exports, imports, and the balance of trade c. 1688
Appendix 3 (lines 1326–3000) — King’s Natural and Political Observations upon the State and Condition of England (1696), the famous demographic and economic survey
Appendix 4 (lines 3001–3150) — King’s Letter about Queen Anne’s Bounty
Appendix 5 (lines 3151–4127) — George Chalmers’s early biography of King (source for King’s life)

Content Summary
Appendix 1 — King’s Autobiography
King’s own account of his life: his birth in Lichfield (1648), his education, his work as a herald and genealogist, his employment by the Earl Marshal’s office, his involvement in the coronations and funerals of James II, William & Mary, and Queen Anne, his work as a surveyor and mapmaker, and his gradual turn to demographic and economic calculation. Written with the modesty of a working scholar.
Appendix 2 — King on the Naval Trade of England
King’s detailed analysis of English foreign trade around 1688. Contains original numerical tables showing:

Gross exports and imports by trade region (European, African, Levant, Plantation, East India)
The proportion of trade carried in English vs foreign shipping
The profit made by foreign nations trading with England in their own ships
Estimates of freight earnings and the balance of trade

Appendix 3 — Natural and Political Observations (1696)
This is King’s most famous work and the centrepiece of the source. Written in the midst of the Nine Years’ War, it is a comprehensive statistical survey of England’s population and wealth. The contents are:
1. Population of England & Wales
Calculated from the assessments on marriages, births, and burials. King estimates the number of inhabited houses (1,300,000) and the number of souls (5,500,000), broken down by parish, city, and village. He includes detailed tables showing the number of people per house in London (5.4), other cities (4.4), and villages (4.0).
2. Proportion of England to France, Holland, Europe, and the World
Comparative geography: England has 7 acres per head, France 9, Holland far less. England is “between 5 & 6 Times better peopled than the Known world in General” and “Exceeded only in populousness by Holland & China.”
3. Distinctions of the People
A famous social table: 1,900,000 husbands and wives, 90,000 widowers, 240,000 widows, 2,500,000 children, 560,000 servants, 210,000 sojourners and single persons — all broken down by London, great towns, and villages.
4. Ages of the People
Age distribution: those under 16 (2,240,000), between 16 and 60 (fighting men: 1,310,000), above 60 (600,000). The number of communicants at 3,260,000.
5. Income and Expense of the Nation (1688)
The famous “Scheme of the Income & Expence of the Several Families” — a table ranking English families by social rank from temporal lords down to vagrants, showing the number of families, the income per family, and the total income and expense for each rank. This is the most cited of all King’s tables.
6. Land, Livestock, and Agricultural Production
The several sorts of land in England and their value, the live stock of the nation in cattle, the flesh yearly consumed as food.
7. Beer, Ale, and Malt Consumption
The annual consumption and the revenue of excise arising thereby.
8. Tax Yields
Calculations of the produce of the poll bills, the tax on marriages, births, burials, houses, and windows.
9. State of the Nation in 1695
Projections of the effect of continuing the war to 1698.
10. Comparative State of France and Holland
The state and condition of England, France, and Holland compared in 1688 and 1695.
Appendix 4 — Letter about Queen Anne’s Bounty
King’s letter concerning Queen Anne’s Bounty — the fund established in 1704 to augment the incomes of poor clergy. King was involved in the statistical work underlying this scheme.
Appendix 5 — The Life of Gregory King by George Chalmers
An early biographical account (c. 1793) by Chalmers, who was responsible for preserving and publishing King’s manuscripts after his death. Essential for understanding how King’s work came down to posterity.
OCR Quality
Good. This text is born-digital from the Taylor book, so the OCR is clean. The tables are reproduced as ASCII approximations of tabular data, which preserves the numbers accurately. The original page numbers (e.g., “126”, “Appendix 3. King’s Natural and Political Observations 1696”) appear as running headers throughout.

sources/halliwell-letters-science.title: Halliwell — Collection of Letters Illustrative of the Progress of Science
sources/halliwell-letters-science.content:
Halliwell — Collection of Letters Illustrative of the Progress of Science
James Orchard Halliwell (later Halliwell-Phillipps, 1820–1889) — A Collection of Letters Illustrative of the Progress of Science in England from the Reign of Queen Elizabeth to that of Charles the Second. — Printed for the Historical Society of Science by R. and J. E. Taylor, London, 1841.
A slim volume (164 pages) published by the short-lived Historical Society of Science. Halliwell was a noted Shakespearean scholar and antiquary who also worked extensively on the history of mathematics and science. This collection prints 83 original letters drawn from the British Museum manuscripts, covering roughly 1562 to 1682.
The volume contains 164 page-files, extracted as 7,825 lines (~0.2 MB).
Scope and Value
This is a source document collection, not a narrative. Each letter is transcribed from the original manuscript with Halliwell’s annotations. The letters cover mathematics, astronomy, navigation, calendar reform, hydrostatics, and the organisation of early scientific inquiry.
The most substantial correspondences are:

Thomas Harriot and his circle (William Lower, Thomas Aylesburie) — 1610s, covering astronomy, optics, and mathematics
John Pell and Sir Charles Cavendish — 1640s, covering analytic geometry and algebra; Cavendish was importing Continental mathematical ideas
Henry Briggs and John Pell — logarithms and computation
Thomas Lydyat — an astrologer/scientist corresponding on chronology and astronomy
John Collins and Henry Oldenburg (Secretary of the Royal Society) — 1670s

Key Contributors
Most of the letters revolve around a small network of mathematical correspondents:


John Pell (1611–1685) — mathematician, the central figure of the collection; professor at Amsterdam and Breda, later Cromwell’s diplomatic agent in Switzerland. His equation (Pell’s equation) is famous though misattributed. The volume draws extensively from his vast manuscript collections in the British Museum.


Sir Charles Cavendish (1591–1654) — mathematician and patron; brother of the Duke of Newcastle. He travelled on the Continent, meeting Mersenne, Descartes, and Fermat, and acted as the conduit for Continental mathematics into England.


Thomas Harriot (c. 1560–1621) — the great but unpublished mathematician and astronomer (Raleigh’s mathematical tutor, the “English Galileo”). His optical and astronomical observations, including telescopic drawings of the moon and sunspots, precede Galileo’s. The letters from his circle illuminate his work after his death.


Henry Briggs (1561–1630) — the first Gresham Professor of Astronomy, then Savilian Professor at Oxford. Promoter of decimal logarithms (Briggsian logarithms).


Henry Oldenburg (c. 1619–1677) — Secretary of the Royal Society, editor of the Philosophical Transactions.


OCR Quality
Very good. This is a 19th-century printed book with clean modern typography. The OCR is near-perfect. Mathematical notation and marginal notes are occasionally fragmented.

sources/hume-history-of-england-vol5.title: Hume — History of England, Vol. V
sources/hume-history-of-england-vol5.content:
Hume — History of England, Vol. V
David Hume (1711–1776) — The History of England from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688. To Which is Prefixed, a Short Account of His Life, Written by Himself. A New Edition, in Eight Volumes. Vol. V. — Printed by J. F. Dove for Baynes and Son, London, 1822.
This is Volume V of David Hume’s 8-volume History of England. It covers the latter half of Elizabeth I’s reign (from c. 1562) through the early years of James I (to c. 1612).
The volume contains 508 page-files (OCR’d from the University of Chicago Library copy, shelfmark 12846423), extracted as 21,324 lines (~1 MB) of plain text.
Scope note for the 17th-century wiki: Only the final ~60 pages (Chaps. XLV–XLVI, covering James I from 1603 to ~1612) fall within the 17th century. The bulk of the volume is Elizabethan (16th century), though the Appendix III essay on government, revenue, and commerce is relevant background for understanding early Stuart governance.
Contents Overview

































































SectionTopicPageLineChap. XXXIXElizabeth (1562–)1119Chap. XLElizabeth — Puritans, Norfolk, Northern Rebellion, Massacre of Paris873,882Chap. XLIElizabeth — Scotland, Drake, Anjou marriage, Low Countries, war with Spain1647,165Chap. XLIIElizabeth — Babington, Mary’s trial & execution, Spanish Armada, Portugal2149,267Chap. XLIIIElizabeth — French wars, Henry IV, Peace of Vervins, Essex29212,658Chap. XLIVElizabeth — Tyrone’s rebellion, Essex in Ireland, Essex’s fall, death of Elizabeth33314,409Appendix IIIElizabethan government, revenue, commerce, military, manufactures, learning33316,838Chap. XLVJames I — Introduction, Raleigh’s conspiracy, Hampton Court, peace with Spain43118,709Chap. XLVIJames I — Gunpowder Plot, parliament, truce with Spain, death of Henry IV, Arminianism, Ireland46019,953
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. XXXIX — Elizabeth (line 119, page 1)
Covers c. 1562–1568. Opens with a survey of Europe after the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis — Philip II of Spain and Elizabeth as the great rival powers. The French Wars of Religion begin; Elizabeth takes Havre de Grace as security, but it is lost to plague and French Catholic forces. Affairs in Scotland: Mary Queen of Scots marries Darnley, the murder of Rizzio, the murder of Darnley, Mary’s marriage to Bothwell, insurrections, Mary’s imprisonment and flight into England. Conferences at York and Hampton Court to adjudicate the charges against Mary.
CHAP. XL — Elizabeth (line 3,882, page 87)
Covers c. 1568–1572. The character of the Puritans and the rise of religious dissent. The Duke of Norfolk’s conspiracy to marry Mary Queen of Scots. The Northern Rebellion (1569) — Catholic earls rising in the North. Assassination of the Earl of Murray (Regent of Scotland). Parliament and the succession question. The French Wars of Religion continue. Affairs of the Low Countries and the Dutch Revolt. Norfolk’s second conspiracy, his trial and execution (1572). The Massacre of St Bartholomew (1572) and its impact on English politics.
CHAP. XLI — Elizabeth (line 7,165, page 164)
Covers c. 1572–1585. Affairs of Scotland — the regency of Morton, James VI’s minority. Spanish affairs and the growing rivalry with England. Sir Francis Drake’s circumnavigation (1577–1580) and his raids on Spanish America. Parliament and the succession debate. Negotiations for Elizabeth’s marriage to the Duke of Anjou. The Scottish Reformation and the fall of Morton. Mary’s letters and conspiracies. The ecclesiastical commission. Affairs of the Low Countries — English intervention in the Dutch Revolt. Open hostilities with Spain begin. The assassination of William the Silent (1584).
CHAP. XLII — Elizabeth (line 9,267, page 214)
Covers c. 1585–1588. The climax of Elizabeth’s reign — the crisis with Mary Queen of Scots and the Spanish Armada. Babington’s conspiracy (1586) and Mary’s fatal correspondence. The trial of Mary at Fotheringhay, the sentence, James VI’s intercession, and Mary’s execution (8 Feb 1587). Elizabeth’s affected sorrow. Drake’s raid on Cadiz (1587), “singeing the King of Spain’s beard.” Philip II’s project to invade England. The Spanish Armada (1588): English preparations, the Armada’s arrival in the Channel, the running battles from Plymouth to Gravelines, the fireship attack, the Armada’s disastrous flight around Scotland and Ireland. Parliament and thanksgiving. The expedition against Portugal (1589) — Drake and Norris’s failure.
CHAP. XLIII — Elizabeth (line 12,658, page 292)
Covers c. 1589–1598. French affairs: the murder of the Duke of Guise (1588), the murder of Henry III (1589), the accession of Henry IV of Navarre. English naval enterprises against Spain — privateering, the Azores voyages. Henry IV’s conversion to Catholicism (“Paris is worth a mass”). Scottish affairs: the struggle between James VI and the Presbyterian kirk. Naval enterprises continued — the Earl of Cumberland, Sir Richard Hawkins. The Peace of Vervins (1598) between France and Spain. The Earl of Essex’s rising influence.
CHAP. XLIV — Elizabeth (line 14,409, page 333)
Covers c. 1598–1603. The final years. State of Ireland: the Tyrone rebellion (Nine Years’ War). Essex sent to Ireland (1599), his disastrous campaign, his unauthorized return to England. Essex’s disgrace, his intrigues, his abortive insurrection (1601), his trial and execution. Mountjoy’s success in Ireland: the defeat of the Spaniards and Irish at Kinsale (1601), Tyrone’s submission. Parliament and the monopolies debate. Elizabeth’s final sickness, her death (24 March 1603), and her character — one of Hume’s most famous set-pieces, praising her firmness, intelligence, and mastery of her kingdom.
APPENDIX III — Elizabethan Government, Revenue, Commerce, etc. (line 16,838, pages 333–429)
A thematic essay covering the state of England during Elizabeth’s reign. Not a narrative but a structural analysis:

Government — the prerogative, Star Chamber, the ecclesiastical commission, the abuse of power under colour of law (imprisonment without trial, press gangs, monopolies)
Revenues — crown lands, parliamentary supply, the sale of monopolies, Elizabeth’s parsimony contrasted with her successors’ difficulties
Commerce — the East India Company (founded 1600), the Hanseatic League’s decay, the Merchant Adventurers, the growth of English shipping
Military force — the militia system, the navy, the artillery, the ammunition shortage
Manufactures — the low state of English manufacturing compared to foreign imports
Learning — the flourishing of English literature under Elizabeth (Spenser, Shakespeare), the state of the universities
Prices — the rise in prices during Elizabeth’s reign, the influx of American silver
Manners — the decay of the aristocracy, the growth of the gentry and middle classes

The appendix concludes with a reflection on Spenser’s Faerie Queene and the peculiarities of Elizabethan literary taste, then transitions to the Stuart era.
CHAP. XLV — James I (line 18,709, page 431)
Covers 1603–c. 1606. The accession of James VI of Scotland to the English throne — the smooth transition from Tudor to Stuart. Key topics:

The Accession — the peaceful succession, James’s journey from Edinburgh to London, the shower of honours and knighthoods
State of Europe — the Habsburg-Bourbon rivalry, James’s vision of a peaceful foreign policy
Rosni’s Negotiations — the French envoy’s mission to secure James’s alliance against Spain
Raleigh’s Conspiracy — the Main Plot and the Bye Plot (1603): Sir Walter Raleigh, Lord Cobham, and Lord Grey of Wilton accused of treason. Raleigh’s trial, his dramatic conviction, and his imprisonment in the Tower
Hampton Court Conference (1604) — the meeting between the Anglican bishops, the Puritan clergy, and James I. The Puritan millenary petition, James’s famous retort to the Scottish presbyterians, the decision to produce a new translation of the Bible (the King James Version)
The First Parliament — the debate over the Union of England and Scotland, the Buckinghamshire election case (Goodwin v. Fortescue), the question of wardships and purveyance
Peace with Spain (1604) — the Treaty of London, ending the 19-year Anglo-Spanish war

CHAP. XLVI — James I (line 19,953, page 460)
Covers c. 1605–1612. Key topics:

The Gunpowder Plot (1605) — Hume’s dramatic narrative of the conspiracy: Robert Catesby, Guy Fawkes, the discovery of the gunpowder under the House of Lords, the pursuit and death of the conspirators, the trial of Henry Garnet (the Jesuit superior), and the harsh recusancy laws that followed
Parliament and the Union — the continued debate over the Anglo-Scottish union, the failure of the Great Contract (1610) — James’s proposal to exchange wardships and purveyance for a permanent parliamentary revenue, which collapsed when the Commons demanded the redress of grievances first
The Truce with Spain and the United Provinces (1609) — the Twelve Years’ Truce between Spain and the Dutch Republic
The Assassination of Henry IV (1610) — the murder of the French king by Ravaillac, the consternation in England, the fear of Catholic conspiracy
Arminianism — the rise of the Arminian (anti-Calvinist) party in the Church of England, James’s involvement in the Dutch Remonstrant controversy
State of Ireland — the Plantation of Ulster, the introduction of English law, the abolition of Irish customs (Gavelkinde, Tanistry), the suppression of the O’Dogherty rebellion
The volume ends with James’s first parliament (which sat for nearly seven years) dissolved in 1611, and a discussion of Irish policy extending to 1612

OCR Quality
Good. Text is fully readable, from the University of Chicago Library scan. The only artifacts are the library stamps at the beginning and end of the scan (shelf mark 12846423). A few page-number and running-header fragments appear inline.

sources/hume-history-of-england-vol6.title: Hume — History of England, Vol. VI
sources/hume-history-of-england-vol6.content:
Hume — History of England, Vol. VI
David Hume (1711–1776) — The History of England from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688. Vol. VI. — Printed by J. F. Dove for Baynes and Son, London, 1822.
This is Volume VI of Hume’s 8-volume History of England. It covers from the later years of James I (c. 1612) through the opening of the Civil War (1643), filling the gap between Vol. V (which ended c. 1612) and Vol. VII (which starts at Marston Moor, 1644).
The volume contains 492 page-files (OCR’d from a UC Library copy, barcode 31158008788845), extracted as 20,921 lines (~1 MB) of plain text.
Contents Overview



























































SectionTopicPageLineChap. XLVIIJames I — Prince Henry’s death, Overbury scandal, Somerset, Buckingham111Chap. XLVIIIJames I — Raleigh’s execution, Palatinate, Bacon’s fall, parliament30—Chap. XLIXJames I — Spanish Match, Prince Charles in Madrid, Buckingham’s character——Chap. LCharles I — First parliaments, Isle of Ré, Buckingham’s impeachment138—Chap. LICharles I — Petition of Right, Buckingham’s assassination175—Chap. LIICharles I — Personal Rule, Strafford, Laud, Ship Money, Hampden215—Chap. LIIICharles I — Scottish Covenant, Bishops’ Wars, Short Parliament, Newburn254—Chap. LIVCharles I — Long Parliament, Strafford’s impeachment, Civil War opens297—
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. XLVII — James I (line 11, page 1)
Covers c. 1612–1615. The sudden death of Henry, Prince of Wales (Nov 1612) — the promising heir who admired Raleigh and chafed at his father’s pacifism. The marriage of Princess Elizabeth to Frederick V, the Elector Palatine. The rise of Robert Carr, Earl of Somerset, as the king’s favourite; his marriage to Frances Howard (divorced from the Earl of Essex). The poisoning of Sir Thomas Overbury in the Tower, who opposed the marriage. Somerset’s fall from favour. The rise of George Villiers, later Duke of Buckingham, as the new favourite. The cautionary towns (Flushing, Brill) delivered back to the Dutch. Affairs of Scotland.
CHAP. XLVIII — James I (page 30)
Covers c. 1616–1621. Sir Walter Raleigh’s release from the Tower, his expedition to Guiana (1617), the attack on San Thomé, the death of his son, his return empty-handed. Raleigh’s execution (1618) under the old 1603 treason sentence — sacrificed to Spanish demands. The outbreak of the Thirty Years’ War: insurrection in Bohemia, the loss of the Palatinate to Spanish and Imperial forces. James’s negotiations with Spain. The summoning of parliament (1621) — the first in seven years. The parties in parliament: the country opposition vs. the court. The fall of Francis Bacon, Lord Chancellor, convicted of bribery. The rupture between king and commons over foreign policy. The Protestation of the Commons (Dec 1621), which James tore from the Journal.
CHAP. XLIX — James I (c. 1622–1625)
Negotiations with Spain for the marriage of Prince Charles to the Infanta Maria, and for the restoration of the Palatinate. The character of Buckingham — his charm, ambition, and increasing influence. The rash journey of Prince Charles and Buckingham to Madrid (1623) — the “Spanish match” adventure, the romantic failure, the humiliating return. The marriage treaty broken; Charles and Buckingham now advocate war with Spain. A parliament (1624) — Buckingham’s popularity, the Spanish war voted. The return of Bristol (the ambassador from Spain) and his conflict with Buckingham. James’s declining health and death (March 1625).
CHAP. L — Charles I (page 138)
Covers 1625–1627. The accession of Charles I — his marriage to Henrietta Maria of France (a Catholic). The first parliament at Westminster: distrust of Buckingham, refusal of adequate supply. The second parliament at Oxford: the impeachment of Buckingham demanded, Charles dissolves. The forced loan. The naval expedition against Spain: the disastrous Cadiz expedition (1625) under Sir Edward Cecil — total failure, men starved and diseased, the fleet returned in disgrace. War with France begins. Buckingham’s expedition to the Isle of Ré (1627) — the attempt to relieve the Huguenots of La Rochelle, the siege of St Martin’s, the disastrous retreat, the loss of thousands. Buckingham’s mismanagement becomes a national scandal.
CHAP. LI — Charles I (page 175)
Covers 1628–1629. The third parliament (1628): the Petition of Right — the great constitutional document forbidding arbitrary imprisonment (habeas corpus), martial law, forced billeting, and non-parliamentary taxation. Charles’s reluctant assent. The prorogation. The assassination of Buckingham (Aug 1628) at Portsmouth by John Felton — the nation’s rejoicing. A new session of parliament: the dispute over tonnage and poundage (customs duties). The rise of Arminianism in the Church. The dissolution of parliament (1629) — the speaker held in his chair, the three resolutions against innovations in religion and unconstitutional taxation. Charles begins his Personal Rule.
CHAP. LII — Charles I (page 215)
Covers 1629–1639. The Personal Rule (or “Eleven Years’ Tyranny”). Peace with France (1629) and with Spain (1630). The state of the court and ministry: the queen’s influence, the rise of Wentworth (later Earl of Strafford) in the North. William Laud, Archbishop of Canterbury — innovations in the church, the imposition of uniformity, the persecution of Puritans. Irregular levies of money: knighthood fines, forest fines, tonnage and poundage collected without consent. Severities in the Star Chamber and High Commission: the cases of Prynne, Burton, and Bastwick. Ship Money extended from coastal to inland counties. The trial of John Hampden (1637) — the great test case against the legality of Ship Money, decided narrowly for the crown but Hampden became a national hero.
CHAP. LIII — Charles I (page 254)
Covers 1637–1640. Discontents in Scotland over the introduction of the English canons and the new Prayer Book. The tumult at St Giles’ Cathedral, Edinburgh (1637) — Jenny Geddes throws her stool. The National Covenant (1638) — mass subscription across Scotland. The General Assembly in Glasgow abolishes episcopacy. War with Scotland: the First Bishops’ War (1639) — the Pacification of Berwick, a standoff. Renewal of war: the Second Bishops’ War (1640). Charles summons the Short Parliament (April 1640) for funds — it refuses supply and is dissolved after three weeks. Discontents in England: the rout at Newburn (Aug 1640) — the Scots army invades, defeats the English. The Treaty of Ripon: the Scots occupy the North pending a settlement. The Great Council of Peers at York. Charles summons the Long Parliament.
CHAP. LIV — Charles I (page 297)
Covers 1640–1643. The meeting of the Long Parliament (Nov 1640) — the greatest parliament in English history. The impeachment of Strafford (Earl of Wentworth) and Laud. Finch and Windebank flee. The Triennial Bill — parliament to meet every three years. The attainder and execution of Strafford (May 1641) — Charles’s capitulation, his guilt over abandoning his minister. The abolition of the prerogative courts (Star Chamber, High Commission). The Grand Remonstrance (Nov 1641) — the comprehensive indictment of Charles’s rule. The Irish Rebellion (Oct 1641) — the massacre of Protestant settlers. The militia dispute: who controls the armed forces? The attempted arrest of the Five Members (Jan 1642) — Charles enters the Commons, a fatal breach. The king leaves London. The raising of the royal standard at Nottingham (Aug 1642) — civil war begins. Edgehill (Oct 1642). The opening campaigns of 1643: royalist advances, the Irish Cessation. The volume ends with the war in its first phase, the king negotiating with the Irish, and the parliament consolidating control of London and the southeast.
OCR Quality
Good. Text is fully readable. UC Library stamps and barcodes appear at the beginning and end.

sources/hume-history-of-england-vol7.title: Hume — History of England, Vol. VII
sources/hume-history-of-england-vol7.content:
Hume — History of England, Vol. VII
David Hume (1711–1776) — The History of England from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688. Vol. VII. — Printed by J. F. Dove for Baynes and Son, London, 1822.
This is Volume VII of Hume’s 8-volume History of England. It covers from the climactic battles of the Civil War (1644) through the Restoration to the end of the Third Anglo-Dutch War (1674).
The volume contains 522 page-files (OCR’d from a UC Library copy, barcode 31158003319687), extracted as 21,511 lines (~1 MB) of plain text.
Contents Overview

































































SectionTopicPageLineChap. LVIICharles I — Marston Moor, Cropredy Bridge, Self-Denying Ordinance1—Chap. LVIIICharles I — Naseby, Montrose, end of the First Civil War41—Chap. LIXCharles I — Army vs Parliament, Pride’s Purge, king’s trial, execution79—Chap. LXThe Commonwealth — Cromwell in Ireland, Dunbar, Worcester154—Chap. LXIThe Commonwealth — Navigation Act, Dutch War, Blake, Barebone’s218—Chap. LXIIThe Commonwealth — Richard Cromwell, Monk, the Restoration287—Chap. LXIIICharles II — Clarendon, Uniformity, Dunkirk sold, Indulgence342—Chap. LXIVCharles II — Second Dutch War, Four Days’ Battle386—Chap. LXVCharles II — The Cabal, Third Dutch War, Test Act439—
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. LVII — Charles I (page 1)
Covers 1644. The year of decision. Invasion of England by the Scottish army of the Solemn League and Covenant. The Battle of Marston Moor (2 July 1644) — Cromwell’s cavalry decisive, the North lost to the king. The Battle of Cropredy Bridge — Waller defeated, but Charles fails to exploit. Essex’s army disarmed at Lostwithiel — a royalist success. The Second Battle of Newbury (Oct 1644) — indecisive. The rise of the Independents as a political faction. The Self-Denying Ordinance — removing members of parliament from military command. The rise of Fairfax and Cromwell. The Treaty of Uxbridge — failed peace negotiations. The execution of Archbishop Laud.
CHAP. LVIII — Charles I (page 41)
Covers 1645–1646. Montrose’s brilliant royalist campaign in Scotland: a series of stunning victories (Tippermuir, Aberdeen, Inverlochy, Auldearn, Alford, Kilsyth). The New Model Army created — Fairfax commander, Cromwell as cavalry general. The Battle of Naseby (14 June 1645) — the decisive defeat of the Royalist army, the king’s private correspondence captured. The surrender of Bristol — Prince Rupert disgraced. Fairfax conquers the West Country. Montrose finally defeated at Philiphaugh. Ecclesiastical affairs: the Westminster Assembly, the rise of Presbyterianism. The king goes to the Scots at Newark (May 1646). The end of the First Civil War. The Scots deliver the king up to parliament in exchange for arrears of pay.
CHAP. LIX — Charles I (page 79)
Covers 1647–1649. The army mutinies against parliament. Cornet Joyce seizes the king at Holmby House. The army marches on London and subdues parliament. Charles’s negotiations with the army (the Heads of Proposals) and with parliament. The king flees to the Isle of Wight, imprisoned at Carisbrooke Castle. The Second Civil War (1648) — royalist risings in Kent, Essex, and the North; the Scottish invasion under Hamilton. Cromwell crushes the Scots at Preston (Aug 1648). The Treaty of Newport — futile negotiations between Charles and parliament. Pride’s Purge (Dec 1648) — Colonel Pride ejects Presbyterian MPs, leaving the Rump. The trial of the king: the High Court of Justice. The execution of Charles I (30 Jan 1649) — Hume’s famous reflection on the king’s dignified death.
CHAP. LX — The Commonwealth (page 154)
Covers 1649–1651. The state of England after the king’s death. The state of Scotland: the Covenanters proclaim Charles II. The state of Ireland: the Confederate Catholics hold most of the island. The Levellers suppressed at Burford. The siege and storming of Drogheda (Tredah, Sept 1649) — Cromwell’s massacre of the garrison. The storming of Wexford. The conquest of Ireland continues. Montrose taken prisoner in Scotland and executed. Cromwell invades Scotland: the Battle of Dunbar (3 Sept 1650) — a stunning victory against superior numbers. Charles II crowned at Scone. Cromwell’s masterstroke: the Battle of Worcester (3 Sept 1651) — the “crowning mercy,” the end of the Civil Wars. Charles II’s escape and exile.
CHAP. LXI — The Commonwealth (page 218)
Covers 1651–1653. The establishment of the Commonwealth as a European power. The Navigation Act (1651) — aimed at the Dutch carrying trade. The First Anglo-Dutch War (1652–1654): the great admirals emerge — Blake, Monk, Dean, Penn. The battles of Dover, the Kentish Knock, Dungeness, Portland, the Gabbard, Scheveningen (Texel). Blake’s victory at Santa Cruz (1657). The Rump Parliament: its growing unpopularity, its failure to reform. Cromwell’s expulsion of the Rump (April 1653). The Little Parliament (Barebone’s Parliament) — nominated by the churches, its experiment in godly rule.
CHAP. LXII — The Commonwealth (page 287)
Covers 1653–1660. The Instrument of Government — England’s first and only written constitution. Oliver Cromwell as Lord Protector. Foreign affairs: Cromwell’s Western Design, the capture of Jamaica. Richard Cromwell succeeds his father (1658). Richard’s parliament — the Cabal of Wallingford House (army grandees). Richard deposed by the army (1659). The Long Parliament (the Rump) restored. The conspiracy of the royalists — Sir George Booth’s rising. General Monk in Scotland: his ambiguous manoeuvring. Monk declares for the parliament, marches into England. Monk enters London, declares for a free parliament. The secluded members (Presbyterians) restored. The Long Parliament dissolves itself. A new, free parliament is elected. The Restoration: Charles II invited back (May 1660). The king’s return, the Declaration of Breda. Manners and arts.
CHAP. LXIII — Charles II (page 342)
Covers 1660–1667. The new ministry: Clarendon as chief minister. The Act of Indemnity — the settlement of accounts, the land restored. The settlement of the revenue. The trial and execution of the regicides (the men who signed Charles I’s death warrant). Prelacy restored; the Savoy Conference (1661) between Anglicans and Presbyterians — the arguments for and against comprehension. The Corporation Act and the Act of Uniformity (1662) — the Great Ejection, two thousand Puritan ministers removed. The king’s marriage to Catherine of Braganza. The trial and execution of Sir Henry Vane. Dunkirk sold to the French. Clarendon’s fall: the Dutch War, his impeachment and exile.
CHAP. LXIV — Charles II (page 386)
Covers 1664–1667. A new session of parliament. The rupture with Holland: the Second Anglo-Dutch War. The victory of the English fleet at Lowestoft (1665) under the Duke of York. The rupture with France and Denmark. The Sea-fight of Four Days (1666) — a hard-fought English defeat under Monk and Prince Rupert. The victory on St James’s Day (July 1666). The Great Fire of London (Sept 1666). The Dutch Raid on the Medway (June 1667) — de Ruyter’s devastating attack on Chatham, the burning of the English fleet at anchor. The Treaty of Breda (1667) — peace with Holland, the Navigation Acts modified.
CHAP. LXV — Charles II (page 439)
Covers 1668–1674. A new parliament (the Cavalier Parliament continues). The Cabal ministry: Clifford, Arlington, Buckingham, Ashley-Cooper, Lauderdale — their characters and secret counsels. The Secret Treaty of Dover (1670) — Charles’s alliance with Louis XIV, the promise to declare himself Catholic. The Third Anglo-Dutch War (1672–1674): the Battle of Solebay (1672), the Earl of Sandwich killed. The Declaration of Indulgence (1672) — suspended penal laws against Catholics and Nonconformists. Parliament forces its withdrawal. The Test Act (1673) — requiring all office-holders to receive Anglican communion. The Duke of York (James) resigns the Admiralty rather than take the Test. The Exchequer shut. Coventry Act against duelling. Colonel Blood’s theft of the crown jewels. The volume ends with the conclusion of the Third Dutch War and the Peace of Westminster (1674).
OCR Quality
Good. Text is fully readable. Minor page-number artifacts. UC Library stamps on first and last pages.

sources/hume-history-of-england-vol8.title: Hume — History of England, Vol. VIII
sources/hume-history-of-england-vol8.content:
Hume — History of England, Vol. VIII
David Hume (1711–1776) — The History of England from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688. Vol. VIII. — Printed by J. F. Dove for Baynes and Son, London, 1822.
This is Volume VIII — the final volume — of Hume’s 8-volume History of England. It covers the last years of Charles II (1674–1685), the reign of James II (1685–1688), and the Glorious Revolution (1688–1689), ending with Hume’s concluding essay on manners and arts.
The volume contains 476 page-files (OCR’d from a UC Library copy, barcode 31158008788514), extracted as 31,765 lines (~1.5 MB) of plain text. The larger size includes the extensive index for the entire 8-volume set.
Contents Overview



























































SectionTopicPageLineChap. LXVICharles II — Cabal, Temple, Nimeguen, William & Mary’s marriage1—Chap. LXVIICharles II — Popish Plot, Oates, Coleman, Godfrey’s murder60—Chap. LXVIIICharles II — Exclusion Crisis, Danby’s impeachment, dissolution114—Chap. LXIXCharles II — Oxford Parliament, Tory reaction, Rye House Plot155—Chap. LXXJames II — Monmouth’s Rebellion, dispensing power, Magdalen, bishops206—Chap. LXXIWilliam III — Invasion, Revolution, settlement264——Manners & Arts — concluding essay307——Index to all 8 volumes447—
Chapter-by-Chapter Summary
CHAP. LXVI — Charles II (page 1)
Covers 1674–1678. The aftermath of the Cabal ministry. The schemes of the Cabal exposed; Sir William Temple’s remonstrances. The campaign of 1674 — the Dutch War ends, the Peace of Westminster. A parliament: the debate on passive obedience vs. resistance. The campaign of 1675 — the French advance in Flanders. The Congress of Nimeguen (1676–1678) — the general peace negotiations. The uncertain conduct of Charles: his secret French subsidy from Louis XIV, his public pro-Dutch stance. The campaign of 1677. Parliament’s distrust of the king. The marriage of William of Orange to the Lady Mary (Nov 1677) — the Protestant alliance cemented. Plans for peace; negotiations. The campaign of 1678. The Peace of Nimeguen — France gains Franche-Comté, the Dutch satisfied. The state of affairs in Scotland — the Duke of Lauderdale’s repressive rule.
CHAP. LXVII — Charles II (page 60)
Covers 1678–1679. The Popish Plot — the most extraordinary political crisis of Charles II’s reign. Titus Oates’s narrative: his story of a Jesuit conspiracy to murder the king, burn London, and impose Catholicism. Oates’s character — Hume’s skeptical portrait of the informer. Coleman’s letters — a real correspondence with the French Jesuit confessor, suggesting Catholic hopes. Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey’s murder (Oct 1678) — the magistrate who took Oates’s deposition found dead, the nation convulsed. General consternation: the search for conspirators, the arrest of Catholic peers (including Lord Stafford, Arundel, Powis). The parliament: its zeal against Popery. Bedloe’s narrative — corroboration of the plot. The accusation of Danby, the Lord Treasurer, for allegedly negotiating with France without parliament’s knowledge. Danby’s impeachment and fall.
CHAP. LXVIII — Charles II (page 114)
Covers 1679. The Popish Plot hysteria at its peak. The execution of William Staley, Coleman, Ireland, Grove, and other accused plotters. The trial and execution of Lord Stafford (Dec 1680) — the last Catholic peer judicially murdered. The crisis of the Exclusion Bill: Shaftesbury and the Green Ribbon Club move to exclude the Duke of York (a Catholic) from the succession. The parliament passes the Exclusion Bill in the Commons; Charles dissolves parliament. The Habeas Corpus Act (1679) passed in this session. The king’s health; the fear of a Catholic succession. The struggle over the militia: who controls the army? The second general election of 1679 — the “Exclusion Parliaments.” Charles rejects exclusion, begins to reassert his authority.
CHAP. LXIX — Charles II (page 155)
Covers 1680–1685. The Oxford Parliament (March 1681) — Charles summons parliament to Oxford (a royalist stronghold), the Exclusion Bill re-introduced, Charles dissolves parliament after one week and never calls another. The Tory reaction: the tide turns against the Whigs. The Rye House Plot (1683) — a Whig conspiracy to assassinate Charles and his brother. The discovery and suppression of the conspirators: Lord Russell, Algernon Sidney, the Duke of Monmouth implicated. The trial and execution of Lord Russell — his dignified death. The execution of Algernon Sidney — based on his unpublished republican writings. The trial of Monmouth — he confesses, is pardoned, and exiled. The king’s authority restored; the Tory ascendancy; the attacks on the corporation charters.
CHAP. LXX — James II (page 206)
Covers 1685–1688. The accession of James II (Feb 1685) — his speech to the council promising to preserve the constitution. Monmouth’s Rebellion (June 1685): the landing at Lyme Regis, the popular support in the West Country. The Battle of Sedgemoor (6 July 1685) — James’s army under Feversham and Churchill crushes the rebels. The Bloody Assizes: Judge Jeffreys’s brutal punishment of the rebels. The execution of Monmouth. James’s Catholicising policies: the dispensing power used to appoint Catholics to office. The case of Godden v. Hales — the legal validation of the dispensing power. The state of Ireland: the Catholic Earl of Tyrconnell put in charge. The breach between the king and the Church of England. The Court of Ecclesiastical Commission revived. The suspension of the penal laws and the Declaration of Indulgence (1687). The attempt on Magdalen College, Oxford — the king’s demand for a Catholic president resisted. The trial and acquittal of the Seven Bishops (June 1688) — the great popular triumph. The birth of the Prince of Wales (June 1688) — the prospect of a Catholic dynasty. The Invitation to William of Orange.
CHAP. LXXI — William III (page 264)
Covers 1688–1689. The Glorious Revolution. The conduct of the Prince of Orange: his league against France, his refusal to concur with James’s policies. The invitation from the Immortal Seven — the Whig and Tory lords who ask William to intervene. William’s preparations: his fleet and army assembled. Louis XIV’s offers to James — rejected. James’s desperate attempts to conciliate: the concessions to the Church, the repeal of the Test Act, the dismissal of Catholic officers. William’s fleet sails (Oct 1688), driven back by storms. The second sailing: the “Protestant Wind” carries William’s armada to Torbay. William lands at Brixham (5 Nov 1688). James’s army — the defection of Churchill and other officers. James’s flight: his first attempt to escape, his capture, his second flight to France. The Convention Parliament. The Declaration of Rights. The offer of the crown to William and Mary (Feb 1689). The Revolution settlement: the Bill of Rights, the Toleration Act. The volume concludes with Hume’s assessment of the Revolution.
MANNERS AND ARTS (page 307)
Hume’s concluding essay on the state of English society, culture, and commerce during the 17th century. Topics include: the progress of learning, the growth of science (the Royal Society, Newton, Boyle, Locke), the state of literature (Milton, Dryden, Butler’s Hudibras), the improvements in commerce and navigation, the rise of the public credit, the changes in manners and social life. A comprehensive assessment of the century’s civilising process.
The volume also contains a detailed index to all eight volumes (pages 447–460).
OCR Quality
Good. Text is fully readable. UC Library stamps and barcodes on endpapers.

sources/sprat-history-royal-society.title: Sprat — History of the Royal-Society of London
sources/sprat-history-royal-society.content:
Sprat — History of the Royal-Society of London
Thomas Sprat (1635–1713), Bishop of Rochester — The History of the Royal-Society of London, For the Improving of Natural Knowledge. — Printed by T. R. for J. Martyn and J. Allestry, Printers to the Royal Society, London, 1667.
The classic contemporary account of the founding of the Royal Society, published only five years after the Society received its Royal Charter (1662). Sprat was a founding Fellow and later became Bishop of Rochester. The book serves as both a history and an apology — defending experimental science against its critics (theologians, humanists, and Aristotelians).
The volume contains 506 page-files (Ohio State University copy), extracted as 19,176 lines (~0.5 MB) of plain text. It includes the Royal Charter, the list of Fellows, and various accounts of early experiments.
Structure
Preliminary Matter

Dedication to King Charles II — Sprat praises the King as the patron of experimental philosophy, comparing the discovery of natural knowledge to the discovery of new worlds
“To the Royal Society” — a poem by Abraham Cowley in heroic couplets, celebrating the Society’s break from ancient authority and its turn to observation
Advertisement to the Reader — Sprat explains that the book was written over two years; the First and Third Parts were written earlier; only the Second Part is strictly historical

THE FIRST PART — The State of Ancient Philosophy (line 473)
Not a history of the Society but a sweeping survey of the history of philosophy from the Greeks to the 17th century, arguing that the experimental method is the true path to knowledge. Key sections:

Section I — Preface: The design of the work. Sprat presents the Society’s method as a middle way between dogmatic rationalism and scepticism
Section II: The causes of the slow progress of knowledge — the authority of the ancients, the disputes of the schools, the lack of a systematic experimental method
Section III: The character of the experimental philosopher — modest, industrious, collaborative, avoiding both enthusiasm and pedantry
The intellectual heroes: Francis Bacon is presented as the prophet of the new philosophy; Sprat traces the experimental method back through Gilbert, Harvey, and others
A critique of scholasticism, alchemy, and the “wits” who prefer elegant discourse to solid knowledge

THE SECOND PART — The History of the Royal Society (line 2,885)
The core of the book, divided into three periods:
Period I — The Origins (c. 1645–1660)

The first meetings began “some space after the end of the Civil Wars” at Oxford, in Dr. Wilkins’s lodgings at Wadham College — the birthplace of the Society
The original group included John Wilkins, John Wallis, Seth Ward, William Petty, Robert Boyle, Christopher Wren, John Goddard, Thomas Willis
Their meetings continued through the Commonwealth and Protectorate, focussing on “experimental philosophy” and avoiding political and theological disputes
After the Restoration, the group moved to London, meeting at Gresham College

Period II — The Formation (1660–1662)

The formal establishment after the King’s return: regular meetings at Gresham College
The first official meetings: 28 November 1660, with a list of 41 founding Fellows
The election of Lord Brouncker as first President
The granting of the Royal Charter (1662) — Charles II’s personal interest and patronage
The formal incorporation: the Council, the officers, the Fellows

Period III — The Early Work (1662–1667)

The Society’s method: regular experiments at weekly meetings, correspondence with foreign philosophers, the repository of natural objects
The early experiments: blood transfusion, air pump (Boyle’s experiments), weighing the air, dissection, botanical observations
The establishment of the Curators of Experiments (Robert Hooke was the first)
The correspondence network: Henry Oldenburg as Secretary, corresponding with Continental scientists
The formation of committees: for agriculture, for trades, for mining, for navigation
The publication of the Philosophical Transactions (from 1665)
The building of the repository and museum of natural curiosities

THE THIRD PART — Defence of Experimental Knowledge (line 5,770)
An extended apology for the Society against its critics:

Against the divines: experimental philosophy does not threaten religion; on the contrary, the study of Nature confirms the wisdom of the Creator
Against the “wits” and rhetoricians: the plain, unadorned style of scientific writing is superior to rhetorical flourish — one of the most famous passages in the book, arguing for a “close, naked, natural way of speaking”
Against the statesmen: the Society’s work will benefit navigation, trade, industry, and national prosperity
Against the universities: experimental knowledge complements rather than competes with the traditional curriculum
The positive benefits: improvements in agriculture, medicine, navigation, mining, manufactures

Appendix — The Royal Charter (line 6,200)
The full text of the Charter of the Royal Society (1662), including:

The names of the first Council and Fellows
The privileges and powers granted by the Crown
The provisions for elections, meetings, and governance

Scientific Accounts (line 9,000+)
A selection of accounts of experiments and observations, including:

Blood transfusion experiments (dogs, and an attempted human transfusion)
Observations of the planet Saturn and its ring
Accounts of dissections (e.g., a dog’s spleen)
Reports of unusual natural phenomena
The text of the Philosophical Transactions early issues

OCR Quality
Fair. The 1667 edition uses dense 17th-century typography (long-s, v/u interchange, ligatures) which the OCR handles imperfectly. Some passages are garbled. Footnotes and marginal notes are partially preserved. The errata list at the end can be used to correct some readings.
